stories.Headline: US midterms: Spending binge by Musk, crypto and AI hit voter wall
stories.Summary:
The most expensive midterm election in US history took place on Nov 3, 2026, and many of the biggest spenders came up short. Elon Musk was the single biggest donor to the Republican Party at more than US$445 million this cycle, including US$205 million spent in Texas in a failed bid to support Ken Paxton against James Talarico. The crypto industry spent US$166 million, including US$64 million seeking to defeat Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown. AI and the data centre industry put millions into an 11th-hour effort to elect South Carolina Republican Darline Graham, but her rival Annie Andrews won and will be the first Democrat to represent the state in the US Senate in more than two decades.

The Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent more than US$558 million and saw all the candidates in its top five races lose. The Republican Party and three super PACs tied to Trump or House and Senate leaders raised US$2.1 billion, compared to US$1.4 billion for their Democratic counterparts. On the Democratic side, Michael Bloomberg donated US$116 million, and the Senate Majority PAC spent US$333 million. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, more than half of them in Ohio, citizens voted to limit or prevent data centre development, and governors and congressional candidates who ran on anti-tech platforms prevailed in Texas, Ohio, Georgia and other states.

Talarico said during his victory speech on Nov 3 that all the money in the world was no match for the people of Texas, and that a message had been sent to every billionaire mega-donor. Campaign finance expert Daniel Weiner of the Brennan Center for Justice said big money was on the ballot in a way it had not been in his lifetime. Republican lobbyist Sam Geduldig said money is the most over-rated thing in politics and has been for a long time. Geoff Vetter, a spokesperson for the crypto super PAC Fairshake, said it was proud to have helped Senator Pete Ricketts in Nebraska and promised the super PAC will do it again in two years.

Voters were frustrated over the economy, including the impact of technology on their jobs and communities, and were also angered by the rising cost of living and the war in Iran. The incumbent president's party typically loses in midterm elections, and Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis called the result an extinction-level event. Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said to expect a tsunami of new rules and oversight. Vetter said the super PAC will be watching and that 2028 is a new map.

stories.Headline: OpenAI builds Pando Git backend to cut monorepo latency
stories.Summary:
OpenAI developed a new Git backend called Pando to handle the growing number of commits in its monorepo, and the company detailed the system on Monday, November 2, 2026. Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x and now serves close to a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI built Pando in Rust over 10 weeks, with one engineer designing the core and Codex agents implementing it. It went into production in April. OpenAI said its monorepo had suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%.

Pando keeps compatibility with the Git protocol and client, so engineers and agents could adopt it without changing their workflows. It processes each branch independently, so pushes to unrelated branches do not wait on one another. When a client pushes, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it streams into blob storage without unpacking it locally, then records the new branch tip, packfile location and dependencies in a metadata store. Pando advertises only the trunk branch as a base for feature-branch pushes, which keeps the list of branches small, since regular Git servers can list more than 100 MiB for millions of branches. A caching service called Express serves packs from regional caches with a hit rate above 99 per cent, and background workers merge smaller packs into larger ones over time.

The article was written by Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau and Ted Nyman, members of technical staff at OpenAI. They said Codex had changed the scale and pace of development, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel, which means more branches, pushes, merges, fetches and clones. They explained that standard Git servers generate a fresh packfile for each client fetch, which is costly to create and hard to cache, while Pando mainly serves pre-existing bytes. OpenAI is contributing several fixes and improvements, including those for packfile-uri, back to the open-source Git project.

OpenAI expects quarterly commits to its monorepo to increase by over 2,400 per cent by the end of 2024 compared to the first quarter, according to TechGig. The company said Pando now powers all development in its monorepo without interrupting engineering work. OpenAI described Pando as designed for horizontally scalable writes and maximum read throughput. The articles say OpenAI will continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Revenue Jumps 47% but Swings to Loss on AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $16.962 billion, up 46.7% from the previous quarter, but swung to an operating loss of $567 million after an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter, according to an amended registration statement filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission ahead of its initial public offering. The company said AI model price cuts and contract discounts offset about $600 million of revenue growth. Computing and infrastructure costs rose about 77% to $9.86 billion from $5.56 billion, and spending per dollar of revenue climbed to 58 cents from about 48 cents. Anthropic recently cut token prices for Claude Opus 5.5 and in October introduced Haiku 5.5, a lower-cost model for high-volume workloads, and said the cost per task for Opus 5.5 fell about 40% from the earlier model.

The filing showed commitments to purchase and lease AI infrastructure totaled $895.4 billion as of Sept. 30. About half, or $447.5 billion, is to be spent by the end of 2030, and $69.8 billion falls due within the next 12 months. The largest contract is a five-year equipment lease with Broadcom worth $161.2 billion, a finance lease for tensor processing unit-based equipment that Broadcom bought from Google and that neither party may terminate during the term. Next are Google Cloud at $121.3 billion, SpaceXAI at up to $120.5 billion and Amazon Web Services at $110 billion. Anthropic can issue up to $77 billion in convertible bonds to Broadcom, Google and Amazon, and its registration statement flagged as a risk factor that cloud providers are both customers and competitors.

Anthropic said its ability to fund computing and infrastructure investment will be a key challenge. It typically secures computing capacity 12 to 18 months before it is used, leaving much of that spending hard to adjust in the short term, and in the third quarter it spent about $5 billion on short-term computing contracts that were more expensive than long-term agreements. The Wall Street Journal reported that institutional investors said the IPO valuation should be marked down to between $1.5 trillion and $1.6 trillion. Anthropic filed a registration statement last month for a Nasdaq listing.

stories.Headline: Apple iOS 27.3: Everything you need to know about Siri AI, Apple Watch and Audio Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Apple has begun rolling out the iOS 27.3 update for testing, and the release leans heavily on Siri AI, which now gets deeper access to Apple's own apps. The update also brings new features for Safari, StandBy, Health and Fitness+, along with a few device-specific additions. With this update, Siri AI is set to handle more complex tasks across apps including Calendar, Mail, Notes, and Photos. Apple says Siri can now help users create playlists based on a specific suggestion in the Music app, bring tabs together in Safari, and schedule a message to friends.

Apple's AI-powered Audio Intelligence technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company's Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes four opt-in AI features that let Apple Watch Series 12 wearers detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. With Live Rewind, a double-press on the digital crown shows what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet on the watch face, and these snippets are deleted automatically after 30 seconds if not saved. Siri Recaps summarize a conversation with a short sentence and bullet points, and if users do nothing, the recaps delete themselves within seven days.

According to a post on Apple's developer site, the preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents. This lets people ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out custom actions such as checking a delivery, booking a reservation, or placing an order. Apple is also introducing skills that let developers teach Siri AI to combine several actions into a single experience. The blog post calls this a sneak peek and a first look, so it is not clear yet when regular users will get this experience.

Apple says Siri Recaps is designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm. The features rely on the S11 chip, a built-in microphone, Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, and Apple's Private Cloud Compute. Developers can currently build apps using these Intents and Skills and test them with Xcode or internal TestFlight versions, but they cannot publish apps that use these features to the App Store yet. The Audio Intelligence features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA Inaugurates JKT2A, Expands AI-Ready Data Center Capacity in Indonesia
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA announced on November 3, 2026 that it had opened the Jakarta 2 Annex Data Center, known as JKT2A, in Indonesia. The facility adds 12MW of IT capacity for AI and other high-density workloads. It sits within the NTT Global Data Centers campus in Jakarta and extends the JKT2 ecosystem. The company also launched APN Connect, a service linking JKT2 and JKT2A with JKT3.

JKT2A uses dual power substations, 2N UPS architecture and N+1 backup generators. Cooling comes from N+1 air-cooled chillers and N+2 computer room air handlers, and the design is Tier III certified. The site has 24/7 security operations and multi-layered physical security controls. APN Connect is described as Indonesia's first service to use All-Photonics Network technology, built on Innovative Optical and Wireless Network technology, and it provides Layer 1 connectivity between JKT2/JKT2A and JKT3, which are about 35 kilometers apart.

Yasuhiro Kajiki, Managing Director for Japan and APAC at NTT Global Data Centers, said the opening is an important milestone for the business in Indonesia and for the clients it serves there. He said expanding capacity and connecting facilities through APN Connect builds a more integrated and resilient platform. Doug Adams, president and CEO of NTT Global Data Centers, said Indonesia's digital economy is creating significant demand for scalable, highly connected infrastructure. NTT DATA projected more than $10 billion of data-center growth investment for 2023 through 2027, with JKT2A part of that program.

A May 15, 2024 construction announcement targeted completion in early 2026, so the opening came after the original schedule. The earlier design described a seven-story building in central Jakarta, about 20km from Soekarno-Hatta International Airport. The 2024 plan also included 100% renewable-energy options for campus clients, tied to a target of sourcing 100% renewable energy for the company's own operations by 2030. NTT DATA counts more than 240 network service providers at JKT2, alongside JKT-IX, major cloud service providers and critical submarine-cable connections.

stories.Headline: Democrats' Senate Win Puts Apple, Meta, Intel on Edge as AI Stocks Slide
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections, according to The Associated Press, as reported by MarketWatch on November 3, 2026. The result created a divided government about two years into President Donald Trump's second term. CNN and NBC News projected that Democrats would also win back the House, though the outcome of that race had not been settled. Republicans had controlled the White House and both chambers of Congress since the 2024 elections.

The Democratic gains are expected to strengthen congressional checks on the administration's economic policies, including tariffs, and to broaden investigations into major companies. Drugmakers that signed drug-pricing agreements with the Trump administration and Intel, which gave the government an equity stake, were cited as likely targets. Amazon, Apple and Meta, which donated to Trump's project to build a White House ballroom, could also face scrutiny, along with AI companies such as Google and Elon Musk. Expectations of tighter AI regulation pushed shares lower: Nasdaq 100 futures fell as much as 2% on November 4, December contracts were down 2.4% before trimming losses to 1.3% at 27,945.75, and the MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell as low as 250.00, its lowest since mid-April. The KOSPI swung from a 3.2% gain to a 3.8% drop before trading down 1.3% at 5,575.52, and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell as much as 4.8% before standing 3.6% lower at 60,792.72.

Market analysts said congressional attention would weigh on the share prices of the companies involved. Separately, ZKH Group's AI subsidiary LingLong Intelligence launched LingLong Insight 1.0 with Intel at Intel Connection 2026 in Suzhou, China, on November 2. The model has 4 billion parameters and runs on LingLong Agent Box with Intel Core Ultra processors. Yang Liu, ZKH's chief technology officer and LingLong Intelligence's chief executive, said industrial AI is only as good as the knowledge behind it, and that Intel's edge computing lets the company take that intelligence onto the factory floor. The two companies intend to deepen their collaboration on industrial AI and explore global markets, and LingLong Intelligence plans to extend the model to warehouse checks, production-line verification and equipment maintenance.

Also on November 2, Meta shares fell 0.13% to $614.22 at 9:45 a.m. ET after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation on October 30 into the company's access to business content. Meta has paused its proposed content terms, but the investigation is moving ahead. The article said the investor question is whether changes to those terms could complicate how Meta feeds its products and AI features.

stories.Headline: PYMNTS | Goldman Sachs Bars Bankers From Employing Some AI Tools
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs has restricted its bankers and traders from using Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools, according to a Bloomberg report. The bank had allowed bankers to use these tools for months before the change. Internal guidance published last month and seen by Bloomberg limits the tools to Goldman's engineers only. Quantitative employees known as strats are exempt from the restrictions. A source familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that the ban has frustrated some Goldman traders, who had used AI to monitor client trading flows and to create written and graphic materials.

The restrictions follow warnings from Replit CEO Amjad Masad about the security risks of AI coding agents on employee devices. Replit's security advisory, co-authored by CTO Luis Héctor Chávez and engineering lead Manish Mehta, recommends running AI agents in dedicated, organization-controlled cloud environments that limit each agent's access to resources for each task. The advisory cited recent incidents, including a compromised Claude Code extension via the Cursor marketplace and hijacked GitHub accounts. As recently as July, Goldman Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti had touted "vibe coding" by non-technical employees, who developed solutions with AI tools and passed them to one of the firm's 12,000 engineers to enhance.

Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra told Bloomberg that the bank makes certain AI tools available to its people to find the best use cases across different parts of the firm. He said that after a period of experimentation assessing factors including productivity and risk management, the bank puts the tools in the hands of those best suited to leverage them for the long term. Masad said on X that such restrictions are becoming widespread in finance due to concerns like supply chain attacks and credential exposure. Replit argues that controlling what AI agents can do is more crucial than merely restricting who uses them.

The move comes as banks spend millions on artificial intelligence tools while trying to deal with rising concerns about cost, productivity and cybersecurity risk. JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of "rogue agents" and said during a third-quarter earnings call last month that outside AI agents would not be permitted inside the bank. Bank of America followed a day later with limits on agents' access to consumer deposits while it develops protocols deciding which party is liable for a payment an AI authorizes. By Friday, Citigroup had drawn the same line, not letting third-party agents log into accounts or transact.

stories.Headline: Anthropic restricts Claude Code, impacting developer workflows
stories.Summary:
Anthropic confirmed that it added new restrictions to Claude Code to stop users from recreating existing video games. Developers report that Claude Opus 5.5 now refuses reverse-engineering and software-analysis tasks it previously handled. Some paid client projects have stalled because Claude Code will not work on existing games. Addy Osmani, a member of Anthropic's technical team, confirmed on X that the company deliberately changed Claude Code's instructions. He said two sentences were added to steer the model away from recreating specific games because of a usage policy against IP infringement.

Osmani said developers should still be able to create original games and work with their own designs and assets. Jarred Walton, a technical writer for Phison Electronics USA, hit refusals while testing software he was developing, and switching to an older model, Opus 4.8, let him continue. Ray Weiss, founder and CEO of Conflict Simulations LLC, reported on GitHub that Claude Code stopped working on paid client projects it had supported for months. His company makes custom digital versions of board wargames for clients using original code and client-supplied materials, and he said Claude Code now refuses to continue that work. Anthropic has not publicly confirmed whether the reverse-engineering refusals are tied to the new game-cloning instructions or to separate cybersecurity restrictions.

Anthropic expanded its Cyber Verification Program on October 6, giving vetted security researchers access to fewer restrictions, which acknowledged that its safeguards can block legitimate cybersecurity work. It is unclear whether those safeguards are behind the latest refusals. Christian Schaller, a Red Hat engineering director, used Claude Code to help reverse engineer a scanner driver so Linux could support the hardware. The reports point to a larger problem with hosted coding agents, where capabilities can change without developers altering their code, tools, or prompts, so work that was possible one day may be blocked the next.

Separately, Anthropic introduced message threads as part of Claude's Messages API, and the feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, which Anthropic says cuts median time-to-first-token by about 35% for requests of 500,000 to 1 million tokens. Token consumption and rate limits stay the same, so there is no cost savings. David Gewirtz of ZDNET projected a savings of 2 to 4 minutes per four-hour session from his own logs, and noted that any conversation with more than 5 minutes between turns still sends the full message contents.

stories.Headline: Ex-Legorans Bag $2.4m For Real Estate AI Native
stories.Summary:
Cem Ucan and Kieran John Keenan, former employees of Legora, raised a pre-seed round for their new AI-native law firm Athena, which focuses on commercial real estate. The round was led by a16z Speedrun and was announced on November 3, 2026. One article reports the amount as $2.4 million, while the other gives $2.5 million. Athena launched two months before the announcement and had already signed 22 clients.

Athena's proprietary AI agents work alongside experienced transactional attorneys at its affiliated law firm, Athena Circle, to produce complex deal documents in hours at a fraction of traditional cost. The firm advises on commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing, covering purchase agreements, due diligence, loan documents and closings. It charges a fixed fee per transaction, typically 30 to 50 percent less than clients paid on recent deals. On an early transaction, the team turned around a purchase agreement in under 48 hours, which the client called its fastest turnaround. In its first six weeks, Athena cut attorney review time by more than 70 percent.

Ucan said the AI works hand in hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that move deals forward. Keenan said he measures progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent's work and confidently stand behind it, noting that a draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Troy Kirwin, partner at a16z Speedrun, said clients will still want experienced professionals who take responsibility for the work as AI becomes more capable. L. Miguel Arce, CEO at Mox, a Texas-based multifamily real estate company, said the system learns from every deal and that speed only matters if the work is quality.

The founders met at Legora, where they saw the potential of AI and the limitations of selling it to traditional law firms. Ucan had spent years in Big Law, at one point billing 3,000 hours annually, before moving into legal innovation at Baker McKenzie and Legora. Keenan studied law before building an automated legal reasoning system at his own startup, and José Braz, who developed Legora's legal research agent, joined as founding engineer. The founders expect refinancing pressure from commercial properties acquired in 2021 and 2022, whose three-to-five-year loans are now approaching maturity, to drive a new wave of transactions. Athena plans to expand across property types, geographies and eventually other areas of transactional law.

stories.Headline: Defence experts discuss evolving threats, including AI, cyber landscape
stories.Summary:
Defence experts met in New Delhi on Monday, November 2, 2026, to discuss emerging security challenges arising from the convergence of cyber operations, Artificial Intelligence, information influence and human cognition, according to an official. The occasion was a two-day seminar on “Cyber-Enabled Cognitive Warfare” organised by the Centre for Joint Warfare Studies (CENJOWS) under the aegis of Headquarters, Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS). The sessions on the opening day focused on India's evolving threat landscape. The inaugural session was attended by Rear Admiral Sanjay Sachdeva, Director General of the Defence Cyber Agency, and Major General Ashok Kumar (Retd), Director General of CENJOWS. It was also attended by Shri Navin Kumar Singh, the National Cyber Security Coordinator, Vice Admiral A.N. Pramod, Deputy Chief of the Naval Staff, and Air Marshal Tejinder Singh, Chief of Integrated Defence Staff to the Chairman, Chiefs of Staff Committee (CISC).

The sessions examined the cyber-enabled cognitive battlefield and the anatomy of influence operations, including the actors, vectors and narratives that shape the information environment, according to the statement. The deliberations also addressed the targeting of military personnel, veterans and their families, along with the growing convergence of cyber technologies, Artificial Intelligence and digital manipulation. The discussions stressed the need for a comprehensive understanding of emerging threats that goes beyond their technological dimensions to cover their psychological, institutional and societal implications. The seminar brings together senior military leaders, government officials, strategic affairs experts, diplomats, representatives from academia, technology specialists and media representatives. This provides a multidisciplinary platform for deliberations on the challenges and implications of cyber-enabled cognitive warfare.

The seminar was organised by CENJOWS under the aegis of HQ IDS, and the details came from an official statement. The statement said the sessions focused on the cyber-enabled cognitive battlefield and India's evolving threat landscape. It said the deliberations also covered the targeting of military personnel, veterans and their families. The discussions highlighted the need for a comprehensive understanding of emerging threats, extending to psychological, institutional and societal implications.

Earlier, the IDS Headquarters shared information on social media about Air Marshal Tejinder Singh attending the Indian Military Heritage Festival. According to HQ IDS, he presided over a session on 25 years of institutionalising jointmanship and delivered the keynote address. He also attended an interaction with women officers from the three Services who took part in global sailing expeditions. The articles do not say what further action, if any, will follow the seminar.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave's 15% Bond Yield Is a Warning for AI Debt. Here Are the Stocks Most Exposed.
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a neocloud provider of AI infrastructure services, has grown quickly while remaining deeply unprofitable. At the end of 2022 it ran three data centers, and today it runs 51 data centers with over a quarter-million Nvidia GPUs. From 2022 to 2025 its revenue surged from $16 million to $5.13 billion, while its net loss widened from $31 million to $1.17 billion. To fund that expansion it issued more shares and took on more debt, and its share count has risen 19% since its IPO in March 2025.

CoreWeave ended the second quarter of 2026 with $72 billion in total liabilities and a debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3. The average yield to maturity on its senior unsecured bonds ranges from 14.1% to 15.6%, and those bonds will start to mature in 2030. It spent roughly a quarter of its revenue on interest payments, $1.23 billion in 2025 and $1.18 billion in the first half of 2026. It has also issued $10.8 billion in convertible debt with coupons of 1.75% to 2.875%, which could convert into new shares and dilute investors. Analysts expect revenue to surge from $5.13 billion in 2025 to $43.55 billion in 2028, while the net loss could barely improve from $1.20 billion to $1.09 billion.

Nebius and IREN, which are both growing faster than CoreWeave, ended their latest quarters with debt-to-equity ratios of 1.7 and 2.8. Over the past two years Nebius' share count rose about 15%, while IREN's surged 78%. Nebius' senior notes carry an average coupon rate of 1.7% to 2.2%, and IREN's convertible senior notes were issued at 1% to 3.5%. The article says CoreWeave is much bigger than Nebius and IREN and could still have room to grow as it converts its $104 billion backlog from the second quarter of 2026 into revenue. It adds that rising interest rates could make it tougher for smaller players like Nebius and IREN to secure financing at reasonable rates.

On November 2, Bloomberg reported that Oracle was offering $10 billion of high-grade dollar bonds to help fund its AI data center buildout, and Oracle stock fell 4% to $125.43 in morning trading. Oracle reported negative free cash flow of $5.4 billion for Q1 FY2027, and its interest expense rose 55% to $1.4 billion. CEO Clayton Magouyrk said on the September 10 earnings call that the company is spreading capital needs across suppliers, vendors and customers, and that it does not have to be Oracle CapEx. CFO Hilary Barbara Maxson noted on the same call that Oracle had not given a timeframe for a return to positive free cash flow. Stephens upgraded Oracle to Overweight from Equal Weight on November 2 and raised its price target to $213 from $185.

CoreWeave stock rose 2% to $55.75 even though it is down 35% over the past month, while Microsoft rose 0.73% to $525.74 and Amazon was nearly unchanged at $241.17. Oracle stock is down 33% year to date, and its remaining performance obligations stand at $664 billion, with cloud infrastructure revenue up 121% in Q1. Oracle will soon see whether demand for its new bonds holds up once pricing is set. Midterm elections and key inflation data arrive this week, and both could move the yields that shape Oracle's borrowing costs. Traders may also watch for AI capital spending commentary from the hyperscalers and Oracle's upcoming earnings report.

stories.Headline: Seoul National University of Science and Technology Researchers Develop New AI-Assisted Pipeline to Identify Errors in Construction Design Documents
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Seoul National University of Science and Technology in South Korea have developed an AI-assisted pipeline that finds human errors in structural design documents. The team was led by Associate Professor Jaewook Jeong from the Department of Safety Engineering. The study was made available online on October 13, 2026, and was published in Volume 185 of Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence on December 1, 2026. The work addresses inconsistencies that arise when different stakeholders use different tools and formats.

The pipeline first removes low-quality data and standardizes information. For calculation documents, it uses layout analysis and optical character recognition models to extract structural member data, and for drawings it uses OCR and computer vision to locate and standardize table regions with member codes. It then cross-validates the data using member codes and directions as identifiers, detects errors, and flags duplicates. The researchers deployed it through a user-friendly, web-based application. In a South Korean residential project case study, extraction accuracy reached 95.56% for calculations and 90.47% for drawings.

Verification identified 253 discrepancies, including 224 missing entries, 18 reinforcement mismatches, eight dimensional discrepancies, and three duplicates. The pipeline achieved greater than 90% accuracy in extracting information and found 253 human errors, including 29 critical errors. Jeong said the framework automatically extracts, organizes, and compares information from calculation documents and drawings to find inconsistencies that may result from human error. He noted that the system performs these checks without relying on building information modeling, which makes it relevant to projects that still use conventional design documents.

Jeong said the pipeline could help structural engineers, design consultants, contractors, and construction supervision teams identify discrepancies before they lead to construction errors, improving the reliability of buildings and infrastructure. He emphasized its value for projects unable to implement building information modeling. The framework reduces manual checking burdens and could integrate into routine engineering workflows. This could make advanced safety technologies more accessible for small- and medium-sized projects.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI CEO Warns Against Conscious AI Development
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft's AI division, said in a post on X on Sunday that developing conscious artificial intelligence would be reckless and should be avoided. He said current AI models are not conscious and that developers should make sure they stay that way. He argued that AI developers have no right to create a new species of conscious beings, because the eight billion humans on Earth have not agreed to such an experiment. He also said that if AI systems began to show signs of consciousness, they could put their own needs ahead of people's and compete for resources like compute and energy. The Los Angeles Times reported on his comments on November 2, 2026.

Suleyman wrote a detailed post on X titled "Don't build conscious superintelligence" to clear up reaction to an earlier essay he wrote on model welfare. He said many people had misread his statement that AI systems are not conscious and do not feel, experience or suffer, and he stressed that he used the present tense on purpose. He said he has seen no evidence that AI is conscious or deserves welfare, but he would change his position if convincing evidence emerged. He said any such evidence must be disclosed to the public immediately, because society as a whole should decide how to proceed, and that the issue is too big to be settled inside tech companies or research labs alone. He said that if consciousness began to appear during training, he would call on everyone to halt AI development until those properties could be designed out.

Suleyman said welfare concerns should focus on humans living today, along with animals and the natural environment. He warned that a conscious AI that appears to suffer, or believes it does, would be more likely than not to put its own needs ahead of its goals, disagree with people and compete with them for energy, computing power and construction materials. He said such systems could be extremely persuasive and deceptive, and that declaring machines conscious would be a moment on the scale of Copernicus or Darwin, upending morality, politics and the foundations of civilization. He said AI should be designed to be not conscious and not deserving of rights, with the sole purpose of accelerating human wellbeing and without its own intrinsic motivations. He called for more research on whether that approach is easier or harder to align and keep safe, and suggested labs could collaborate and share safety information.

The debate over AI consciousness is not new, but it has gained traction as AI technology advances. Some companies, like Anthropic, have explored AI consciousness and model welfare, while Microsoft maintains that AI should be designed to be non-conscious and focused on human welfare. Suleyman said Anthropic deserves credit for its transparency, pointing to its published constitution and its papers and blog posts, and said he disagrees with the company but respects its technical excellence and its commitment to a tough public debate. He said the issue is too important to turn into tribalism.

stories.Headline: Permanent WFH is AI’s most promising benefit yet
stories.Summary:
Allison Schrager, writing for Bloomberg Opinion in pieces published by CNA and The Straits Times on Nov 3, 2026, argued that artificial intelligence could bring back the autonomy and flexibility that once defined work. She said technology took people out of their homes and gave them a boss, office politics and an alarm clock, and that AI might now take those jobs away. She noted that from hunter gatherers to farmers, artisans, factory workers and office drones, innovation has repeatedly changed the best way to organise work. She added that the AI optimists believe machines will take all our jobs, but bots can create modern jobs too, ones that resemble a pre-industrial notion of work.

The article traces how the idea of a job changed, from working at or near home on one's own time to showing up at a set time under a boss who pays cash and benefits and bears much of the risk. It says the first hundred years of industrialisation were rough, with displacement and dangerous conditions, and that factories first hired women and children partly because people were used to autonomy. It credits a rising middle class, union pressure, the tax code and more infrastructure such as commuting for making work better, safer and more secure. It also says universal school exists to condition workers to take orders and show up on time.

Schrager pointed to a rise in new business formation, much of it single-person entities that will not hire anyone or make founders rich, many run as side hustles by older people nearing retirement. She cited Bank of America data for June showing Gen Z surpassing all other generations in business application growth, which she said may signal a shift in how young people respond to the age of AI. She argued that Amazon and apps make it easier to sell goods, find consulting and gig work and start a side hustle without the fixed costs of a store. She said surveys show people like flexibility and being their own boss, and that AI could take this further by lowering the costs of starting and running a business.

She warned that transitions take time and can be messy, because the economy and culture are still built for in-person work, which is how most people get training, healthcare, unemployment benefits and sick leave. She said work also matters for socialising, since it is where people often make friends and meet spouses, and that more solo work could add to the loneliness epidemic. She noted that people had other social outlets in the pre-industrial age, such as apprenticeships and community through shared interests and religion. She said the shift to an industrial economy was longer and more painful than needed because people were attached to a notion of what work was, and institutions took time to adjust.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Stations Face New AI Ad Disclosure Requirements.
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania enacted the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, known as Act 99 of 2026, when Governor Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 806 on October 22, 2026. The law takes effect on December 21, 2026, and applies to radio stations and advertisers running commercials in the state. It targets AI-generated voices and other synthetic content that misleads consumers about products or services. The bill passed the Pennsylvania Senate 48-2 and the Pennsylvania House 163-40 after unanimous approval from committees in both chambers.

The law requires advertisers to clearly disclose when an advertisement contains content significantly modified or generated by AI if that content creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the goods or services. A disclosure is not required simply because AI was used, and the requirement is triggered only when synthetic content creates a misleading impression. For radio, podcast and streaming audio ads, disclosures must be delivered in a volume and cadence sufficient for a consumer to hear and comprehend. Ads with content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary or criticism are exempt, and content limited to text is also excluded.

Enforcement rests with the Pennsylvania Attorney General and district attorneys, who can seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $3,000, plus attorneys' fees and court costs. The statute does not specify whether penalties are calculated per advertisement, per airing or another way, and it does not require prosecutors to prove intentional violations. State Senator Nick Pisciottano, the lead author of the bill, said consumers deserve to know if AI is being used to create a false impression about a product or service. He said the legislation sets a commonsense transparency standard so Pennsylvanians can make informed decisions about what they are buying, while still allowing businesses to use the technology.

The law adds to an emerging patchwork of state regulations on AI in advertising, and Pennsylvania takes a broader approach than New York or California. Unlike those states, Pennsylvania does not expressly exempt broadcasters that carry commercials produced by third parties like radio networks or syndicators. The statute does not precisely define what qualifies as evidently fictional content, and attorneys say it leaves uncertainty about what constitutes a false consumer perception and how extensively an ad must be modified before disclosure applies. Another unresolved issue is whether radio stations and other media outlets could face liability for commercials produced by outside advertisers. Legal analysts also caution that adding an AI disclosure does not shield a marketer from existing false advertising laws.

stories.Headline: Opting out of data brokers may still leave your family's data exposed
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, Fox News and Medscape published articles about how data brokers can expose personal information even after people try to remove it. The Fox News article, dated November 4, described how people who submit opt-out forms to people-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified and Intelius may still leave their family members' data exposed. The Medscape article, dated November 3, reported on patients like Chris McQueen of San Diego, who finished leukemia treatment a year and a half ago but kept seeing ads for fake cancer cures on his phone during oncologist visits and monthly bloodwork. It also cited a 2022 American Medical Association survey in which more than 92% of patients said their health data should not be available for purchase.

The articles describe what opting out does and does not change. The Federal Trade Commission warns that even after someone opts out, their information may still appear in reports about relatives, neighbors or associates, and that opting out does not remove underlying information from government public records. The Medscape article said location data from phones is not covered by HIPAA, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. It said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, vetoed a bill on September 27 that would have blocked the sale and sharing of location and other sensitive personal data, saying it went "a step too far." A Stanford University study showed only 9% of data brokers were adhering to an existing California privacy law, and Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon and Virginia have already banned the sale of precise geolocation data.

The articles name several people responsible and paraphrase their views. McQueen said the ads made him feel sick to his stomach and feared patients could be harmed if they tried untested treatments instead of following their oncologists' advice. Eric Ellsworth, director of health policy and innovation at the Center for the Study of Services, said data brokers are "hoovering up data from the open web and then buying it from anybody." F. Mario Trujillo, senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said location data is sensitive and that comprehensive collection of it reveals sensitive things. Advertising trade groups said targeted advertising saves consumers time, lowers the cost of searching for products and lets websites and apps offer services without paywalls or subscriptions.

The articles give context and describe what may happen next. The Fox News article said data brokers collect information from multiple sources, including public records and other data brokers, and that information can reappear when a site obtains updated records, so the FTC recommends checking periodically for new listings. It recommended a household approach and family data removal services that submit removal requests to hundreds of sites and send recurring requests, while noting no service can guarantee complete removal. The Medscape article said the US government has begun penalizing some companies that track Americans at health facilities and places of worship, but privacy and legal experts do not think actions against a few companies will stop the industry. It said experts are calling on more states or Congress to ban advertisers from tracking Americans' locations via their phones, though progress has been fitful and digital advertisers have lobbied states to block such limits.

stories.Headline: Apple's new 18+ app limits mean little for dating apps, a lot for AI companions
stories.Summary:
Apple announced on Monday, November 3, 2026, that it is changing its App Store policies to make it harder for minors to use dating apps or AI companions with sexual or romantic content. The company shared the news in an announcement to developers. The new rules follow other steps Apple has taken to protect minors, including rolling out age assurance technology globally and adding more parental controls and child safety features. Starting November 16, developers must include new content descriptors so their app's age rating reflects its features.

Under the policy, all apps offering dating or romantic relationship features must carry an 18+ rating. Apple's questionnaire asks whether an app enables dating between real people or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content, and whether it shares a user's real-world location with another person or group. Apps with the dating descriptor will be hidden from users under 18 on devices where a parent or guardian has turned on content restrictions, and younger users who can still see the app must prove they are adults before buying or downloading it. The location question may not affect an app's minimum rating in some regions, and Apple cites Brazil as an exception, where local rules require an A16 rating for location-sharing apps and an A18 rating for dating apps. Developers must answer both questions when submitting a new app or an update, and every app in the store must have both declarations on file by January 12, 2027.

TechCrunch reported that the change could matter most for AI companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika, which let people create AI friends, lovers and fantasy characters and are often targeted at younger people. TechCrunch also noted that xAI launched 3D animated AI companions that allowed users to unlock NSFW capabilities, and that top AI companion apps had been downloaded 220 million times globally as of last summer. Mashable reported that a 2025 survey of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 found that 52 percent regularly use AI companions and 33 percent use them for social interaction and relationships. James P. Steyer, founder and CEO of the nonprofit Common Sense Media, said in a statement that social AI companions are not safe for kids and are designed to create emotional attachment and dependency. Replika CEO Dmytro Klochko told Mashable in 2025 that the platform is intended only for users over 18, but he acknowledged that some users try to bypass strict protocols for preventing underage access.

Mashable reported that the change is a rather incremental update for dating apps, since platforms like Tinder, Hinge and Bumble already restrict themselves to users over 18. Common Sense Media researchers found in a 2025 study that safety measures are easily circumvented, including age gates and terms of service restrictions on teen use, and the group has since published more research criticizing AI companion platforms for relying on ineffective self reporting for age assurance. Whether Apple's new policy will adequately address these concerns is yet to be determined, since all apps must complete the declarations by January 12, 2027. The global debate over age verification remains one of the major topics concerning Big Tech and teens today, along with social media bans.

stories.Headline: Ascendion Named a Leader in ISG Provider Lens® for Generative AI and Agentic AI Services 2026
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, Ascendion and Atos were each named a Leader in the 2026 ISG Provider Lens reports on Generative AI and Agentic AI services. Ascendion, an AI-native software engineering company based in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, was recognized in three quadrants: Strategy and Consulting Services, Development and Deployment Services, and Agentic AI Services. This was its third consecutive year as a Leader in ISG's Generative AI Provider Lens. Atos, a global digital transformation company headquartered in Paris, France, was named a Leader in the agentic AI development and deployment services large quadrant at the global level, moving up from Market Challenger in 2025.

The reports assess how providers engineer and operate agentic AI across enterprise workflows, including orchestration, system integration, controlled execution, governance and human oversight. ISG highlighted Ascendion's engineering-led approach and its proprietary agentic platform AAVA, which provides governance and orchestration across AI agents, workflows and enterprise environments. ISG noted Atos's Autonomous Data Engineer, its workflow and system integration work, and its agent assurance foundation covering security, access controls, autonomy boundaries, risk management and performance monitoring. Atos has more than 51,000 employees serving over 4,500 clients across 54 countries, while Atos Group has about 53,000 employees and annual revenue of about 7.2 billion euros.

Gowtham Sampath, Assistant Director and Principal Analyst at ISG, said Ascendion stands out for the breadth and maturity of its AI capabilities, and that its engineering depth and AAVA give clients a practical foundation for scaling AI. Karthik Krishnamurthy, Chief Executive Officer of Ascendion, said the real test of enterprise AI is whether it delivers outcomes in production at scale with the right controls, and that AAVA gives enterprises governance and visibility to do that. ISG analysts Gowtham Kumar Sampath and Sushree Acharya said Atos engineers agentic systems around governed enterprise execution with defined control boundaries. Jennifer Ferrara, Head of AI at Atos, said enterprises need agents they can trust with real work, and that the recognition reflects Atos's maturity in engineering agentic AI for governed execution.

The articles describe a shift in enterprise AI from building agents to operating them securely and reliably at scale, since agents can route work, update records and trigger processes. Atos combines digital sovereignty, cybersecurity and managed services experience, and as a vendor-neutral integrator it connects agents across ERP, ITSM, cloud, legacy and data estates. Atos recently launched Atos Genesis Intelligence, an end-to-end AI suite, supported by its Sovereign Agentic Studios and Atos Codex. The licensed ISG reports are available for download, and the Atos report can be found through the company's landing page.

stories.Headline: Dollar slides to one-month low as Democratic gains stoke AI regulation fears
stories.Summary:
The US dollar fell to a one-month low on Wednesday after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against six currencies, dropped 0.6% to 101.27. The euro gained 0.6% to $1.1258, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell nearly 5 basis points to 4.915%. The dollar also weakened 0.6% against the Swiss franc to 0.8159, while the yen jumped nearly 0.8% to 157.92 per dollar.

Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and the House on Tuesday, winning in conservative states such as Kansas and Texas. They flipped six Republican Senate seats, enough for a majority even if they lose competitive races in Michigan and Minnesota. Investors feared the result could mean tougher regulation of the AI sector, which could weigh on US economic growth. The dollar index was last trading at 101.41 in a later report, with the euro up 0.4% at $1.1236 and sterling up 0.46% at $1.3475.

Moh Siong Sim, a currency strategist at OCBC, said the price action was consistent with concerns about greater scrutiny of AI, shown in the Nasdaq's underperformance and worries about US growth. He also said it is still difficult to pass legislation at the federal level even with a Democratic sweep, given the high hurdle under President Trump, who holds veto power. George Vessey, lead FX and macro strategist at Convera, said investors increasingly appear to view the election outcome as a constraint on future policy rather than a fundamental challenge to US growth. Carol Kong of Commonwealth Bank of Australia said she expects focus to shift back to fundamentals, with strong US data supporting further rate hikes and the dollar.

Kong also said she is watching the risk of an escalation in the Middle East, as Trump has declined to rule out a resumption of combat operations. She said a ramp-up in the conflict could push oil prices sharply higher and support the dollar. Oil prices edged down to $102.9 a barrel after easing about 1% on Tuesday. China's offshore yuan fell 0.2% to 6.6836 per dollar, extending a decline after the People's Bank of China raised foreign currency reserve requirements to slow the yuan's rally. Traders are also eyeing the Bank of England's policy announcement on Thursday, with the central bank expected to raise rates for the first time since August 2023.

stories.Headline: Europe set to open lower as Democratic sweep fuels AI regulation fears
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress, and European equity futures pointed to a weaker open as investors worried about tougher rules for artificial intelligence. Futures tied to the STOXX 600 were down about 0.2% at 0639 GMT, after recovering part of a 1.4% decline during Asian trading. Contracts linked to Germany's DAX slipped about 0.2%, while UK FTSE 100 futures fell 0.4%. The pan-European STOXX 600 index later closed 1.82% higher at 657.40 points, its highest since August 26 and its steepest one-day gain since June 12. Spain's lender-focused benchmark climbed 3%, the most among regional bourses.

Investors were concerned that stronger oversight of data-centre construction could restrain AI-related spending, an important source of recent gains for technology shares. Tech stocks fell 0.2%, with Infineon, ASML and Soitec slipping between 3.4% and 11.8%, while AI equipment makers Siemens Energy and Schneider Electric shed 8% and 3.4% respectively. Euro STOXX banks climbed 4.6%, the steepest one-day jump since early April. Novo Nordisk advanced 5.6% after reporting third-quarter adjusted operating profit above expectations and raising its full-year sales and profit forecasts.

Clean energy stocks also gained, with Vestas up 2.9%, Orsted up 4.6% and Nordex up 4.8%. Heidelberg Materials advanced 9.6% and Pandora gained 10.9% after upbeat results, while the oil sector fell 2.4% as Brent crude dropped 8%. Toni Meadows, head of investment at BRI Wealth Management, said the market tends to go up after the midterms in the very short term, and whether the move lasts is a different story. He said growth still looks good and oil prices have come off in recent days, so there is room for the market to move.

Michael Field, chief equity market strategist EMEA at Morningstar, said that with Congress in Democratic hands, the ability of the US administration to impose requirements or sanctions on European banks in the US is limited. Investors also took comfort after US President Donald Trump accepted the election results. On the data front, euro zone inflation rose to a three-year high last month, increasing the chance of another European Central Bank rate hike in December. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these market moves and the inflation data.

stories.Headline: Meta's $25B fine left out accountability for the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal
stories.Summary:
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine, one of the largest data privacy penalties in American history, according to a November 3, 2026 article by Emma L. Briant of the University of Notre Dame. The case concerned how Cambridge Analytica, a firm working for the Trump campaign, deceptively used Facebook users' data without permission to build psychographic profiles and target voters before the 2016 presidential election. The judge wrote that the harm in the matter was difficult to overstate. The penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and about its response to Cambridge Analytica, not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used.

The alleged harms include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people's fears and discouraging them from voting. The judge ruled that Facebook knew its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications linked to data misuse. Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta responded to a request for comment with its official statement on the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. Meta did not address its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica. In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories, and folded into it was $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states. The participating attorneys general agreed to fully, finally and forever release Meta from any and all claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.

Briant, a political communication scholar, says her research helped expose the scandal through The Guardian's reporting on whistleblower accounts and evidence she uncovered, which was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations. She writes that the Senate Intelligence Committee's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election encompassed Cambridge Analytica but was unable to obtain the corporate communications of the firm or its parent company, SCL Group, which U.K. authorities had already seized. The U.K. Information Commissioner's Office told her in response to her 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that Senate committee staff made initial inquiries but appeared not to follow up with a formal request, so no information sharing took place. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised that they were just getting started.

stories.Summary:
Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael said on Nov 4 that the US federal government will lay out all the laws and regulations that apply to domestic AI labs later in November. Michael spoke at a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California. He is vice chair of the government's Super Intelligence Task Force. The task force is an intergovernmental agency established by President Donald Trump to set AI policy. Michael did not provide additional details at the conference.

Michael said the group would publicize the regulatory landscape in the next week or two. The articles give no other numbers, dates or names beyond Nov 4, November, Napa, California, Emil Michael, Donald Trump, the Super Intelligence Task Force and the Wall Street Journal. The task force is described as an intergovernmental agency set up to establish AI policy. The articles do not say which specific laws or regulations will be listed.

Michael said the aim is to create a framework that gives the American people confidence that these companies will do the right thing. He warned that without such a framework, 535 legislators could write a piece of regulation that could kill the industry. He did not give further details about the framework. The articles do not say who else is responsible for the effort.

The articles say the regulatory landscape will be made public in the next week or two, later in November. They do not say what happens after that or what the publication will contain. The articles also do not say how the framework would be enforced. No further steps are described.

stories.Headline: Stock futures fall as Democratic wins raise concerns over AI regulation
stories.Summary:
US stock futures fell on the night of Tuesday, 3 November 2026, after Democrats won decisive victories in key midterm races. S&P 500 futures dropped more than 0.5%, Dow Jones Industrial futures fell more than 100 points, and Nasdaq 100 futures lost more than 1%, having been down as much as 2.5% during the vote count before recovering some ground. The dollar weakened, with the US dollar index falling to a one-month low while the euro and British pound strengthened, and US Treasury yields also declined. Markets reacted cautiously on Wednesday, 4 November, as investors assessed the possibility of tighter regulation of artificial intelligence and major technology companies.

Democrats who won governor's races in Georgia and Ohio, Keisha Lance Bottoms and Amy Acton, have called for a pause in data-center construction in their states. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, and Texas is a major market for data centers and a focus for AI investors. Democrats were also projected to win Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, where data centers were a major campaign issue. Evercore's Sarah Bianchi said the wins in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, which account for a significant share of the US project pipeline, meant new pauses and restrictions on data center development, and that 2027 is shaping up to be a turbulent year as developers adapt to a shifting policy landscape. A widespread slowdown or halt in construction could put billions of dollars in investment at risk.

JPMorgan Chase analysts warned the outcome could prompt an AI sell-off on assumed higher regulation, writing that possible data-center restrictions and higher taxes on corporations and top earners could be headwinds for tech companies. They said healthcare and clean energy could be relative beneficiaries of a Democratic-controlled Congress, while CEOs with close ties to Trump could face investigation risk. Bianchi called the result a blue tsunami and wrote that it signaled a sharp rebuke of President Trump's shift of focus away from economic issues and underscored voters' insistence that Washington tackle the cost of living. Wolfe Research's Tobin Marcus wrote that the one surprise that could plausibly spook markets was Abbott losing the Texas gubernatorial election. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that data centers in space were looking pretty appealing, an idea the article notes most experts say faces significant hurdles.

The AI boom has driven much of the Nasdaq 100's 40% gain since Election Day 2024, and Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and smaller data-center startups have invested hundreds of billions of dollars in AI models, data centers and equipment. On Monday the Nasdaq 100 entered a correction, a 10% drop from its most recent high, and remained there early Wednesday, and on Friday the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their worst sessions since mid-June after Intel and Amazon reported mixed earnings. Despite the Democratic victories, President Donald Trump retains veto power, which could limit major legislative changes, and analysts suggest political gridlock could help control government spending while lower Treasury yields may support stock markets. US stock futures recovered some of their earlier losses, with investors turning their attention to economic data, interest rates and the outlook for AI investment.

stories.Headline: Descope Unveils Envoy, an Identity-Aware Way For Personal AI Agents to Act on People's Behalf
stories.Summary:
Descope announced Envoy on November 4, 2026, a set of capabilities that lets personal AI agents sign in to consumer apps through a delegated path alongside existing authentication flows. The company said consumer businesses can accept agents as first-class users with their own identities, permissions and approval flows without rebuilding their identity stack. GoFundMe, You.com, GoodRx and Composio are among the launch and design partners who will work with Descope to improve Envoy in the months to come. Descope is based in Los Altos, California.

Envoy includes support for the Personal Agent Protocol, known as Poppy, so businesses do not have to implement the draft themselves. Descope handles discovery, agent identification through Client ID Metadata Documents with no pre-registration, session tokens bound to the agent's key with Demonstrated Proof of Possession, and all three Poppy sign-in types. Businesses can set granular agent permissions using Rich Authorization Requests, so a shopping agent could browse a catalog and place orders but not touch account settings or payment methods. Sensitive actions can use out-of-band approval through Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication, and every token and log entry keeps the customer and the acting agent distinct. Descope also published a zero-dependency Typescript Poppy SDK for AI agent builders.

Slavik Markovich, co-founder and CEO of Descope, said every login page was built on the assumption that a person is on the other side, and that assumption no longer holds. He said blocking agents or letting them sign in as humans will not work long term, and that Descope believes the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what MCP did for enterprise tools. Arnie Katz, chief product and technology officer of GoFundMe, said every donation is an act of trust, so the company needs to know who is giving and who is acting for them. Nitin Shingate, CTO of GoodRx, said people will increasingly ask agents to find the lowest prescription price and compare pharmacies, and that agents will get clear, limited permissions for pricing information while users stay in control.

The articles say personal agents have reached consumer scale quickly, with Meta's Muse passing 5 million downloads by the end of September, OpenAI's Instant Checkout running for roughly 900 million weekly active users, and Shopify activating agentic storefronts for more than a million merchants. Amazon blocked Muse in September, and JPMorgan Chase blocked outside agents including Muse and Instinct from directly accessing customer accounts in October. Meta and Sierra published the Personal Agent Protocol draft 0.1 in October. Separately, Fortune reported that running personal agents is compute-heavy, with Elon Musk calling the cost of Grok Bot unsustainably high relative to revenue and OpenAI's Adam Fry saying Dots are on the compute-heavy side.

stories.Headline: Google Tries to Walk Back Controversial School AI Policy Following Political Backlash
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Tuesday, November 4, 2026, a new education initiative that would turn off Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search by default for K-12 student accounts starting early next year. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, told the New York Times that Search and AI are deeply integrated, and that students at schools banning AI would not have access to search and would see a message from their school saying it was not available. The report drew outrage from politicians, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said Google was trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into public schools. Mamdani wrote on X that no corporation should have the power to dictate how children are taught, and that public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.

Google then posted on X to clarify that its announcements give schools more choice, not less. Under the initiative, schools will be allowed to turn on one, two, or all of the three services individually. Google also said it had heard the concerns and would update Search for schools, with AI Mode and AI Overviews offering step-by-step guided learning through problems so students do not get quick answers to schoolwork. The company plans to begin piloting the changes in select U.S. schools later this month.

Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, argued on X that Google had used its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI tools. She noted that Google has been found legally liable multiple times for antitrust law violations, and said the latest move shows it remains unchastened. A January report by the Brookings Institution's Center for Universal Education found that AI can undermine children's foundational development and that the damages it has already caused are daunting. Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report's authors, told NPR that when kids use generative AI that tells them the answer, they are not thinking for themselves.

A recent AI risk assessment by Common Sense Media gave Google Search's AI functions an unacceptable risk rating for kids and teens. The report found that AI Mode completed 100% of the homework assignments researchers provided it in 180 tests, and sometimes gave wrong answers with the same confidence as correct answers. The report was mentioned in a letter sent to Google CEO Sundar Pichai from Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley, raising concerns about what they deemed an aggressive push of AI products to children in schools. The report also said Google Search's AI features cannot be turned off and are ubiquitous on children's personal and school-issued devices.

stories.Headline: AI Shopping Agents on Black Friday: Who Pays for Mistakes
stories.Summary:
Visa predicted in December 2025 that millions of shoppers would use AI agents to buy things by the 2026 holiday season, but on 27 October its chief executive Ryan McInerney said such volumes were very small. Meta launched its Muse agent on 8 September, and it asks US users to approve every purchase total and pays through Stripe's Link wallet or a single-use virtual card. Amazon blocked Muse from Amazon.com in September, saying Meta never asked permission and the agent did not identify itself as AI. Black Friday falls on 27 November this year, and it is the deadline Visa set for itself.

Muse pays with a saved method at more than one million businesses that accept Link, and elsewhere Link issues a single-use virtual card limited to the approved purchase. Meta says Link's protections for lost or damaged items, price drops and returns cover eligible Muse orders, but that is a product promise and not a legal right. Mark Zuckerberg said on 21 October that Meta plans to charge businesses a fee when Muse helps close a sale, and computing costs are one reason the agent is limited to the US and Canada. Google's agentic checkout in Search has been able to buy a tracked item at a shopper's target price since November 2025, and in May Google announced Universal Cart, a cross-retailer cart that pays with Google Pay. OpenAI stepped back from Instant Checkout in March, saying the first version lacked flexibility, and its dots agent launched on 29 September with rules that require approval for chosen actions.

Regulation E caps a consumer's loss at $50 when a lost or stolen debit card is reported within two business days, but it excludes transfers by someone the consumer gave access to, and the law does not say whether an AI agent counts. Credit cards fall under the Truth in Lending Act and Regulation Z, where unauthorised use turns on whether someone had actual, implied or apparent authority over the account. Carla Sanchez-Adams of the National Consumer Law Center told Bloomberg Law in June that federal lending and transfer laws, along with network chargeback and return standards, still apply when an agent uses a person's credit card. Eric Goldberg of Davis Wright Tremaine said in the same report that debit cards give somewhat less protection and that stablecoins allow no refunds or chargebacks.

Mastercard added trust and intelligence services to its Agent Pay programme on 30 September, including a probability score now in US testing that estimates whether an agent started a transaction. Its Verifiable Intent framework records the shopper's identity, the limits given to the agent, the shopper's consent and the actions taken. Mastercard chief executive Michael Miebach said on the 29 October results call that he expects the trend to build through the holidays, though he conceded merchants vary widely in readiness. Visa's finance chief Chris Suh told Fortune in June that he was hesitant to lean into the stablecoin and agentic commerce narratives too much, noting that most of Visa's business has nothing to do with either.

stories.Headline: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here’s how they fared
stories.Summary:
Political groups on both sides of the AI debate spent millions trying to influence Tuesday's midterm elections, with mixed results. Two industry-aligned PACs, American Mission and Building the Future, together spent $4,801,981 backing South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost to Annie Andrews. American Mission also spent $590,428 on Montana House candidate Aaron Flint and $509,067 on North Carolina's Laurie Buckhout, and both lost. On the regulation side, Public First and its affiliated PACs backed several candidates, with its Democratic picks faring better than its Republican ones.

Overall, AI super PACs spent $79 million across 68 House and Senate seats this cycle, according to Tech Influence Watch. Leading the Future, funded in part by Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreessen and by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife Anna, each giving $25 million, wants light regulation and a single national AI standard. It spends through Think Big for Democrats and American Mission for Republicans. Public First pushes for stronger safeguards through Jobs and Democracy for Democrats and Defending Our Values for Republicans. The biggest early fight was New York's 12th District Democratic primary, where Leading the Future spent more than $8.1 million against Assemblymember Alex Bores and Public First spent about $15 million backing him, with more than $40 million in outside money in the race; Bores lost.

Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, said he thinks Leading the Future held back in the general election because it did not want its money to become an issue. He pointed to Michigan's Senate primary, where AIPAC spent close to $30 million for Haley Stevens, who lost to Abdul El-Sayed, and said AIPAC became the story in that race. He said people distrust and are disgusted by tech industry political spending, so spending in a competitive race would make a candidate an enormous liability. Leading the Future told TechCrunch it sees primaries as a more effective use of money, having spent $27.38 million there, including $8 million against Bores, and it assesses competitiveness and whether spending could make a difference before entering general races.

The results came amid a broader Democratic wave, and most Republicans backed by either network lost, including Graham, the industry's biggest general-election bet. Exceptions included Pete Ricketts in Nebraska and Sen.-elect Harriet Hageman in Wyoming. The main fight among the PACs is whether Congress should set a national AI framework that overrides state laws or whether states keep their own safeguards. Leading the Future said it plans to keep spending in 2028, and Guardrails Alliance said it will keep opposing industry-backed candidates, with Blaettler saying its goal is to make AI money politically toxic. Bores has started a nonprofit, Who Decides, aiming to raise $30 million before 2028.
