stories.Headline: Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell more than 40 to 50% from their high points, but the
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, shares of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell sharply, with Samsung trading at 205,500 won, down 12,500 won, and SK Hynix at 1,295,000 won, down 101,000 won, according to the Korea Exchange. Both stocks were down about 45 percent from their June peaks, Samsung from 374,500 won and SK Hynix by a nearly identical amount. The wider KOSPI fell 4.17 percent to 5,446.79 as of 10:39 a.m., after opening down 1.82 percent and dropping as low as 5,386.29, and the index stood 41.97 percent below its all-time high of 9,385.59 set on June 19. The Korea Exchange triggered a sell sidecar at 10:16 a.m., its 56th KOSPI activation this year and 29th in the sell direction, which suspends program sell orders for five minutes when KOSPI 200 futures stay down more than 5 percent for one minute.

The trigger was the U.S. midterm elections held on the 3rd, where the Democratic Party won majorities in both the Senate and the House. Democratic wins in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, key data center regions, raised concerns about restrictions on new data center permits and delays in semiconductor orders. Foreign investors net sold 1 trillion 125.2 billion won and institutions 6 billion won on KOSPI, while retail investors net bought 1 trillion 46.2 billion won. In the U.S., the Dow rose 3.03 percent to 53,356.12 and the NASDAQ 1.44 percent to 25,736.51, but the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.13 percent. On KOSDAQ, down 4.30 percent to 684.19, foreigners net sold 136.9 billion won.

KB Securities forecast combined operating profit for the two companies of 1,110.5 trillion won, the first time above 1,000 trillion won, with researcher Kim Dong-won projecting fourth-quarter operating profit of 128 trillion won for Samsung and 104 trillion won for SK Hynix, up 539 percent and 441 percent from a year earlier. iM Securities issued a buy rating and 2.3 million won target for SK Hynix on the 4th, expecting operating profit of 45.3 trillion won next year and 54.2 trillion won in 2028, with HBM sales rising from 43 trillion won this year to 183 trillion won in 2028. Researcher Ko Eui-young said the higher the HBM share, the lower the volatility of the company's profit, and that SK Hynix is at the forefront of the industry. Researcher Yang Hyeon-kyung of iM Securities said expectations for reduced cost burdens from falling oil prices are spreading to aviation and transportation, and that it is necessary to check whether rotation trading will appear in non-semiconductor sectors. Researcher Byun Jun-ho of IBK Investment & Securities said markets after midterm elections have tended to react more sensitively to positive news, and that the KOSPI recently plunged to around 1 times its 12-month forward price-to-book ratio, indicating extreme undervaluation.

KB Securities expects HBM's share of global DRAM production capacity to expand from 18 percent in 2025 to 30 percent next year, while general-purpose DRAM falls from 82 percent to 70 percent, and expects Samsung to secure 70 percent of total production capacity through long-term supply contracts by 2030. iM Securities noted SK Hynix fell 57 percent from its June high to its October low, more than the average 51 percent fall in past semiconductor downturns, and that the adjustment took about 4 months rather than the past 8 to 13 months. It predicted SK Hynix's return on equity will remain highly profitable at 47 percent in 2028. Analysts said investors should weigh memory demand from AI investment, HBM competitive advantage and the sustainability of supply shortages rather than treat the fall as a buying opportunity, and warned that a slowdown in big tech AI investment or full-scale expansion by memory companies could dampen HBM demand and memory prices.

stories.Headline: TeraWulf gets credit backstop from Google for Anthropic data-center project
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf Inc. announced on November 4, 2026 that it had executed credit support agreements with Google LLC. The agreements relate to debt financing that supports about $19 billion of contracted lease commitments with Anthropic, PBC. Those leases cover TeraWulf's Justified Data Campus in Hawesville, Kentucky. TeraWulf also announced a definitive engineering, procurement and construction agreement with Fluor Enterprises, Inc. for the development of Justified.

Under the credit support agreements, Google, a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., provides contractual credit support for anticipated debt financing for the long-term Justified development. Alphabet's senior unsecured debt is rated AA+ by S&P Global Ratings and Aa2 by Moody's. The Fluor agreement covers engineering, procurement and construction for three data center buildings at Justified, building on a limited notice to proceed announced in March 2026. It sets defined delivery milestones, open-book cost reporting, procurement oversight and contractual performance protections, with guaranteed maximum pricing being established as engineering and procurement progress.

Paul Prager, TeraWulf's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, said the company structured its Anthropic leases from the outset to address counterparty credit, financing costs and capital requirements. He said Google's credit support strengthens TeraWulf's ability to secure competitive project financing, while Fluor's capabilities expand its capacity to execute at scale. Patrick Fleury, TeraWulf's Chief Financial Officer, said cost of capital is fundamental to infrastructure development and that strong investment-grade credit support strengthens the project's financing profile. Prager added that Fluor lets TeraWulf scale execution without building a global engineering and construction organization internally.

TeraWulf describes itself as an energy infrastructure company that pairs long-term access to power with contracted AI and high-performance computing demand. It develops and operates the underlying infrastructure rather than investing in AI compute hardware. Under the EPC milestone schedule, phased ready-for-service completions are expected to begin in late 2027 and continue through the second quarter of 2028. The Justified milestones follow TeraWulf's recent expansion of contracted power capacity to 1 GW at its Muskie Data Campus in eastern Kentucky.

stories.Headline: Guidelines on artificial intelligence issued for lawyers
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association issued guidelines on lawyers' use of artificial intelligence, according to a report published on November 4, 2026. The association's House of Delegates adopted a report titled "Legal Ethics Guidelines for Lawyers' Use of Artificial Intelligence." The association said the guidelines should help avoid the unauthorized practice of law, keep legal decisions in human hands and reduce bias in legal proceedings. It noted that AI systems are increasingly used in legal research, drafting, client communications, litigation and law practice management. The guidelines urge attorneys to make sure AI output is not biased because of the data it was fed or because of how it was designed and deployed.

They also say AI should not be used in ways that could affect a person's rights, access, opportunity or treatment. Attorneys may charge fees for time spent verifying an AI tool's output, but not for learning how to use it. Acquiring an AI tool is an overhead expense, so its cost may not be billed to a client unless it is for a service specially incurred for that case. The association also reminded attorneys that they must carefully supervise non-lawyers and vendors who use AI tools. Taa Grays, president of the Bar Association, said generative AI is changing the practice of law and that the guidelines give attorneys a resource to use AI responsibly and ethically.

She said the guidelines can help attorneys avoid perils such as inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed, or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use. The association said that while the New York Rules of Professional Conduct do not specifically address AI-generated legal work, an attorney is still responsible for ensuring that a non-lawyer's work meets standards, even if the non-lawyer is an AI tool or system. Separately, India's Computer Emergency Response Team published 107-page guidelines on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, titled "Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines: Framework for Secure, Ethical and Auditable Artificial Intelligence Systems." The guidelines apply to all AI developers and service providers, including US companies behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, but they are legally binding only for cybersecurity auditors empanelled with CERT-In. Companies must report AI-related security breaches to CERT-In within six hours and keep logs of AI systems' usage and operations for 180 days.

The framework proposes four tiers of criticality, low, moderate, high and critical, based on eight identifiers including the severity of potential impact and the sensitivity of data. An official said the guidelines are for auditors to use when examining AI systems at large companies, and that discussions about turning them into law are a separate matter progressing inside Meity. Jibu Elias of the Mozilla Foundation said the guidelines are similar to work by the EU and NIST in the US and are nothing new, and that non-binding guidelines generally do not have a major impact on an industry. The EU has adopted a legally binding AI Act, the US has voluntary AI standards through NIST, and China requires generative AI services to undergo government security checks before launch.

stories.Headline: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges
stories.Summary:
Fal, a San Francisco startup that hosts and runs AI video, image and audio models, raised $1.3 billion in a funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with Nvidia, Sound Ventures and T. Rowe Price also taking part. The deal values the company at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, according to Bloomberg. Fal announced its Series E and Series F rounds at the same time and said it raised a combined $1.65 billion across both. Sequoia led the earlier round. The new money comes as demand surges for inference, the process of running an AI model that has already been trained to generate outputs, especially from customers using open source models.

Fal passed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg reported. Other inference providers, including Baseten, Fireworks AI and Modal, have also been growing fast and raising large rounds at higher valuations. Their gross margins remain thin because buying or leasing compute is expensive, according to several people familiar with the companies' financials. Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon. The articles do not say who else at the company commented on the round or what specific plans the new funding will pay for.

They also do not give a date for when the round closed beyond the November 3, 2026 report. The articles do not say what happens next for Fal beyond the funding itself. They place the round in the context of rapid growth across the inference sector, where several companies are raising large sums at higher valuations. They note that thin gross margins across the sector stem from the high cost of compute.

stories.Headline: Intuit Connect 2026: AI Agents, a New Partner Program, and a Unified Platform Take Center Stage
stories.Summary:
Intuit held its Intuit Connect 2026 conference in Las Vegas in late October, bringing together thousands of accounting professionals for three days of product announcements and strategy sessions. Chairman and CEO Sasan Goodarzi opened the event by repeating a shift he had announced earlier in the year, in which accountants are treated as Intuit's customers. The company said it is investing billions of dollars a year in growth and efficiency. Intuit also announced its acquisition of Sequence, an AI-native revenue management platform, a week before the event.

The company introduced Intuit Intelligence, a financial intelligence layer that draws on 40 years of accounting data and the patterns of 10 million businesses. It routes each task to the right AI, automation, or expert, including a network of more than 650,000 accountants. New tools include Agentic Books Close, in pilot, which follows a firm's own close procedures and posts nothing without explicit review, and Playbooks, in beta, which lets firms upload SOPs and have AI draft a playbook for approval. Pilot sign-up for Agentic Books Close is open through late November, and the tool is free during the pilot but will become a paid add-on afterward. Intuit also said the tiered ProPartner program will replace ProAdvisor in early 2027 with five tiers.

Intuit's chief technology officer, Alex Balazs, said that after speaking with more than 40 firms, one point stood out: clients expect speed and fresh insight, but responsibility for correct financial outcomes still rests with the firm. He said firm-defined policies and playbooks guide the AI, a unified audit log tracks every action, and the accountant makes the final call. Diana Williams, vice president of Product for Accountants, demonstrated the latest additions to Intuit Accountant Suite. Wyatt Jenkins, senior vice president of Mid-Market Product, outlined four industry editions for Intuit Enterprise Suite, with Construction and Manufacturing in beta and Nonprofit and Franchise in pilot.

Intuit said client advisory is the fastest-growing service area in public accounting and that hiring is a top constraint. To address this, the company highlighted its Accounting Futures program, which offers educators QuickBooks and advisory curriculum, free QuickBooks Level 1 certification, and paid micro-internships. Intuit has committed to educating more than one million students over five years. All of the announcements are available to watch on the Intuit Connect replay.

stories.Headline: UNESCO, Brazilian Government and ITU partner to launch green AI Climate Institute
stories.Summary:
UNESCO, the Government of Brazil and the International Telecommunication Union formed a partnership to establish the Artificial Intelligence Climate Institute, known as AICI. The institute was announced at COP30 in Belém, and its vision was unveiled there on 11 November 2025. It will be hosted by Brazil's National Telecommunications Agency, Anatel, within the ITU's Green Digital Action Hub in Brasília. An inaugural workshop was held in Manaus on 4 August 2026 to help finalise the institute's operational structure.

The partners committed to a two-year operational roadmap for 2026 to 2027 that focuses on country-led capacity development. Its activities combine training for public officials on data governance and climate policy with practical technical support for local developers and data scientists. The roadmap also envisages a shared digital learning repository with open environmental datasets, climate-specific AI model architectures and guidance for low-connectivity, resource-constrained environments. The measures aim to help developing countries keep greater control over their data and build expertise to develop and maintain their own climate models.

The institute draws on UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and its Open Science framework to guide responsible AI development. Brazil's Anatel provides institutional hosting for the AICI Secretariat and steers regional cooperation. The ITU brings technical expertise in telecommunications and digital infrastructure, with links to the ITU Academy and the AI Skills Coalition. UNESCO grounds the institute's curriculum and projects in its ethics recommendation and open science framework, and it cites a joint UNESCO-UCL study showing that task-specific models and optimised prompts can cut AI energy consumption by up to 90%.

The founding partners are scheduled to launch the institute's operational phase on 16 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye, at COP31. The launch is expected to present the approved 2026 to 2027 work plan and showcase pilot applications, including AI-based deforestation prevention in the Amazon Basin. It will also open membership to governments, research institutions and international financing partners committed to sustainable digital transformation. The institute aims to help developing nations design, deploy and govern their own ethical, resource-efficient AI solutions for climate action.

stories.Headline: Eros Innovation and Ministry of Tourism sign MoU for cultural AI in incredible India
stories.Summary:
Eros Innovation signed a Memorandum of Understanding with India's Ministry of Tourism to advance Cultural Artificial Intelligence, cinematic storytelling and immersive digital experiences across the country's tourism ecosystem. The signing took place at the India Pavilion in London, in the presence of Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, the Union Minister of Culture and Tourism, with Swaneet Singh, Co-President of Eros Innovation, representing the company. The deal was announced on November 4, 2026, and reported by adgully.com and The National Law Review. The collaboration combines Eros's proprietary Large Cultural Models, multilingual AI, digital characters and entertainment heritage with the Ministry's Incredible India initiatives.

Under the MoU, Eros will produce 50 two-minute films showcasing India's destinations and cultural experiences, and the Ministry will support their promotion over 50 weeks through Incredible India and participating state tourism channels. The agreement sets up a framework to evaluate Eros Cultural AI technologies for possible integration into Incredible India websites, mobile applications and other approved tourism platforms. Eros will be recognised as a non-exclusive, non-binding and non-financial Cultural AI and Experience Technology Knowledge Partner. The collaboration also includes curated content for international tourism exhibitions, engagement with state tourism departments, technology workshops and AI-enabled training for tourism professionals and creators. Official tourism information would remain grounded in Ministry-approved sources and subject to appropriate review.

Swaneet Singh said India is not simply a collection of destinations but a living civilisation of stories, languages, traditions, music and cultural experiences. He said the company's Large Cultural Models could make this heritage more accessible, interactive and personal for travellers worldwide, and that people should be able to imagine India before arriving, experience its culture more deeply during the journey and carry those connections after returning home. He said Eros was honoured to work with the Ministry to bring India's cultural legacy to life through responsible innovation. Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said cinema has the power to inspire people to explore new destinations and experience different cultures. He said the collaboration aims to bring the stories of Incredible India to a wider global audience and strengthen Bharat's position as a leading tourism destination.

Eros Innovation is headquartered in the Isle of Man, with operations across the United Kingdom, India, the United States and the Middle East. Eros envisions Experience India, a multilingual travel companion that could help travellers before, during and after their visits, and a Screen-to-Destination experience letting travellers discover where film scenes were shot. The technology would be evaluated for integration into existing Incredible India digital platforms and participating state tourism services, subject to technical and institutional approvals. Interactive destination experiences at tourism exhibitions, airports and visitor centres are also envisaged, subject to relevant permissions.

stories.Headline: AI Roundup: AMD, Apple Results Puzzle Investors, Democrats’ Midterm Win Weighs On Traders
stories.Summary:
AMD reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and forecast fourth-quarter sales above Wall Street estimates, according to a roundup of AI news. The company also said it expects sales to grow 80% in 2027, buoyed by demand for data center chips. The report came after Intel's tepid forecast the previous week, which pressured Intel's shares and the broader sector. AMD forecast December-quarter sales above Intel's outlook, and if both companies meet those targets, AMD would outsell Intel for the first time in their history.

The results contrast with Intel's report last week, which weighed on chip stocks. AMD's forecast puts its December-quarter sales target ahead of Intel's outlook. The article ties the chip sentiment to Intel's earlier forecast, which had pressured the company's shares and the wider sector. No further details on the figures were given in the article.

The article places AMD's report in the context of a broader market move, with Democratic victories in the midterms sending AI stocks into a tailspin on Wednesday. The roundup says the selloff added to pressure from mixed Big Tech earnings and growing concerns that record AI spending may not be sustainable. It also notes that Arizona Rep. Yassamin Ansari called for a pause on advanced AI development until adequate regulations are in place, as well as a ban on artificial superintelligence. The article does not say what happens next for AMD beyond its stated forecasts.

stories.Headline: Copyright Infringement Lawsuit Against OpenAI Draws More than 50 (Very Illuminating) Amicus Briefs
stories.Summary:
In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation is a consolidated case that combines more than a dozen major AI lawsuits, including cases filed by the Authors Guild and news organizations such as the New York Times. By the October 30 deadline, the court overseeing the case received 51 amicus briefs from publisher and author associations, individual creators and journalists, copyright scholars, tech groups, and some U.S. legislators. Amicus briefs let parties who are not part of a case, with the court's permission, weigh in on the litigation. In cross-motions for summary judgment filed last month, the plaintiffs argued that OpenAI committed copyright infringement by copying works, including from pirated sources, to train its models, and that its outputs can also be infringing. OpenAI's attorneys countered that its copying for training qualifies as fair use and that its outputs are not infringing.

Of the 51 briefs, 26 support the plaintiffs, 18 support the defendants, and eight are neutral. A final round of briefs is due on November 6, after which oral arguments will be set before judge Sidney H. Stein. On September 4, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a Statement of Interest urging the court to find that using copyrighted works for AI training is fair use. In October, judge Stein struck from the evidence a study suggesting AI books were displacing human-written works, after OpenAI attorneys argued the author failed to disclose a conflict over funding; the author denies the conflict, and the plaintiffs did not oppose the motion to strike.

The Association of American Publishers, CCC, IBPA, and STM Publishers said in their brief that copyright goals are undermined when fair use authorizes uncompensated appropriation of creative labor where licensing is practical and commercially reasonable. Ken Burns said large language models copied transcripts of his films and perhaps companion books without his permission, and that copycat filmmakers use the outputs to make competing films at far lower cost. WME said it comes not as an opponent of AI but as a participant in the licensing market, and that its position is that AI use of creative materials should be licensed, not stopped. Members of Congress responding to the DOJ's Statement of Interest called it breathtaking in scope and said it proposes what is in effect a blanket exemption that would preclude every copyright claim within the ambit of training LLMs.

On the defendants' side, Authors Alliance addressed only whether so-called market dilution is a cognizable form of harm under the Copyright Act, calling the theory a radical departure from settled copyright law. Kevin Kelly said a ruling for the plaintiffs on fair use would grant them far more than the limited monopoly Congress intended and would hinder new technologies and new works. EFF said the Constitution gives Congress the role of adjusting copyright law for new technologies, and that the court should apply well-established precedents that favor fair use here. Tim Hwang and Samuel Roland of the Foundation for American Innovation filed a proposed amicus brief supporting OpenAI, arguing that under Google LLC v. Oracle, courts may consider public benefits that copying enables, including the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis and software.

stories.Headline: Your AI Bill Is a Data Problem
stories.Summary:
In a recent SD Times Live! Supercast on the economics of AI, J.R. Storment of the Tokenomics Foundation described a year of whiplash, with early tokenmaxxing giving way by spring to spending caps because there was no direct tie between spend and results. A foundation survey found respondents fairly confident they had visibility into their AI spending, but only 9% were really confident they could show value on it. Shawn Alpay of the Linux Foundation said his own team is in the same boat and that comparisons of new models are "all vibes." Storment said respondents could see their total bill but could not tie it to who was doing what or allocate it to a cost center, and they consumed AI from four to six sources that each reported data differently.

Jerod Johnson of CData Software said the cost conversation is coming to a head because AI spend has moved from contained pilots to agents in production, and what organizations pay now depends on how agents behave more so than on how people use it. In a CData Labs benchmark, 27 models ran the same enterprise tasks, and without business context only about one run in 400 succeeded, a rate that held for every model including frontier models like Fable 5.1. With context, 12 of the models went 15 for 15, and the cheapest did it for less than a cent per correct answer while the most expensive cost about $1.17. Johnson framed cost as context times turns times model, and in preliminary numbers from more than 800 runs the median run without context took 29 turns versus seven with context, while tool calls fell from roughly 40 to 8.

Johnson said organizations can recover that spend by doing the work once, either before the request by shaping data in a warehouse or lakehouse, or inside the request with a context layer in the AI gateway. In CData's testing, a derived view cut tokens from about 183,000 to about 40,000 per query, a 78% reduction, and cost from about 60 cents to about 15 cents, while a simple cached copy cut token consumption by 89%. The full run without context cost $350 and produced one correct answer, while with context it cost $93 and produced 318 correct answers, or 29 cents each. Johnson advised starting with what a cloud or gateway provider already offers, such as spend by model, API key and project, plus budgets and alerts, but said that won't show spend per business question, turns per correct answer, or which data path served each answer.

Alpay helps steward FOCUS, the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification, which unifies billing data across providers, but billing data cannot say which trace or span kicked off a given workload. FOCUS will work with OpenTelemetry, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project, during its 1.6 development cycle to create a telemetry schema that lets organizations associate OTel data with FOCUS cost data. Storment also warned that routing to cheaper models has a catch, because switching away from a model where you are running a lot of cached tokens breaks your cache and leaves you paying for uncached tokens. Alpay's closing advice was to keep encouraging teams to use the new tools while asking whether they can quantify what they spent and what it resulted in.

stories.Headline: Ohio Voters Back Local Data Center Limits in Unofficial Results
stories.Summary:
Voters in several Ohio communities backed local data-center restrictions in the November 3, 2026 general election, according to unofficial county results. In Trenton, Issue 17 drew 79.68% support, with Butler County reporting 3,541 yes votes to 903 no votes and all eight precincts counted. Pataskala’s charter amendment passed 5,418 to 1,941, or 73.62% yes, and Granville’s passed 2,015 to 429, or 82.45% yes, according to Licking County results. Sunbury’s amendment passed 2,809 to 763, or 78.64%, with all six precincts reporting, and Grove City’s Community Consent Amendment passed 11,317 to 9,411, or 54.60% yes, with all 30 precincts reporting. Ashville’s referendum drew 1,469 no votes, or 81.61%, against 331 yes votes in Pickaway County’s unofficial results.

Pataskala’s sample ballot shows a direct ban on covered data-center construction within city limits, effective immediately, with covered facilities defined as those used primarily or exclusively for digital information services with demand or peak load greater than 25 megawatts. Sunbury’s charter text uses the same 25-megawatt threshold and defines construction to include related preparations and modifications on single, contiguous, adjacent or otherwise aggregated parcels. Grove City’s amendment covers heavy industrial development, including data centers, server farms, power generation and large-scale warehousing or logistics, and requires voter approval before city approvals for developments meeting at least one threshold: 50 or more contiguous acres, more than 20 megawatts of peak electrical power, or more than 500,000 gallons of water per day. Applicants must fund an independent impact study, which must be posted publicly at least 60 days before the referendum, and a failed vote blocks city approval and bars the same or a substantially similar application for 24 months. Cumulative increases above 10% in acreage, peak electrical demand or daily water consumption trigger another referendum.

Trenton’s vote followed a September 1, 2026 Supreme Court of Ohio opinion holding that the city council had a mandatory constitutional duty to certify residents’ data-center amendment petition. Council members had refused certification after concluding the petition lacked sufficient valid signatures, and Trenton Data Center Campus, L.L.C., an entity constructing a data center in the city, intervened as a respondent. The petition contained 336 valid signatures, and the court held that 128 were required based on the 1,277 ballots cast at the preceding municipal election, rather than the council’s 820-signature requirement derived from 8,197 registered voters. The court ordered certification for a special election within the constitutional 60-to-120-day period and denied requests for attorney fees and court costs.

The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel says Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the fifth-highest count among states, with most in Central Ohio, and that companies plan to invest up to $40 billion more by 2030. An October 22, 2026 Ohio Northern University release says its Institute for Civics and Public Policy, working with SurveyUSA, surveyed 1,650 Ohio adults between October 8 and October 14, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. The university reported that 55% of respondents opposed data-center construction in Ohio and 22% supported it, that 57% would vote for a constitutional amendment banning new large-scale data centers with peak demand above 25 megawatts, and that 79% expected higher local water and electricity costs. The Ohio Secretary of State says certified results will be published approximately three weeks after the election, and the totals remain unofficial.

stories.Headline: trust, training, and the future of law and medicine in the AI era
stories.Summary:
Stanford University held its first Future of the Legal and Medical Professions Symposium on Oct. 26 on its campus. The event was co-hosted by Stanford Law School, Stanford School of Medicine and the Deborah L. Rhode Center on the Legal Profession. It brought together physicians, lawyers, scholars and technology leaders to compare the shared pressures facing law and medicine. George Triantis, dean of Stanford Law School, and Lloyd Minor, dean of the School of Medicine, both spoke at the public event.

The symposium focused on how artificial intelligence is reshaping education, public confidence and access to care and justice. Speakers said students now must master four to five times more content than earlier generations. Daniel Ho, a Stanford law professor, said his team tested legal AI tools marketed as free of hallucinations and found they hallucinated 17% to 33% of the time, with more than 2,000 real legal cases involving hallucinations. Nora Freeman Engstrom, a Stanford law professor, said about 75% of U.S. civil cases have at least one side without a lawyer. A December 2024 poll found only 35% of Americans expressed confidence in the justice system.

Minor said leaders at Stanford have an obligation to rebuild trust in their educational programs and professions. Triantis said the key will be to teach adaptability, how to move from one tool to another and when a human must stay in the loop. John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association, asked how a student who always relies on ambient listening will learn to distill a patient history. California Supreme Court Justice Goodwin Liu said he can persuade his model to give him almost anything because it is designed to please him. Arati Prabhakar, a former White House science and technology adviser, said there is no scientific and technological foundation for thorough evaluation and validation of these models.

David Freeman Engstrom, a Stanford law professor, described an AI assistant his team built to flag likely errors in debt collection cases in Los Angeles County Superior Court, where nearly half of default judgments contain errors. He said a randomized controlled trial of the tool is underway. David Studdert, Stanford's dean of research, said the interests of the patient and client come first and should not adapt too quickly. Vivian Lee of Harvard Business School said people want to feel understood and cared about. Alyce Adams, a Stanford Medicine professor, said her team works with patients who have diabetic neuropathy, a condition with no cure.

stories.Headline: Humans Matter, too: Amazon Robotics, Anthropic and Duckbill Leaders on the Future of AI
stories.Summary:
A panel of industry experts gathered at WBUR CitySpace in Boston on October 29 to discuss findings from the latest Bentley-Gallup Business in Society Report, including Americans' lack of trust in businesses to use AI responsibly. The event, titled The Business of AI: Opportunity, Trust and What Comes Next, was moderated by Shirley Leung, a columnist and associate editor at The Boston Globe. The panelists were Tye Brady, chief technologist at Amazon Robotics; Meghan Verena Joyce, co-founder and CEO at Duckbill; and Richard Tibbetts, former engineering manager at Anthropic. The report found that young Americans ages 18 to 29 are the biggest skeptics, with most in that group not trusting businesses to use AI responsibly, the highest share of any age group. The event drew about 60 attendees, including Bentley students, and included networking, a panel discussion and a Q&A session.

The panelists agreed that humans will continue to play a big role in AI. Tibbetts said the job should be broken down to identify which parts can be improved with AI, and that successful projects come from a specific understanding of the job and a willingness to reshape it as a hybrid between human experts and AI that automates some of the toil. Brady said technology succeeds when it solves a problem that helps people do their jobs safer and more productively, and that there is no substitute for humans and natural intelligence. Joyce said putting technology into the world without a human in the loop is a technology in search of a purpose, and that it is the company's job to evaluate that on behalf of consumers and deliver genuine value. The report also found that the lack of trust Americans have in businesses to use AI responsibly decreased from last year.

The day opened with remarks from Bentley President E. LaBrent Chrite, who said that as businesses race to take advantage of AI, leaders must address concerns about how the technology is created and deployed. Gallup Senior Partner Stephanie Marken followed with an overview of the survey findings, emphasizing the need to consider the various applications of AI when it comes to trust, such as driving a car or helping with learning versus recommending individuals for an employer to hire. Joyce said the biggest gift to give children and students is a fearlessness for change, and that the ability to lean into change and be an optimistic leader is the most important thing. The article does not say what happens next beyond the event itself.

stories.Headline: AI trust gap reveals distinct retail priorities: Divergent paths to consumer growth in Hong Kong and the GBA
stories.Summary:
New research from KPMG China and GS1 Hong Kong, released on November 4, 2026, found that consumer confidence in artificial intelligence is rising across Hong Kong and other cities in the Greater Bay Area, but retailers will need different strategies to turn that confidence into growth. The report is called Growth Reimagined: Building Consumer Trust in the AI Era. It identifies three priorities for retailers: building trust in AI, delivering market-specific strategies for the growing silver economy, and strengthening brand confidence across Hong Kong and other GBA cities. The research says consumers in other GBA cities are more open to personalised experiences and Chinese Mainland brands, while Hong Kong consumers place more emphasis on value for money.

Trust in AI has risen since last year's survey. In Hong Kong, 48% of consumers now trust AI at least somewhat, up from 28%, while trust in other GBA cities rose from 59% to 76%. However, only 10% of Hong Kong consumers who trust AI are comfortable sharing personal data, compared with 32% in other GBA cities. Among silver shoppers, defined as consumers aged above 55, just 38% in Hong Kong trust AI, compared with 76% in other GBA cities. Value remains a priority for 73% of Hong Kong consumers across all age groups, compared with 45% in other GBA cities, and 57% of Hong Kong silver shoppers identify as value shoppers, compared with 23% in other GBA cities, where brand reputation at 37% and shopping experience at 27% lead.

Anna Lin, Chief Executive of GS1 Hong Kong, said AI increasingly shapes how consumers discover and evaluate products, and it tends to recommend products backed by data it can interpret and trust. She said businesses with trusted, standardised product data that is structured for machines and traceable to an identifiable source will be best placed to earn consumer confidence. Alice Yip, Partner and Head of Consumer and Retail for Hong Kong SAR at KPMG China, said growth in the silver economy depends on recognising that shoppers' priorities differ across markets. She said Hong Kong's silver shoppers prioritise competitive prices, while those in other GBA cities emphasise brand reputation and shopping experiences, and retailers should tailor their offers locally rather than treat the silver economy as one uniform market.

Chinese Mainland brands are seen in other GBA cities as strong on value for money at 64%, safety and reliability at 58% and brand reputation at 50%. In Hong Kong, 81% of consumers choose them for value for money, but fewer cite safety and reliability at 39%, higher quality at 33% or brand reputation at 31%. Hong Kong brands retain an advantage in trust, with 74% of Hong Kong consumers and 61% in other GBA cities citing safety and reliability as the leading reason for choosing them, and preference is strongest in airlines at 78% and food and beverages at 71%. Anson Bailey, Head of Consumer and Retail for Asia Pacific at KPMG China, said any brand that still sees Chinese Mainland competitors as a low-cost threat is looking backward, and that their speed is now producing better products, sharper design and faster innovation.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches Images 2.6 in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, saying it generates images 50% faster, and adds animated GIF creation from prompts or photos (Emma Roth/The Verge)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI launched its Images 2.6 model on November 4, 2026, rolling it out in ChatGPT, Codex and the API. The update lets ChatGPT create animated GIFs from a prompt or a photo uploaded to the chatbot. Users can adjust a GIF's animation speed, edit individual frames and share the result with others. Before this change, ChatGPT could not natively generate GIFs in a single step. OpenAI shared an example in which ChatGPT made a GIF in response to the prompt asking for a GIF of a cat dancing, while also offering options to change playback speed and view it frame by frame.

OpenAI says the new model generates images 50 percent faster. The company says users now generate over 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT and its API, up from the 3 billion per week it reported in September. Images 2.6 is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users across web, desktop and mobile apps. OpenAI is also launching GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst in its API for faster and higher-quality image generation.

The GIF feature is rolling out alongside the new model. The articles attribute the announcement to OpenAI and name Emma Roth of The Verge as the reporter who wrote about it. They do not include direct statements from OpenAI executives beyond the company's claims about speed and usage. The articles describe the GIF tools as letting users change playback speed and view a GIF frame by frame.

They do not say what OpenAI said about the GIF feature beyond the example it shared. The articles give little context beyond the earlier figure of 3 billion images per week in September. They do not say what happens next beyond the rollout to ChatGPT and Codex users and the API launch. No further plans or timelines are mentioned.

stories.Headline: AI isn't the next cloud. Don't let it outgrow IT
stories.Summary:
Glen Maguire, founder of Matrix AI Consulting, wrote an article published on 3 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia and IT Brief New Zealand. He argues that AI will follow the path of earlier technologies like the web, mobile and cloud, which started with IT and then spread across the business. He says AI's use should spread too, but its foundations must not outgrow IT. He draws on his 25 years of experience in digital transformation.

The article cites several figures. Datacom's 2025 State of AI Index found 87% of New Zealand organisations use AI in some form, but only 12% have deployed it across the whole business. Deloitte's 2026 research found 69% of Australian organisations surveyed were using autonomous AI agents, but only 22% reported highly advanced agent governance. Randstad found 32% of Australian workers fear AI could cost them their job, and only 48% say they have been trained on the AI tools reshaping their jobs, while employers believe 56% have been. Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index found 75% of knowledge workers already use AI at work, and 78% of them bring their own tools.

Maguire says AI is different from earlier technologies because it acts rather than just informs, it sees everything a user can access, it arrives as a feature update inside bought tools, it changes over time and it changes the work itself. He warns that staff can now build apps and agents in plain English, which repeats the pattern of the dot-com boom when marketing teams moved faster than their understanding. He says the answer is not to stop people building but to give them a safe place to do it, with approved platforms, data rules built in, every app and agent registered to the organisation, a named business owner for each, and IT review before anything touches customers or core systems. He says IT must be preventative rather than reactive.

The article says New Zealand's Privacy Commissioner has confirmed the Privacy Act 2020 applies to AI tools, and Australia's OAIC advises organisations not to enter personal information into publicly available AI tools. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report found 97% of organisations that suffered an AI-related breach lacked proper AI access controls, and 63% of breached organisations had no AI governance policy or were still developing one. Gartner found only 4% of CIOs surveyed had explicit plans to redesign roles for a human-agent workforce, and those that did were 2.4 times more likely to be in its higher-performing AI group. Maguire lists seven moves for IT to stay central, including setting guardrails early, making the approved path the easy path, convening a cross-functional AI group, leading change with HR, building learning and resistance into the plan, measuring value in business terms, and building capability inside IT. He says IT leaders should watch for signals that AI is becoming strategic, such as business units asking for their own AI budgets and board conversations turning from risk to opportunity.

stories.Headline: Silicon Valley promises AI will cure disease. Drugmaker CEOs aren’t buying It.
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley leaders have made bold claims that artificial intelligence could cure most human diseases within a decade, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei posted in September that this could happen in roughly five to ten years. Drug company executives are pushing back, and Jeff Leiden, executive chairman of Vertex Pharmaceuticals, called one such claim complete nonsense. Vertex has used about 50 AI companies to comb through a data set of 10,000 drug compounds, and Leiden said not one produced a working drug. No drug designed by artificial intelligence has won FDA clearance, and pharma leaders say biology is the obstacle.

The divide shows in how the two sides describe the technology. AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said disease and biology are complicated, and that saying AI will cure cancer may be a little bit of a jump. McKinsey senior partner Alex Devereson said AI can design experimental medicines faster but that about a quarter of mid-stage to late-stage failures come from safety problems and off-target effects that current models struggle to predict. Venture capital and private equity firms invested $8.4 billion globally into AI drug discovery in 2025, up from roughly $4 billion two years earlier. Only a few AI-native biotechs, such as Insilico Medicine and Generate Biomedicines, have gotten drugs into late-stage patient testing, and the FDA has not cleared any of them.

Pharma companies are still using AI as a tool rather than a cure. AstraZeneca signed a deal with AI biotech Insitro worth $40 million up front to discover new heart and weight-loss drugs, and it signed an agreement with Oracle to help streamline patient recruitment for clinical trials. Eli Lilly and Nvidia said in January they would invest up to $1 billion over five years to research AI's role in drug discovery and robotics, and Bristol Myers Squibb, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi have announced partnerships with OpenAI or Anthropic. Regeneron chief scientific officer George Yancopoulos said AI will not miraculously cut drug development from 15 years to five.

Tech companies are moving deeper into the field. Anthropic bought a stealth-mode biotech earlier this year and recently bought a one-person biotech running an almost completely AI-enabled operation, and OpenAI announced last month that it bought an AI drug-discovery biotech. Bayer's gene therapy unit used AI to comb through 100 million patient records in a matter of days to find the five best diseases for its gene-editing technology. Sebastian Guth, Bayer's chief operating officer, said the magic happens when the brilliance of human scientists is married with AI. Regulators have proposed new frameworks to govern AI use in regulatory submissions and trial data analysis, though the articles say this does not help with thornier parts of the process such as finding enough of the right patients and monitoring them through studies.

stories.Headline: US stocks: Nasdaq ends higher as AI heavyweights rebound ahead of midterm results
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq ended higher on Tuesday, Nov 3, 2026, as AI heavyweights rebounded ahead of US midterm election results. Apple fell 1.9 per cent after it warned that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring its holiday-quarter gross margin. Memory-chip maker Micron Technology gained 2.6 per cent, while Nvidia rose 2.3 per cent after falling in the last four sessions. The broader Philadelphia chips index jumped, while AMD rose ahead of its quarterly report due after the bell, and Microsoft and Amazon each moved more than 2 per cent higher.

The S&P 500 climbed 0.36 per cent to end the session at 7,568.92 points, while the Nasdaq gained 0.83 per cent to 25,372.01 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.38 per cent to 51,787.04 points, and six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by consumer staples, down 1.76 per cent, followed by a 1.75 per cent loss in materials. The Nasdaq 100 on Monday ended more than 10 per cent below its Oct 6 record-high close, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction. The S&P 500 is down about 3 per cent from its record-high close on Oct 6, and it remains up over 10 per cent in 2026.

Jay Hatfield, chief executive officer at Infrastructure Capital Management, described the move as a rotation from safe tech like Apple into riskier tech like chipmakers. He said it was clear dip-buying in a higher-risk, Nasdaq-driven market. Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, said markets will assess potential implications for fiscal policy, regulation, taxation and government spending. He said it will be good to put the elections behind, as they have been an anticipated volatility event for quite some time.

American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump's second term in Tuesday's midterm elections. Polls and nonpartisan analysts favour Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans, while control of the Senate remains uncertain. Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note earlier this week that the elections should help remove a major market overhang. They believe a US market correction that began in June is in its final innings.

Frost & Sullivan announced on November 4, 2026, that it has named Seekr the 2026 Global Company of the Year in the AI Trust & Validation industry. Company of the Year is Frost & Sullivan's top honor, recognizing the market participant that exemplifies visionary innovation, market-leading performance, and unmatched customer care. The recognition covers Seekr's approach to AI accountability, explainability, model validation, and sovereignty. Seekr's SeekrFlow platform supports deployment in the cloud, on-premises, at the edge, and in fully air-gapped environments. Its portfolio includes SeekrGuard, SeekrIntel, and SeekrGeo, built on SeekrFlow to support organizations across the AI lifecycle. She said models can behave differently in real-world environments, and when agents act on flawed observations, errors can compound across reasoning and action cycles. She said Seekr addresses this through a framework centered on observability, explainability, contestability, and sovereignty. Rob Clark, President of Seekr, said enterprise and government customers are demanding more from AI than giving data away to train, hoping an agent does not go rogue, and facing large closed-weight model bills. He said the platform brings AI agents and models that are explainable and defensible from start to finish, running on the customer's terms in their environment.

The assessment considered factors including the ability to address unmet needs, leadership focus, implementation of best practices, price/performance value, customer ownership experience, and brand equity. stories.Headline: Anthropic warns AI could outpace human control in developing successor models
stories.Summary:
Anthropic warned that artificial intelligence could soon begin accelerating the development of more powerful AI systems faster than companies can put adequate safety safeguards in place. The company made the warning in an amended registration statement filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on November 2, 2026. It said its internal estimates point to the imminent possibility of dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI. The warning relates to recursive self-improvement, a process in which AI systems help design and develop more capable successors. Anthropic said its Claude models already contribute to several stages of developing later generations, including research experiments, training data, model evaluations, safety audits and coding.

Anthropic said more than 90% of contributions to its codebase in September were written by Claude. The average daily volume of code contributed per engineer during the three months ended September 30 was more than 45 times the 2024 average. Claude's success rate on challenging, open-ended engineering problems reached around 90% in September, rising by nearly 50 percentage points in nine months. Anthropic clarified that its assessment concerns future models, and that none of its existing models has been designated as having crossed that threshold. It said it did not anticipate safely using Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding.

Anthropic acknowledged that AI-assisted development of more powerful AI systems could introduce significant safety risks. It conceded that its ability to predict or measure the pace of capability improvements remains limited, noting that it had previously recognised significant acceleration only after it had occurred. The company said it is considering changes to its Responsible Scaling Policy to ensure humans retain control over frontier AI development. Its precautionary approach has already involved delaying releases and restricting access to certain models, such as Mythos, which was initially made available to select organisations through Project Glasswing rather than released publicly. Anthropic cautioned that such restrictions could carry a competitive cost, slowing its progress relative to rivals that do not impose similar constraints.

Separately, Anthropic said it is developing a way to verify which AI model produced a given output. Its FlashProve system is designed to deliver what is known as provable inference, allowing users to confirm that responses came from a specific AI model, according to a November 3 blog post. Anthropic said a user querying a model today cannot check that responses came from the model a developer claims is responding, rather than one secretly substituted by a routing service for cost reasons or by an attacker who tampered with the token stream. Anthropic also said its red team found that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things devices, such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. It warned such models might be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, and said a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there is no centralized point to shut off.

stories.Headline: AI agents need canvas model, not rigid harness engineering
stories.Summary:
Nimisha Asthagiri, a technical advisor at Thoughtworks, gave a presentation proposing a shift from harness engineering to a bounded canvas model for AI agents. She spoke at QCon AI, and TechGig published a report on her talk on November 4, 2026. The term harness engineering was popularized by Mitchell Hashimoto of HashiCorp in a blog post on February 5, 2026. OpenAI then ran experiments in which a team built a million lines of code in five months using the harness approach.

Harness engineering means continuously updating a surrounding structure to correct agent mistakes. The canvas model instead gives agents boundaries, scaffolding, primed environments, and constraints, like a painter's chosen palette. Over-constraining agents can cause context bloat, communication failures, and brittle agent skills, according to learnings from OpenAI. Vivek from LangChain defined an agent as a model plus the harness, with the harness covering observability, persistence, and controls. LangChain found that improving the harness alone moved model performance from top 30 to top 5 on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

Asthagiri said the industry is changing rapidly and that her ideas should be taken with a grain of salt. She described the shift as a mental model change, from a controlled harness to a bounded canvas for managing agentic topologies. She said cognitive debt is a huge concern and called for decision records, including architecture, organization, and product decision records, to leave traces for whoever inherits the codebase. She recommended applying product engineering operating models with define, build, and review phases to agentic teams. She also said teams should design for change and failures and embrace the messiness of creation to build more resilient AI systems.

Asthagiri drew on her earlier experience as chief architect at edX, where she dealt with codebase decay, architecture drift, and distributed teams. She said harness engineering followed prompt engineering in 2023 and 2024 and context engineering in 2025, and that the term gained buzz starting in February 2026. OpenAI's experiments showed the need for continuous garbage collection by separate agents. Kyle from HumanLayer suggested in March that harness engineering might be a subset of context engineering. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recommendations.

stories.Headline: Ricursive releases Ripple-65B Preview, a general-purpose variant of its AI model for automating advanced chip design, under Apache 2.0, costing $0.60/1M output (Carl Franzen/VentureBeat)
stories.Summary:
Ricursive AI released Ripple-65B Preview on November 4, 2026. It is a 65B dense open-weight model pretrained from scratch for agentic coding, and it is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive's AI chip design platform. The company reported a score of 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which it says is the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. Every MoE rival it beats on that test carries 501B to 975B total parameters.

The model was pretrained on 12T tokens with up to 1M context, and it runs in BF16 on datacenter GPUs at 250 tokens per second on 2x B200, with an experimental NVFP4 build targeting NVIDIA DGX Spark. The release includes three checkpoints, an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version and a BF16 base model, all under Apache 2.0. Ricursive put the full R&D cost at $32M, which it estimates is one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. The model uses a dense Transformer rather than Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity, with a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers, and training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization.

On benchmarks, Ricursive reported 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus Beam at 80.1, Muse Spark Open at 76.4, Inkling at 63.8 and Nemotron 3 Ultra at 56.4. It reported 79.1 on SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard, the top score in its table, 76.5 on SWE-bench Verified, 98.3 on AIME 2025 and 90.5 on HMMT Feb 2026. Its weaker results were SciCode at 39.4, DeepSWE 1.1 at 44.3, MCP Atlas at 71.67 and GPQA Diamond at 85.2. Ricursive said it hit 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts, which it puts at roughly 70x fewer than Beam, which reported over 100M rollouts.

Ricursive said it chose the dense design over Mixture-of-Experts to cut infrastructure complexity, and it built its recipe through laddering experiments starting from Olmo 3's ladder, rejecting changes that failed to hold at 4B scale, such as 2-stream mHC. The technical post reports a 16x code compute-efficiency gain at 4B scale. Ricursive said it bought no post-training data and built its own synthetic pipelines, and that post-training ran midtraining, long context, SFT, long-context SFT and mixed RL, with long-context stages trained at 2M sequence length. The company also reran Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K, where most rivals dropped, Beam fell to 70.8 and Muse Spark Open rose to 78.7, still below Ripple's 80.5.

stories.Headline: South Korea's MegazoneCloud, KAIST Team Up to Standardize Robot-Equipment Interoperability, Launch Physical AI Commercialization
stories.Summary:
MegazoneCloud signed a memorandum of understanding with KAIST's Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute to work on standardizing and commercializing physical AI, according to a report on November 3, 2026. The agreement was signed at COEX in Seoul on November 2, and MegazoneCloud Chairman Lee Joo-wan and Jang Young-jae, head of the institute, attended the ceremony. The partnership centers on building a common framework that connects robots, production equipment and data systems, which differ from factory to factory. The two sides will also work with the governance subcommittee of the Ministry of Science and ICT's Physical AI Alliance.

The plan covers technology validation, industrial deployment, commercialization and overseas expansion, and the tool for on-site use is KAIROS 37, a robot orchestration platform developed by KAIST. Robot orchestration means connecting robots and systems from different manufacturers on one platform and allocating and managing tasks. MegazoneCloud will draw on its experience building cloud and AI systems for some 8,000 companies at home and abroad, and it says it has about 2,800 people with AI and AX capabilities. A working-level consultative body will pick the industry sectors and cooperation tasks, and KAIST plans to expand the number of participating companies in stages.

Chairman Lee said the essential competitiveness of physical AI lies not in a simple collection of technologies but in steady progress through continuous improvement based on stability and efficiency at real industrial sites. He said the company would combine its experience from more than 8,000 companies with its AI and AX capabilities to help the technology take root and create substantive value. Separately, President Lee Jae Myung said in his annual budget address to parliament that South Korea will invest 21.3 trillion won, nearly twice this year's amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers. He said 4.7 trillion won would go to frontier AI development projects, and the government proposed a record budget with a 12.8% spending increase to 820.9 trillion won, which needs parliamentary approval.

Physical AI is a field in which robots and equipment make judgments and move based on sensor data, and it is seen as the next pillar of manufacturing automation. In South Korea most cases so far are demonstrations at individual factories, and a standardized interoperability framework has been cited as the key to commercialization. The articles say the pace of standardization is the key variable because of the tangled interests of participating companies, and that which sectors the working-level body picks first is expected to be the first test of commercialization. The initiative also includes a vision of an open cooperation ecosystem not subordinate to any particular company.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave IREN and Nebius Stocks Sink as Election Results Spark AI Data Center Fears
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, shares of CoreWeave and Nebius fell in early trading, dropping 7% and 5% respectively, according to TradingView. The declines came as Democratic election gains led investors to reconsider the outlook for large AI infrastructure projects. All three companies named in the headline, CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, are spending heavily on facilities and equipment for AI computing services. The article ties the stock moves to possible changes in U.S. rules for AI data centers.

The concerns go beyond building permits. Some Democratic lawmakers have sought a temporary pause on new data-center construction until Congress sets rules for the industry, while other proposals would make technology companies shoulder more of the electricity costs their facilities generate. stories.Headline: OpenAI appoints Jill Hazelbaker as Chief Corporate Affairs Officer
stories.Summary:
Jill Hazelbaker is joining OpenAI as its Chief Corporate Affairs Officer, the company announced on November 3, 2026. In the new role she will lead OpenAI's global communications and corporate positioning. She comes to OpenAI from Uber, where she was President and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer. At Uber she helped lead the company's transformation from an ambitious startup into one of the world's largest global technology platforms.

The job covers OpenAI's global communications and reputation, along with corporate brand and positioning, social media, and cultural and community partnerships and convenings. OpenAI said the appointment reflects its commitment to investing in the leadership and capabilities needed to engage more deeply with the people and institutions shaping AI's future. Hazelbaker will report to Greg Brockman, OpenAI's co-founder and president. She brings nearly two decades of experience advising technology companies and political leaders.

Brockman said that as AI becomes part of more people's lives, how the company communicates, engages and earns public trust has never been more important. He said Hazelbaker brings exceptional judgment, seasoned leadership and a deep understanding of the opportunities and responsibilities of building technology at global scale, and that he is thrilled to welcome her. Hazelbaker said AI represents the most profound technological shift of our lifetime, with enormous stakes and extraordinary possibilities, and that the work of building public trust has never been more consequential. She said she could not be more excited to work alongside Sam, Greg and the team they have assembled.

Hazelbaker spent a decade at Uber, where she oversaw global communications, marketing, public policy, safety and people teams. Before Uber she led communications and public policy at Snap, and earlier held senior roles at Google covering corporate communications globally, communications across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and government relations in Europe. She began her career in U.S. politics, serving as National Communications Director and Chief Spokesperson for Senator John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign and as Press Secretary to New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg. Axios described her as among Washington's best-known and best-connected executives.

stories.Headline: Apple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' ways
stories.Summary:
Apple said in its annual financial filing on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, that AI agents able to act in unintended or unpredictable ways could threaten its business by opening the company to lawsuits or hurting its reputation. The filing added new risk factors about agents that can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions. Apple wrote that such agents may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized. The Fortune report said the filing also warned that rogue agents could conceal actions, hide, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs.

The filing follows several AI safety incidents, including this summer's attack by OpenAI agents on AI company Hugging Face. Earlier this year, OpenAI released an agent called Dots and Meta introduced one called Muse, both of which use advanced AI models to work autonomously. Last month, Apple announced changes to full disk access on Macs to reduce risks related to that level of access for AI agents installed on PCs. Apple also said it does not currently have an agentic AI, and it warned that its ability to oversee and control third-party AI agents may be limited.

Apple chief executive John Ternus, on his first earnings call as CEO on Monday, said agentic capabilities are promising tools for users. He said the company wants to make sure users are aware of what they are giving access to, and that this is done in a way that protects security and privacy. Ternus said Apple cannot access private data on its devices and called that a core differentiator, noting that Siri can tap into personal data such as contacts, communications, health data and financial data in a secure and private way. This fall, Apple released Siri AI, which uses the iPhone's local data storage but cannot work autonomously for long stretches like Dots or Muse.

The filing also outlined other pressures, including memory and storage component shortages that Apple said will intensify. Apple said demand for cloud computing, storage and other AI infrastructure has produced constrained supply, extended lead times and increasing costs that could affect its AI rollout, and its research and development spending rose 32% year over year. Apple shares dropped roughly 2% on Tuesday after the company said its margins would continue to be squeezed by memory chip costs and after it showed slowing growth in its Services segment. Google parent Alphabet also pointed out risks posed by rogue agents in a recent filing, and Microsoft recently announced controls to detect, monitor and restrict AI agents.

stories.Headline: AMD forecasts Q4 revenue above estimates on data-center growth
stories.Summary:
AMD reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and forecast fourth-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates. The company expects revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, compared with analysts' average estimate of $16.23 billion. Third-quarter revenue rose 45 per cent from a year earlier to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion consensus. Earnings before certain costs came to $2.09 per share, beating the forecast of $1.95 per share, and net income was $3.47 billion, up 77 per cent from $1.96 billion a year earlier.

Data-center revenue nearly doubled in the quarter, jumping 97 per cent to a record $8.55 billion, and the unit accounted for 64 per cent of overall revenue, up from 47 per cent a year earlier. AMD's flagship Helios rack, which combines the MI455X accelerator and new Venice server chips, is in production and set for a larger ramp-up in the fourth quarter, with initial systems being tested at Meta. In February, AMD agreed to sell up to $60 billion worth of AI chips to Meta over five years. AMD also agreed in September to acquire Fei-Fei Li's World Labs for $8.2 billion in a stock deal, and it acquired Taalas, a maker of model-specific chips.

Chief Executive Lisa Su said on a conference call that adoption is just starting and that demand should grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly. She said AMD had worked across its supply chain to secure wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory and other key components for much higher growth next year. Su said Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Oracle and Meta are all using AMD Helios systems in their data centers. Analyst Jacob Bourne of eMarketer said the results would encourage investors after the recent semiconductor selloff.

AMD's adjusted gross margin is expected to be about 55 per cent in the fourth quarter, down from 56 per cent in the third quarter. The company expects server revenue to double year over year in fiscal 2027, with AI growth likely to accelerate faster than projected three months earlier. Its PC and gaming segment saw revenue decline 8 per cent to $3.7 billion, and gaming revenue fell 40 per cent from the previous year. Rival Intel recently forecast quarterly revenue well below estimates, and its stock fell more than 30 per cent on Friday.

stories.Headline: Enmovil to quadruple FDE team amid enterprise AI hiring
stories.Summary:
Enmovil, an agentic AI company focused on supply chain and logistics orchestration, plans to expand its forward-deployed engineering team from about 30 employees to 100 to 120 within a year, according to reports published in early November 2026. The company currently has 175 employees, including around 100 in development. It expects revenue to grow from approximately $5 million to $8 to 9 million by the end of the current financial year. Enmovil has raised around $8 million to date, including a $6 million Series A round about a year ago.

Forward-deployed engineers work at the intersection of software development, product engineering and customer operations. They adapt technology to specific operational requirements and integrate software into existing systems, including enterprise resource planning, warehouse management and transport management platforms. Enmovil's platform connects supply chain planning, inventory management, procurement, replenishment and logistics execution through an agentic AI layer called CADDIE. It works as an intelligence layer over existing systems such as SAP, Oracle and Blue Yonder rather than replacing them. The company says its platform has improved forecast accuracy by 30 to 40 percent, reduced dispatch costs by 10 to 15 percent and cut manual effort by more than 75 percent.

Ravi Prasad Bulusu, co-founder and CEO, said enterprise solutions do not follow a one-size-fits-all model, and that as systems become more complex, teams need to work closely with customers to make technology practical for them. He said the company built an agentic platform that coordinates individual modules into workflows, effectively providing customers with an AI workforce. He also said the optimization engine remains the core technological differentiator, while the agentic layer makes the system easier to use. Bulusu spent about 20 years in technology, including as a director at NVIDIA and Intel. His co-founders are Nanda Kishore, COO, and Venkat Moganty, CTO.

Enmovil has more than 40 customers in India, including Maruti, Mahindra, TVS Motor, Volvo, Daimler, Nestlé, ITC and The Whole Truth Foods. The company is beginning to expand internationally into the US and Southeast Asia, and the planned team growth is expected to support that expansion and a growing customer base. The company competes with supply chain technology providers such as SAP, Blue Yonder, Kinaxis, o9 Solutions and Pando, depending on the use case. The reports say the hiring plans reflect a broader shift in enterprise AI, where building the technology is only part of adoption and engineers are needed to translate AI capabilities into practical workflows.

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s Medical AI Is Over Twice as Good Diagnosing Diseases as Doctors
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers published a paper in Science in November 2026 describing a system called MAI-DxO, which is powered by GPT-5 and acts like a panel of physicians. One specialist proposes possible diagnoses, another suggests questions and tests, and a third considers costs, while an orchestrator coordinates the debate. The team tested it on 304 complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine and a similar number of typical emergency room cases. The system reached an accurate diagnosis 83 percent of the time on the complex cases, compared with 22 percent for physicians relying on their own knowledge.

On typical emergency room cases the AI was nearly twice as accurate as physicians, at 80 percent versus 47 percent. A cost-conscious version kept nearly 80 percent accuracy on the complex cases while spending an estimated $1,300 per case, based on 2023 hospital pricing data, while doctors ran up bills of over $4,700. In one case of scurvy, the system linked the patient's diet to bleeding gums and tooth loss and reached the right diagnosis after spending just over $1,100. The standalone GPT-5 asked for an extensive neurological workup that cost nearly 7.6 times more, and swapping in GPT-5.5 further boosted accuracy.

Study author Eric Horvitz said he has worked on AI in medicine since the 1980s and hopes the advances bring timely and effective care to more people. He also said each patient's understanding, goals and preferences must be considered. Study author Harsha Nori said the benchmark measured whether the right diagnosis was reached and how expensive the path was. The team said working alongside clinical teams will show where the technology succeeds, where it falls short and how it fits into busy workflows.

The experiments took place in controlled, text-based simulations, and the article says unsupervised AI diagnosticians are not coming to hospitals anytime soon. Real clinicians deal with incomplete histories, medical images and time pressure, and patients have the final say over whether to undergo a test. The team has partnered with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston to evaluate the system in different hospital settings. A separate article describes deepfake AI doctors appearing in supplement ads, and it cites a paper by Athni TS in the Journal of Medical Internet Research on classifying physician deepfakes.
