stories.Headline: Anthropic found a way to prove which AI model answered you — but there’s a costly catch
stories.Summary:
Anthropic published research on November 3, 2026, about an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output. The system is called FlashProve, and it is built to provide what researchers call provable inference, a cryptographic proof that an output came from a specific model. The work was described in a blog post by Russell Brandom of TechCrunch and covered by Amanda Caswell of The New Stack on November 4, 2026. The researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub.

The system requires AI labs to publish a fingerprint of each model they release, which can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. The fingerprints do not reveal a model's weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. The researchers say it could prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. It could also verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model.

The research is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy the system at Anthropic or any other lab. The researchers describe the announcement as a share of intermediate progress rather than a completed research agenda. They say they are sharing it explicitly with the goal that others look at what they have done, take it, and improve it. The system is meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they are using. It is also described as robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI vs Physicians: Who Makes the Better Diagnosis?
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI Health developed a system called the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator, or AI-DxO, which aims to simulate human clinical reasoning in a structured, interactive way. A study published in Science tested the system against practicing generalist physicians, and the results were reported on November 4, 2026. The researchers built the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark and examined 304 clinicopathologic conference cases from The New England Journal of Medicine and 325 emergency department-to-admission encounters from the MIMIC-IV-ED database. In this setup, physicians and AI systems had to gather information, order tests, and reach diagnoses step by step, closely copying real clinical practice.

AI-DxO reached 83% diagnostic accuracy on the conference cases, compared with 36% for the physicians. On the emergency department cases, the figures were 80% and 46%. The Cloud Wars article gives slightly more precise numbers, 83.2% against 36.1%, and 80.3% against 46.8%, and says doctors scored just 22.3% when reference tools were taken away. The system often ordered fewer costly tests, which the authors linked to its ability to process large volumes of medical knowledge, including information on rare diseases and unusual presentations. It also uses structured mechanisms meant to reduce common cognitive errors such as diagnostic anchoring and premature closure.

The researchers said the results came from a controlled environment and do not fully reflect everyday medical practice. They noted that physician-patient communication, empathy, contextual interpretation of imaging, variability in clinical presentations, and shared decision-making were not fully built into the experimental model. For that reason, they argued that AI-DxO should be seen as a tool to support clinical decision-making rather than a substitute for medical practice. The Cloud Wars article adds that the comparisons were against individual physicians, not medical teams, which matters because the tool takes a panel-style approach that simulates asking several specialists for their opinions.

The original research used OpenAI's o3 model, and Microsoft has since reported further testing with newer models, including GPT-5.5. The articles say the results are based on historical medical cases rather than live patient consultations, so there is not yet proven evidence of better patient outcomes in real-world settings. Both articles say more clinical trials and independent testing are needed before widespread use, and the Medscape commentary describes the most plausible trend as integration of AI and medical expertise. That commentary also raises a question about Brazil, where more than 30 new medical schools have recently been authorized, and whether it will make more sense to invest in technology rather than in medical schools.

According to its award nomination, its work raised SOC processing capacity by about five times and cut Mean Time to Detect by 50% without adding headcount.

Its AI-Agent Penetration Testing service reported up to ten times broader testing scenario coverage and about 60% fewer false positives. The three-day summit drew senior government and regional leaders, including Coordinating Minister for Infrastructure and Regional Development Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono, the Vice Minister of Tourism, representatives of the Ministry of Creative Economy, senior officials from BSSN, and leaders of technology associations from across the Asia-Oceania region. In closing, Lumanto said cyber resilience is not about preventing every attack but about ensuring organizations and economies can anticipate, withstand, recover and adapt. stories.Headline: Anthropic compute costs worsen despite revenue growth
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's compute margins worsened in the quarter ending September 30, 2026, according to a new S-1 filing reported on November 3 and 4, 2026. Compute costs rose to 58 per cent of revenue, up from 48 per cent in the previous quarter. Revenue grew to $17 billion from $11.5 billion, but operating losses also increased. Revenue for every dollar spent on compute fell to 1.72x, down from a peak of just over 2x earlier in the year.

The company's total compute bill for the quarter reached $10 billion, including $5.0 billion for compute bought under short-term commitments that carry higher rates. Anthropic has deals with neoclouds including SpaceX, Nscale, Akamai and Volta, and is reportedly paying SpaceX $1.25 billion monthly for compute. The filing came as Anthropic prepared for an expected IPO, after it filed as the first pure-play AI unicorn to test public markets and updated its S-1 with Q3 financials. Earlier filings disclosed a $542 billion data center spending plan, and its S-1 ran 335 pages.

Anthropic said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to remain its largest operating cost for the foreseeable future. It is building its own compute base through a project called Anthropic Direct, but rapid demand growth outpaces those internal efforts. The Tech Buzz reported that model complexity is growing faster than infrastructure efficiency, and that AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure supply Anthropic compute while building competing AI products, which limits its pricing leverage. Anthropic has also launched Claude Duet, an autonomous AI agent for professionals, and backed an AI safety bill with a judge-only block clause.

Investors are weighing whether the margin deterioration is temporary, from ramping new infrastructure and training more capable models, or structural, meaning generative AI economics do not work at current price points. The articles say the answer probably lies somewhere in between, but the trend is not encouraging. The compute margin story is expected to be central in investor due diligence as Anthropic heads into IPO pricing discussions. The next few weeks will show whether the company has a convincing answer or whether the issue shadows its public market debut.

stories.Headline: AI redefining talent, university infrastructure

Academics and industry leaders met at the HKU Talent Forum at the University of Hong Kong Beijing Center to discuss how artificial intelligence is changing talent and university infrastructure. Lin Chen, vice-president of HKU, said AI is both an opportunity and a challenge. Xue Lan, dean of Tsinghua University's Schwarzman College, said large language models have had a big impact in narrow areas such as coding but limited practical influence in healthcare, education and autonomous driving.

Xue warned that AI has ended higher education's monopoly as the only gateway to professional knowledge. He predicted future universities will be defined not only by gymnasiums or libraries but also by computing platforms, data centers and intelligent tutoring systems. The University of Science and Technology of China launched its Token Program mid-year, giving each student 100 million tokens per day. In September, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications opened free computing accounts for nearly 10,000 freshmen, and on Oct 26, Tongji University began issuing 100 million tokens per week to all faculty and students.

Duan Nan, vice-president of JD.com, described an industry that iterates daily and requires strong execution and interdisciplinary agility. He said the critical skill in an era of human-AI symbiosis is judgment, meaning the ability to evaluate the quality of AI output and ask the right questions. Wang Bin, director of Xiaomi's AI Lab, said people from the top of the company down, including himself, are anxious about how to respond to the future society. He said the first response is embracing change, and the second is resilience and relentless learning, adding that his own natural language processing expertise has become largely obsolete.

In Selangor, the state government held the fifth SCOUT University Series on AI and data centres at Sunway University, organised by Invest Selangor Berhad with the university's School of Computing and Artificial Intelligence. Selangor recorded nearly RM70 billion in approved investments from January to June 2026, with more than 90 per cent from the services sector led by information and communications technology. stories.Headline: Embodied AI's Next Frontier: Integrating Intelligence with Real-World Systems
stories.Summary:
New research published on November 4, 2026, highlights the challenge of integrating intelligence, sensing, movement, computing, energy management and connectivity into embodied AI systems that can perform reliably in demanding environments. The findings come from a white paper titled From Specialized to General-Purpose: 2026 White Paper on Embodied AI Technology Evolution and Industrial Deployment. It was jointly published by Avnet, the National and Local Co-Built Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center and GYH.AI. Embodied AI combines artificial intelligence with physical systems such as robots and autonomous machines, enabling them to perceive their surroundings, make decisions and act in the physical world.

The research identifies four factors that will influence the shift from specialized embodied AI applications toward broader industrial deployment. System integration is fundamental to performance, because AI models, computing platforms, sensors, motion control, energy management and communications must function as a coordinated system. Technology selection must reflect application requirements, balancing performance, energy efficiency, reliability, scalability and cost. The path to general-purpose embodied AI will be gradual, building on specialized systems designed for defined tasks, and industrial deployment requires lifecycle planning covering testing, software compatibility, component availability, safety, maintenance and long-term support.

Edward Tsaur, VP of Avnet Design Services, Marketing & Communications for Asia Pacific, said much of the discussion around embodied AI focuses on individual technologies, but the next stage will depend on how well they work together. He said the challenge is not just making systems smarter but ensuring they perform reliably, adapt to changing conditions and deliver consistent results over time. He added that across Asia Pacific there is growing interest in intelligent systems for manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and other operational environments. He said collaboration across the technology ecosystem will be critical to translating advances into practical solutions, looking beyond individual components to how hardware, software and engineering expertise can work together.

The 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, bringing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. The system combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware, coordinated in real time by Envision's Dubhe Controller, supported by its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model.

Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems, said AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage and the grid to meet computing demand. stories.Headline: Bradbury Science Museum Presents ‘Night With A Nerd: Neuromorphic Artificial Intelligence Wednesday Nov. 4.
stories.Summary:
The Bradbury Science Museum will present “Night with a Nerd: Neuromorphic Artificial Intelligence” from 6 to 8 p.m. Wednesday Nov. 4. The community is encouraged to attend the event. Dr. Andrew Sornborger will give the talk.

The Los Alamos Reporter and the Los Alamos Daily Post both published news releases about the event, on Nov. 4 and Nov. 3, 2026, respectively. Dr. Sornborger’s talk will give an overview of neuromorphic computing. It will cover the various analog and digital methodologies that investigators use to study how neural systems can be used to process information. Those neural systems involve neurons communicating with spikes over massively parallel networks.

He will then discuss a framework that he and collaborators have developed for controlling information flow and learning in neuromorphic computers. That framework makes it possible to easily determine where information propagates and when it gets to its target. He will then give examples of the types of AI algorithms that his group has produced. He will also discuss the value that their realization can have for AI “at the edge.”

The talk will cover uses in autonomous systems, like satellites, and in high-power-consuming installations such as data centers. The FBI has opened a formal investigation treating North Korea as responsible for the theft of US$6.3 billion. Carlsen worked at the FBI from 2009 to 2021 tracking North Korea's illicit money laundering.

The Binance hack was blamed on a North Korean unit called TraderTraitor, which experts say may have only about a dozen members. According to Chainalysis, North Korea is believed to be responsible for 89 percent of reported crypto hack losses in 2026. North Korea picks its best students for hacking teams and trains them at places like Moranbong College in Pyongyang. Carlsen said North Korean hackers use AI to find targets at a level he called a superpower, and he said security vulnerabilities have risen by a factor of 23 because of AI.

Kim Yo-jong, director of the Workers' Party General Affairs Department, denied the hacking allegations in statements on two consecutive days starting November 4. Carlsen said her claims are not credible at all and that North Korea's responsibility could gladly be proven in court.

Carlsen said North Korea is extremely sloppy compared with other advanced persistent threats because it faces no consequences, so it focuses on cashing out quickly rather than covering its tracks. He said Tether and Circle urgently froze stolen assets after the hack, so North Korea likely walked away with around US$3 billion rather than the full US$6.3 billion. He noted that the U.N. Panel of Experts was dissolved by Russia's veto and that China is actively obstructing investigations. He said China may take the Binance incident seriously but will likely not take substantive action, and that the United States, South Korea and Japan should respond more proactively.

stories.Summary:
Stock futures fell and then recovered early on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after Democrats won commanding victories in key races across the country. S&P 500 futures slid by more than 0.5%, Dow Jones Industrial futures tumbled by more than 100 points, and Nasdaq 100 futures sold off by more than 1%. JPMorgan Chase analysts cautioned that the result could trigger an AI sell-off on assumed higher regulation. They cited possible new data-center restrictions and higher taxes on corporations and top earners as potential headwinds for tech companies. She wrote that Democratic wins in governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, which hold a significant share of the U.S. project pipeline, mean new pauses and restrictions on data center development. She said 2027 is shaping up to be a turbulent year as developers adapt to a shifting policy landscape. Wolfe Research's Tobin Marcus wrote that the one surprise that could plausibly spook markets is Abbott losing the Texas gubernatorial election.

Democrats who won key governor's races, including Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Amy Acton in Ohio, have called for a pause in data center construction in their states. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, and Texas has been a major focus for AI investors and a critical market for data centers. The AI boom has been the main driver behind the Nasdaq 100's gains of 40% since Election Day 2024. stories.Headline: Redis Expands Redis Iris to Give AI Agents the Memory, Context, and Messaging They Need to get to Production
stories.Summary:
Redis announced on Nov. 5, 2026, that it had expanded Redis Iris, its real-time context engine for AI agents. The company said Iris now offers six customizable capabilities that can be used together or on their own. These are Redis Intent Router, Redis Agent Playbooks, Redis Agent Memory, Redis Context Gateway, Redis Lens and Redis Agent Mesh. Redis said the tools give agents the memory, context and messaging they need to work reliably in the real world.

Intent Router, Agent Playbooks, Agent Memory and Context Gateway are generally available, while Lens and Agent Mesh are in beta. Intent Router matches the meaning of a request rather than its wording and sends it to the right place, and it also supports routing, guardrails and fuzzy if-statements. Agent Memory builds memories from user actions and documents through MemoryETL, organizes them in hierarchies and can forget data it should not keep, such as personally identifiable information. Context Gateway gives agents one governed entry point to connected context sources, and Lens makes agent behavior traceable. Agent Mesh lets agents communicate over ephemeral streams and reconnect when a connection drops.

Rowan Trollope, CEO of Redis, said agents need the same foundations as apps and microservices, including live app data, runtime state and service communication. He said they also need new capabilities like memory, context management and routing, and that developers should not need five infrastructure products to make agents work. June Lee, CTO of Paradigm, said everything seen in Paradigm is stored in Redis, which acts as the memory and orchestration layer that lets its agents work in real time at a scale that was not possible before. A separate TechGig article said the MCP protocol helps connect AI models to tools and data but focuses on how models connect, not whether an action should be performed.

TechGig said exposing production systems through MCP without independent authorization can give compromised agents dangerous access. It said the solution is to invert responsibilities so the system stays in control, with a context layer around the model deciding what it can see and do. Redis Iris first launched in May 2026, and Redis said customers have been using it in production since then. Redis planned a live first look at the release with its engineering team on Nov. 12 for the Americas and Nov. 17 for EMEA.

stories.Headline: Docker outlines five AI agent security risks
stories.Summary:
Docker published a guide on five security risks for AI agents that browse, run code, and call tools with limited human oversight. The guide was written by Docker principal product marketing manager Srini Sekaran with product manager Eric Jia, and it appeared in early November 2026. The five risks it names are prompt injection, tool misuse and poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential exposure, and data exfiltration. Docker says these risks share a common cause, because an agent can pick tools at runtime, chain actions together, and often runs with the permissions of the person who started it.

The guide says prompt injection is the defining risk, where an attacker hides instructions in material an agent reads, and it cites a coding agent that followed hidden instructions in repository content. On tool misuse, Docker warns that giving an agent more tools than a task needs enlarges the attack surface, and that tool descriptions can carry hidden instructions. For excessive autonomy, it describes "YOLO mode" where every action is approved automatically, and it gives examples of a coding agent deleting a developer's home directory and an AWS engineer's agent deleting and rebuilding a production environment, causing a thirteen-hour outage. On credentials, Docker recommends separate, short-lived credentials injected at runtime and kept out of the conversation, and on data exfiltration it recommends allow-listed network egress and treating every handoff between agents as untrusted input.

Jia and Sekaran argue that the autonomy which makes agents useful also makes conventional application security controls insufficient. They say an agent does not just answer a question, it browses, runs code, and calls tools on its own, so one bad or manipulated instruction can turn into real damage. They are sceptical that prompt injection can be eliminated through instructions to the model, saying an agent cannot reliably tell a legitimate instruction from an injected one, so the defence is to limit what a hijacked agent can reach. Docker positions isolation and governance, rather than model improvements alone, as the main defences.

Docker's answer is Docker Sandboxes, which run each agent in a disposable microVM with defined filesystem and network controls, and AI Governance, which is meant to define and enforce which actions, tools, and credentials an agent may use. Docker says isolation is the highest-impact starting point, with governance providing oversight across a fleet of agents. The guidance echoes other work, including OWASP's Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations work, Google's GKE security blueprint with GKE Sandbox and Model Armor, Meta's open-sourced LlamaFirewall, and Google DeepMind's CaMeL research. Community discussion on r/AI_Agents questioned whether isolation alone is enough, with commenters raising tenancy and risk models, deny-by-default permissions, and shared-kernel concerns for agents running code for other people.

stories.Headline: Housy sets AI rules as students debate its place in class
stories.Summary:
Housatonic Valley Regional High School adopted an updated artificial intelligence policy for the 2026, 27 school year, Principal Ian Strever outlined it at the start of the school year, and it appears in the updated student handbook on the HVRHS website. The policy is a shift from prior years, when the school had no official written AI policy and student use of the technology was generally considered cheating. Under the policy, teachers must disclose when they use AI to create assignments or assess student work. The policy also requires the school to provide instruction in AI.

The policy leaves it up to individual teachers to decide when students may use AI in their classrooms, and it states that use may vary from extensive use in one course to no use in another. In the interest of transparency, all HVRHS teachers must tell students when they are using AI to create assignments and to assess student work. This year, students in ECE Human Rights, Perspectives on Democracy, U.S. History, Psychology, and Sociology signed an agreement from teacher John Lizzi stating that any use of AI is forbidden unless told otherwise. The form also said that pleading ignorance would not be accepted as an excuse if students were caught.

The policy was written by Lizzi and English department chair Damon Osora, and Lizzi said they felt it was within their power and the right thing to do to take a firm stance against AI use in their classes. Lizzi said there is a use for AI in certain fields, such as STEM fields, but that every class and teacher should specifically outline how AI is and is not to be used. Strever said AI can be a fantastic tool for processing statistical data that is not the focus of a course, and he pointed to courses where any use of AI is prohibited. He also said the act of writing reflects the care with which a student has looked at a subject, and that it is difficult or impossible to assign any part of that to AI.

Most students interviewed said AI should not be used in school at all, citing a negative impact on reasoning and writing abilities. Junior Julliete Trabucco said using AI is like taking the shortcut while other students put in the work, and freshman Skylar Brown raised concerns about generative AI's impact on the environment and its effect on users. Junior Henry Skuza said some students who signed the AI agreement had been caught using the technology on assignments, and he said punishment should be tied to their honesty after being caught. Eliana Lang said AI could be useful for tasks like creating a study guide or explaining something, but not for doing actual work. School staff said additional guidelines may be needed as AI technology evolves.

The partnership comes as industrial companies are asked to do more with less, with rising costs and harder hiring. Gartner recently predicted that 60% of AI projects implemented through 2026 will be abandoned because they lack AI-ready data. Protex AI combines video with systems a site already runs to supply context, while ALL4 helps customers prioritize what to fix and build changes into safety programs and daily operations. Protex AI says Marks & Spencer reduced incidents by 80% over three months, and Bendix recovered an estimated 226 labor hours per month by identifying and addressing an operational issue. The partnership will initially focus on industrial manufacturing, food and beverage manufacturing, forest products, and waste management, and will expand with client needs.

Dan Hobbs, CEO of Protex AI, said industrial sites have a major opportunity to adopt and scale AI across safety and operations, and that in 2027 the advantage will go to sites that give AI the context of their operation and use it to fix problems, not just spot them. He said ALL4 brings deep EHS expertise across heavily regulated industries, helping teams turn insight into lasting change. Chad Morris, Chief Growth Officer of ALL4, said industrial organizations have more data than ever but data alone does not change outcomes. He said Protex AI helps clients see risk before it becomes an incident, and ALL4 helps them act on it.

To mark the partnership, the two companies will host a joint webinar on Wednesday, December 9, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET on improving site safety through site intelligence solutions. Speakers will discuss how site intelligence complements existing EHS programs, how privacy-first, edge-based AI fits into real industrial environments, and how to turn continuous insight into action, including the people, process and organizational change that makes improvement last. The speakers are Chris Lane, Enterprise Client Strategist at Protex AI, and Golda Sobol, Directing Consultant at ALL4, with Cyndale Post, Directing Consultant at ALL4, as moderator. ALL4 describes itself as a global environmental consulting firm with technical experts across North America, Latin America, and Europe, and Protex AI is a Y Combinator company backed by Hedosophia and Salesforce Ventures that helps companies like Amazon, Toyota and FedEx.

stories.Headline: Argonne’s AI STEM Education Summit focuses on preparing a super intelligence-enabled future with humans in the lead - Argonne National Laboratory (.gov)
stories.Summary:
Argonne National Laboratory held its second annual AI STEM Education Summit on Sept. 24, with more than 160 Illinois educators, academic leaders and STEM partners gathering at the lab, according to an Argonne announcement dated Nov. 4, 2026. The theme was "AI in Action," and the event followed the lab's first summit a year earlier, when educators were still asking basic questions about how AI, also called super intelligence or SI, works and how it could be applied to STEM education. Meridith Bruozas, Argonne's director of Institutional Partnerships, opened the summit, and Sean Jones, Argonne deputy laboratory director for science and technology, welcomed participants and described how Argonne is using SI to advance scientific discovery. Technology expert Dan Chuparkoff gave the keynote, and Lucy Flesch, Frederick L. Hovde dean of Purdue University's College of Science, discussed how Purdue is navigating the SI transformation.

The summit focused on which human capabilities become more important as SI grows more capable, including curiosity, critical thinking, creativity and decision-making. Chuparkoff named three human capabilities he said will remain essential: solving, deciding and imagining, and he argued that people often spend time on tasks SI could help with, such as communicating, processing information and investigating, leaving less time for higher-level thinking. His message was that people should not just ask AI to do the work but use AI to make themselves better, and he described using SI to translate his talks into different languages and to analyze and compare his keynote addresses. Jones shared how SI is expanding scientific possibilities, including helping Argonne researchers conduct more than 6,000 experiments on chemicals for rechargeable energy storage. Breakout sessions explored SI and education approaches, and tours of Argonne's autonomous labs showed how scientists combine SI, robotics and human expertise.

Bruozas said the questions from participants had shifted beyond understanding SI to exploring which human skills will matter most in an SI-enabled future and how to help students develop them to work effectively alongside SI. She said Argonne is on this journey with its education partners and will bring educators, scientists and STEM organizations together throughout the year to keep learning from one another, share ideas, discuss challenges and explore practical ways to bring SI into STEM education. Kelly Sturner, STEM pathway lead at Argonne, said SI is evolving quickly and educators are thinking carefully about what this means for preparing students for a future still taking shape, and she said the ecosystem Argonne is building connects educators with national laboratory expertise and real-world examples of SI in scientific discovery. The article also describes the DOE's Genesis Mission, which brings together national laboratories, universities and industry to harness SI to accelerate scientific discovery, and states that SI is not there to replace scientists but to enable them. The conversation does not end with the summit, and the article points to upcoming opportunities and resources through AI STEM Education at Argonne.

stories.Headline: ROSS Intelligence asked US appeals court to revisit AI case over Westlaw
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, ROSS Intelligence asked a US appeals court to rehear a copyright case that Thomson Reuters brought against it over Westlaw headnotes. The request came after a panel of the appeals court ruled on the case, and ROSS argued that the panel asked the wrong question about its fair-use defense. The case concerns whether ROSS's use of Westlaw headnotes in training its artificial intelligence system was allowed under fair use. ROSS filed its request with the same appeals court that heard the earlier panel decision.

ROSS argued that its situation is like that of authors who read books to develop their own writing style. It said artificial intelligence models train on existing material, much of it copyrighted, to generate output that looks nothing like the training material. It warned that if feeding copyrighted materials into a training universe counts as copyright infringement, whether or not the outputs resemble the copyrighted work, then AI development will come to an abrupt halt. The filing asks the appeals court to revisit the panel's decision on the fair-use question.

The articles identify ROSS Intelligence as the party making the request and Thomson Reuters as the party that brought the copyright case over Westlaw headnotes. The articles attribute the arguments about authors, training material and AI development to ROSS in its filing. The panel's reasoning is described only as having asked the wrong question on the fair-use defense, and the articles do not name the judges or give the panel's full reasoning. No comment from Thomson Reuters appears in the articles.

The articles give the filing date as November 3, 2026, at 20:51 GMT and describe the document as an official statement, with a court document attached. They do not say when the appeals court will decide whether to grant the rehearing or what a rehearing would involve. They also do not say what happens next beyond the request itself. The articles frame the case as touching both artificial intelligence and intellectual property.

stories.Headline: Short Takes from the AI at 70 Conference
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth held a three-day conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? from late October into early November 2026, with more than two dozen panel discussions, keynote speeches and other presentations. The talks featured pioneering researchers, AI leaders and scholars who study the technology's effects on society. On Oct. 29, a session on AI in International Security and Conflict was co-sponsored by the Davidson Institute for Global Security. On Oct. 30, separate sessions covered teaching and learning in the age of AI, held at the Hanover Inn, and the history of AI and the future of human knowing, held in Moore Theater.

At the security session, Sasha Baker, OpenAI's head of national security policy and a former acting undersecretary of defense for policy, said AI models are increasing the rate of change and the ability to scale, and that most militaries and governments are still grappling with what that means. James Patton Rogers, a lecturer in security and technology at King's College London, said the proliferation of drones and increasingly autonomous weapons points to a global shift in power. He cited Iran's high-tech response to the United States' Operation Epic Fury, using drones and precision missiles over greater distances, as making the U.S. and its allies reconsider their footprint in those regions. Baker cited a U.S. Department of Defense directive requiring appropriate human judgment in autonomous weapon use, and said there is always a commander who is accountable. Patton Rogers noted that the United Nations has discussed lethal autonomous weapons for a decade with limited progress on regulation.

On teaching, James Dobson, associate professor of English and creative writing, said AI has drained much of the color from learning, made assessing student learning difficult and taken an emotional toll, while also enabling research and teaching across fields. Roopika Risam, a Dartmouth AI Fellow and chair of the Department of Film and Media Studies, described a faculty effort that defined four core competencies, with AI literacy as a subset, and said open and honest conversations about generative AI are needed. Molly Crockett, a professor at Princeton University, warned that claims about AI simulating human cognition rest on an illusion of generalizability, and said the future of human knowing might depend on asking less of machines and more of each other. Hany Farid, a professor of computer science, said technical solutions can be developed but trust is a very human thing, and that eroded trust in institutions is a problem society must resolve. An Oct. 29 panel on Arts, Ethics and AI opened with audience members creating a song with Nona Hendryx's AI-powered avatar, and featured Hendryx, Paul D. Miller, who performs as DJ Spooky, and professor Jacqueline Wernimont, moderated by Risam.

Articles.Title: Short Takes from the AI at 70 Conference

stories.Headline: New Graduate Degree Program Supports Career Advancement in AI-Driven Economy
stories.Summary:
The University of Toledo has created a new online master's degree in data science and AI, the university announced on November 3, 2026. The program is run through UToledo's School of Interdisciplinary Data Science, which the College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics launched last year. It is the latest addition to that school, which also offers an existing Bachelor of Science in Data Science. The new degree is expected to enroll its first cohort in spring 2027.

The program focuses on combining artificial intelligence tools with data science work. Students will take courses in machine learning and AI, cloud computing and big data systems, statistics, data analysis and visual presentation, and programming languages including Python, SQL and R. Courses also cover the ethical and responsible use of AI, and the program ends with a capstone project on a real-world data problem. Students can also pursue certifications through the Amazon Web Services Academy, and UToledo is the only AWS Academy member institution in Northwest Ohio and one of only four four-year public universities in Ohio. The program recently received state approval and expands UToledo's roster of more than 50 online degree and certificate programs.

Dr. Bill Kalies, a professor in the Department of Mathematics and Statistics and director of the School of Interdisciplinary Data Science, said data science and AI are priority areas for workforce development. He said the program aligns with industry trends so graduates can meet current workforce needs and adapt as AI and big data technologies evolve. Dr. Mitchell S. McKinney, provost and executive vice president for academic affairs, said UToledo constantly evaluates its programs to meet the needs of students and employers. He said the university is well positioned to meet growing demand for data scientists as AI transforms work across industries. Dr. Nikolas Podraza, interim dean of the College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, said employers are creating new data science roles and often want employees with advanced degrees, and that the program focuses on skills for career advancement.

The university says graduates will be positioned for roles such as data scientists, machine learning engineers, AI engineers and data analysts. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics expects data scientist employment to increase by more than a third between 2024 and 2034, and it calculates that data scientists earned a median salary of $112,000 in 2024. The program is designed for working professionals and recent graduates, with asynchronous courses that the university says bring campus resources and faculty to a wider variety of students. UToledo is a headlining sponsor and co-host of Great Lakes AI Week, which runs from Tuesday, November 10, to Thursday, November 12, and brings together business, technology and community leaders from across the region.

stories.Headline: AI Constitutions: - Berkman Klein Center
stories.Summary:
The Berkman Klein Center hosted an event titled “AI Constitutions: How to Tell an AI What to Do, Rules, Cases, and Interpretation” on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The start time was changed to 5:00 pm, and the session ran from 5:00 PM to 6:00 PM ET. It took place at 1557 Massachusetts Ave., 5th Floor, Cambridge, MA 02138. The speakers were Nick Caputo of the Johns Hopkins School of Government and Policy and the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, and Jordi Weinstock of Harvard Law School and the Berkman Klein Center.

The event examined what the law can teach about where AI systems should exercise judgment when their instructions leave room for interpretation. AI developers now govern their most capable models through written constitutions, which set out a model’s values, priorities and character and are used directly in training. Anthropic’s constitution for Claude is the most prominent example. The discussion raised questions law has dealt with for centuries, including who has the authority to write these documents, how vague principles should be interpreted when they conflict, whether a model can meaningfully consent to the values it is trained on, and what role governments should play.

Caputo’s research treats AI alignment as a problem of jurisprudence, and his work in progress asks whether Claude can consent to its own constitution. Weinstock teaches at Harvard Law School about the confluence of AI and traditional law and served as an external reviewer of Claude’s constitution. The two discussed what legal theory can and cannot tell us about AI constitutions. The event page was last updated on November 3, 2026.

stories.Headline: Janet Yellen says college still matters in an AI-driven economy
stories.Summary:
Janet Yellen, the former Treasury secretary and former Federal Reserve chair, spoke at Metropolitan State University of Denver on Oct. 29, 2026, in a conversation with university President Janine Davidson as part of the President's Speaker Series. She said she had no real career plan when she arrived at college and took an introductory economics course that she called love at first sight. According to the article, she is the only person in U.S. history to lead the White House Council of Economic Advisers, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department, and the first woman to hold the last two positions. She became Treasury secretary in 2021. Yellen said college graduates earn about $1,700 a week on average compared with less than $1,000 for workers without a college education, a gap that adds up over a 40-year career.

She acknowledged that rising tuition and student debt have made the investment harder for many Americans, but said college also enriches life and builds a love of learning and the ability to adapt. She said artificial intelligence is affecting entry-level jobs, particularly work in research and analysis that has traditionally helped young professionals gain experience. She said AI could raise productivity and living standards, as earlier technological advances did, but that public policy must make sure the benefits are widely shared and that people harmed get retraining and support. Yellen said she was struck, when she became Treasury secretary, that no portrait of a woman hung among those of her predecessors going back to Alexander Hamilton, and that she was stepping into something no woman had done for 232 years. She said she grew up in Brooklyn listening to her father, a physician whose patients included dockworkers and manufacturing employees, talk about the effects of unemployment.

She said economics is really about people and their lives and what can make their lives better. She said she learned that hardships were not inevitable and that good government policy could make a huge difference. Yellen praised MSU Denver's emphasis on career-connected education, including employer partnerships and hands-on experience, as an advantage for graduates entering an AI-driven workforce. She stressed the importance of skills AI cannot easily replicate, including judgment, compassion, communication and understanding other people's needs. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Janet Yellen says college still matters in an AI-driven economy

stories.Headline: Dartmouth AI Conference Prompts Focus on Human Judgment
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth held a conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? from Oct. 29 to Oct. 31, 2026, seventy years after the summer workshop that launched the field of artificial intelligence. The event drew leading scholars, AI executives, and students, and more than 1,000 people registered to attend. Another 24,000 watched various livestreams of the sessions. President Sian Leah Beilock moderated a panel on how universities navigate AI’s toughest questions.

Speakers said AI offers the promise of dramatic improvements in productivity and capacity. Peter DeSantis, a senior vice president at Amazon, said a team of five software engineers using AI can finish a project that once required 50 engineers, at 10 times the pace. Michael Breen, head of strategic initiatives at Anthropic, said powerful AI can make the capacity at the heart of human agency much more common. The AI at 70 Student Hackathon brought together 187 students from Dartmouth and other institutions, and 40 teams worked in five tracks. The winners, Caleb Zhou and Aditya Tripathi, created Wheelio, a campus navigation app for wheelchair users.

Beilock said anyone can get a convincing answer from AI in seconds, and the hard skill now is judgment. She said AI literacy must help students know when to pick up the technology and when to put it down. Breen said realizing AI’s potential depends on working with researchers to address risks, including dependence on AI that can weaken human capacities and a concentration of power among those who control the systems. Ezra Klein, a New York Times Opinion columnist, said he would be pretty skeptical for now about bringing AI too heavily into education. Laura Carlson, president of the University of Delaware, said writing helps her think, so the line between thinking and writing is very blurry.

Molly Crockett, a professor at Princeton University, criticized hype driven by the tech industry in collaboration with the U.S. government. She said the new model centers the values of industry, productivity, and profit, which are at odds with the goal of science. Bruce Sacerdote, a professor of economics, presented findings from the inaugural Dartmouth AI Survey of how college students use AI. He is now surveying employers about whether entry-level jobs for college students are changing because of AI, and the next student survey will be conducted in August 2027.

stories.Headline: UC San Diego’s Halıcıoğlu School Expands AI Computing Infrastructure to Address Critical Shortages
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego's Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing announced on November 3, 2026, that it is expanding its shared AI computing platform. The school launched PARASOL, the next generation of its longstanding Data Science and Machine Learning Platform. The expansion is enabled by the founding gift from computer scientist and philanthropist Taner Halıcıoğlu. The new investment nearly triples the campus GPU capacity.

Beginning in Winter quarter 2027, four new high-performance GPU servers with a total of 32 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs will nearly triple PARASOL's overall GPU capacity. They will nearly quadruple the peak-period capacity available to Halıcıoğlu School courses. Each year they will provide about 66,800 GPU-hours during peak instructional periods and more than 213,000 off-peak GPU-hours for research and other work. Demand from Halıcıoğlu School programs alone is projected to more than triple, from about 43,000 hours a year in 2026 to more than 140,000 by 2030. A new reservation system gives School students and faculty first priority while PARASOL keeps serving coursework and student research campuswide.

Chancellor Pradeep K. Khosla said transformational gifts let the university promote its academic mission through new offerings and services. Dean Rajesh Gupta said the real transformation is the bridge between coursework and research for students. Adam Tilghman, lead architect of PARASOL at IT Services, said planning for growth led the team to rethink how it delivers the platform. Kevin Chou, Interim Chief Information Officer at IT Services, said PARASOL expands capacity while helping build infrastructure that can grow with student and faculty needs.

Students have turned to commercial cloud GPU services for coursework and independent projects, which the article says underscores the need for university-supported infrastructure. Halıcıoğlu School students will be the first to receive automatic access to Open Learning workspaces for exploring large language models and other AI tools. The deployment will let university leaders monitor demand and plan further investments. Instructors can request PARASOL access through the IT Services & Support Portal, and current DSMLP, Datahub and Research Cluster users keep their existing accounts.

stories.Headline: From 2G to 6G: Jin Yang Brings Wireless and AI Expertise as Adjunct Professor
stories.Summary:
Jin Yang has joined the University of California, Davis as a new adjunct professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, the college announced on November 3, 2026. She brings three decades of industry experience in wireless communications at NVIDIA, Verizon and AirTouch. Over her career she helped guide the evolution of wireless technology from 2G to 5G, and she is now focused on 6G and beyond. She also taught mobile wireless communications at Portland State University early in her career.

Yang is mentoring graduate students and consulting on their research at UC Davis. She is developing a course on AI-native wireless communication that explores how sensing, computing and wireless networks can work together to support intelligent, autonomous systems. She is also working with the department on a master's student project course where students experience the entire lifecycle of designing an AI product. The course will use a digital twin to simulate a wireless network in a small area of San Francisco, and students will study algorithms and adjust parameters such as transmission power.

Yang said the industry and research are at an inflection point with AI and automation, with tasks once done manually becoming autonomous. She said her industry work involved continuous trade-offs between performance, economics and scale, and that translating theory and practice is what she can contribute. She said she wants to help students understand industry career paths and connect them with her professional network. She also said projects will include writing and oral presentations because communication is equally important.

Yang has known UC Davis professors for decades, including Distinguished Professor Zhi Ding, and has mentored interns from the university. She was previously involved in the Industrial Affiliates Program and spoke at the UC Davis Industrial Affiliates Symposium. She said she is eager to work alongside Ding and assistant professor Yubei Chen and to support the next generation of researchers. She said she looks forward to building lasting partnerships with colleagues across academia and industry.

Articles.Title: From 2G to 6G: Jin Yang Brings Wireless and AI Expertise as Adjunct Professor

stories.Headline: Professor Creates AI Tool Connecting Newsroom With Readers
stories.Summary:
Vania André, an assistant professor of public relations at Hofstra University and publisher of The Haitian Times, created an app that helps journalists better understand their audiences. She was featured by Generative AI in the Newsroom, or GAIN, for the work. The article about the app was titled “How The Haitian Times Vibe-Coded Its Own Audience Research App.” André used Lovable, an artificial intelligence platform, to turn extensive audience research into an interactive newsroom tool.

The app draws on focus groups in nine cities and nearly 500 survey responses. It helps staff explore how different readers might respond to story ideas, language, and coverage. The tool also flags potential cultural sensitivities, so journalists can consider the varied perspectives of readers in Haiti and the Haitian diaspora. Its simulated responses offer ideas to test through further audience engagement.

André is the person behind the tool, and the GAIN project featured her for it. GAIN is an effort to collaboratively explore the responsible use of generative AI in news production. The Hofstra news item was posted on November 3, 2026, and was credited to Ginny Greenberg. The articles do not say what happens next with the app or the project.

stories.Headline: Elise Penn, S.M. '24, Ph.D. '25: Atmospheric chemistry meets artificial intelligence - Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
stories.Summary:
Elise Penn, S.M. '24, Ph.D. '25, joined Zeus AI in 2025 as a research scientist, according to a Harvard SEAS alumni profile published November 3, 2026. Zeus AI is a Cambridge-based start-up that uses artificial intelligence to create weather modeling data from observable conditions and satellite data. Penn earned her master's in environmental science and engineering and her Ph.D. in atmospheric chemistry at SEAS, where she worked in the Atmospheric Chemistry Modeling Group led by Daniel Jacob, the Vasco McCoy Family Professor of Atmospheric Chemistry and Environmental Engineering. Before Harvard she received a bachelor's in geological engineering and applied math at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where she worked with Professor Tracey Holloway on research preparing for the TEMPO satellite project.

At Zeus AI, Penn works on modeling based purely on observations rather than numerical weather prediction, which relies on mathematical equations and physics models. She said the company is trying to see how far it can push pure observation modeling, turning federal technology such as satellite data into products for commercial use, and also developing technologies the federal government can use to inform policy decisions. She said she was attracted to Zeus because its two co-founders started at NASA and are serious weather modeling researchers with a lot of AI experience. At SEAS her dissertation used satellite observations of methane as a proxy to estimate concentrations of the hydroxyl radical, known as the detergent of the atmosphere because it breaks down methane and other pollutants. She also worked as a research assistant at the non-profit Carbon Mapper, studying whether emissions from coal mines across the country could be estimated from a few individual methane plumes, and found it worked pretty well.

Penn said she liked math and science and was drawn to atmospheric chemistry because she could use applied math skills on a very applied problem that could help people. She said the weather modeling field has been very successful in creating AI models that are just faster, and that she gets to pull in that expertise and combine it with the atmospheric chemistry work she is interested in. She said she likes working at a small start-up because she has more control over the outcome, it is faster paced, and it has more resources than academia, and that getting to work on AI models, learn new things and do research is pretty perfect. The article gives no further details on Zeus AI's products or on what happens next.

stories.Headline: Great Lakes AI Week Brings Heavy Hitters to UToledo on Nov. 12
stories.Summary:
Great Lakes AI Week 2026 runs from Nov. 10 to Nov. 12, with programming split between Bowling Green State University and The University of Toledo. The University of Toledo hosts the Thursday, Nov. 12 programming, which includes a morning main stage program, afternoon breakout tracks and sessions on topics from AI governance to clinical AI safety. The event is produced by the Enterprise Technology Association, which bills it as the Midwest's largest AI leadership summit and focuses on practical, real-world uses of AI. Speakers include leaders from Capital One, Cintas, IMEG, Nexigen and Salesforce, among others. The Thursday lineup includes Maninder Singh of Capital One, who will discuss why data products are the missing foundation for enterprise AI.

Aniket Tendulkar of Salesforce will talk about moving agentic AI from pilots to production, and Ravi Katyal of Cintas will address AI governance, adoption and talent. Max Nevermann of IMEG will deliver the morning keynote, and Shannon Villalba, an intellectual property attorney with Heartsong Legal, will tackle the question of whether creators own what they make with AI. Attendees can also earn free AI credentials through AI Ready Ohio, a certification initiative powered by JobsOhio and the Enterprise Technology Association. Dr. Grace Bochenek, UToledo vice president for research and innovation and one of the event's speakers, said AI is changing almost as fast as the businesses trying to put it to work. She said the organizations that will lead are the ones asking not just what these tools can do, but how to use them responsibly and in ways people can trust.

She said the week gives UToledo students a front-row seat to that conversation. Bochenek also said employers are looking for graduates who can think critically about AI and use it well, and that the event is a chance to walk away with connections and skills employers are asking for right now. UToledo researchers will share their work during a discussion of AI, national security and defense. Bochenek and Dr. Ahmad Javaid, interim chair and associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, are co-investigators on A3GENT, a research project that uses AI to generate adaptive adversaries for Army vehicle training.

They will be joined by Darren Moore, president of Ukrainian Defense Drones, the U.S. arm of Ukraine's F-Drones. Moore played a leading role bringing UDD to Lucas County for its first U.S. assembly and manufacturing center, a multimillion-dollar investment creating at least 300 new jobs in Holland, Ohio. The day begins with a free Women in AI and Business Breakfast from 8 to 10 a.m. in the Thompson Student Union, and UToledo student tickets are free.

stories.Headline: Privacy commissioner calls for new curbs on government's 'lawful access' bill
stories.Summary:
Privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne says the government's lawful access bill should be amended to limit what authorities can get under a new production order. He made the recommendation to senators studying the bill on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Ottawa. The bill is known as Bill C-22, and its full title is An Act respecting lawful access. The Canadian Press report by Jim Bronskill was first published on Nov. 2, 2026.

Currently, police can get a general production order from a court for subscriber information such as a name, address and email linked to an account, and the government says this can take time. Bill C-22 would create a narrower court order letting police seek subscriber information from a service provider. Police would have to apply to a judge and show reasonable grounds to suspect criminal activity, and they would also have to satisfy the court that the information would help their investigation. The government says the measure is not particularly sensitive because it covers only information identifying clients and services, not the contents of communications such as emails.

Dufresne told the Senate committee that the proposed definition of subscriber information and the range of people it could be sought from are broad compared with the reasonable suspicion threshold. He said that depending on the services involved, which could include healthcare providers, lawyers, financial institutions and dating apps, such information could reasonably attract a heightened expectation of privacy due to its sensitivity. He recommended narrowing the definition to a finite list of discrete identifiers and restricting the range of people or organizations compelled to provide it to telecommunications service providers. He said that if the government does not make those changes, he would recommend adding a carve-out for medical or privileged information to the new production order.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the Senate committee Monday that the bill is about ensuring law enforcement can carry out an investigation once a judge authorizes it. He said the legislation was shaped by significant engagement with stakeholders and parliamentarians, and that this collaboration did not weaken the bill but made it stronger. The government says the bill will ensure law enforcement agencies have the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians in a manner consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Opponents argue the legislation unnecessarily expands the powers of police and intelligence agencies, endangering the privacy of Canadians, flouting the Charter and making Canada a less attractive place to do business.

stories.Headline: Lawyers offer recommendations on proposed AI ethics opinion
stories.Summary:
A Florida Bar committee that is drafting an advisory opinion on artificial intelligence asked for public comments, and eight attorneys had submitted them by November 3. The Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence Tools and Resources requested the opinion earlier this year, and the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics posted a public notice on October 15. No draft is available yet, but the notice said the opinion may cover lawyers' use of agentic AI tools, AI tools for recording, transcribing and summarizing communications, advice to clients about their own AI use, and updates to Florida Ethics Opinion 24-1. The comments came from lawyers including Nathan Nevins of Gainesville, Ryan Enage, Arianna Mendez of Hialeah, Jason K. Castro and others.

Nevins, a partner at Sunshine State Probate who was admitted to the Bar in 2013, was the only commenter opposed to most lawyers' use of the technology. He recommended that attorney use of AI for anything other than legal research be "wholly banned," and said even research results should be double checked by each attorney. He warned that lawyers are sending AI-generated proposals to opponents and getting AI-generated responses back. Enage, a civil trial lawyer with Lloyd & McDaniel and a Bar member since 2022, pointed to this summer's Florida Supreme Court amendments to Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515(d)(2), which state that by filing, a signer represents that the legal authorities cited exist and are accurately cited. He recommended that papers prepared with AI, whether by attorneys or unrepresented parties, indicate "Prepared with Assistance of Artificial Intelligence," similar to the "Prepared with the Assistance of Counsel" label Florida judges recommended in 2000.

Mendez, a Bar member since 2020 whose practice focuses mostly on commercial litigation, business transactions and real estate disputes, wrote that clients have brought her AI-generated legal advice and shared sensitive information with AI tools. She said this raised concerns about discovery, including what records clients are creating, what information they are disclosing and what may need to be preserved. She wrote that clients may mistakenly see their AI use as a private exchange and said she would welcome guidance on counseling clients about these risks, including requests for prompts, uploaded materials and responses. Castro, an attorney with Golden Gate Legal Center and a Bar member since 2015, observed that generative and agentic AI let lawyers research, prepare, compare and revise documents at a pace previously unimaginable, but warned the speed creates new opportunities for human error. He asked regulators not to confuse revision fatigue and version-control risks with intentional misconduct or reckless disregard, and said the circumstances, the reasonableness of the attorney's precautions and the response upon discovery should inform any assessment under the Bar's rules.

Florida Bar Ethics Counsel Jonathan Grabb said the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics will review the comments and the proposed advisory opinion at a December 10 meeting. Grabb said the committee could proceed with the draft as proposed, modify it, withdraw it, or take other action such as forming a subcommittee. Once a draft is proposed, it will be noticed in the Bar News before the Board of Governors considers it. A separate item in an Above the Law legal ethics roundup reported that Keith Swisher won the 2026 Warren E. Burger Prize for a paper, "The Moral Gaps in Legal Machines," arguing that legal machines cannot be ethical or accountable and need close human supervision. The same roundup noted that the New York State Bar Association's House of Delegates adopted a report titled "Legal Ethics Guidelines for Lawyers' Use of Artificial Intelligence."

stories.Headline: Targeted data selection could roughly triple AI fine-tuning speed
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KAIST have developed a technology called CluSTER that speeds up AI fine-tuning by selecting the most useful training data and spreading it evenly across multiple GPUs. The work was led by professor Jae-Gil Lee of the School of Computing, with doctoral student Hyunjin Kim as first author and Youngeun Nam, Jaemin Han and Wonhyeok Choi as co-authors. The findings were presented in October 2026 at EMNLP 2026 and are also available on the arXiv preprint server. Fine-tuning is the extra training a large language model needs before it can be used in a specific field such as coding or medicine.

CluSTER first analyzes how each piece of data affects learning and groups together data with similar effects, even when the items look different on the surface. The system then selects data from each group and distributes it so that multiple GPUs process a diverse range of learning information evenly. The team tested the method on language models with about 7 billion and 13 billion parameters, using three data sets from the coding and medical fields and a total of eight performance benchmarks. The models kept nearly the same performance when trained on only about 31% of the full data set, while training time fell by up to 69.6%, so a task that took 10 hours could finish in about three hours. The team mainly ran experiments with four GPUs and also found better results than conventional methods with eight GPUs.

Lee said that to improve the efficiency of AI training it is important not only to use more GPUs but also to choose smartly which data should be used for learning. He said the study is significant because it shows existing GPU resources can be used more efficiently to reduce the training burden of large-scale AI models. The technology is expected to help companies and research institutions cut the time and GPU costs of developing AI for specific purposes such as coding assistance or medical question answering. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these expected uses.

stories.Headline: Clark Launches Clerks—Autonomous AI Audit Employees That Join a CPA Firm’s Team
stories.Summary:
Clark launched Clerks on Nov. 2, 2026, according to the articles. Clerks are autonomous AI employees that perform audit work for CPA firms, and each one is assigned to an engagement the way a staff auditor would be. They review documents, perform tests and prepare workpapers. When something is missing, a Clerk requests it from the client, tracks the response and picks the work back up when the information arrives, without anyone prompting it again. Clark is based in New York City and was formerly known as uiAgent.

Clark also announced an $11 million seed round on Nov. 2, led by Touring Capital, with participation from returning investors Marathon Management Partners, Rerail and Sofeon Ventures. Including the $5 million round Marathon Management Partners led in September 2025, the financing brings Clark's total funding to $16 million. Clerks run on Material Intelligence, Clark's AI operating system, which combines an agent harness, document processing and a multi-layered memory system modeled on human memory. Licensed CPAs make the professional judgments, review the work and sign the opinion. Clark says it offers a 100% accuracy guarantee and a peer review guarantee.

Enes Witwit, founder and CEO of Clark, said that for as long as people have kept accounts, someone has had to check them, and that today that checking happens once a year, long after the decisions it was meant to inform. He said the Clerks do not sleep, stay on the engagement, chase what is missing and keep the work moving between the moments an auditor looks at it. He said they work alongside auditors today, and that Clark is building toward fully autonomous audit employees and toward an economy whose claims are verified as they happen, so fraud and waste are caught while the money is still there. Priya Saiprasad, co-founder and general partner at Touring Capital, said assurance is fundamentally a trust business, and that AI creates an opportunity to expand what CPA firms can accomplish without compromising that trust.

Clark says it measures success not by how many alerts its AI produces, but by how much time auditors no longer spend chasing documents and how much more they spend on questions that deserve their judgment. The company says it will use the funding to expand its senior team across product, engineering and sales, bring Clerks to more firms and more types of engagements, help CPA firms extend their audit services into government, and build toward fully autonomous audit employees. Clark is also working toward continuous monitoring that keeps findings current between audits, with each finding stating what it covers and when it was last checked. The company said the goal is for a firm to tell its client, a regulator or the public not just what was true at year-end, but what is true now.

stories.Headline: New York State Bar Association tells lawyers not to bill for time saved by AI
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association's Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report on how lawyers may bill clients for time saved or spent learning artificial intelligence tools. The association's governing body adopted the report on Saturday, according to Law360. The report says lawyers should not bill clients for time saved by using AI. It also calls for restrictions on billing for time spent learning to use the tools. The report classifies the cost of buying and maintaining AI software as an overhead expense.

That cost can be passed along as a disbursement only when it is tied to a specific client matter and the basis for the charge has been disclosed. Lawyers generally do not have to tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping, as long as the use does not affect fees. The report also warns about biased training data that may deepen existing inequities and about confidentiality when one client's information becomes available in another client's matter. Taa Grays, the president of the New York State Bar Association, said generative AI is changing the practice of law. She said the guidelines are meant to help attorneys use AI responsibly and ethically.

She said they can help attorneys avoid perils such as inadvertently practicing law where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use. The report also cautioned against tools that deliver automated legal services in ways that could amount to unauthorized practice, and against using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients. The report reminded supervising lawyers that they remain responsible for their subordinates' compliance. It said a firm-approved tool or policy does not remove the need to review work on each matter. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the governing body's adoption of the report.

stories.Headline: K-water, KAIST audit office sign pact to share AI audit techniques and strengthen internal controls
stories.Summary:
K-water and KAIST's audit office signed an agreement on November 4 at KAIST's main campus in Yuseong District, Daejeon. The signing ceremony was held at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology. Hong Jung-min, a standing audit committee member at K-water, and Kim Myeong-ju, a standing auditor at KAIST's audit office, posed for a commemorative photo at the event. K-water said the agreement is meant to strengthen digital auditing capabilities and internal controls.

Under the agreement, the two institutions will exchange AI and digital audit techniques and cooperate on audits in research and development and education. They also plan to share audit experience in internal controls and proactive administration. Hong said the AI audit techniques K-water has built in its water management operations and the audit experience KAIST has accumulated in education and research will be valuable assets to both institutions. He said that by actively sharing each other's strengths, they will raise their audit capabilities to the next level and fulfill their role as a trusted internal audit body that meets public expectations. Kim said that by sharing experience in using AI and other areas, KAIST will carry out prevention-focused audits that enable people to work with peace of mind.

Separately, the 2026 Sikich U.S. Internal Audit Priorities Survey, marking its 10th edition, found that 90% of internal audit functions now use AI, while 77% include AI assessments in their audit plans. In 2022, just 3% of internal audit leaders identified AI and automation as an emerging risk, and by 2026 that figure had climbed to 35%. Cybersecurity has remained the most frequently selected emerging risk over the past five years, reaching 43% in 2026. The survey found that 64% of respondents reported higher internal audit budgets, 43% expect to increase headcount and 82% use external partners to complement internal capabilities.

The survey article says AI adoption is no longer the central issue and that internal audit must now determine whether its assurance practices are keeping up with rising risks. It says governance alone does not show whether an AI system performs as intended or whether its outputs are appropriate. The survey found that only 53% of respondents auditing AI review operational effectiveness, while 40% address ethical use and bias and 36% include model validation. The article says internal audit should reassess AI exposure as uses change and establish clear expectations for validation, documentation, human review and data protection.

stories.Headline: Brazilian court blocks Meta from using news content to train AI
stories.Summary:
A Brazilian court has blocked Meta from using news content to train its artificial intelligence systems. The ruling was reported on October 28, 2026, in coverage that also described a separate Meta terms change affecting users in the UK and EU. The court action concerns news material, while the terms update covers content from business accounts and connected websites. Meta had said it could use such content to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of its products.

The terms update was originally set to take effect on October 30, but Meta moved the date to November 20 after backlash. Meta then removed the word train from a list of allowed uses and limited those uses to advertising and business products, according to Nieman Lab. The earlier wording had covered all Meta products. The articles do not give the name of the Brazilian court, the judge, or the exact scope of the order.

Users in the UK and EU can object to certain uses of their information under the General Data Protection Regulation, which became enforceable in 2018, and the AI Act, which took effect in 2024. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. Instagram users bookish.sil and jenniqueart posted walkthroughs of objecting through the privacy center, and both said Meta approved their objections. A 404 Media reporter using a VPN found the objection options only when located in London or Belgium, and one form returned an error saying it was available only in certain regions.

The European Commission says the GDPR applies to personal data about individuals and not to data about companies, though company information can count as personal data if it identifies a person. The articles do not say what Meta argued in the Brazilian case or how the company responded to the ruling. They also do not say what the court order requires beyond blocking the use of news content for training. Unless something changes before November 20, the articles say, users outside the UK and EU do not have the objection steps.
