stories.Headline: Acton Declares Ohio Win as Data Center Pause Advocates Advance
stories.Summary:
Amy Acton's campaign announced on November 4, 2026 that she had won Ohio's governor's race, after she spoke to supporters on November 3, 2026. She addressed more than 1,000 people at the Hilton Columbus Downtown and promised to govern for all Ohioans. She named lower costs, action against corruption, and a fair shot for residents as her priorities. Ohio's Secretary of State says election-night results stay unofficial until certification, with the official canvass finished about three weeks after the election.

In Georgia, complete but unofficial returns last updated at 4:19:07 a.m. on November 4, 2026 showed Keisha Lance Bottoms leading Rick Jackson with 54.31% of the vote. The figures gave Bottoms 2,268,462 votes and Jackson 1,908,261, with all 159 localities reporting and Jackson at 45.69%. Both candidates have proposed restricting new data center development through a moratorium or a construction pause. The results extend election-night gains for restriction advocates beyond Gina Hinojosa's declared victory in Texas.

Acton first announced her conditional-moratorium position on July 27, 2026, promising immediate action as governor if projects failed her requirements. Developers would have to bear the full cost of gas, water, and electricity rather than taxpayers or nearby communities, and invest in their own generation. Projects would also have to show they would not raise electricity prices or weaken regional reliability, and construction would use union labor exclusively. Her platform would end data center nondisclosure agreements, add clawbacks to tax incentives, and require siting on brownfields or previously developed industrial land rather than farms.

Bottoms' August 31, 2026 proposal called for a pause on new data center construction, citing environmental effects, utility costs, and risks to community water supplies. She would hold a comprehensive discussion with developers, technical and environmental experts, and community leaders before deciding Georgia's path forward. Hinojosa's Texas policy calls for an immediate moratorium until the legislature enacts protections and gives Texans a role in deciding whether and how data centers enter communities. Governor Greg Abbott had already ordered a permit halt on September 21, 2026 pending grid and water reviews, and Hinojosa said Abbott called to congratulate her and offer transition assistance.

stories.Headline: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, Hugging Face published an update by Tarek Ziadé about a bug in the Transformers library. The bug affected the T5 model and its scaled dot-product attention, known as SDPA. As a side effect, the decoder of UMT5 could attend to future tokens, so during training it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in the main code for almost two months.

The update describes model integration contracts, which are published once and then reused. On a pull request, the team picks contracts based on the files the patch changes. One detail mattered because the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. A test took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup, and log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22.

The team runs fast integration tests to catch bugs before they reach main. They check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite, and they reject failed builds. For a new model, a draft contract comes from a language model through Inference Providers. The team also trained a small model on a few tones paired with words such as red and green, because random audio made a poor test of the audio path.

The article says coverage is still partial across model families and the APIs people use. It asks how many real bugs the contracts catch on pull requests and how often they send the team chasing false alarms. It also asks whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. The team invites people to contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

stories.Headline: TSE Growth Market 250 Falls for Fourth Straight Session as AI Regulation Fears From U.S. Midterms Weigh
stories.Summary:
The TSE Growth Market 250 Index fell 0.57% to 769.27 on November 4, 2026, its fourth straight decline. During the session the index dropped more than 3% at one point. Reports that the Democratic Party was gaining an edge in the U.S. midterm elections chilled investor sentiment over fears of tighter AI regulation. Later reports that the Democratic Party had recaptured majorities in both the House and Senate brought a selling on the news view.

As the Nikkei Stock Average pared its losses, bargain-hunting buying emerged and supported the market. Among individual stocks, MTG and Humameid declined, while Oncolys and QD Laser rose. Data Section, Terra Drone and Cybertrust also traded weak, and Tier IV and Ftsuper rose. Newly listed Allganize Holdings got off to a firm start, and MabGenesis, in its second day of trading, briefly hit the daily limit-up.

Market participants said it is uncertainty over regulation, rather than the election results themselves, that is widening the market's swings. The articles say U.S. political developments tend to directly affect the valuation of high-tech stocks. Investor attention will now shift to the specifics of regulation and the direction of U.S. interest rates. Many expect a nervous trading environment to continue in the near term as investors watch for U.S. policy announcements.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion IPO Faces Investor Doubts as AI Spending Bill Soars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is preparing for a stock market debut that could become one of the largest technology IPOs in history, and the plan is facing investor scrutiny. The company behind the Claude AI platform is dealing with concerns about its enormous valuation, slowing revenue growth and almost US$900 billion in AI infrastructure commitments. According to reports, some investors are now considering a valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, which is approximately A$2.14 trillion, down from expectations close to US$2 trillion. The concerns follow the release of Anthropic’s latest financial figures, which showed revenue expanding rapidly but growth slowing while infrastructure costs rise.

According to Reuters, Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% quarter-on-quarter to US$16.96 billion, a substantial slowdown from the 144% sequential growth recorded in the second quarter. The company reported a net loss of US$23.29 billion for the quarter, narrower than its US$66.3 billion loss in the previous quarter, and an operating loss of US$567 million. Anthropic has approximately US$895.4 billion in commitments tied to AI infrastructure development, including computing capacity, data centres and cloud services, and almost half of that spending is expected before the end of 2030. The company also recorded an additional US$5 billion in computing costs during the quarter.

Anthropic is planning an international retail share offer that will include Australian investors, with CommSec, Bell Potter, LGT Wealth, Macquarie, Morgans, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, Sharesies and Stake among the institutions expected to participate. The company is not planning to list on the Australian Securities Exchange and has applied to list its Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the proposed ticker symbol ANT. The Australian retail offer is expected to be made under a prospectus lodged with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Anthropic has cautioned that the participating broker list is specific to the proposed offering and advised investors to wait for the official prospectus before making any decisions.

The proposed listing could become an important test of investor confidence in the AI sector more broadly, as technology companies have committed enormous sums to AI infrastructure and investors increasingly question whether AI revenue will justify the capital expenditure. Anthropic’s dependence on major cloud infrastructure providers, including Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet, adds complexity, since both are investors in Anthropic but also supply computing infrastructure and compete in the AI market. Rival AI developer OpenAI is also considering a major stock market listing. Anthropic’s debut could provide an early indication of how much investors are prepared to pay for the future of the technology.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion IPO Faces Investor Doubts as AI Spending Bill Soars

stories.Headline: Alphabet (GOOGL) Commits $15 Billion To Malaysia As AI Lawsuit Lands
stories.Summary:
Alphabet plans to invest US$15 billion to expand Google data centers and AI infrastructure in Malaysia, the company announced. The buildout includes new facilities to support AI services in Southeast Asia, along with sustainability and workforce programs. Shareholders have also filed a lawsuit alleging that Google trained AI models, including Lyria music tools, on copyrighted material without permission. The article frames both the Malaysia data center push and the AI copyright lawsuit as only part of what matters for Alphabet today.

The Malaysia plan covers new facilities for AI services in Southeast Asia, plus sustainability and workforce programs. The article says Alphabet has also issued multiple euro denominated bonds, including notes maturing from 2028 out to 2045. It says the US$15 billion buildout points to Alphabet using its balance sheet and access to debt markets to keep pushing AI capacity without relying only on near term cash generation. The article says the lawsuit alleges Google trained AI models, including Lyria music tools, on copyrighted material without permission.

The article does not name the shareholders who filed the lawsuit or give a court or filing date for it. It says the Narrative the market trades on hinges on Alphabet turning large AI infrastructure and custom TPU investment into durable demand for Gemini and Google Cloud while managing pressure on free cash flow. It says the US$15 billion regional data center push and the copyright lawsuit both reinforce the same tension, between big AI spend on one side and mounting legal and regulatory risks on the other. It points to a US$408 fair value figure tied to how these catalysts shape Alphabet's path.

The article says the clearest sign of whether the AI story is working will be whether Google Cloud and AI related revenue, including the AI weighted backlog already referenced by analysts, keep scaling fast enough to cover rising depreciation and interest costs from bonds and data centers. It says quarterly updates on Cloud margins and group free cash flow will be the key checkpoints, especially through 2027 when capex is flagged to rise. It describes Alphabet as running global search, video, cloud and advertising platforms across regions that include the US and Asia-Pacific. It says large AI data center projects and legal disputes over training data both sit close to how its core services are built and delivered.

Articles.Title: Alphabet (GOOGL) Commits $15 Billion To Malaysia As AI Lawsuit Lands

stories.Headline: Markets overreacting to AI regulation fears after US elections, says Roundhill Investments strategist
stories.Summary:
Global markets appear to be overreacting to fears of tighter artificial intelligence regulation after a strong Democratic showing in the US elections, according to Drew Pettit, Chief Investment Strategist at Roundhill Investments. Pettit said the Democratic performance exceeded polling expectations. He argued that corporate earnings and business fundamentals, not political outcomes, will keep driving stocks. He also said the chance of sweeping policy change remains low. Pettit said Democrats do not hold the two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress needed to advance major legislative changes.

He noted that Donald Trump has indicated he will veto new bills. Pettit said markets seem to be pricing in a Democratic president after Trump, which he described as getting ahead of developments. He said he has never made money trading politics and makes money by trading fundamentals and what businesses do. Opposition to data centre expansion is not purely partisan, and both Republicans and Democrats have raised concerns about the pace of development. Moratoriums on new data centres are already in place in Texas, where the governorship is Republican-controlled.

Pettit argued that a full reversal of the AI trade based on election results alone would require a complete sweep of Congress, the Senate and the White House, which he said the current political arithmetic does not support. He noted that voters remain focused on inflation, affordability and the war in Iran. Pettit referenced historical US market behaviour, noting that rallies have occurred in the months following each of the last 19 midterm elections since World War II. He stressed that as long as business resilience and earnings revisions remain strong, the passing of the midterms should support equity performance rather than undermine it. The article says India's AI-linked technology sector and global institutional investors track US regulatory signals closely when making capital allocation decisions.

Articles.Title: Markets overreacting to AI regulation fears after US elections, says Roundhill Investments strategist

stories.Headline: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
stories.Summary:
Dharma-AI released the Dharma Field Extractor on November 4, 2026, in a post on Hugging Face. The model is a 2-billion-parameter system that takes a document image and returns structured JSON. It is built on DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the model in the team's earlier paper. The authors are Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso, Paulo Henrique de Medeiros Araujo, Bruno Duarte and Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves.

The model works in two modes. In open mode, no schema is supplied, and the model works out which parts of the page are structured fields and returns them as key-value pairs. In schema-directed mode, you name the exact fields and types, string, number or boolean, under the key names your system already uses. A field that is not on the document comes back as null instead of an invented value, and the output follows the schema exactly with no extra fields. The adapter was trained on 43,384 examples covering English multi-domain data, real Brazilian documents in Portuguese, and a smaller share of other European and Asian languages.

The benchmark covered 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases. The model scored 0.834, above Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 and GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741. The quality gap over general-purpose LLMs runs from 1.8 points to 9.3 points, and cost runs from roughly 6 times lower to roughly 147 times lower. The authors say the model runs self-hosted on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour, and they note that this is not a sales price because self-hosted cost depends on hardware, volume and latency.

The team frames the result as evidence for its thesis that on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. They point to their earlier OCR paper, where a 3-billion-parameter model beat every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese, and say the gap held three months later when newer models arrived. The post says parameter count sets the ceiling while training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. It invites readers to try the model on their own documents and to visit dharma-ai.com to learn more.

Articles.Title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

stories.Headline: Bill Gates freezes everyone: 4 jobs AI will never steal
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder, published a forecast on 4 November 2026 about which jobs artificial intelligence will not take over. He named four fields: programming, biology, the energy sector and professional sports. The article was written by Carolina Vivianti for redhotcyber.com. Gates said algorithms and robots will be able to handle a significant share of the work people do today.

In programming, Gates said AI can already generate code, find bugs and automate routine tasks, but developers are still needed to configure and fine-tune the systems AI builds. They also handle infrastructure, security and integration. In biology, AI can analyze large amounts of data, find patterns and model processes, but research also means asking questions, testing hypotheses, running experiments and interpreting results. Energy workers are needed because the sector runs critical infrastructure that homes, businesses, hospitals and transport depend on, and people must inspect equipment and respond to emergencies. Professional sport is the fourth field, because its value lies in human abilities, emotions and the spectacle of competition, and Gates said spectators are unlikely to want to watch computers play baseball.

Gates is responsible for the forecast, and the article paraphrases his view that people will still be in demand in these professions even with widespread use of new technology. He said AI could take on much of the work in manufacturing, goods transportation and food production. He also said the scenario does not mean all professions outside his list will disappear. The impact will depend on specific tasks, technological capabilities and how fast companies adopt automation, which for some workers could mean less routine work and for others the need to learn new skills or change specialization.

The article sets this against AI's growing role in writing texts, analyzing data and creating images, and against concerns that algorithms could replace part of a company's workforce and that some specializations risk disappearing in their current form. It gives no date for when Gates made the forecast beyond the article's own publication. It does not say what happens next beyond the dependence on tasks, technology and the pace of automation. It ends by pointing readers to the site's Google News page and newsletter for updates.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates freezes everyone: 4 jobs AI will never steal

stories.Headline: Siemens Energy: A 210 MW Mexican Electrolyser and a Hokkaido Wind Pact Sit Behind the AI Sell-Off - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Siemens Energy shares fell 5.6% on the day, making the company one of the DAX's clearest decliners, as investors worried about tighter artificial intelligence regulation after the US midterm elections. Traders pointed to the prospect of a Democratic hold on both congressional chambers as a reason to expect slower investment in data-centre capacity, and that anxiety spread from pure AI names to infrastructure suppliers tied to the build-out. No order cancellations have been announced, and the pressure stems from the wider market backdrop rather than a company disclosure. On 22 October, according to media reports, the research house mwb Research reiterated its sell recommendation with a price target of €100 while expecting a strong closing quarter.

On Thursday, Japan's METI and Siemens Energy signed a cooperation agreement covering floating offshore wind development, supply-chain expansion and workforce training, alongside a planned strategic operations and maintenance hub in Hokkaido. The pact establishes a framework for further collaboration and is not the same as booked revenue. The Mexican project carries a firmer status: Transition Industries signed a binding EPC contract with Siemens Energy and Techint E&C on 28 October for an electrolyser of roughly 210 MW at the Pacifico Mexinol project in Sinaloa. A binding contract and a cooperation agreement represent different stages of commitment.

The real arbiter is the outlook for 2027, which the company has signalled will accompany fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results on 11 November. That release should show how management reads its own trajectory, letting shareholders judge whether political unease and corporate expectations are diverging or pointing the same way. For the bullish case to hold, the guidance would need to make a demonstrable case for why the expected development is achievable, and a more cautious view would carry more weight than the hope that today's selling is purely political. Should the regulatory worry persist and weigh on investment decisions, the stock could struggle even without a confirmed deterioration, and it would be a mistake to treat the Japanese and Mexican announcements as a hedge against any disappointment.

Articles.Title: Siemens Energy: A 210 MW Mexican Electrolyser and a Hokkaido Wind Pact Sit Behind the AI Sell-Off - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Satellite images expose potential trouble behind Microsoft's $5 billion AI spending shortfall
stories.Summary:
Microsoft spent $5 billion less than expected on AI infrastructure last quarter, and satellite images may show why. On Microsoft's quarterly earnings call last month, chief financial officer Amy Hood said delays by third-party cloud providers contributed to the lower-than-expected spending. Microsoft cut its annual capital expenditure forecast by $5 billion, and the news sent neocloud stocks tumbling. Microsoft did not name the providers, but satellite analysis from research firm Aterio points to two data center projects from neoclouds IREN and Nebius. In Texas, IREN is building four data centers under a $9.7 billion deal with Microsoft.

An October 21 satellite flyover found that one building, Horizon 4, was still missing backup power generators and cooling equipment and risked missing its scheduled delivery by the end of the year, Aterio said. IREN previously said equipment shortages had delayed the first building, Horizon 1, which Microsoft accepted in August. In New Jersey, data center operator DataOne is developing the second project for Nebius under a $17.4 billion deal with Microsoft, and Aterio said roughly 140 megawatts of that project's planned capacity could slip into 2027. Aterio data analyst Daud Shiraz said DataOne struggled to get permits for its original power generators, then faced more approval delays after switching to fuel cells. Regulators fined DataOne $1 million in September for operating generators without the required permits.

A Microsoft spokesperson said its approach to infrastructure is built on flexibility and optionality, combining its own data centers with leased facilities and third-party providers. IREN and DataOne declined to comment, and Nebius did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The potential delays point to broader struggles, and in October Microsoft axed a deal with another neocloud, Nscale, due to power-supply delays. The research firm Currence estimates that 30% to 50% of planned data center capacity initially scheduled to come online this year could be pushed into 2027 or later due to electricity shortages and other construction issues. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those estimates and the companies' responses.

Articles.Title: Satellite images expose potential trouble behind Microsoft's $5 billion AI spending shortfall

stories.Headline: EU AI act: the world’s first law on artificial intelligence - Meer | English edition
stories.Summary:
The European Union introduced the AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive law governing artificial intelligence, after the European Commission launched its proposal in 2021. The European Parliament approved the final text in March 2024, and EU governments in the Council backed it two months later. On August 1, 2024, the AI Act officially entered into force. Some bans on the most dangerous AI systems took effect within six months, while other provisions will be phased in over the next three years.

The law sorts AI systems by risk. Unacceptable risk systems, such as social scoring and unauthorized real-time biometric surveillance, are banned completely. High-risk systems used in healthcare, policing or hiring are allowed only under strict conditions on transparency, oversight and safety testing. Limited risk systems like deepfakes must tell users they are interacting with AI, and minimal risk tools such as spam filters face little regulation. From August 2025, providers of general-purpose AI such as ChatGPT must share technical documentation with regulators, publish a summary of training data and adopt copyright policies.

The law covers any foreign business whose AI systems are used inside the EU, though military and national security AI and lab research are excluded. The European AI Office, a body within the European Commission, will monitor compliance, with help from national authorities, an independent panel of scientists and an advisory forum. Companies using banned systems can be fined up to €35 million or seven percent of global revenue, and lesser violations up to €15 million or three percent, under Article 99. Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has called parts of the law confusing and burdensome, while supporters say clear rules build public trust.

Industries are already adjusting, with fashion AI tools needing human oversight and generative media required to be labeled or watermarked. The United States has issued executive orders and voluntary guidelines but no binding law, and China has drawn up its own rules. The EU is positioning itself as a champion of trustworthy AI, though whether other powers follow remains uncertain. The article says AI will no longer develop in a vacuum and the rules written in Brussels will be impossible to ignore.

Articles.Title: EU AI act: the world’s first law on artificial intelligence - Meer | English edition

stories.Headline: Why AI Order Backlogs Matter After Democrats Win Control Of Congress
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, according to the articles. The Associated Press called the Senate for the Democrats after Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative, beat Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson in Iowa. Democrats were projected to reach the 218 seats needed for a House majority, with NBC News projecting a final total of as many as 244. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, is in line to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027.

The result closes the path Republicans were building toward federal preemption of state AI and privacy laws, at least for the next two years, and puts the FTC under new scrutiny. Democrats will not be able to write the rules on their own, because President Donald Trump keeps his veto and the Senate keeps the 60-vote threshold for most legislation. The likeliest consequence for advertisers, publishers and AI companies is the survival, and probable expansion, of the state-by-state regime the industry spent 2025 and 2026 trying to replace. The articles also say the next eight weeks of the lame-duck session are unusually important, since anything that can pass then will become law under the old arithmetic.

Jeffries said Democrats were relentlessly focused on driving down the high cost of living and fighting for an affordable America, and that they were willing to work with the other side of the aisle whenever and wherever possible. On impeachment, he said Democrats had not ruled anything out when it comes to all of the tools available to hold people accountable, and had not ruled anything in. Robert Garcia, the Californian expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, told the administration to lawyer up, according to ANI. Neither Jeffries nor Garcia mentioned artificial intelligence or advertising on election night.

The articles say the campaign was fought on prices, health care, the war with Iran and the president, with technology entering mainly through electricity bills and data centres. An early CBS News exit poll put Trump's approval at 38%, and CNN's exit poll found about 90% of voters calling the cost of living a crucial or major factor. Jeremy Kahn, writing in Fortune's Eye on AI newsletter, said any legislation Congress does pass faces a likely veto from Trump, so new AI law will still require a bipartisan bill with very broad support. The Brookings Institution framed the coming two years as a backdrop of government divided along political fault lines, which tends to produce fewer laws and more investigations.

Articles.Title: Democrats win Congress: what changes for AI rules, privacy and advertising - PPC Land
