stories.Headline: China to explore AI applications in financial regulation, services: report - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China will explore using artificial intelligence in financial regulation and services, according to a report submitted to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature. The report was submitted by the State Council and was under deliberation at the session, Xinhua reported on November 3, 2026. It set out five priorities for the next stage of financial development. These include keeping an appropriately accommodative monetary policy, strengthening financial regulation and improving financial services to the real economy.

The report said China will use various policy tools to ensure ample liquidity and will keep evaluating and improving its monetary policy framework. On regulation, the country will crack down on illegal financial activities, explore AI applications in financial management and services, and strengthen protection of financial consumers. It will also increase support for infrastructure networks, technological innovation and small businesses. The report called for expanding the international use of the yuan, attracting more foreign financial institutions and long-term capital, and further developing an independently controlled cross-border yuan payment system.

On risk prevention, the report highlighted the use of monetary policy tools to support the capital market and continued implementation of the property sector's white-list mechanism. It said China has stepped up financial support for the real economy. From October 2025 to September 2026, new aggregate financing to the real economy totaled 33 trillion yuan, about 4.9 trillion U.S. dollars. A total of 88 companies went public on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, with nearly 90 percent of them being high-tech firms.

Articles.Title: China to explore AI applications in financial regulation, services: report - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Global AI governance requires multilateral cooperation on innovative regulatory tools
stories.Summary:
The article, published by China Daily on November 3, 2026, argues that global AI governance requires multilateral cooperation on new regulatory tools. It says human intelligence still exceeds machine intelligence, since the human brain is 10 to 100 times more complex than today's most advanced AI models. It adds that this gap is narrowing fast and that humanity may soon face a technological singularity, a point where AI surpasses human capabilities. The piece was presented as part of the discussion around the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai.

The article points to research on digitally reconstructed brains, including Google's digital fruit fly brain, which copies the exact neuronal wiring of a real fruit fly. In trials, these digital flies played gobang, simulated car driving, transcribed text such as "Hello, world" and even simulated slicing doner kebabs. The article also cites optogenetics, recognized by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, which allows precise control of neural circuits such as those governing sleep and wake cycles. It says a neural circuit's function is plastic, defined and reshaped by its training and operational environment.

The article says responsibility for governing AI rests entirely with humanity, because all artificial systems are built, trained and nurtured by people. It cites OpenAI's release of AI-derived solutions to long-standing unsolved mathematical puzzles, but says these results were not autonomous. It notes that human-defined research priorities, investor funding and teams of mathematicians and computer scientists made them possible. It also invokes philosopher John Searle's Chinese Room Argument to show that AI systems lack full autonomy and cannot progress without human support.

The article says medical AI deployment must be bound by multi-layered guardrails, including ethics committee approval, regulatory authorization and patient consent. It adds that interdisciplinary collaboration among data scientists, clinicians, pharmacists and nursing staff is needed. It suggests traditional physical supervision can be modernized, just as physical fences are gradually replaced by GPS-powered virtual fences. It concludes that both the promises and perils of AI stem from human choices, and that multilateral cooperation on next-generation regulatory tools is urgently needed.

Articles.Title: Global AI governance requires multilateral cooperation on innovative regulatory tools - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Microsoft Delays Default Copilot Usage-Based Billing Again, Citing Partner Feedback
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has again delayed its plan to turn on usage-based billing by default for new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business subscriptions bought through Cloud Solution Provider partners. The company now expects to enact the policy sometime between January and March 2027, its third fiscal quarter, it said on Wednesday. This is the second delay, after Microsoft previously moved the policy's Nov. 2 effective date to Dec. 1. Microsoft has about 500,000 partners worldwide, according to CRN's 2026 Channel Chiefs.

The policy will apply to new purchases of Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses in CSP, including standalone offers and bundles. Solution providers will still have a default spending limit of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month across eligible services for users in a customer's organization, and partners can set the limit to zero to stop usage-based spending. Copilot Cowork, Work IQ application programming interfaces and GitHub Copilot Harness are among the offerings that require usage-based billing. Microsoft is also delaying Partner Center sandbox environments for testing the policy without giving a new date, and it promises readiness guidance and at least 30 days of sandbox testing before default billing becomes generally available. The timelines for sandbox availability and usage-based billing apply to Australia, Belgium, Brazil, France, Germany, India, Italy, Korea, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and other markets.

Microsoft said it heard feedback and is adjusting the effective dates to give partners extra time to prepare and support their customers. Chris Miller, chief revenue officer of Chesterfield, Mo.-based Microsoft solution provider ATB Technologies, told CRN that working with Microsoft's Azure cloud has helped ATB understand cloud economics. He said he can imagine license-based AI offers disappearing one day and the market moving entirely to token-based pricing. ATB helps clients understand their AI consumption bills, stay within budget and determine which Microsoft AI capabilities are covered by licenses and which trigger consumption charges. Miller said there is a way to do it so a customer does not end up with a $5,000 bill at the end of the month, and that ATB is monitoring its own ways to keep costs in line.

ATB recommends targeted rollouts of Copilot licenses to select users before exploring products such as the Microsoft Fabric data analytics platform and deciding whether consumption-based capabilities make sense for particular users. Miller said consumption is sometimes a better model than licensing, since 80 percent of a customer's users could be wasting a license. Microsoft executives have said publicly that the future of AI pricing is a basic allotment of compute under a license with metered charges for more advanced uses. On Microsoft's latest quarterly earnings call, CEO Satya Nadella said the number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew more than 75 percent over the quarter, and credit consumption from agentic features on GitHub more than doubled. Nadella said consumption plus seat subscriptions increase Microsoft's total addressable market and average revenue per user.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Delays Default Copilot Usage-Based Billing Again, Citing Partner Feedback

stories.Headline: China Regulator Warns AI Investment Boom Crowds Out Traditional Industries
stories.Summary:
Xiao Yuanqi, a vice minister of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, warned on Tuesday that excessive global investment in AI is crowding traditional industries out of financing and driving up their borrowing costs. He made the remarks at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit in Hong Kong on Nov. 3. He said massive capital inflows into technology companies are pushing up leverage levels and could fuel excessive expansion. The article also cites estimates that AI adds 0.5 to 1 percentage point to US growth and 0.1 to 0.3 percentage points to Europe's.

The warning concerns the effect of heavy AI investment on borrowing costs and credit risks for traditional industries. The article says past tech bubbles have not always caused downturns, because productivity gains often support long-term growth. It gives no further details on any specific measures or policy changes. The figures it provides are the estimated growth contributions for the US and Europe.

Xiao is responsible for raising the issue, in his role as a vice minister of the National Financial Regulatory Administration. According to the article, he warned that the capital flowing into tech companies is raising leverage and could lead to excessive expansion. The article does not say what he proposed as a response. It also does not give further comments from him beyond these points.

The context is a global boom in AI investment and concern about its side effects for other sectors. The article notes that past tech bubbles have not always ended in downturns, since productivity gains can support growth over time. It does not say what happens next or what steps, if any, the regulator will take. It also does not give a timeline for any action.

Articles.Title: China Regulator Warns AI Investment Boom Crowds Out Traditional Industries - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Meta faces R$1m daily fine if it scrapes Brazilian media sites for AI
stories.Summary:
On November 3, a state court judge in São Paulo suspended the clause in Meta's revised Commercial Terms that would let the company crawl the websites of its business users. Judge Guilherme Madeira Dezem of the 44th Civil Court of the Central Civil Forum granted the measure without hearing Meta, on a joint application from ABERT, ANJ and ANER. He signed the decision at 15:36 local time. It was the second court order against the terms in a week, after an Oslo court temporarily blocked them on October 28. The reasoning rests on copyright and contract law rather than competition law.

The order requires Meta to keep the associations' members' Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads accounts fully active if they refuse the new terms. Meta must stay off their portals and must not use automated tools to access, index or crawl their domains, or use that content to train or feed its AI systems, until final judgment. The penalty is 1 million reais for each day of non-compliance, capped at 100 million reais. Meta has five days to contest the order, and the associations have 30 working days to file their main claim. The case number is 4214874-21.2026.8.26.0100.

The judge found that scraping news sites to build AI is reproduction under Article 29 of Brazil's Copyright Law, Law No 9.610/1998, which requires prior and express authorisation. He said Brazilian law provides no general text and data mining exception for commercial AI training. He also declared ineffective a clause sending disputes to courts in California, citing Article 21(I) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Marco Civil da Internet, Law No 12.965/2014. The decision describes November 20, 2026 as the date the terms take effect.

Meta's revised terms were made available on October 16, 2026, and originally contained the word train, which was deleted in a further change on October 19. On October 28, Andy Stone, Meta's vice president of communications, said the company would not change its policies without a full consultation with industry groups, and that implementation would be delayed if the consultation ran past November 20. The decision does not refer to that pause. The order is temporary and holds until the full case is decided.

Articles.Title: Meta faces R$1m daily fine if it scrapes Brazilian media sites for AI - PPC Land

stories.Headline: Ansari Wants a Day-1 AI Pause; Her Bill Sets a 10^25 Line
stories.Summary:
Representative Yassamin Ansari, an Arizona Democrat, posted on X at 18:54 UTC on 4 November that a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry and a ban on artificial superintelligence should top the Democratic agenda on day 1. The post came the day after the Associated Press called her re-election in Arizona's 3rd Congressional District on 3 November. Her post did not name a bill. She is one of 10 House members named on H.R. 10538, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, which was introduced on 24 September by Representative Greg Casar.

The bill would create a Department of Artificial Intelligence and pause systems trained on 10^25 or more integer or floating point operations. Under Section 8, those systems may not be trained, modified or fine-tuned, including through recursive self-improvement, and unreleased ones may not be deployed. The threshold is adjusted each year by the Secretary to reflect gains in training efficiency. The pause has no fixed end date and runs from enactment until the Secretary determines the Department is fully staffed and has issued rules on pre-development plans, monitoring, auditing and final pre-deployment approval.

Section 13 sets a fine and up to 20 years in prison for policymaking individuals or rogue actors who recklessly violate the pause. Ansari made a similar call at a 9 September press conference in Phoenix, where she said she wanted an immediate pause on further AI development from major companies because they are not regulating themselves. She also called for a ban on artificial superintelligence and a pause until federal regulations are in place and Congress can regulate the industry. Casar's release of 23 September described the bill as pausing advanced AI development until a new federal AI regulatory body is up and running.

By the article's reading of the introduced text, the bill has no provision on data centers. The article connects the post to a wider debate in which local ballot limits target data centers while the federal bill targets model training. It notes that OpenAI's Chris Lehane wrote on 4 November that 2028 Democratic hopefuls could be asked to show support for a moratorium on data centers. The article states that her post sets out a position, not a party plan, and that nothing establishes which agenda the next Congress will take up or whether the bill will move.

Articles.Title: Ansari Wants a Day-1 AI Pause; Her Bill Sets a 10^25 Line

stories.Headline: IREN Shares Drop 10% Amid Fears of AI Regulation and Construction Delays
stories.Summary:
IREN Ltd. shares fell 10.06% to $22.00 on Wednesday, reaching a fresh 52-week low, according to Benzinga Pro data. The drop came amid a broader decline in AI cloud stocks after Democratic midterm gains. Democrats now hold both chambers of Congress. Traders fear tighter regulation will delay data center construction and limit AI infrastructure expansion.

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott after promising tighter construction restrictions, starting with an immediate statewide freeze. Wells Fargo estimates Texas will account for 27% of the gigawatts planned for U.S. data centers. Georgia accounts for 7% of planned capacity, while Pennsylvania and Ohio each account for 5%. Democrats won or retained the governorships in Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio, and those states plus Texas represent about 44% of planned capacity.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co wrote Wednesday that Democratic gains should slow U.S. data center construction in the coming years. He named Texas as a particular concern and called Hinojosa a known opponent of data centers. He wrote that Democratic control of the Senate should make AI legislation harder. However, he said President Donald Trump's veto threats may push technology executives to negotiate with Congress.

AI stocks were already under pressure before the election results, and the Nasdaq-100 entered correction territory in late October. Wells Fargo chief equity strategist Ohsung Kwon warned earlier in the week that a Democratic win in Texas could be an unusually severe worst-case outcome for the sector. IREN will report first-fiscal-quarter earnings after trading ends on November 5, Thursday. IREN shares have lost nearly 45% over 30 days, and analysts expect a loss of 67 cents per share on revenue of $223.19 million.

Articles.Title: IREN Shares Drop 10% Amid Fears of AI Regulation and Construction Delays

stories.Headline: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Predicts the Bitcoin Price: Is This Actually Possible?
stories.Summary:
Meta AI, the artificial intelligence system from Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, published a prediction that Bitcoin could reach very high prices by January 1, 2027, according to an article by Ahmed Barakat published on cryptonews.com on November 4, 2026. The prediction describes a hypothetical scenario in which several of the world’s largest energy producers and commodity trading companies settle a significant portion of cross-border trades in oil, gas and refined products using Bitcoin. In that scenario, Bitcoin would move from being only a store of value to a preferred method for settlement and liquidity in physical energy markets. The article says this could create a new, high-velocity demand channel not seen in previous market cycles.

The article states that Bitcoin was trading around $77,000 at the time, after rebounding 1.8% overnight from a selloff that pushed it to $75,800. It says the fall came as US Midterm results rolled in, with Democrats winning 53 seats to 42 for Republicans. The article says Bitcoin has been trading between roughly the mid-$70,000s and the low-$80,000s, and that a decisive weekly close above the $90,000 to $95,000 zone would mark a clear shift in momentum. It adds that if the energy-settlement catalyst gained real traction alongside a return of broad risk appetite, Bitcoin could trade in the $280,000 to $420,000 range by January 1, 2027, with an extreme stretch scenario pushing toward $550,000 or more.

The article describes the prediction as deliberately aggressive and highly speculative, and says the catalyst would require a fundamental change in how global energy markets operate, something it calls a long shot. It says the scenario is unconventional but not impossible. The article also says Bitcoin needs to reclaim $80,000 quickly for the bullish prediction to play out. It does not say that Meta AI or Mark Zuckerberg commented beyond the prediction itself.

The article also covers Bitcoin Hyper, a Bitcoin Layer 2 built on the Solana Virtual Machine, and says its presale has raised over $33.2M with fewer than 22 days remaining at a price of $0.0136877. It says staking is available only for presale participants at a 30% annual percentage yield. The article carries a disclaimer that crypto is a high-risk asset class and that the article is for information only and not investment advice. It does not say what happens next beyond the price levels and the January 1, 2027 date.

Articles.Title: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Predicts the Bitcoin Price: Is This Actually Possible?

stories.Headline: AI agents surge on protected transactions, Arkose says
stories.Summary:
Arkose Labs published its Q3 2026 State of Agentic AI Trust Report on 3 November 2026, finding that personal AI agents are increasingly carrying out online transactions for consumers. The report is based on production data gathered between July and September. It found that 97.7% of legitimate AI agent sessions included no verified identity disclosure. More than 65% of Arkose Labs customers encountered AI agents on protected transactions such as logins, registrations and checkouts, across banking, gaming, technology and travel sites.

Sessions from Meta's Muse, described as a personal AI agent built for consumer use, rose more than 30-fold in September, while other agents remained broadly flat. Arkose Labs classified 77.4% of AI agent sessions as legitimate, compared with 7.9% of known bot sessions. It also found that 70.5% of registration sessions were identified as fake-account attempts. The report groups agents into three categories: self-disclosing good agents, non-disclosing good agents and malicious agents, and it describes Muse as a non-disclosing good agent because it appears on networks as a Chrome browser.

Kevin Gosschalk, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Arkose Labs, said the findings reflected a wider concern among security leaders. He recalled that at a recent banking industry summit, the CISO of one of the world's largest banks said a technology had arrived ahead of the controls for the first time in his career. Gosschalk said the report makes clear how difficult it has become for companies to distinguish legitimate, revenue-driving agents from malicious ones. Mitchell Davies, Lead Researcher in the Arkose Cyber Threat Intelligence Research team, said the presence of automation alone is no longer the deciding factor, and that the real question is what the agent came to do and what its intent is.

The report says businesses face a new problem as consumer-facing AI agents become more common in routine digital activity, and the challenge is no longer only identifying automation but deciding whether an automated session reflects a legitimate customer action or a malicious attempt at fraud. It notes that the automated flows used by AI agents overlap with those commonly targeted by attackers. Arkose Labs said Instinct was designed in a way that made 96.8% of its sessions appear medium or high risk, yet neither Instinct nor Muse had a single session linked to an attack. Davies said each company must decide how to handle agents accordingly, taking its industry and risk posture into consideration, and that a bank will have different controls in place than a retailer.

Articles.Title: AI agents surge on protected transactions, Arkose says - TechDay US

stories.Headline: Investment, AI and regulation: the keys to Mobile World Congress 2027
stories.Summary:
The 2027 Mobile World Congress will be held from March 1 to 4 at the Gran Via venue of Fira de Barcelona, in its 21st edition. GSMA Ltd. president and director John Hoffman presented the event's novelties on Wednesday. The congress will cover about 240,000 square meters and expects around 100,000 attendees. It will focus on robotics and artificial intelligence, and on building bridges between companies, investors and visitors.

Hoffman said the event creates conversations between countries through the ministerial program, a closed-door space where political leaders are expected to debate AI regulation. He called it the largest gathering of policymakers outside the United Nations and said more than 200 countries and territories consider MWC a meeting point. SoftBank Group Corp is making its debut with a large stand. The event adds three new sectors, health, automotive and aviation, and confirmed companies include Vodafone, Deutsche Telekom, Orange, SK Telecom, Telefónica, Starlink, Amazon, Cisco, Ericsson, Google, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Huawei, Meta, Nokia, Qualcomm, Samsung, Xiaomi and ZTE.

Speakers will include Anima Anandkumar, Mati Staniszewski, Amy Webb, Dr. Hany Farid, Tarek Mansour and Yoon Young Park. Connect Health, with Mobile World Capital, will bring together AstraZeneca, Garmin Health, HPE, Medtronic and NUHS. Connect Auto will feature 5GAA, AVATR Technology and Chery Mobility Iberia, and Laia Ripoll, general director of GSMA Spain, said Chery will present the Omoda 4, which has an AI system that lets you interact with the car as if talking to another passenger. Connect Aviation will include Cranfield University, Imagine Wireless, Barch and Seamless Air Alliance.

Hoffman denied that companies would present defense application projects and said the event will focus on civilian applications. He said 4 Years From Now remains a major pole of capital attraction and that the Talent Arena is the skills part of MWC. He did not say whether the Talent Arena would return to the same facilities as the congress. He also would not reveal the use of pavilion 0 when works finish in spring 2027, saying they have the answer but cannot say anything yet.

Articles.Title: Investment, AI and regulation: the keys to Mobile World Congress 2027

stories.Headline: Fermaca Unveils NVIDIA-Powered AI Factory Platform to Power Mexico and Latin America
stories.Summary:
Fermaca announced on November 4, 2026, that it has become the first NVIDIA Cloud Partner based in Mexico and unveiled an AI factory platform meant to make the country a producer of advanced AI capabilities for Mexico and Latin America. The rollout begins with Fermaca Digital Origins in Mexico City and combines Fermaca's infrastructure and operating experience with NVIDIA accelerated computing. The platform is intended to expand access to the computing capacity that businesses and institutions need to build and deploy AI. Fermaca describes its strategy as reaching from gas molecule to token, bringing together gas infrastructure, energy development, fiber connectivity, AI facilities and accelerated computing.

The first deployment uses an initial NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra cluster, and a later roadmap includes NVIDIA Vera Rubin. Inventec is providing compute systems and DDN is providing storage, while Fermaca is responsible for infrastructure development and operations. Fermaca's near-term plan targets 60 MW of total facility power supporting operational AI facilities by December 31, 2027, including computing, cooling and supporting facility systems. Beyond that, Fermaca Digital City in Durango is a longer-term ambition of up to 1 GW of IT capacity, which measures computing equipment only, and the company says these are separate milestones with deployment phased as the platform expands.

Manuel Calvillo of Fermaca said the company is investing in Mexico's capacity to produce intelligence, create economic value and shape its own technological future. He said the ambition runs from gas molecule to token and that NVIDIA accelerated computing extends the infrastructure Fermaca knows how to build into the computing capacity businesses across Mexico and Latin America will increasingly depend on. Marcio Aguiar, NVIDIA's director of enterprise for Latin America, said the company is excited to support Mexico's growing AI ecosystem and to bring NVIDIA accelerated computing to more businesses and developers. Paul Bloch of DDN said Fermaca is connecting the infrastructure that powers industry with the infrastructure that will power intelligence, and Inventec called the announcement the beginning of a long-term partnership with Fermaca.

Fermaca says it has full support from Mexican government authorities at the federal, state and municipal levels, which it links to the national development objectives of Plan México. The company says the platform is designed to strengthen Mexico's digital sovereignty by building capacity to develop and deploy AI on infrastructure located in Mexico, which could help businesses, universities and institutions retain more of the knowledge and economic value created by AI. Fermaca is also working with NVIDIA on an education initiative called México Aprende IA con Fermaca y NVIDIA, which started in Durango and is designed to equip university teachers with AI knowledge and practical training. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the phased rollout and the 2027 power target.

Articles.Title: Fermaca Unveils NVIDIA-Powered AI Factory Platform to Power Mexico and Latin America

stories.Headline: Using AI to advance the Rule of Law, Trust and Democracy - King's College London
stories.Summary:
Dr Stephen Daly, a Reader in Tax Law at The Dickson Poon School of Law, King's College London, published a feature on 4 November 2026 arguing that AI could strengthen the Rule of Law, build trust in public institutions and advance democracy. He said lawyers have mostly focused on AI's risks, such as breaches of constitutional rules, human rights instruments and GDPR. In work co-authored with Tofigh Nisi and Francien Dechesne, published in Intertax, he set out guidelines for tax authorities regulating AI against risks including bias, opacity, lack of accountability and hallucinations. His Cambridge Law Journal article argued that AI can advance the Rule of Law by making systems more transparent, giving taxpayers better guidance on their obligations and rights, speeding up tax disputes and reducing non-compliance. In "Trustworthy AI and HMRC," published in the British Tax Review, Daly argued that HMRC can use AI to better meet its strategic objectives and so increase its trustworthiness, including simple tools such as Co-Pilot to write letters and summarize meetings and to sift through job applications.

In 2025 he concluded the "Taxing Better" project, funded by the British Academy and Leverhulme Trust, which considered whether AI can advance democratic norms. The resulting policy paper, "Taxing Better: Using AI to Advance Democracy," makes five recommendations to HMRC on using AI-enhanced surveys to gather feedback on tax rules, priorities and policies. Daly said the papers generally take the existing legal system as a given, but that serious consideration should be given to whether advances in information-sharing and AI call fundamental tenets of the tax system into question. Daly argued that tax authorities hold broad discretionary powers because they are better placed to decide how to collect taxes, but that AI changes this. He said that if an AI system can enable better tax collection, failing to use it could be seen as irrational, and that coercive powers were necessary where collection was painstaking and labour intensive, while AI-facilitated investigations make them less necessary.

He said AI-enabled risk profiling now provides a coherent basis for deciding which taxpayers to audit, where previously there were no good answers. He also said taxpayers once knew their own affairs better than the tax authority, but authorities now hold masses of bespoke and population-level information on which systems can be trained to compute liabilities, so it is less obvious that taxpayers should bear responsibility for determining their own liability. The feature appears in King's College London's Artificial Intelligence and Technology in Law series, which the university describes as driving forward extraordinary changes in how legal scholars understand the intersection of law, AI and technology. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Using AI to advance the Rule of Law, Trust and Democracy - King's College London

stories.Headline: NASDAQ Index, SP500, Dow Jones Forecasts – NASDAQ Rallies Despite AI Regulation Worries
stories.Summary:
On November 4, 2026, US stock indexes rose after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections. The S&P 500 gained 2.04% to 7,715.60, the NASDAQ 100 rose 1.71% to 28,574.40, and the Dow Jones climbed above 53,000, according to FXEmpire. Oil prices fell 9% as traders bet that Trump would not be able to restart the military operation against Iran. Vice President Vance said the war in Iran was the reason Republicans lost.

The S&P 500 was trying to settle above resistance at 7,690 to 7,700, with the next level at 7,770 to 7,780. The NASDAQ's nearest resistance was 28,850 to 28,900, then 29,400 to 29,450, with support at 28,500 and 28,250 to 28,300. The Dow Jones rose above resistance at 52,800 to 52,900 and was trying to settle above 53,300, with the next level at 53,600 to 53,700. The 2-year Treasury yield fell toward 4.58% and the 10-year settled below 4.90%. The ISM Services PMI fell from 54.9 in September to 54.5 in October, against a forecast of 54.8, and ADP reported 86,000 private jobs added in October, against a forecast of 69,000, with the previous figure revised from 86,000 to 90,000.

Traders believed Democrats would slow the development of AI data centers, and CoreWeave fell 9.65%, Sandisk fell 7.97%, and Seagate fell 7.84%. Consumer cyclical and consumer defensive stocks were among the biggest S&P 500 gainers, while energy stocks came under pressure from the oil sell-off. 3M was the biggest Dow Jones gainer, up about 10%, and only three Dow stocks fell. The article says the economic reports did not have a material impact on stocks because traders focused on the election results.

Articles.Title: NASDAQ Index, SP500, Dow Jones Forecasts – NASDAQ Rallies Despite AI Regulation Worries

stories.Headline: Two-thirds of Australian businesses expect no AI impact on job vacancies: ABS - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
About two-thirds of Australian businesses do not expect artificial intelligence to affect their job vacancies over the next 12 months, according to official data released on Wednesday. The figures came from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. About 8 percent of businesses expect AI to reduce job vacancies, while 1 percent expects an increase. Sean Crick, head of labor statistics at the ABS, gave the figures in a statement.

The data showed that AI has had a limited impact on job vacancies so far, with about 82 percent of businesses reporting no impact in August. Four percent of businesses said AI had reduced their vacancies in August, while less than 1 percent reported an increase. The impact varied by industry. Information media and telecommunications had the highest share of businesses reporting a fall in vacancies due to AI, at 16 percent, followed by wholesale trade at 8 percent and manufacturing at 6 percent.

Electricity, gas, water and waste services had the highest share reporting an increase, at 10 percent, followed by public administration and safety at 4 percent and health care and social assistance at 2 percent. The ABS said the estimates cover only the impact of AI on job vacancies and do not reflect its impact on existing jobs. Total job vacancies in Australia stood at 325,000 in August 2026, down 0.9 percent from May. That number was 31.2 percent below its peak in May 2022.

Articles.Title: Two-thirds of Australian businesses expect no AI impact on job vacancies: ABS - Xinhua

stories.Headline: AI Could Give the Billable Hour New Life. Here's Why Legal Departments May Welcome It
stories.Summary:
Integreon's Rhett Lemmel, director of legal spend and analytics, warned in a November 4, 2026 Law.com article by Trudy Knockless that AI could give the billable hour new life. As corporate legal departments push for lower law firm rates, Lemmel said the discounts they negotiate may disappear through excessive hours, inefficient staffing and work that goes beyond the agreed scope. The article reports that legal departments expect AI to reduce outside counsel costs. Lemmel believes AI could make some alternative fee arrangements less attractive to corporate clients.

The article gives no specific figures, dates beyond the November 4, 2026 publication, or named law firms and companies other than Integreon, Rhett Lemmel and the author, Trudy Knockless. It says the piece runs about nine minutes of reading time. It does not describe any new rule, policy or requirement, only the shift Lemmel expects in how legal departments and law firms handle fees. The full text sits behind a subscription, so the article's detailed arguments are not available.

Lemmel is responsible for the warning, and he works as director of legal spend and analytics at Integreon. According to the article, he cautions that the rate discounts corporate legal departments negotiate may be undone by excessive hours, inefficient staffing and work outside the agreed scope. The article frames his view as a belief rather than a finding. It also notes that legal departments expect AI to reduce outside counsel costs.

The context is the push by corporate legal departments for lower law firm rates, which the article describes as ongoing. The article does not say what happens next beyond Lemmel's expectations about alternative fee arrangements becoming less attractive to corporate clients. It offers no timeline, no announced plan and no response from law firms or legal departments. The rest of the article's analysis is not visible without a subscription.

Articles.Title: AI Could Give the Billable Hour New Life. Here's Why Legal Departments May Welcome It

stories.Headline: Texas Political Shift Deals Blow to AI Infrastructure as Democratic Governor-Elect Moves to Pause Data Center Approvals
stories.Summary:
In the U.S. midterm elections, Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term, to become Texas's first Latina female governor. Democrat James Talarico also defeated Trump-endorsed Republican Ken Paxton in the federal Senate race, becoming the first Democrat to win a Texas federal Senate seat since 1988. The result ends more than three decades of Republican control of the Texas governorship. After the announcement, Nasdaq-100 futures fell as much as 2%, more than double the decline in Dow futures.

Hinojosa advocates an immediate moratorium on accepting new data center permit applications until the state legislature enacts comprehensive safeguards. She also calls for repealing the existing 20-year tax exemption for hyperscale data centers, which she says costs Texas at least $1 billion in tax revenue annually. Talarico likewise advocates stronger data center regulation, proposing to end some tax subsidies and raise labor, environmental, and grid usage standards. According to Wells Fargo estimates, 27% of all planned U.S. data center power capacity is located in Texas, and the state is expected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center capacity through 2030.

Abbott announced in September a pause on approvals and grid connections for some data center projects, saying that Texans must come first, and Hinojosa dismissed that limited pause as lacking urgency and credibility. Wells Fargo Chief Equity Strategist Ohsung Kwon warned before the election that a Democratic win in the Texas governor's race could become a left-tail risk event for the AI trade. Horizon Investments Chief Investment Officer Scott Ladner noted that Texas has long been fertile ground for building data centers, and a change of governor could make that ground largely barren. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said on election night that a Democratic victory could slow data center construction, but that fears of a policy shock may be exaggerated.

The election result does not mean existing data centers will halt immediately, and the specific impact depends on the policy formulation and scope of implementation once the new government takes office. Texas still has advantages in industrial clusters, energy resources, and existing infrastructure, but grid connections, environmental reviews, and tax incentive terms all face tightening. Going forward, attention should be paid to whether Hinojosa delivers on her pledge of a broader permit pause, and whether new power and tax policies will alter tech companies' investment plans in Texas. The Nasdaq-100 Index had already pulled back at least 10% from its high by late October, entering technical correction territory, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 19% over the past month.

Articles.Title: Texas Political Shift Deals Blow to AI Infrastructure as Democratic Governor-Elect Moves to Pause Data Center Approvals - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Anthropic Uses Claude to Show Bacterial and Phage Proteins Form Vaults
stories.Summary:
Anthropic reported on November 4, 2026 that it used Claude to help show that bacterial and bacteriophage relatives of the major vault protein can assemble into vault particles when produced in E. coli. Vaults are large, hollow protein shells whose biological function is unknown. The team searched a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins and found major vault protein homologs in 29 bacterial phyla and four archaeal phyla, though the proteins appeared in less than 1% of species with sequenced genomes. They tested 44 proteins, 15 of 24 candidates produced soluble protein, and seven of those 15 formed vault-like particles under electron microscopy, with cryo-electron microscopy confirming the shape in four, two from phages and two from bacteria. Claude helped map one bacteriophage-derived shell, called L05, at a nominal resolution of 3.2 angstroms, which Anthropic describes as the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells.

L05 contains 96 copies of one protein, 48 in each half, compared with 78 copies in mammalian vaults, 39 per half. Each L05 protein has seven repeating wall segments versus nine in human major vault protein, and the shell is shorter and wider than the human vault but encloses about 25% more volume. The team made 15 altered versions of L05, and some single substitutions near the wall seam or cap produced open, rosette-like particles or aggregates instead of closed vaults. Duplicating two wall segments gave L05 nine repeats and produced closed particles with about 20% more enclosed volume, which the authors interpret as evidence that repeat duplication can adjust vault size without preventing assembly. Claude converted chosen protein sequences into DNA designs, added gene-control sequences, and prepared designs for ordering, and Anthropic says its optimized size-exclusion chromatography method cut the journey from cells to a microscopy grid to about 90 minutes, compared with about three days for the conventional sugar-gradient method.

The authors directed the work and accepted responsibility for the content, while various Claude models and interfaces, including Claude Science and Claude Code, wrote the study's code and performed its computational analyses. Anthropic says most steps could be performed by a typical laboratory using existing Claude products, though the parallel cryo-EM analysis used hundreds of GPUs beyond what many academic institutions may have available. The workflow also produced consequential errors: one Claude-written protocol specified a growth-medium additive that interfered with introducing DNA into cells, delaying the project by two weeks, and an early cryo-EM run skipped a standard step and generated a flawed map blended with its mirror image. Anthropic shared the laboratory notes with its model-training researchers and says subsequent Claude models appeared to make fewer DNA-design errors and identify experimental pitfalls more effectively.

Each L05 protein copy contains a pocket with unresolved density from an unidentified small molecule, and a computational search of 25,000 molecules identified coenzyme A or a derivative as a candidate ligand, though neither the molecule's identity nor any functional implication has been confirmed. The particles have so far been produced only in E. coli, and the researchers have not tested whether they form in the bacteria and phages where the proteins naturally occur. Anthropic has submitted the technical report to bioRxiv and plans to release the structures and additional data later. The immediate advance is experimental control over a family of protein shells that can now be produced in bacteria, mapped in detail, and resized through repeat duplication, while the larger question remains whether that simpler system and the unidentified ligand can help explain what vaults do.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Uses Claude to Show Bacterial and Phage Proteins Form Vaults

stories.Headline: India’s AI regulation consultation paper nearing completion: Report
stories.Summary:
India's government is close to finishing a consultation paper on artificial intelligence regulation and expects to ask the public for feedback soon, according to a report by Moneycontrol cited by Storyboard18. A senior government official said the government studied regulatory frameworks used in other countries and held talks with several stakeholders, including academics, while preparing the document. Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw first announced the planned consultation on October 8, saying the government intended to publish the paper within a month and naming AI safety as a key focus. On October 23 he said the document would be released in the coming weeks and that the government would invite responses from citizens, businesses and AI users.

The consultation is expected to cover AI safety, the spread of deepfakes and the possible psychological impact of the technology on users. It will also look at skilling requirements and ways to make the gains from AI accessible to a wider section of society. The paper is expected to examine accountability, copyright, data protection, deepfake detection and institutional mechanisms as India considers a broader framework for AI governance. Vaishnaw also indicated that the scale of emerging AI-related risks warranted consideration of legislative measures and additional regulations.

The exercise builds on the India AI Governance Guidelines released in November 2025, which set out seven guiding principles for developing and deploying AI, including human oversight wherever feasible, accountability in proportion to potential harm and transparency for users and regulators. The committee that drafted the guidelines found that several AI-related risks could be addressed through existing legislation, but recommended examining gaps in the legal framework, particularly around accountability when AI systems cause harm, the application of data protection requirements to AI development and copyright issues involving material used to train AI models. The guidelines also called for uniform mechanisms to establish the origin and authenticity of digital content, especially amid growing concerns over deepfakes. On the institutional side, the framework proposed an AI Governance Group to coordinate policymaking across government departments, backed by a Technology and Policy Expert Committee, and recommended an AI Safety Institute to support research and testing.

Articles.Title: India’s AI regulation consultation paper nearing completion: Report

stories.Headline: AMD Turns to Long-Term Memory Contracts to Ease HBM Cost Burden — Samsung Electronics Emerges as Likely Supplier
stories.Summary:
AMD said on its third-quarter earnings call that it has signed long-term supply agreements with some memory suppliers, though it did not name them. Industry watchers believe Samsung Electronics is the likely counterparty, given a meeting this spring between AMD CEO Lisa Su and Samsung Chairman Lee Jae-yong and the HBM4 volumes involved. Samsung is currently supplying AMD with substantial volumes of sixth-generation High Bandwidth Memory, known as HBM4, and is also understood to be supplying general-purpose DRAM. The disclosure is read as AMD's effort to manage component procurement risk ahead of expected growth next year.

AMD forecast revenue growth of more than 80% next year and said it has secured wafer, substrate, advanced packaging and memory capacity. Third-quarter data center revenue rose 97% to $8.55 billion, a quarterly record, and fourth-quarter revenue guidance was $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, above analyst forecasts. Total third-quarter revenue was $13.38 billion, up 45% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings per share were $2.09. Adjusted gross margin was 56%, and the company expects margins to slip to around 55% next year.

Asked about cost pressure from rising HBM prices, Su said AMD has long-term contracts with some memory suppliers and is also in talks with customers, including large cloud operators, on sharing the cost increases. Su said data center chips will account for 80% of 2027 revenue and will drive most of the revenue and profit growth. Samsung said on its own earnings call that it has completed multi-year supply contracts with 10 large customers so far and is negotiating with 10 more. Samsung also said it has wrapped up HBM supply negotiations for 2027.

The global semiconductor industry is facing a shortage of expensive HBM used in AI processors, and supply remains tight even as manufacturers ramp up output. The long-term contract shows how AI chip buyers and suppliers are locking in a structure in which each guarantees the other's supply stability. For AMD, it locks in HBM procurement costs to defend margins, while Samsung ties major AI customers to multi-year contracts. Some observers say that if the memory shortage continues, the cost gap could widen between companies with long-term contracts and those without.

Articles.Title: AMD Turns to Long-Term Memory Contracts to Ease HBM Cost Burden — Samsung Electronics Emerges as Likely Supplier - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: AI May Speed Up Legal Research, But That Doesn’t Automatically Shrink The Bill
stories.Summary:
A unanimous Tenth Circuit panel affirmed a $114,663.11 fee award to the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck. The ruling came after Flux Drive’s trade secrets suit was dismissed. Flux Drive had argued that the firm’s use of AI and online research tools should have reduced its fees. Judge Carolyn McHugh wrote for the panel that plaintiffs had not shown the use of AI made the hours actually expended unreasonable.

The court said Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated billing entry. The panel acknowledged that AI may reduce research time. It also noted that lawyers still must verify their authorities and arguments. The decision was issued on 2026-11-04, according to the Above the Law article.

Brownstein partner Christopher Ottele welcomed the ruling. He said AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still must exercise in court filings. Judge McHugh’s opinion was written for a unanimous panel. The article was written by Staci Zaretsky, the managing editor of Above the Law.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the ruling itself. It frames the case as a quote of the day feature. The panel’s reasoning ties any fee reduction to specific billing entries rather than to the use of AI alone. The article gives no further dates or names beyond those above.

Articles.Title: AI May Speed Up Legal Research, But That Doesn’t Automatically Shrink The Bill

stories.Headline: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan Warns Safeguarding ‘Thousand Millions’ Of AI Agents From Unauthorized Actions Is A Key Challenge Of The AI Wave
stories.Summary:
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan spoke about artificial intelligence in a discussion with Hyperbolic CEO Jasper Zhang, published on November 4, 2026. The talk came after Hyperbolic raised $30 million in a round backed by Tan's venture capital firm, Walden Catalyst. Tan said AI momentum will continue and be even bigger than the internet. He also raised concerns about security as AI agents spread.

Tan said the main question is how quickly the technology can scale. He listed memory, GPU and power shortages as constraints on data center construction. He added that financing has become a bottleneck for growth. He also said he expects some correction in the sector.

Tan said he expects "thousand millions of agents" and asked how so many agents would be safeguarded from moving into areas they are not authorized to do. He remained optimistic that the sector would keep growing once the constraints are addressed. In October he predicted hardware shortages would last three years and said return on investment was paramount. He is not the only executive to voice concerns, as Elon Musk predicted "death" for some AI companies late last month.

Tan has discussed agentic AI several times in recent months. In late September he said he left AI agents working overnight before evaluating their output in the morning. His remarks mirrored Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, who also uses AI agents in his regular workflow and sees agent security as a key concern. Tan concluded that once the constraints are addressed, the sector would continue to grow.

Articles.Title: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan Warns Safeguarding ‘Thousand Millions’ Of AI Agents From Unauthorized Actions Is A Key Challenge Of The AI Wave

stories.Headline: AI Reads the Classics: Machine Learning Extracts Themes from Political Theory
stories.Summary:
Stephen J. DeCanio published a commentary in the journal AI Perspectives arguing that Alan Turing’s 1950 paper on machine intelligence raised a problem that is still unsolved. Turing had imagined that artificial intelligence would develop much like the education of a child, an idea that came long before modern machine learning took shape. The problem DeCanio points to is how humans might teach or shape artificial intelligences to behave in ways that match moral standards. As one small step, he applied a natural language processing technique to works of classical political theory.

The technique is called Latent Dirichlet Allocation, or LDA, and it belongs to a family of “bag-of-words” methods that count word frequencies while ignoring sentence structure. DeCanio applied it to classical political texts downloaded in machine-readable form from Project Gutenberg. The results showed that even corpora made up of only a few authors and works could be processed successfully, and that the method works on texts distant in time from the present day. All the calculations ran on a desktop PC using Mathematica 12, so no supercomputing resources were needed. The three contributors to The Federalist Papers were treated as a single author.

DeCanio is emphatic about what the results do not show, saying the findings cannot demonstrate human-level understanding of texts by an unsupervised AI. He notes that the LDA topics are not summaries of the works, and that texts with opposing political implications might show very similar topic signatures. He uses an “M” prefix before words like analysis and comprehension to mark that machines are doing the operations, which sidesteps the question of what thinking is. He concludes that we have no idea what it is like to be an AI, and that the gap between word patterns and genuine grasp of an argument remains wide.

The commentary places the demonstration within a larger argument about moral development in machines, suggesting that an emergent AI’s motivations might partly be formed by absorbing human writings on ethics and politics. It cites an estimate that raising a child in the United States cost roughly 233,610 dollars in 2015, excluding college, and that combined public and private spending on education plus childrearing comes to roughly 10 percent of U.S. national output. It also cites an estimate that even careful software engineering in industry rarely achieves an error rate better than one error per 1,000 lines of code. One cited analysis suggests reasonable accuracy from LDA sampling may often be achieved with 5,000 iterations or less. The paper makes clear that the distance between topic signatures and moral understanding is still enormous, and no current technique closes it.

Articles.Title: AI Reads the Classics: Machine Learning Extracts Themes from Political Theory

stories.Headline: Democratic-led US Congress to turn up heat on Beijing over AI, Taiwan: analyst
stories.Summary:
US midterm elections were held on November 4, 2026, and the results so far were described by Chinese analyst Zhao Minghao as a "blue tsunami" and a "big win" for the Democrats. Zhao is a professor at Fudan University's Institute of International Studies. He said the results would turn US President Donald Trump into a "lame duck." The article was published by the South China Morning Post on November 4, 2026, with reporting by Dewey Sim in Beijing.

According to the article, a Democratic-controlled US Congress will ramp up pressure on Beijing over Taiwan, artificial intelligence and export controls. The article says the US midterm results will not upend Washington's broader China strategy. It says the "blue tsunami" could still shift Washington's tactics. The article does not give further numbers or dates beyond the November 4, 2026 publication and update times.

Zhao, the analyst cited in the article, said the results were a "big win" for the Democrats. He said they would make Trump a "lame duck." He said a Democratic-controlled Congress would increase pressure on Beijing over Taiwan, AI and export controls. The article attributes these views to Zhao and does not say what US officials said.

The article frames the midterms as unlikely to change Washington's overall approach to Beijing. It says the shift would come in tactics rather than strategy. It does not say what happens next beyond the expected pressure from a Democratic-led Congress. The article does not give further details on timing or specific measures.

Articles.Title: Democratic-led US Congress to turn up heat on Beijing over AI, Taiwan: analyst

stories.Headline: The Value of the Fine Arts in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
Rachel Toor, a professor of creative writing and contributing editor at Inside Higher Ed, wrote the article about her experiences in fall 2026. She attended a week-long "Fitness and Embodiment" retreat in Crete in early September, which combined body training with acting coaching. She had never taken a theater class before and signed up at the last minute before a series of upcoming presentations. At the retreat, an acting coach led eight participants in improvisation exercises, including an imaginary ball game, reading lines aloud, and blindfolded dancing. She also visited the Manhattan School of Music with its president, Jim Gandre, where she watched students rehearse a reinterpretation of Verdi's Otello.

The article argues that colleges should teach students skills that AI cannot replace, such as presence, collaboration and honest communication. Toor describes how the retreat taught her to stay in her body and in contact with other people rather than leaving her body during stressful moments. She notes that AI tools like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT can now write prose, insert jokes, simulate a personal touch and shape arguments. She says employers she interviewed for her book cared about attitude, not majors or credentials, and looked for applicants who were humble, hungry and smart.

She suggests colleges give students more chances to practice being fully present with others, listening, responding and recovering from a stumble. Toor says she is not ready to give up her view that writing is the most important skill, even with the advent of the bots. She describes herself as uncomfortable speaking to groups and says she often cannot remember what she said after a talk. She writes that she is not ready to sign up for an improv group but could use public-speaking lessons from actors.

She credits the retreat with teaching her about presence and honest communication rather than faking sincerity or performing confidence. The article does not say what happens next at any institution or whether any programs will change. It presents Toor's reflections and her suggestion that colleges teach more students how to act as humans with bodies who need to communicate with other humans. She frames this as one thing colleges can teach in the age of AI, alongside writing better prompts or sorting through bot-generated prose and music.

Articles.Title: The Value of the Fine Arts in the Age of AI

stories.Headline: What Teenagers' AI Use Reveals About the EU Kids Act
stories.Summary:
A YouGov survey of 970 French children and teenagers aged 11 to 17, and 1,138 parents of children in the same age range, was commissioned by Interface and carried out between June 24 and 30, 2026. It found that 40% of French 11- and 12-year-olds report using general-purpose generative AI at least weekly, compared with 26% according to parents' own estimates. Among 11- and 12-year-olds who use generative AI, 14% say they turn to these tools to confide in them. The study also found that 23% of children in that age group regularly use generative AI embedded in social media and 16% regularly use AI companions, even though most of these services' terms and conditions restrict access under the age of 13. Among teenagers who use generative AI, 92% report spending more time than they would like on at least one of the tools covered, rising to 59% for users of AI companions and 57% for users of AI embedded in social media, compared with 45% for general-purpose generative AI users.

In September 2026 the European Commission presented its EU KIDS Act, a proposal introducing obligations across social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, and AI chatbots and companions. It sets a three-tier system for social media and video-sharing services presenting certain risks: children under 13 would generally be prohibited from holding accounts, those aged 13 and 14 could use limited accounts supervised by a parent or guardian, and teenagers aged 15 and above could open their own accounts. AI chatbots and companions are treated differently: the proposal does not establish an equivalent general prohibition on access for children under 13, and Article 14 requires their access to be enabled and controlled through parental tools. These services would also face safety-by-design obligations, including measures addressing potentially addictive designs and emotionally dependent relationships. Providers would have to avoid designs that simulate interpersonal relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency, refrain by default from using information from previous interactions in later conversations, and conduct risk evaluations before placing their systems on the market.

The article says the reliance on parental controls deserves scrutiny, noting that only 32% of parents feel sufficiently supported in helping their children navigate generative AI and 42% report receiving no support at all. It argues that the primary responsibility for mitigating risks should remain with the companies designing the systems. It also questions why the KIDS Act prohibits children under 13 from holding accounts on certain platforms while allowing them to access AI companions under parental supervision, saying such distinctions should be supported by evidence rather than assumptions. The article adds that 44% of parents whose children use generative AI say they do not feel at ease with that use, and that 38% of all surveyed teenagers report negative emotions at least weekly, rising to 50% among regular users of AI companions, while cautioning that correlation does not imply causation.

The article says the findings come at a timely moment as negotiations on the KIDS Act get underway. It calls on policymakers to pay greater attention to AI features that encourage prolonged, personalized or emotionally significant interactions, to ensure consistency in how risks are approached across different categories of digital services, and to invest in independent, longitudinal research on how children's interactions with generative AI evolve over time. It says the current evidence remains limited and that self-reported surveys cannot establish causal relationships between AI use and well-being. It adds that regulation must preserve the opportunities generative AI can offer children, including learning, creativity and access to information, while ensuring they are not left alone to navigate potentially harmful systems.

Articles.Title: What Teenagers' AI Use Reveals About the EU Kids Act

stories.Headline: As Shoppers Warm to Agentic Commerce, Terms of Use Have to be Clearly Defined
stories.Summary:
Riskified, a digital fraud and risk intelligence company, released its latest Agentic Commerce Pulse report on November 4, 2026, based on a poll of more than 5,100 consumers globally. The report found that 80 percent of those surveyed have used AI for some part of the shopping process. Half of all consumers said they were more comfortable than six months ago with an AI shopping agent completing a purchase without immediate approval. The findings suggest comfort with AI shopping is running ahead of actual adoption.

The data showed a gap between using AI to browse and letting it buy. Seventy-four percent said they would allow agentic purchases in some form, and 68 percent said they were likely to use AI for holiday shopping. Yet just 11 percent had completed a purchase inside an AI tool, and only 7 percent were comfortable letting AI buy something without their approval. On control, 43 percent still want to approve every purchase, while 29 percent would allow automatic purchases within rules they set.

On responsibility, 51 percent said the AI platform should issue refunds when AI makes a mistake, even though the terms of agents like Muse and Instinct say users are responsible for their agents' actions. Asked who they would trust to run a shopping agent, one-third named a general AI platform such as ChatGPT or Gemini, 17 percent named a retailer or brand they already shop with, and 9 percent named a bank, credit card company or digital wallet. Jeff Otto, chief marketing officer at Riskified, said consumers are getting comfortable delegating shopping to AI but have not delegated the blame. He said agentic commerce only scales if merchants can tell a real customer using a legitimate agent from a hijacked account or malicious automation.

The report's authors said the findings point to issues of control and governance that still need to be addressed for confident adoption and growth. They described an emerging relationship of conditional autonomy, in which consumers give AI greater authority if they set the limits. Riskified said it is extending its identity risk intelligence to the person behind the agent, for the order and the service interactions that follow. The company said retailers and brands will need to distinguish trusted customers and legitimate AI agents from fraudsters as agentic commerce expands.

Articles.Title: As Shoppers Warm to Agentic Commerce, Terms of Use Have to be Clearly Defined

stories.Headline: Binance $6.34 billion breach reveals DevSecOps architectural flaws
stories.Summary:
Attackers moved about $6.34 billion in digital assets from Binance's hot wallets on October 29, 2026, according to the company. About $2.85 billion of those assets were frozen or intercepted, and Binance replenished 98 per cent of affected tokens from its own reserves by October 31. The incident was detailed in Binance's November 3 report. The report says the breach began months earlier with a poisoned package install and escalated through a fake job interview that used an internal AI tool. The initial compromise in June 2026 involved an engineer on the Wallet DevOps team who downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation.

Binance's security team replaced the device and rotated credentials, but attackers gained access to the organisational chart, which exposed roles in the wallet infrastructure team. In September 2026, a second engineer was targeted through a fake job interview, including a video call with a false HR representative and a chat with a fictitious company's CEO. That engineer downloaded an interview assignment containing malicious code onto a work computer, and the code hijacked the local Python version manager by replacing its legitimate wrapper script. On October 29, 2026, attackers logged onto a third engineer's computer, used stolen credentials from another engineer, and deployed a container that triggered a malicious script against the internal wallet signing service, starting the drain at 20:05 UTC. Binance reported about $3.8 billion drained on Ethereum, along with 18,270 BTC, 233.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP.

Binance suspended withdrawals and shut down hot wallet services, but on Ethereum the attackers used EIP-7702 authorizations to create a persistence layer that gave an attacker-controlled smart contract partial execution rights over a hot wallet. The team had to develop a specialised procedure to revoke the authorizations, and the final unauthorised transfer of 2,961.9 ETH completed at 23:56 UTC. The report highlights five operational laws for Cloud Operations and DevSecOps, including containing the blast radius of internal AI tools, eliminating long-lived tokens on laptops, moving local development environments out of user-owned host paths, using allowlists for package managers, and game-daying un-revocable architecture. It says internal AI infrastructure should be treated as Tier-0 assets with isolated execution environments and strict least-privilege role-based access control.

Articles.Title: Binance $6.34 billion breach reveals DevSecOps architectural flaws
