stories.Headline: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist
stories.Summary:
Binance says hackers stole $6.34 billion from its hot wallets last week after a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers' computers, one through a fake job interview. The exchange published its initial incident report on November 3, and about $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted. The FBI has blamed the theft on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group. Binance said the intrusion was not a single breach or a simple phishing incident but unfolded in stages using fake recruiters, malicious downloads, hijacked employee computers and an internal AI tool.

The campaign began in June, when a Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while searching for a popular AI coding tool. Binance's security team caught it, replaced his device and reset credentials, but the attackers had already learned about his work and colleagues on the wallet infrastructure team. In September, a second engineer was approached by someone claiming to be a project director and invited to two interviews, the first with a fake HR representative and the second with the alleged CEO of a company that did not exist. The second interview ended with a request to download a coding assignment onto his work computer, and the assignment hid malicious code that ran as soon as he set it up. Binance said the 0-day malware was not detected by endpoint security tools at the time.

On October 20, the attackers used the infected machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of the first engineer's system and a third wallet engineer's system, though the report does not explain how the AI tool was used. On October 29, they signed into the third engineer's computer, deployed a container with credentials taken from the first engineer and started the attack with a malicious script. Binance says the attackers exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to move XRP, SOL, OP and BTC out of its hot wallets, and used the same service to abuse Ethereum's EIP-7702 mechanism, giving a contract under their control partial execution rights over a hot wallet. Because the hot wallet used multi-party computation, Binance had no single key to cancel the delegation right away; the last unauthorized transfer settled at 23:56 UTC and the delegation was cleared shortly after midnight.

Binance said it has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool, replaced devices and retired the engineers' credentials and tokens, and is engaging independent security firms to review the incident. It is also working on a research fund focused on AI security in blockchain environments and said it detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats this year. North Korea rejected the FBI's attribution, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, calling it a grave political provocation in a statement carried by state media. Co-CEO Richard Teng said 98% of the impacted tokens have been replenished and withdrawals have broadly resumed after reopening in phases from November 1. Elliptic says the stolen funds passed through about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in under four days, and as of November 3 roughly $3.18 billion remained in theft-linked addresses.

Articles.Title: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: Supreme Court examines DPDP Act's impact on journalism
stories.Summary:
The Supreme Court of India has issued notice to the Centre on a petition filed by the Digital News Publishers Association, which represents 21 digital news publishers. The petition challenges the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, arguing that it has no exemption for journalism. The association contends that the Act's consent, notice and erasure rules could hinder investigative reporting. The court is examining the matter, and a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, heard the case.

The petition, filed under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeks to declare Sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37 and 44(3) of the Act unconstitutional. It also challenges provisions of the DPDP Rules, 2025, and Section 36 read with Rule 23 and the Seventh Schedule, which deal with the Centre's power to request information from data-handling entities. Section 44(3), which amends the Right to Information Act, is challenged separately. The articles note that earlier drafts of India's data protection laws in 2018, 2019 and 2021 included provisions excluding journalists, but these were removed from the 2022 draft and the final legislation.

Senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the association, told the court that requiring journalists to seek consent from the people they report on could amount to pre-censorship. She said journalism cannot function if permission must first be obtained from individuals being investigated. Ankit Sahni, a partner at Ajay Sahni Associates, suggested that any exemption should be purpose-based rather than a blanket provision, distinguishing commercial use of personal data from journalistic use. Anirban Mohapatra, a partner at Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, noted that the GDPR and UK data protection regimes expressly include journalistic exemptions, unlike India's Act. Ronil Goger, managing partner at Blaze Legal, recommended an express, purpose-based exemption that would disapply consent, notice and erasure requirements only where they would materially prejudice public-interest journalism, while keeping data security and accountability duties.

Sahni also warned of potential conflicts under Section 12, which covers rights of rectification, updating and erasure, when legally and truthfully published reports are later disputed. He suggested appending corrections or updates instead of deleting reports, with redaction for sensitive information where necessary. The articles say the court's decision on data erasure could affect brand safety, contextual targeting and the stability of digital archives for advertisers. The bench observed that citizens' rights and press freedom must be balanced. The matter is listed for further hearing on November 17.

Articles.Title: Supreme Court examines DPDP Act's impact on journalism

stories.Headline: Google Legend Starts AI Firm at 58, Targeting $50 Billion Value
stories.Summary:
Jeff Dean, the former Google chief scientist who led work on the Gemini artificial intelligence models, founded a startup called Discovery Loop in August with three Google researchers. The company is seeking funding at a target valuation of $50 billion, about 67 trillion won, foreign media reported on Nov. 2. Dean had spent 27 years at Google, joining in 1999 as its 30th employee, and he also led development of the Tensor Processing Unit, Google's custom chip. He left the company in August, and Google shares fell 4% on Aug. 5, the day news of his exit emerged.

Discovery Loop is building an automated system in which AI proposes research hypotheses, runs thousands of experiments at the same time and then adjusts the hypotheses based on the results. The goal is to automate machine-learning research itself, leading to recursive self-improvement, in which AI builds better AI. The industry was stirred again last month by news that Chen Guangyu, a prodigy born in 2009 who worked on the Kimi K3 model at China's Moonshot AI, had joined the firm. Dean, 58, declined an interview request at an AI event held on Oct. 28 at Stanford University in Palo Alto, California.

Dean said he was at a stage of focusing on building the organization. In a lecture at the event, he explained that the reason for automating machine learning is to achieve faster scientific discovery. He said that if a system has solved 5,000 problems through AI innovation, the 5,001st should be something it can learn to solve on its own from the problems that came before. He said the company has built the agents and the harness it uses for its own development and automation, and that about 20 automatic improvement loops are running now.

Dean left Google, a large corporation, to found the venture as a public-benefit organization because he wants to concentrate on research goals. Inside Google, his departure had a bigger impact than the step back from frontline management by Demis Hassabis, the DeepMind chief known as the father of AlphaGo. The global tech industry is watching Dean's next move, and Silicon Valley paid particular attention to the startup because of his long record at Google. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported funding effort.

Articles.Title: Google Legend Starts AI Firm at 58, Targeting $50 Billion Value - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: The CFO’s Guide to LLMjacking: When Stolen AI Becomes a 7-Figure Cloud Bill
stories.Summary:
Cybercriminals are hijacking corporate AI credentials and reselling access to premium language models, leaving the victim companies to pay the cloud bills. Google's cyber threat intelligence division published a report on Monday, Nov. 2, documenting these attacks, which researchers call LLMjacking. The report found fraudulent AI consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day at some organizations, with cumulative charges reaching $1 million before access was revoked. Financial services, retail, technology and transportation companies across multiple continents were affected.

The attacks exploit exposed API keys, compromised service accounts, stolen identity tokens and credentials embedded in software repositories. Attackers sometimes expanded their privileges, activated unused AI services or created new credentials, and in one case enrolled compromised accounts in pay-as-you-go agreements and used short-lived service accounts to evade rate limits. Intermediary services called LLM Mixers aggregate stolen credentials and resell access at discounted prices. One such service, Jet Night, advertised unlimited access to frontier models for about $60 per month, and Google linked it to an attacker who made more than 500,000 API calls in under eight hours, passing nearly $1 million in token costs to a victim.

Google says the problem is that a cloud platform can correctly authenticate a request and bill the account without the business ever authorizing the expense. For finance teams, this raises the accounts payable question of who may incur an expense and what stops spending beyond that authorization. Google expects the criminal marketplace for stolen AI access to expand as premium models and autonomous workloads become more widely deployed. The same infrastructure that lets businesses buy intelligence instantly lets criminals consume it just as quickly.

Articles.Title: The CFO’s Guide to LLMjacking: When Stolen AI Becomes a 7-Figure Cloud Bill

stories.Headline: More Democratic Governors Could Shake $2.5 Trillion AI Buildout
stories.Summary:
U.S. midterm elections began on Nov. 3, with voters filling 35 Senate seats, all 435 House seats, and governorships and state legislative seats in 36 states. Washington's political establishment broadly expected Democrats to win the House by a wide margin, with the Senate seen as a close contest. Attention also focused on governorships, where Democrats were seen as having a chance to win a majority for the first time since 2010. Wall Street estimates that AI infrastructure investment exposed to Democratic governors alone exceeds 3,300 trillion won, or about $2.5 trillion.

Democrats were expected to win 230 to 240 of the 435 House seats, where the current split is 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies. Governorships currently stand at 26 Republicans and 24 Democrats, and Democrats were seen as likely to add two to four. The 100-seat Senate is divided among 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats and two independents who lean Democratic, and 35 seats were being contested. Even a 50-50 split would let Vice President JD Vance cast tie-breaking votes as Senate president. The dominant issue was severe inflation, with U.S. gasoline at $4.13 a gallon on Nov. 3, and a Financial Times poll with Focaldata from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1 found 68% of respondents dissatisfied with Trump's handling of prices.

Trump said in a podcast interview released by the New York Post on Nov. 1 that he would probably become "Mr. Veto" if Democrats won congressional majorities, and predicted they would come to him to cut a deal after bills were repeatedly rejected. The Justice Department, led by Todd Blanche, said on Nov. 3 it had deployed about 1,000 election monitors and observers across all 50 states, triple the scale of the 2022 midterms. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned on X that people who vote illegally would be tracked down and prosecuted, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement wrote that it would find, track, arrest and prosecute them. Democratic governors in Washington, North Carolina and Colorado mobilized National Guard members for election monitoring.

Financial markets focused on gubernatorial races and data center regulation, because community opposition to data center construction is emerging across the United States. The outcomes in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where large-scale AI infrastructure projects are planned, could have a decisive impact on the industry, and Texas accounts for about 25% of U.S. data center capacity expected to be operating by 2030. If Democrats capture both chambers, Trump could slide into an early lame-duck period, and Britain's Telegraph reported on Nov. 2 that parts of the White House and the Republican Party were worried Democrats would pursue impeachment. Britain's Times reported that officials including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and the White House counsel's office spent months drawing up ways for the president to advance his agenda without congressional approval, and Reuters reported that Miller and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought had been reviewing such steps since April.

Articles.Title: More Democratic Governors Could Shake $2.5 Trillion AI Buildout - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Passes Bill Requiring Disclosure Of Misleading AI In Ads 10/09/2026
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania lawmakers passed Senate Bill 806 on Wednesday, October 8, 2026, according to MediaPost. The bill would require advertisers to disclose the use of artificial intelligence in ads, but only in some circumstances. It mandates disclosure when material generated or modified by AI misleads consumers about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised. The bill now heads to Governor Josh Shapiro. The measure also sets formatting requirements for the disclaimers.

Audio disclaimers must be at a volume and cadence that consumers can hear, and visual disclaimers must appear on screen long enough to be read. Disclaimers must be in the same medium as the ad and, if feasible, should be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove from the synthetic content. The bill was sponsored by State Sen. Nick Pisciottano, a Democrat from Allegheny. Pisciottano said the requirements will help prevent scams and that consumers deserve to know if AI is being used to create a false impression about a product or service. He described the legislation as a commonsense transparency standard that lets Pennsylvanians make informed decisions about what they are buying while still allowing businesses to use the technology.

The tech industry group NetChoice opposed the bill, arguing in an October 4 letter to lawmakers that it is not necessary because federal and state laws already prohibit deception in ads. NetChoice wrote that layering a parallel, AI-specific regime on top of actively enforced laws does not enhance consumer protection, and it raised concerns that rules this prescriptive risk overwhelming short videos, small display ads and audio spots. Pennsylvania is not the only state attempting to regulate AI in ads. Last month, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a law requiring ads that use synthetic performers to clearly disclose that the digital figures were generated by AI. The articles do not say what happens next in Pennsylvania beyond the bill going to Governor Shapiro.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania Passes Bill Requiring Disclosure Of Misleading AI In Ads 10/09/2026 - MediaPost

stories.Headline: EU AI Act Explained – What Is Banned and What Comes Next?
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act sets binding limits on certain uses of artificial intelligence and creates obligations for other systems, according to The European Times. The Act applies to providers and deployers in specified circumstances, including some outside the EU, and its rules can reach providers abroad when a system's output is used in the EU. The framework classifies systems by risk into unacceptable, high, limited and minimal categories, and enforcement is carried out by national authorities and EU-level bodies. The article was published on 5 November 2026.

The Act bans specific practices, including manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behavior and cause significant harm, and exploitation of vulnerabilities linked to age, disability or social or economic situation. It bans social scoring that leads to unjustified or disproportionate detrimental treatment, individual criminal-risk assessments based solely on profiling or personality traits, and untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases. Biometric categorization that infers sensitive traits such as political opinions or sexual orientation is banned, as is emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions except for medical or safety reasons. Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is banned except in narrowly defined cases with strict safeguards and authorization, such as locating a missing person or preventing an imminent terrorist threat.

High-risk systems face requirements covering risk management, data quality, technical documentation, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity. Providers must complete conformity assessments, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking and register applicable systems in the EU database before market placement. General-purpose AI model providers must keep technical documentation, give information to downstream providers and publish a summary of training content, and they must adopt a copyright policy that respects rights reservations under text-and-data-mining rules. Models presenting systemic risk must undergo model evaluations including adversarial testing, report serious incidents to the AI Office and national authorities, and ensure adequate cybersecurity.

The article says compliance is subject to oversight by designated authorities, with enforcement shaped by the system's role and the conduct under review. The framework pairs market surveillance with complaints, investigations and corrective orders rather than relying solely on voluntary disclosures. Prohibited practices receive particular scrutiny under Article 5. The article does not set out further next steps beyond these enforcement arrangements.

Articles.Title: EU AI Act Explained – What Is Banned and What Comes Next? - The European Times

stories.Headline: Google, OpenAI, Anthropic pledge new AI scraping controls
stories.Summary:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic said they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of AI scraping across multiple crawlers. The announcement was reported on October 30, 2026. The standard comes from an Internet Draft that Anthropic's Kevin Kelley submitted to the AI Preferences working group at the IETF on the same date. The IETF's document tracker lists it as an individual draft, which does not represent official IETF standardization activity. Kelley said in a post to the working group's email list that Anthropic has started development to provide the feature.

The draft adds no new directive to robots.txt. A site would write an ordinary rule group under the policy token __usage_ai-training, using Allow and Disallow as usual. The draft's example opts out of AI training on the whole site except the /press-kit/ folder. The token's meaning rests on the working group's vocabulary draft, which defines AI training as using content to modify a generative model's learned parameters, and exempts models that only do non-generative tasks like classification or ranking. A wildcard group can never match the token, and a file without a __usage_ai-training group indicates no preference, which Kelley said is true of every robots.txt file currently published.

Based on the companies' provided timelines, none of the three currently supports the line. Google's John Mueller said that if a site opts out with the shared line and does not specify Google-Extended, Google plans to treat it as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended, and the control also applies to grounding within Gemini Apps. Microsoft wants sites that use its NoArchive and NoCache tags to switch to new preferences by March 1, 2027. Google and Microsoft described how each would handle the line differently.

The token does not control crawling. On October 22, Search Engine Journal covered a different working group draft, co-written by Google's Gary Illyes, that would add a Content-Usage rule to robots.txt. Kelley wrote that the group set that draft aside to make progress on the vocabulary. Rules already placed in robots.txt files will not count as part of any shared training preference.

Articles.Title: Asana lets AI teammates act across Google, Microsoft and Slack

stories.Headline: M’sia acts on AI election threat
stories.Summary:
Malaysia’s Communications Minister, Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, said existing laws will govern any action over alleged foreign interference in Malaysian elections through an artificial intelligence platform. He said the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) would also act under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and other applicable laws. Fahmi said the MCMC is seeking more information and clarification from the US AI company Anthropic. This follows a report alleging that its Claude AI platform was used to run an election manipulation operation targeting users in Malaysia. He gave the reply in writing in Parliament on Wednesday, in response to Pasir Mas MP Ahmad Fadhli Shaari.

The report, titled “Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI: September 2026”, described an alleged operation that used actual census data and millions of voter records. It said the operation targeted Malaysia’s political and social fault lines, including race, religion and the royal institution, across all 222 parliamentary constituencies. Anthropic reportedly uncovered the operation after identifying an account that used its platform to manipulate elections and target Malaysian users. Fahmi said the MCMC would decide on appropriate follow-up action based on the information and evidence obtained. He said this would be done in line with the commission’s jurisdiction and relevant legal provisions, including cooperation with enforcement agencies, security agencies, platform providers and relevant parties if necessary.

Fahmi also said the Digital Ministry is drafting an Artificial Intelligence Governance Bill. He said the bill would strengthen the country’s AI governance framework, including accountability, risk management and the responsibilities of parties developing and implementing AI systems. He said the government will continue to strengthen monitoring of the risks of AI technology misuse. He also said it will keep working with technology providers, digital platforms and relevant agencies to address online harms. The aim, he said, is to ensure the country’s digital environment remains safe, transparent and trusted.

Articles.Title: M’sia acts on AI election threat - The Star

stories.Headline: Korea Display Industry Association, KOSA Join Forces to Expand AI Adoption in Manufacturing
stories.Summary:
The Korea Display Industry Association signed a memorandum of understanding with the Korea Software Industry Association on November 3, 2026, at the KDIA building in Korea. The agreement is meant to speed up the adoption of artificial intelligence across display manufacturing operations. Lee Seung-woo, vice chairman of KDIA, and Seo Sung-il, vice chairman of KOSA, posed after signing the cooperation agreement. KDIA announced the partnership on November 3.

The partnership covers five areas, which are matching technologies and expanding networks between AI and software companies and display manufacturers, training specialists in AI and software for the display industry, advancing technologies that combine display and AI, jointly organizing seminars and conferences, and sharing domestic and international industry trends and information. The two associations aim to connect manufacturing companies' operational needs with relevant AI and software solutions. They want to help small and midsize materials, components and equipment suppliers adopt technologies suited to their production processes and business conditions. They also plan to identify AI implementation projects for individual companies and train specialists to carry them out.

Lee Seung-woo of KDIA said manufacturing AX was an important means of improving productivity and manufacturing competitiveness in the display industry. He added that the association would expand cooperation between AI and software companies and display manufacturers. The two associations previously co-hosted the "AX Connect Day: Display & Manufacturing" event in October. That event showcased AI adoption cases and solutions from display materials, components and equipment companies and facilitated business matchmaking between manufacturers and AI providers.

Articles.Title: Korea Display Industry Association, KOSA Join Forces to Expand AI Adoption in Manufacturing - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: The sovereign AI mandate: How Germany’s HLRS is anchoring Europe’s digital future
stories.Summary:
The High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart, known as HLRS, is at the center of a push for sovereign AI in Europe, according to a sponsored article published by CIO on November 4, 2026. The article says HLRS has built an environment for industrial enterprises and scientific researchers that keeps their data in Germany and conforms to European standards. It describes HLRS as an operational blueprint for European enterprises that want to scale out AI without giving up data sovereignty. The article was written by HPE and AMD, which supply technology to HLRS.

The article says European organizations have faced architectural lock-in, unpredictable data egress fees and compliance headaches when moving sensitive data across borders. It says HLRS uses HPE Cray Supercomputing platforms and HPE liquid-cooling technologies to support massive parallel processing and energy efficiency. It says HLRS also integrates AMD processors and accelerators to handle both traditional high-performance computing simulations and modern AI training workloads. The article says this lets users train multibillion-parameter AI models and run billions of simulation cycles, including for automotive vision models and aerodynamic simulations.

The article presents HLRS as a co-innovation partner rather than just a data center, serving both midsize enterprises and multinational corporations. It says the model offers future-proof compliance, protection of intellectual property and uncompromised performance. HPE and AMD say they are partnering to deliver the next generation of AI and supercomputing infrastructure, combining HPE system design with AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct accelerators. The article directs readers to a podcast episode, This Week in HPC Episode 400, for more on Europe's strategic investments in digital autonomy.

The article ties the shift to the EU AI Act and to European concerns about privacy laws in other jurisdictions. It says sovereign AI is no longer a niche regulatory preference but a core business strategy for CIOs. It argues that organizations building on data autonomy will be positioned to lead as AI matures. The article does not say what specific projects or customers HLRS has signed.

Articles.Title: The sovereign AI mandate: How Germany’s HLRS is anchoring Europe’s digital future

stories.Headline: USCIS Seeks Input on AI-Enabled Contact Center Recompete
stories.Summary:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services posted a request for information on SAM.gov on Monday, according to ExecutiveGov. The notice seeks industry feedback on a cloud-based, artificial intelligence-enabled contact center to replace the agency's Enterprise Customer Experience operations. The new requirement is called Enterprise Customer Experience 2, or ECX2. USCIS described ECX2 as a recompete of an existing task order rather than a follow-on.

The current contact centers handle roughly 15 million toll-free calls a year through about 1,500 agents at 18 sites nationwide, many working remotely. An interactive voice response system resolves about 70 percent of External Affairs calls without a live agent. USCIS wants a FedRAMP Moderate platform with 99.99 percent availability and room for as many as 3,000 live agents, plus links to Salesforce and ServiceNow. The RFI asks whether AI voice systems can top 95 percent intent-matching accuracy, respond in under 700 milliseconds and keep at least 75 percent of calls from reaching an agent, with an 85 percent target.

Responses are due by 8 a.m. Eastern time on Nov. 12, emailed as PDFs to Contract Specialist Brittany Willette. In October the agency forecast a value of $50 million to $100 million for ECX2 and set March 1, 2027, as the expected solicitation release date. The forecast also shows the current arrangement under the Enterprise Infrastructure Solutions vehicle expiring July 2, 2027. Vendors must explain how their solution could run without the incumbent's proprietary tools and how the government would retain control of its data and configurations.

Articles.Title: USCIS Seeks Input on AI-Enabled Contact Center Recompete

stories.Headline: Freshworks crosses $1 billion ARR, Q3 revenue up 14 per cent
stories.Summary:
Freshworks reported its third-quarter results for the period ended September 30, 2026. Revenue rose 14 per cent to $245.4 million, up from $215.1 million in the same quarter a year earlier. The Nasdaq-listed software company also said it crossed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue after the quarter, ahead of its earlier projection of year-end 2026. The growth came from demand for its employee experience platform and AI-led offerings.

The company posted GAAP net income of $18.3 million, compared with a net loss of $4.7 million a year earlier and net income of $3.2 million in the previous quarter. Non-GAAP operating income rose to $73.2 million from $45.2 million in Q3 2025, and the non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 29.8 per cent from 21 per cent. Customers contributing more than $100,000 in ARR rose 25 per cent year-on-year to 1,821, while those contributing over $50,000 rose 18 per cent to 4,257. New customers included Tata Technologies, Texas Christian University, Unilabs (UK) and Jose Cuervo. The company ended the quarter with $697.3 million in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities, and operating cash flow grew 22 per cent to $77.7 million.

CEO and President Dennis Woodside said the company's upmarket strategy delivered another strong quarter. He said momentum upmarket accelerated, with new multi-product employee experience deals increasing over 35 per cent. Last month Freshworks acquired Torii, a SaaS management and AI spend governance platform, and Robusta Dev, an AI-powered IT troubleshooting firm, spending a combined $102.5 million, paid primarily in cash. Earlier, in January 2026, it acquired AI-powered incident management software provider FireHydrant for about $88.7 million in cash.

Articles.Title: Freshworks crosses $1 billion ARR, Q3 revenue up 14 per cent

stories.Headline: US Treasury's COINS Act Proposal Would Broaden AI Investment Prohibitions and Expand Biotechnology and Quantum Restrictions - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
On 22 October 2026 the US Department of the Treasury issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to implement the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025 and expand the Outbound Investment Security Program. The proposal would add countries and technologies, including hypersonic systems and biotechnology, and would widen the existing quantum restrictions to cover associated software and algorithms and specified sensing and networking applications. The biggest change concerns artificial intelligence, which the proposal calls super intelligence, or SI, following Executive Order 14434 of 29 September 2026. Under the proposal, covered transactions by US persons involving foreign persons that develop any SI system would be prohibited, with no notification-only category and no capability threshold. The NPRM was published in the Federal Register on 26 October 2026 at 91 Fed.

Reg. 67396 and would set out the rules as a new 31 C.F.R. Part 851. The existing rules at 31 C.F.R. Part 850 would keep applying until the new rules take effect, and the new rules would not apply retroactively. Congress enacted the COINS Act on 18 December 2025 as part of the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, and the statute calls for final regulations within 450 days of enactment, or by 13 March 2027. Comments on the proposal are due 7 December 2026.

The countries of concern would expand beyond China, Hong Kong and Macau to include Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia. The proposal would also prohibit transactions involving specified biotechnology activities, which could restrict US investment in much of China's pharmaceutical and life sciences tools industries. For semiconductors, prohibited activities would include high-bandwidth memory with bandwidth density above 2 gigabytes per second per square millimeter, radiation-hardened integrated circuits, photonic integrated circuits and advanced packaging. Hypersonic systems would be defined as vehicles or weapon delivery systems capable of sustained flight at Mach 5 or greater.

Treasury has elected to treat all SI development as prohibited even though the COINS Act does not compel that result, and the article says this choice is likely to draw substantial comment. The exceptions for publicly traded securities and SEC-registered fund shares would remain substantively unchanged, but the proposal would eliminate the business development company exception and extend the knowingly directing prohibition to notifiable transactions. Because the public securities exceptions would remain, the expanded prohibitions would fall most heavily on private, venture and pre-IPO investments and on investments carrying governance rights. The proposal would also impose an increased compliance burden on limited partners.

Articles.Title: US Treasury's COINS Act Proposal Would Broaden AI Investment Prohibitions and Expand Biotechnology and Quantum Restrictions - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Democrats seize Congress, advance US AI regulation despite industry spending
stories.Summary:
In the U.S. midterm elections, candidates who called for stronger regulation of artificial intelligence were elected one after another, and Democrats took control of both the House and Senate. The AI and venture investment industry spent tens of millions of dollars to back candidates friendly to deregulation and to unseat regulation advocates, but the effort did not stop the wins. Among the winners, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's U.S. Senate race on Nov. 4 and proposed a "controlled AI" plan to halt AI development until new safeguards are in place, along with a new government agency dedicated to AI oversight. In Colorado, Democrat Manny Lutinel was elected to the U.S. House after introducing AI regulation bills in the state legislature, and he pledged to require safety reviews by an independent body before major AI models are released. In California's 11th District, which includes San Francisco, Scott Wiener led fellow Democrat Connie Chan by about 17,000 votes, an 11-percentage-point margin, with 51% of the vote counted, and he says a federal agency is needed to handle AI safety and oversight.

The industry spending included the super PAC Leading the Future, which received large donations from venture firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman and ran a campaign to defeat AI regulation advocate Alex Bores in New York's Democratic congressional primary. Bores lost the primary, but in the general election Micah Lasher, who introduced a state AI regulation bill with him, was elected. Wiener previously introduced and passed an AI transparency bill in the state Senate, and Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed the bill once but signed it when it was reintroduced the following year. Lutinel received support in this election from the super PAC Public First, which campaigned on AI safety.

With Democrats controlling Congress, some expect a check on the Trump administration's push to limit state-by-state AI regulations. Brandon Steinhauser, a Republican strategist and CEO of the Alliance for Safe AI, told Time magazine that there will be an enormous amount of legislation at the state and federal levels and that the AI industry needs to prepare for that. However, even if Congress passes an AI regulation bill, President Trump could veto it, so some say practical regulation could be crafted at the state government level. Scott Singer, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that if Congress ends up in gridlock, what happens in California will dictate AI in the United States and around the world.

Articles.Title: Democrats seize Congress, advance US AI regulation despite industry spending - Chosunbiz

stories.Headline: Binance reveals LinkedIn lure in $6.3 billion crypto theft
stories.Summary:
North Korean attackers used fake job interviews on LinkedIn to steal $6.3 billion from Binance's crypto accounts, the company disclosed. The attackers contacted an engineer through a legitimate job-hunting platform while posing as a Project Director. The engineer's profile mentioned experience at Binance, which made them a target. The supposed Project Director set up two rounds of interviews with people claiming to be an HR representative and the CEO of a fictitious company. This staged recruitment led the engineer to download a malicious assignment, which gave the attackers access to company systems.

Earlier, the attackers targeted a different engineer through an online advertisement for a tampered version of Homebrew, a software installation tool. Binance said this employee downloaded the tampered tool through the advertisement, bypassing approved company channels. The company found and removed the malicious software, but the attackers had already obtained information about the engineer's responsibilities and other employees who managed company wallets. The information from both attacks let the hackers control several wallets and drain funds, Binance said. The theft took place over several hours, and Binance suspended withdrawals for about 48 hours before restoring them.

Binance recovered around $2.5 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion after Tether and Circle froze stablecoins. The exchange also replenished 98 per cent of the stolen coins using reserves and said customer funds were safe. A Binance spokesperson said employees in non-public facing roles are not allowed to keep LinkedIn profiles. Binance said it had previously detected and prevented 57 North Korea-related hacking attempts in 2026.

Articles.Title: Binance reveals LinkedIn lure in $6.3 billion crypto theft

stories.Headline: Inaccurate information, algorithmic bias undermine justice - Kaduna Attorney-General warns young lawyers
stories.Summary:
James Atung Kanyip, the Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Kaduna State, spoke at the Votive Mass and Opening of the New Legal Year of the National Association of Catholic Lawyers, Catholic Diocese of Kaduna. The event was held at Holy Family Catholic Church in Barnawa, Kaduna, on a theme of AI and legal automation and the opportunities and risks they pose for Catholic lawyers. Kanyip, who is also a member of the association, encouraged lawyers to embrace artificial intelligence and legal automation to improve legal practice and access to justice. He made the call while also urging caution about the risks of the technology.

Kanyip said AI could help lawyers with legal research, document organisation, routine drafting and information management. He said this could reduce delays and costs and let practitioners spend more time on complex legal matters and their clients. He warned that inaccurate information, algorithmic bias and breaches of client confidentiality could undermine justice if the technology is used without proper safeguards. He stressed that lawyers must verify AI-generated information and remain professionally accountable for their work.

Kanyip further emphasised that technological advancement must uphold human dignity, fairness and the common good. He reaffirmed the Kaduna State Government's commitment to strengthening justice institutions and improving access to justice. The articles do not say what specific measures or rules, if any, will follow from his remarks. They also give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Inaccurate information, algorithmic bias undermine justice - Kaduna Attorney-General warns young lawyers - Daily Post Nigeria

stories.Headline: Korea Eximbank commits $170m to Tanzania's first EDCF AI project
stories.Summary:
The Export-Import Bank of Korea will lend $170 million to Tanzania to build an artificial intelligence education center, the bank said Thursday. Senior Executive Vice President Lee Dong-hoon and Tanzanian Deputy Finance Minister Natu E. Mwamba signed the loan agreement in Dar es Salaam on Wednesday. It is the first AI project financed through South Korea's Economic Development Cooperation Fund. It is also the first project under Seoul's K-AI Package, which pairs development financing with Korean AI technologies to help emerging economies and create overseas business for Korean companies.

The center will sit on a 35,000-square-meter site and offer four programs covering AI, robotics, data analytics and the Internet of Things. It will focus on training specialists in physical AI and will have AI laboratories and advanced training facilities. It will use Korean technologies and education systems for teaching, assessments and instructor training. The curriculum will also use cloud-based platforms for sharing courses and managing learning, with the aim of setting a model for AI education in Tanzania.

Lee said the bank would use the project as a first step toward establishing Korean AI technologies in Africa. He pledged continued support for Korean companies pursuing overseas infrastructure projects in AI, digital technology and other strategic sectors. The Tanzanian government plans to develop a large-scale AI data center nearby and set up an AI cluster to attract technology companies. Korea Eximbank said the project could serve as a foothold for expanding Korean AI technologies and infrastructure businesses into Africa.

Articles.Title: Korea Eximbank commits $170m to Tanzania's first EDCF AI project

stories.Headline: Godfather of DevOps Advises Software Engineers to Brace for Agentic AI Impact
stories.Summary:
Patrick Debois, known as the godfather of DevOps and a co-author of The DevOps Handbook, now works as product DevRel lead at Tessl. He spoke at an AI DevCon event hosted by Tessl on November 3, 2026, according to a DevOps.com report by Mike Vizard. He told attendees that DevOps will increasingly revolve around multiple AI agents doing tasks at the same time. He warned that those agents may undo each other's work as code merges pile up without orchestration.

Debois said agents need a way to claim a ticket through a concurrency locking mechanism so they do not step on each other. Once an agent claims a ticket, it should split the request into tasks that sub-agents run in parallel, he said. He also described speculative trains of merges of pull requests to finish work more efficiently. Without orchestration, token consumption and infrastructure use by agents will skyrocket, he noted.

Debois said DevOps teams are responsible for redesigning serial workflows for parallel work. He argued that too many teams simply add agents to existing workflows, which adds tension without delivering the benefits. He said teams need to start designing now for what is becoming the new normal. He added that teams should let engineers' personal agents join workflows and find ways to record output without storing every ticket, so humans can review risks and exceptions.

The article says most DevOps teams have adopted AI coding tools, but few have re-engineered workflows for parallel tasks. Debois said reaching that goal could let end users vibecode applications with the rigor engineers require. The article does not say how far teams are down the path of agentic engineering. It concludes that much work remains before AI lives up to its potential.

Articles.Title: Godfather of DevOps Advises Software Engineers to Brace for Agentic AI Impact - DevOps.com

stories.Headline: Alaska’s U.S. Senate race draws significant donations from AI company employees
stories.Summary:
An analysis of Federal Election Commission records, reported by the Alaska Beacon on November 3, 2026, found that Alaska's U.S. Senate race drew more campaign money from employees of AI companies than any other 2026 Senate race. At least 19 employees contributed approximately $119,000 to the campaigns of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, with most giving close to the legal limit of $3,500 per election, or $7,000 for the primary and general together, and $5,000 a year to a leadership PAC. Many of the donations came from employees of Anthropic, and none of the donors listed an Alaska address, with most living in California. Peltola received at least $56,000, nearly all from Anthropic employees, while Sullivan received about $63,000 for his campaign plus $35,000 through his leadership PAC, True North, for a combined total of about $98,000. Neither campaign responded to requests for comment.

The race also includes Republican Gerald Heikes, who has no campaign and therefore cannot receive donations, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who received no contributions from the AI-company employees examined. The contest became more contentious after a New York Times report that Peltola recruited Daniel J. Sullivan as a spoiler, which her campaign denied to the Times. Once donations to PACs are included, South Dakota Senate campaigns pulled in the most, and the top individual candidate was Republican Mike Rounds of South Dakota with $165,100 to his campaign and PACs. Counting employees of Google, Microsoft, Meta and other big tech firms, Peltola ranked fifth among Senate candidates nationwide and Sullivan 16th, with Peltola supported by close to 150 big tech employees compared with four for Sullivan. Most of the money to both candidates came through joint fundraising committees rather than direct donations.

Brendan Fischer, Director of Strategic Investigations at Campaign Legal Center, said large contributions from a small number of employees in the same industry can suggest donors see a candidate as favorable to their interests, but he cautioned against using employer data as proof of coordinated giving. He said political money often flows toward races where donors believe their contributions can have an impact, and donors wanting to influence the chamber's balance of power may be attracted to Alaska's race since it could determine control of the Senate. Sullivan has advocated expanding data center development in the state and pushed for federal advanced AI data centers on Alaska's military bases, and in April the Air Force sought developers for potential AI data centers on about 4,700 acres across three Alaska installations. Peltola has focused less on data centers and more on affordability and energy costs, according to a Newsweek report, and Sullivan holds approximately $5 million in stock in his family's chemical company, RPM International, whose subsidiaries supply specialized coatings used in data centers, according to The Alaska Current.

An AP-NORC poll from September found that 67% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are worried data centers will impact water supply, and 57% of Democrats and 50% of Republicans believe AI will harm society more than help it in the next 10 years. Krystal Lapp, Interim Executive Director of Alaskans for Data Center Accountability, said the election will have significant impacts on Alaskan land and resource allocation, and that with the boom of AI, politicians and others are inviting people up because of Alaska, adding that the state looks like a cash cow but they are not going to benefit us. In September, the Alaska Beacon reported that the Alaska Department of Natural Resources decided to transfer 30 square miles of land to the state-owned economic development agency AIDEA for a multi-use industrial and energy development district, and AIDEA officials have said there are no existing plans for data centers but that they could potentially be built. Lapp said she is against the executive orders that were put through and against the gutting of the public process, and that by taking away that process they take away that responsibility piece.

Articles.Title: Alaska’s U.S. Senate race draws significant donations from AI company employees

stories.Headline: Nexus Mods adds AI disclosure rules but stops short of a blanket ban
stories.Summary:
Nexus Mods, a website for finding and downloading PC mods, introduced rules requiring authors to disclose whether they used AI and to explain how, Eurogamer reported on Wednesday, 4 November 2026. A new filter lets visitors hide mods that use AI. The requirements also apply to existing mods, and their authors have 60 days to check whether they comply. Changes to the site's interface will make AI labels more prominent, though not all backend updates will arrive at once. The site will not ban AI-generated mods outright.

AI-generated mods are allowed if they meet criteria covering permissions, transparency, presentation and conduct, the post said. Nexus Mods is working on permission options for AI use and training, as well as forks and derivative mods. The site said it will not use mods to train AI or sell or license them to anyone doing so. It has not introduced new rules for AI-generated or AI-assisted thumbnails, describing them as grey zones. Co-owner Foledinho said Nexus Mods was pro-human creativity but that it would be difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable.

He said an outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use, and that the site would prefer the opposite, with AI use out in the open, clearly labelled and regulated under rules it can implement. He acknowledged that not everyone would disclose their AI use and said the site was establishing moderation standards with consequences for rule violations. The post said the site still needs to work through details involving existing licences, forks and how permissions apply to different versions of a mod. It said the changes would take longer as a result, but described the current plans as a good first step.

Articles.Title: Nexus Mods adds AI disclosure rules but stops short of a blanket ban - Mezha.net

stories.Headline: Visitors test their skills against AI tractors
stories.Summary:
Visitors competed against an AI-powered tractor in a simulated field-plowing task at an agriculture expo in Daegu. The event was the 2026 Korea International Exhibition of Machinery, Equipment, Science and Technology for Agriculture. It opened on Wednesday at EXCO in Buk District, Daegu. The article was published on November 4, 2026.

In the simulation, the AI-driven tractor worked at a steady speed and covered a consistent area. The field plowed by the visitor had uneven, overlapping furrows. The comparison was shown on two monitors, with the tractor on the left and the visitor's work on the right. Visitors tested their skills against the machine to see how their plowing compared.

The article does not name any of the visitors who took part. It also does not name the organizers of the expo or the makers of the AI tractor. No one is quoted in the article, so there are no comments to paraphrase. The story gives no figures beyond the year 2026 and the date of November 4.

The article offers little context beyond the expo itself. It does not say how many visitors attended or how the competition was scored. It does not say what happens next or whether the expo runs for more than one day. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Visitors test their skills against AI tractors

stories.Headline: MARA Holdings (MARA) Commits Billions To AI Power, Is It 63% Below Fair Value?
stories.Summary:
MARA Holdings has committed about US$1.5 billion to buy the Long Ridge gas plant and roughly US$600 million for Texas land, the articles say. The company is pushing into AI infrastructure while its revenue and digital asset values decline. Its share price has fallen sharply, with a 1-month return down 38.5% and a year to date return down 30.7%. The 1-year total shareholder return has fallen 59.9%.

The company is building a powered land and data center portfolio of roughly 4.8 GW, anchored by the Long Ridge campus and the planned Matagorda County site. The portfolio could support future AI and high performance computing leases that add new revenue streams. MARA closed at $6.87, while the most followed valuation view puts fair value near $18.61. That view sees the stock as 63% undervalued, and 164 investors share it.

The articles say the narrative can break if MARA keeps posting large losses tied to Bitcoin. They also say it can break if the company struggles to convert its 4.8 GW power portfolio into signed AI leases. The articles describe two important warning signs and key risks to the narrative. They present the bullish fair value story and the headwinds as a normal tension for investors to weigh.

The articles say MARA is rebranding and focusing on AI infrastructure alongside increased Bitcoin backed borrowing and recent power asset deals. They describe the gap between price and narrative as wide and rooted in how the power portfolio might translate into contracts and cash flow. They advise reviewing the underlying numbers and weighing them against the warning signs. They do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: MARA Holdings (MARA) Commits Billions To AI Power, Is It 63% Below Fair Value?

stories.Headline: Foreign AI election interference claims under Online Safety Act probe, ministry tells Parliament
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's Communications Ministry told Parliament on November 4 that the government will use existing communications and cyber safety laws to counter an alleged foreign-linked artificial intelligence influence campaign targeting Malaysian voters. The ministry said this in a written parliamentary reply the day before to Pasir Mas MP Tuan Haji Ahmad Fadhli Shaari, who asked what steps the government would take to investigate foreign election meddling through generative AI platforms, including Claude. The ministry confirmed that the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission is treating the allegations seriously and has sought detailed technical clarification and supporting evidence from Anthropic, the US-based creator of Claude. The controversy began with a September threat intelligence report from Anthropic, which said a commercial actor had used Claude to develop core parts of a covert political influence campaign. Enforcement action will be pursued under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, alongside the Online Safety Act 2025 and related statutes under the commission's purview.

The agency will coordinate with federal security bodies, criminal investigators, and social media platform providers where necessary. At the same time, the Digital Ministry is drafting a standalone AI Governance Bill to codify corporate accountability, risk mitigation requirements, and developer liabilities across the artificial intelligence life cycle. The reply gave no firm timeline for introducing the bill in Parliament. Anthropic attributed the activity to BBS Bilisim Teknolojileri, a technology firm based in Istanbul, saying the operation tried to build synthetic persona networks, automated bot accounts, and bespoke propaganda websites.

The operation reportedly harvested demographic census records and voter data to profile electorates across all 222 federal parliamentary constituencies. The Turkish company denied involvement on September 11, and Anthropic said it had shut down the offending accounts and that the campaign showed no evidence of gaining meaningful organic traction among genuine users. After the disclosures, Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said urged authorities to mount a comprehensive and independent investigation. The ministry did not disclose whether Anthropic has responded to the commission's queries, whether police have registered a formal criminal investigation, or how existing domestic statutes can effectively hold offshore technology operators and foreign-based software firms accountable beyond Malaysian borders.

Articles.Title: Foreign AI election interference claims under Online Safety Act probe, ministry tells Parliament - Yahoo

stories.Headline: Partos urges action on AI copyright use after award win
stories.Summary:
Composer Antony Partos used his win at the APRA AMCOS Screen Music Awards to press his campaign against the use of copyrighted creative work in artificial intelligence systems without permission. He won Best Music for a Television Drama for The Artful Dodger at the event at Brisbane's Fortitude Music Hall, where industry figures wore record-shaped badges bearing the copyright symbol in support of the Australian Guild of Screen Composers' Human Made campaign. The campaign focuses on concerns that AI companies are using copyrighted music and other creative work to train models without consent or payment. Partos chairs the guild's Industrial Relations Committee and co-founded Sonar Music.

APRA AMCOS, which represents more than 128,000 Australian songwriters and composers, estimates that AUD $227 million in revenue for Australian and New Zealand music creators could be at risk by 2028. It has proposed a voluntary licensing framework for AI training, under which AI developers would seek permission and pay rights holders for material used to train systems, while creators could choose whether to opt in. Partos said that if AI needs copyrighted material to train its models, a licence system needs to be implemented to compensate artists who choose to opt in. He said AI systems can learn from a composer's style, orchestration and techniques to create new commercial music without reproducing a specific work or compensating the original creator.

Partos said the issue is already affecting working composers, who are being asked to recreate AI-generated tracks so productions can claim there is a human author. He said creative industries cannot become collateral damage in the race to attract AI investment, and that composers cannot copy something that may have been built from illegally harvested creative work. He argued that copyright should not be traded away in policy negotiations focused on attracting AI investment, and said the Human Made campaign is not opposed to the technology itself but seeks a system in which rights holders are recognised and paid when their work is used. He said the consequences of AI-generated music are no longer hypothetical.

The intervention comes as Australia debates possible changes to copyright settings for AI, and as governments in several markets examine how copyright law should apply to AI training data. In Australia, creators' groups have warned against changes that would weaken existing protections or create broad exemptions for technology companies. The debate comes as the local screen sector grows, with Australian film and television drama production expenditure reaching a record AUD $2.7 billion in 2024-25, up 43 per cent on the previous year, according to figures cited by the campaign. Partos's screen credits include Poker Face, Mystery Road, Last King of the Cross, Total Control, The Rover and the Academy Award-nominated Tanna, and Sonar Music, which he co-founded with Jono Ma, David McCormack, Matteo Zingales and Andrew Lancaster, has worked across television, film and advertising since launching in 2010.

Articles.Title: Partos urges action on AI copyright use after award win - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Generative Legal's Cornell Tech Conference: ‘Productizing’ Legal Work in the AI Age
stories.Summary:
Panelists at Generative Legal's Cornell Tech conference in New York on Wednesday discussed how artificial intelligence is changing legal work and the organizations that do it. The panelists spoke on the condition that their comments not be attributed by name. They said legal professionals are responding to AI by productizing their work, meaning they are embedding their expertise in software. They also said legal professionals are promoting their specialized legal judgment to set themselves and their organizations apart.

One panelist said that to get the best output from AI models across use cases, users need to provide as much context as possible. The panelists said that as teams and firms browse their next AI solution, knowing how to prompt these tools is imperative. The conference discussion covered how AI is reshaping legal business models, from law firms embedding their expertise in software to legal teams fighting decision paralysis in a crowded tech market. The articles do not name the individual panelists or give further details of what each person said.

The articles do not identify who is responsible for any decision or change, beyond the panelists who spoke at the conference. The panelists are described only as speaking on the condition that their comments not be attributed by name, so their identities are not given. The articles do not quote any of them directly by name. The articles also do not say what specific steps, if any, were announced at the conference.

The context given is that law firms and legal departments have had a lot to adapt to in the artificial intelligence age. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the discussion at the conference. They do not give a date for any follow-up event or decision. They do not say whether the panelists' views will lead to any formal change. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Generative Legal's Cornell Tech Conference: ‘Productizing’ Legal Work in the AI Age - Law.com

stories.Headline: Westlaw AI Fight Warrants Full Court Review, 3rd Circ. Told
stories.Summary:
Ross Intelligence has asked the full Third Circuit to revisit a copyright decision that found it was not protected by fair use when it trained its artificial intelligence legal research platform on Thomson Reuters material. The petition was filed with the appeals court, and Law360 reported on it on November 4, 2026. The article gives no further dates, names or figures beyond Ross Intelligence, Thomson Reuters and the Third Circuit. The underlying decision concluded that Ross Intelligence was not protected by fair use.

The article does not set out the specific requirements or changes the petition seeks, and it gives no numbers or dates for the original ruling. It says only that Ross Intelligence urged the full Third Circuit to revisit the copyright decision. The case concerns training an AI legal research platform on Thomson Reuters content. No other details of the requested relief are provided.

Ross Intelligence is the party behind the petition, and the article attributes the request to the company. It does not include any statement from Ross Intelligence, Thomson Reuters or the court beyond the filing itself. The article names Theresa Schliep as the reporter and gives the publication time as November 4, 2026, at 8:23 PM EST. No further comment from any party is included.

The context is a copyright dispute over whether training an AI legal research platform on Thomson Reuters material counts as fair use. The article does not say what happens next beyond the request for full court review. It also does not indicate when the Third Circuit might act on the petition. More to follow.

stories.Headline: A $6 billion hack in a season of AI anxiety
stories.Summary:
On October 29, attackers stole more than six billion dollars in digital assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance. The Federal Bureau of Investigation has attributed the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation. Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's compromised laptop, but the exchange later identified additional points of breach. So far there is no public evidence that AI tools were used to break into Binance's systems. Binance reports that it has replenished about 95 percent of the affected assets using its own resources, though that is not the same as recovering the money from the hackers.

The FBI, the Secret Service, the Internal Revenue Service, blockchain analysis firms and private companies have worked to trace and freeze stolen assets. Chainalysis identified thousands of transactions moving funds repeatedly among digital wallets, and the firm said the attackers appear to be using automation to obscure the trail. The article says the speed at which stolen funds can move may be what is changing, leaving less time to freeze assets. Separately, on October 21 researchers at Wiz, which Google acquired earlier this year, disclosed serious flaws in PHP, a widely used open-source programming language, uncovered with the help of frontier AI models. Node.js also patched a severe vulnerability reported by OpenAI.

Wiz privately reported the PHP vulnerabilities in August, nearly two months before public disclosure and the release of patches in October. JPMorganChase is a launch partner in Anthropic's Project Glasswing, which provides early access to its Claude Mythos model for defensive security work, and a KPMG survey found that 84 percent of banking executives were increasing cybersecurity investment to address AI-related risks. The article says the next five to ten years may bring complicated legal questions at the intersection of cybersecurity, AI and financial technology. A recent Congressional Research Service analysis explains that existing federal criminal laws can apply when a person deliberately uses AI to gain unauthorized access to a computer. The author argues that regulators should distinguish genuinely new problems from familiar misconduct, and concrete risks from conjecture, before reaching for sweeping new restrictions.

Articles.Title: A $6 billion hack in a season of AI anxiety

stories.Headline: Manufacturing leads peers in AI-driven IT issue fixing
stories.Summary:
TeamViewer has published research on AI adoption among manufacturing IT decision-makers, finding the sector ahead of its peers in using proactive and partially autonomous approaches to resolving technology issues. Among manufacturing respondents, 43% said their organisation already resolves issues proactively, while a further 25% reported partially autonomous handling, where AI predicts and prevents issues with some human oversight. That gives the sector a combined total of 68%, ahead of technology at 56%. Across all industries, the figures were 41% for proactive handling and 17% for partially autonomous handling.

Almost a third of manufacturing IT decision-makers, 32%, said uncertainty about AI's value or business impact remained a barrier to adoption, compared with 16% in technology and 21% across all industries. Security, privacy and risk concerns were the most commonly cited obstacle in manufacturing, identified by 47% of respondents. A lack of skills or training followed at 34%, placing those issues alongside doubts over business value as the three main barriers to wider uptake. In the sector, 28% said they would prefer IT teams to use AI to detect issues early and keep them informed, slightly above the 25% cross-industry average. By contrast, only 19% said they would rather report issues themselves and wait for a fix, notably lower than the 25% cross-industry average.

Just 23% of manufacturing respondents said a person should be involved before any action is taken, compared with 31% across industries. At the same time, 46% said they wanted a human involved when security, data or business operations could be affected, above the 40% average. Some 44% said AI is already making them more productive, compared with 39% across industries, and manufacturing respondents who verify AI outputs said they spend an average of 1.6 hours a week doing so, compared with 1.9 hours across industries and 2.7 hours in technology. Manufacturing respondents said they prompt AI an average of 3.08 times a day, compared with 3.28 across industries and 4.72 in technology.

Looking ahead, 35% of manufacturing respondents said they expect to delegate more tasks to AI by 2030 and focus on higher-value work, compared with 28% across industries. Mei Dent, Chief Product and Technology Officer at TeamViewer, said the challenge in manufacturing often lies in proving the value of changes that happen incrementally rather than through full system replacement. She said many manufacturers run on systems built over decades that they cannot simply replace, so the biggest advances come from thousands of smaller decisions, and because that work happens quietly in the background, its impact is easy to overlook. The study was conducted by Sapio Research on behalf of TeamViewer among 4,200 respondents across nine markets: the US, the UK, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Singapore and Brazil.

Articles.Title: Manufacturing leads peers in AI-driven IT issue fixing - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Google is entirely disabling Search in schools that don’t want AI
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026, that it will turn off Google Search entirely for K-12 student accounts in schools that reject its AI features, as The Verge and Education Week reported. The change was shared in a broader education update from Google, which said access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search will be entirely off unless administrators explicitly turn them on. Administrators will not be able to switch off Gemini-powered features while keeping Search, because Google says the two are deeply integrated. Students in schools that disable the AI will see a message from their school saying Search is not available.

Under the new rules, administrators get two levels of control, according to Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education. Search and Gemini will be off by default, and districts can turn on either one or both, with settings that can differ by grade. A district could block AI for one group, limit another to Guided Learning, and give older students the full search experience with AI summaries. Traditional searches without AI summaries will not be an option, and the changes are set to start early next year. Google also said it is updating Search for schools to make it better for learning, with AI Mode and AI Overviews offering step-by-step guided learning through problems rather than just answers, and it will test Guided Learning in select US schools this month.

Phillips said during a November 2 virtual meeting that if a school is not comfortable with AI and simply wants it off, it has the choice to not have Search at all. Google said in its November 3 statement that schools have told the company they want control, and that its goal is to give school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products as they see fit. The statement did not mention a letter from Senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley, who had given Google until November 2 to answer nine questions, including why AI became the default on school devices. Blumenthal told Education Week that Google is once again prioritizing profits over people, this time blocking schools from Search unless they opt into its AI overview.

The announcement comes months after Google turned on its Gemini assistant by default inside Google Classroom, which is used by more than 150 million teachers and students globally. Since then, New York City banned student-facing AI through 8th grade, and Los Angeles Unified imposed a one-year moratorium on generative AI on its devices, and both districts use Google products. Yvette Renteria of Common Sense Media said getting rid of Google Search eliminates the chance to embrace critical thinking in the classroom, and she said having Search without AI search is the best option, one Google is not providing. Critics including former FTC Chair Lina Khan, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Senator Bernie Sanders posted objections on X, and some districts are testing workarounds such as internet filters or a Chrome extension that hides AI Overviews.

Articles.Title: Google’s New Rules Hand Schools Hard Choices About AI and Search - Education Week

stories.Headline: Musk’s Minnesota Deepfake Fight Could Define AI’s First Amendment
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk's company xAI, now renamed SpaceXAI, sued Minnesota in late July 2026 over a new state law on deepfake nude images, just days before the law was set to take effect. The company also sought an injunction to block the law. Minnesota's legislature had passed HF 1606, titled "Prohibition on Nudification Technology," in a nearly unanimous vote last spring. The law lets the state attorney general seek up to $500,000 in fines from a technology company each time it allows a user to nudify an image or video.

The law defines nudify as altering or generating an image or video to show an intimate part not in the original, in a way so realistic that a reasonable person would believe the part belongs to the identifiable individual. It holds the company strictly liable even if it has anti-deepfake policies and safeguards that a user manages to get around. Unlike older nonconsensual intimate imagery laws, it does not require intent or lack of consent, and it has no explicit exception for satire. It also defines intimate parts to include the primary genital area, groin, inner thigh, buttocks, or breast of a human being.

SpaceXAI said it already bans users from generating nonconsensual deepfake nudes and does not contest Minnesota's interest in prohibiting them. The company argued the statute reaches far beyond that goal and exposes protected speech to civil liability and government sanctions, and that the steep fines will chill speech. Minnesota argued that the law targets harmful technology, not ideas, beliefs, or expression. The state also said xAI knows how to identify illegal uses of Grok Imagine but has failed to stop what it called a flood of digital sexual victimization.

On Sept. 4, U.S. District Judge Donovan Frank denied xAI's request for a preliminary injunction without considering the First Amendment issues, focusing mainly on the company waiting nearly three months after the law was signed to file. xAI appealed directly to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, and on Oct. 2 the court granted an injunction in a one-sentence order, temporarily barring enforcement against SpaceXAI while it considers the appeal. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the First Amendment Lawyers Association, and the Woodhull Freedom Foundation filed an amicus brief supporting SpaceXAI. The Eighth Circuit's eventual opinion will address AI, an area with little precedential First Amendment law, and may need to decide what state of mind an AI company must have to be liable for its users' conduct.

Articles.Title: Musk’s Minnesota Deepfake Fight Could Define AI’s First Amendment - Lawfare

stories.Headline: Panel discusses AI's impact on frontend architecture and developer workflows
stories.Summary:
A panel of experts from Meta, AWS, Parallax and Netlify discussed how artificial intelligence is affecting frontend architecture and developer workflows. The discussion took place at an event covered by TechGig and was published on November 5, 2026. The panel looked at hiring, code quality and the growing role of people without technical backgrounds. Y Combinator reported that 95% of codebases in its latest batch were AI-generated.

James Hall, the CEO of Parallax, said experienced engineers are still needed but junior roles remain essential because juniors approach problems differently. He said Parallax now lets candidates use AI during interviews, which has created difficulties for some. Danielle An, a principal engineer at Meta, pointed to the rise of what the article calls vibe coding among non-technical roles such as artists and designers, who can now prototype ideas quickly with AI tools. The panelists agreed that guardrails are needed so AI-generated code follows best practices and regulatory requirements.

The panel also raised concerns that more contributions from non-engineers can lead to architectural debt and problems with code quality and maintenance. They discussed the need to redefine quality and trust as both human users and AI agents interact with frontend systems. The economic model for open-source projects like Tailwind is being challenged, because AI's prevalence may separate usage from traditional ways of making money. The panel concluded that AI can boost productivity but also requires a more disciplined approach to software development and code review.

Articles.Title: Panel discusses AI's impact on frontend architecture and developer workflows
