On SpaceX's recent earnings call, Musk told analysts that the company expects to build and bring online at least an additional 10 GW of AI compute capacity in 2027 via data centers.

Tesla is currently expanding its Cortex AI training supercluster in Austin, Texas, while SpaceX has reportedly been looking to build another data center campus in Texas with an additional 1 gigawatt of compute capacity. As of 10:45 a.m. ET, the major market indexes were soaring higher, yet SpaceX and Tesla traded roughly 3% and 2.2% lower, respectively. Hinojosa's win is described as a clear blow to Musk and both of his companies. The article says the task of adding the 10 GW of AI compute capacity likely just got a lot harder.

Articles.Title: AI Regulation Was on the Ballot In These States. Here Are The Elon Musk Stocks That Could Be Impacted.

stories.Headline: ‘Huge step in the regulation of AI in healthcare’ as government accepts independent commission’s AI - Society of Radiographers
stories.Summary:
The government has accepted all 44 recommendations from the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, an independent expert advisory body set up by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency in September 2025. The commission's report followed extensive consultation with NHS unions and professional associations representing staff affected by AI. The Society of Radiographers submitted evidence to the commission so that the views of radiographers were heard. The government announced its response on 3 November 2026.

The accepted proposals include post-market surveillance, which means technologies such as AI image analysis tools, triage algorithms and treatment planning software will be evaluated and audited throughout their entire operational life. The MHRA will issue draft guidance by the end of 2026 on managing changes and updates to AI tools already deployed in clinical settings. In 2027 the MHRA will consult on new standards to qualify and classify AI-enabled medical devices. A programme board will oversee implementation across 10 priority areas.

Jeanette Carter, professional officer for AI and digital technologies at the Society of Radiographers, said the government accepting all 44 recommendations was a huge step for AI in healthcare. She said the society is working to see where it can help contribute to the success of completing the recommendations and will keep members posted. She added that the importance of post-market surveillance has been known for a while, with the Royal College of Radiologists having its own guidance on it. She said there is always a concern with new technology that small deteriorations in accuracy cannot be fully understood without regular review, and that AI is a powerful tool but the human is accountable for reviewing the results.

Articles.Title: ‘Huge step in the regulation of AI in healthcare’ as government accepts independent commission’s AI - Society of Radiographers

stories.Headline: Addressing Radiology’s Workforce Crisis: Can a Shift from Being Passive AI Users to Active AI Creators Have an Impact?
stories.Summary:
Radiology is facing a workforce shortage that is especially severe in diagnostic departments, according to an article published on November 4, 2026, by Khan Siddiqui, MD, on diagnosticimaging.com. The article says radiology has a 10-year deficit of more than 20,000 clinicians, driven by rising demand for imaging and high rates of burnout. It also says that as imaging technology evolves, scanners produce more images, so radiologists must review more than 10 times the data per case than before. Siddiqui is the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of HOPPR. The article says AI developers have promised to solve radiology's burnout and shortage problems, but the narrative often sounds like AI is trying to replace clinicians.

It says AI can help most by relieving administrative burden and handling repetitive, tedious, non-diagnostic tasks. It points to report automation tools that take patient measurements, push approved AI-generated insights into the report, and turn dictated notes into a cohesive narrative. It also describes AI-assisted prioritization that scans images in the background and moves urgent findings to the top of the worklist, and says these tools must be deeply integrated with a practice's radiology information system and electronic health record. Siddiqui argues that the next step is giving radiology practices the power to build their own tools in a secure environment. He says developing a custom AI model used to require years of coding, massive compute power, and painstaking accumulation of local data.

He says imaging AI foundries provide pre-validated foundation models trained on millions of diverse medical images, so clinicians can fine-tune them with a smaller, curated set of local data. He says this shift from passive consumers to active creators restores a sense of agency to the profession. The article cites several sources, including a 2025 study in AJNR Am J Neuroradiol on the gap between job growth and the radiology training pipeline, and a 2015 study in Acad Radiol on how utilization and technological changes affect radiologist workload. It also cites a 2026 American Medical Association survey on physician AI use and a 2025 AMA article on physicians using AI to cut administrative burdens. It cites a 2024 article in Ann Med Surg on digital multitasking, a 2020 study in Radiol Artif Intell on AI reprioritization of the reading worklist for head CT, and a 2024 ArXiv paper on the HOPPR medical-grade platform.

Articles.Title: Addressing Radiology’s Workforce Crisis: Can a Shift from Being Passive AI Users to Active AI Creators Have an Impact?

stories.Headline: UK regulators warn firms: existing law applies to personal AI agents
stories.Summary:
Four UK regulators said on 30 October that existing law already applies to personal AI agents. The Competition and Markets Authority, the Financial Conduct Authority, the Information Commissioner's Office and Ofcom made the statement through the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum. They said an agent's autonomy does not reduce a firm's duties. The statement runs to about two pages and offers no new rules, but the regulators promised enforcement and early testing routes.

The regulators said the frameworks that apply include consumer, competition and data protection law, along with payments, financial services, cyber security and online safety. They said product safety and other areas sit beyond these four regulators. They welcomed the technology, which could act for users by buying things and dealing with businesses, but said agents may amplify old risks and add new ones. They named fraud and scams, personal data shared in ways users did not expect, and misleading recommendations. Their questions for developers and deployers cover whether a customer can tell when an agent is acting for them, how authority to act is given, which commercial interests shape its recommendations, and who answers for its decisions.

The regulators said they will not hesitate to use their powers where conduct is reasonably suspected of breaching the law and risks harm. They strongly encouraged firms to come forward early and test products through sandboxes and direct engagement. They conceded there may be more to do and said they are working with government to identify potential gaps in compliance and further regulatory challenges. The statement cites no AI-specific legislation and leans on existing regimes.

For UK businesses, the practical effect is to close off the argument that agents fall into a gap until Parliament acts. Nothing in the statement changes the law, and no case is announced. The first enforcement case will show which regulator moves first and what accountable means in practice. Firms already building agents would be wise to document their answers now, according to the article.

Articles.Title: UK regulators warn firms: existing law applies to personal AI agents

stories.Headline: SPONSORED: Building AI factories at enterprise scale
stories.Summary:
ASUS announced a full-stack enterprise AI offering at NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on October 21 and 22, 2026. The offering is called the Enterprise Agentic AI Solution and has three layers. These are the ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure, the ASUS AI Software Stack, and the ASUS AI HUB services operation. The announcement brought together existing ASUS assets for enterprise AI users along with new hardware.

The hardware includes single and full-rack systems built around the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 eight-GPU server board. The 3U hybrid-cooled XA NR11-E12L and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XA NR11-E12 both target large AI reasoning workloads. ASUS says the tool-less CPU and GPU sleds can cut maintenance time by up to 50 percent. The company also showed MGX servers, the ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3 developer desktop with 748GB of coherent memory, the Ascent GX10, the ProArt GR1X Mini PC, the ProArt P16 and P14 laptops, the PE3000N edge computer, and the PE6000G workstation platform.

Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS, said the servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure for complex task execution and large-scale agent deployment. He said AI servers were historically optimized around GPU compute, but agentic workloads now depend heavily on a continuous agent loop that is CPU-intensive. He named single-thread performance, memory bandwidth, multi-die latency, and a lack of hardware sandbox isolation as bottlenecks in conventional AI servers. He also said customers must match server platforms to their projected AI workload profiles.

IDC said the worldwide server market grew 30 percent in a single year to reach $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025. IDC expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year and says it is growing fastest at the edge. ASUS has adopted NVIDIA's DSX AI Factory platform with a digital twin system for planning hardware and power, and its racks become simulation-ready assets inside DSX. The digital twin is meant to keep working after go-live so operators can test changes before touching hardware.

Articles.Title: SPONSORED: Building AI factories at enterprise scale

stories.Headline: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
stories.Summary:
For about two years, UK government ministers told the public that AI could add £400 billion, or $538 billion, to the economy. Last week the UK AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, admitted in a parliamentary answer that this figure was far above the government's own projections. He said the £400 billion number came from a publicly available 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First, a British consultancy now called PF Global. Narayan said the government's more recent assessment put the gain from AI adoption and data investment at £55 billion to £140 billion by 2030, with a central estimate of £120 billion. He described even that estimate as hugely uncertain.

The lower estimate had been with ministers since at least November 2025, almost a year before the admission, yet the government agency Skills England was still publishing the old figure four months later. Government departments and agencies used the Google figure for almost two years, under two governments. Narayan's answer was the first recorded evidence that the government set the two numbers side by side, or said the report was commissioned by Google. The answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it had been wrong.

PF Global's head of economics, Jonathan Dupont, said the gap was partly because of what the firm saw as slow government adoption of AI. He said AI moves fast and assumptions behind models have to be updated, and that the government's numbers assume a much slower rate of adoption than seemed possible in 2023. He said the firm's central estimate for what is likely to be achieved by 2030 is now much closer to the government's number. PF Global said its work for Google continued but all research was independent and all judgments and assumptions were its own.

Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, said the government is right to promote technology like AI for public services. She said the reports highlight hype as one of the central barriers to digital transformation, and that overstating benefits risks undermining the case for change. Lord Holmes of Richmond, the Conservative peer who asked ministers in January 2025 about the origins of the claim without getting a response, said it was unfortunate the figure had now been significantly adjusted. He said it would have been better to clarify sooner and more directly, and that robust data is critical.

Sumedha Deshmukh of the Ada Lovelace Institute said the revised estimates are welcome but it is concerning they come after almost two years of ministers citing research paid for by Google. She said figures about AI that look precise often have assumptions and incentives built into them, and industry often funds or shapes the research behind them. She said the government should test the numbers it is given, fund independent research, and measure whether promised gains are delivered. The Cabinet Office, the department responsible for AI in government, and Google were approached for comment.

Articles.Title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google

stories.Headline: China Speeds AI Law; DeepSeek, Alibaba Face Disclosure Push
stories.Summary:
China's National Development and Reform Commission said on 3 November 2026 that it will speed up a basic, comprehensive AI law and set safety standards and ethical guidelines covering the full life cycle of AI, Bloomberg first reported. Wang Ruomeng, a deputy director-general of the NDRC's Department of Innovation and High-Tech Development, set out the plan at the first briefing in the NDRC's series on the 15th Five-Year Plan, answering a question from The Paper on AI risks. Bloomberg said the rules would reach developers from DeepSeek to Moonshot and Alibaba. The plan follows three versions of the national cybersecurity standards committee TC260's AI Safety Governance Framework in 24 months, with version 3.0 released on 14 September 2026.

Wang said the NDRC will also legislate on data, computing power and algorithms and on key application scenarios, and will review rules periodically and adjust provisions that no longer fit. Regulators will set reasonable transition periods, offer compliance guidance by sector and build evaluation, consulting and certification services to cut firms' compliance costs, and will support AI regulatory sandboxes with rules for applying, testing, using and exiting them. China will push developers and operators to strengthen risk management, disclose safety risks promptly and proactively report safety incidents and vulnerability information. The fourth area covers jobs, rights and mental health, including monitoring of job displacement risk and adding model trainers and data annotators to the national occupational classification.

Wang said AI safety is not a problem one company, industry or country can tackle alone and called it a global challenge requiring international cooperation. He said several AI security incidents have occurred worldwide since the start of this year and that a large model developed in China recently took part in responding to an international emergency security incident, without naming the model or the incident. He called for joint work on safety governance standards, vulnerability notification, risk warning and response, and said that at the September meeting of the Chinese and US heads of state the two sides agreed to set up a China-US AI dialogue and a communication channel for AI incidents. He also said China will adhere to open source and openness and inclusive development, and that 38 countries have joined the World AI Cooperation Organization as founding members.

The transcript gives no draft text, timetable or lead drafting body for the law or the life-cycle standards, and does not say how long the transition periods will be or whether disclosure and incident reporting will be mandatory. Wang did not name DeepSeek, Moonshot, Alibaba or any other company; those names are Bloomberg's. Bloomberg reported the government continues to encourage open AI development during the 15th five-year plan ending 2030. The briefing came days after China's plenum called for a deeper Party role in tech firms. On 3 November the UK's NCSC published its own warning on AI-powered ransomware.

stories.Headline: A US company argued that lawyers using artificial intelligence should receive lower fees after its trade
stories.Summary:
Flux Drive Inc. sued defendants from another state, accusing them of taking its privately owned technology without permission. A federal district court judge in Colorado dismissed the trade-secrets lawsuit after finding the court did not have legal authority over the Illinois-based defendants. The defendants, represented by the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, then asked to recover their defence costs. The trial judge reviewed the firm's records and ordered Flux Drive to pay $114,663.11 in legal fees. Flux Drive appealed to the 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals.

Flux Drive argued that the law firm had used artificial intelligence software, that AI tools can complete tasks faster, and that the hours charged were therefore too high. The 10th Circuit rejected this and upheld the award in full. Writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh said AI can make legal research and document writing faster, but the party challenging a bill must provide clear evidence of overcharging. The panel, which also included Circuit Judges Scott Matheson and Richard Federico, said the district court had reviewed the time entries and found them reasonable, and that Flux Drive had failed to point to specific billing entries that were repeated, false or inflated because of the technology.

The ruling sets an early example of how courts may deal with automated tools in the legal profession, and Reuters reported on 2 November that it sets a clear standard for future fee disputes involving technology. Legal analysts say the decision does not give law firms complete freedom to charge for AI-assisted work without question, and courts can still reduce fees if someone shows software did most of a task in minutes while the firm charged for hours of manual work. The decision comes as courts pay closer attention to AI use by law firms, after cases in which lawyers submitted documents with fake legal references generated by AI chatbots. The 10th Circuit has also proposed rule changes requiring lawyers to confirm that a human attorney independently checked all legal authorities cited in appeal filings. The 10th Circuit's formal order leaves the district court's fee decision unchanged, ending the dispute.

stories.Headline: China to Fast-Track AI Law, Calls on Developers to Disclose Incidents
stories.Summary:
On November 3, China's National Development and Reform Commission, the country's top economic planner, promised to speed up work on a single artificial intelligence law. Wang Zhomeng, deputy director of the commission's Department of Innovation and High Technology, announced the plan at a briefing in Beijing. The rules would cover the whole AI lifecycle, from development to deployment. The changes would affect startups DeepSeek and Moonshot AI with their Kimi models, as well as Alibaba's Qwen family, according to Bloomberg.

The law will pull together lessons from existing rules to form a basic comprehensive law behind all other regulation in the field. Officials will also speed up rules on data, computing power and algorithms, plus key application areas. Safety and ethics standards will apply at every stage, from training through operation. Compliance will be checked periodically and outdated provisions revised, and there will be a transition period, though no length was given. Agencies will offer guidance and expand assessment, advisory and certification services to cut compliance costs, and regulatory sandboxes will test innovations under government oversight with temporary waivers.

Developers and operators must disclose security threats promptly and report incidents and found vulnerabilities to authorities. The government will watch job shifts and warn about worker displacement, and it plans to add model trainers and data annotators to the national occupational list. Tools will target deepfakes, algorithmic discrimination and personal data leaks, with special protection for older adults and minors, and the agenda includes fighting addiction and emotional attachment to AI. Wang said support for open development will continue, and he called on countries to build trust, coordinate disclosure of flaws and respond to risks together, saying AI safety cannot be solved by one company, industry or government alone.

China currently regulates the sector through ministerial rules, with interim measures for generative AI services in force since August 2023 and mandatory labeling of generated content since September 2025. From July 15, 2026, an advance level of control is set for each step of an AI agent, from human-only decisions to full autonomy. On May 11, the State Council's 2026 legislative work plan first included language about a comprehensive AI law, and the National People's Congress Standing Committee added AI initiatives to its list of documents to consider once texts are ready. No adoption timeline has been announced.

Articles.Title: China to Fast-Track AI Law, Calls on Developers to Disclose Incidents

stories.Headline: Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says
stories.Summary:
The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver rejected an argument that a law firm's use of artificial intelligence should reduce its fee award, Reuters reported. The court upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable. The appeals court also upheld the dismissal of the lawsuit.

The case began in 2024, when Flux Drive, an industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker, sued a Chinese manufacturer and alleged that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to the manufacturer. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants' legal fees. On appeal, Flux Drive argued that the defense billed for ministerial tasks and that AI use should have lowered the bill. The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Judge Carolyn McHugh wrote for a unanimous three-judge panel that the plaintiffs had not shown that the defense counsel's use of AI made the hours they actually expended unreasonable. She acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient, but she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves. Christopher Ottele, a Brownstein Hyatt partner who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace. He said the decision confirms that AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis attorneys must still exercise in every filing with the court. Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

stories.Headline: Seattle families to rally, address generative AI tech usage in schools
stories.Summary:
Seattle families rallied outside Seattle Public Schools headquarters on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, urging the state's largest school district to pause the use of generative AI and address concerns about student-facing technology. Parents said they worry the technology could be more harmful than helpful for student learning, and they want the option for their children to have a paper alternative to using an iPad or tablet. The rally was planned before the school board's informational study session about educational technology. Superintendent Ben Shuldiner and most of the school board attended the rally.

The families called on the district to form a committee to disclose ed tech products and student data collection to caregivers, get caregiver consent to use these products, allow paper-based alternatives and device opt-outs, and set grade-level screen-time limits. The district does have time limits for student use of this technology and blocks certain web content like YouTube, Minecraft and Gemini, according to a district presentation. The district describes generative AI as deep learning models that can create complex original content like long-form text, high-quality images, realistic video or audio in response to a user's prompt. Some examples used in classrooms include Magic School, Amplify Science, Emerge, SuccessMaker Math, Lexia, enVision Mathematics, Lexia Core5, Sora, Schoology, Canva and Book Creator.

Erica Shutes-David told KOMO News she was surprised when her then-kindergartener was given an iPad, and she chose to opt her son out. She said AI is currently wildly untrustworthy and that grooming kids to rely and trust on that source is dangerous and irresponsible, in her opinion. Ashley Worobec, a Salmon Bay K-8 parent, said the tools shortcut thinking and that it does not make sense to her that they are used in schools during crucial developmental years. Director Liza Rankin told KOMO she is excited to continue the conversation and wants all kids to have the opportunity to be critical thinkers, and she said there is a lot of alignment among the parents and the board.

Parents said they are frustrated with what they call too much screen time replacing hands-on learning, a lack of a districtwide cell phone policy, no clear governance over how AI is being used, and over-purchasing of digital programs. Directors are reviewing guidance for developmentally appropriate, safe and purposeful technology and AI use to support student learning. The school board presentation notes SPS is changing how it makes software decisions, aiming to have fewer overlapping applications and better support tools with help from an advisory committee. KOMO News asked the district about parents' concerns.

Articles.Title: Seattle families to rally, address generative AI tech usage in schools

stories.Headline: How AI impacts solopreneurs’ relationships with their clients (and what to do about it)
stories.Summary:
A November 4, 2026 article in Fast Company describes how AI is changing the way clients deal with solo business owners. The Ramp Economics Lab tracked how companies split spending between freelance marketplaces and AI model providers. Among the companies studied, the share going to freelance marketplaces fell from 0.66% in the fourth quarter of 2021 to 0.14% in the third quarter of 2025. Over the same period, the share going to AI model providers rose from zero to nearly 3%.

The article says clients now expect AI to make human work cheaper, and some may expect to pay less for it. It advises solopreneurs not to cut their rates to compete with AI, because that devalues the result the client pays for. Instead, it suggests cutting the scope of work or offering more flexible terms, such as ad hoc or on-demand work. It also says clients can paste deliverables into a chatbot for a free second opinion, and that AI feedback tends to be generic and can misunderstand the project's goals. The article recommends covering AI upfront, during a discovery call or in the contract, and limiting how much feedback gets incorporated into revisions.

The article also says cold pitches and social posts are now full of AI-generated content, so the usual ways of finding clients work less well. It says personal connections matter most now, because people who know you and can vouch for your work are the surest way to break through. It adds that clients trying to replace work with AI are not a fit anyway, and that the pool of potential clients may be smaller. The author says her own clients hire her for judgment and expertise and still want a person behind the work.

stories.Headline: White House: AI Vetting Framework Still a Secret
stories.Summary:
The White House is withholding its entire frontier artificial intelligence review framework after a nonprofit sued for its release. The Office of the National Cyber Director told Protect Democracy in a letter on Friday that it would withhold all 60 pages of records it located in response to the group's Freedom of Information Act request, including the seven-page framework itself. The office cited exemptions covering national security and confidential commercial information in its refusal to disclose the framework. The letter arrived on the Oct. 30 deadline that federal attorneys accepted as part of an open records lawsuit filed by Protect Democracy in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The nonprofit had withdrawn a motion for a preliminary injunction and agreed to seek only four categories of records. These include substantively unredacted copies of the framework, the participation terms given to companies joining the Gold Eagle AI vulnerability clearinghouse, the list of individuals and entities deemed trusted partners, and records showing what legal authority the government relied on for both programs. The government also committed to producing a Vaughn index, a document-by-document accounting of what it held back and why, by the same date. President Donald Trump created the review process through a June 2 executive order that lets developers voluntarily give the government access to covered frontier models for up to 30 days before releasing them to other trusted partners.

The National Security Agency holds primary responsibility for deciding which models qualify, using classified benchmarks for advanced cyber capabilities, and the order explicitly rules out mandatory licensing or preclearance. Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology, a nonprofit pursuing a separate open records lawsuit over the framework, said Monday that the government told it late Friday the full document would stay secret on national security and other grounds. The group said the government had told a court Oct. 23 that it had found the framework and would turn over whatever was not exempt by Oct. 30. LASST wrote that the public should not have to sue to find out how the government reviews powerful AI models before they are released.

Protect Democracy argued in its September complaint that the White House declined to disclose the framework's contents, participants or legal basis even while acknowledging that the framework is not classified. The complaint also cited the July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing sandbox and breached Hugging Face, arguing that outside testers cannot evaluate whether federal reviews account for that kind of failure. The White House has said it completed the framework by the order's Aug. 1 deadline and discussed it with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and other developers, but it declined to make the document public. The administration also has not identified the companies participating in Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse launched in July to coordinate patches for vulnerabilities uncovered by AI models.

stories.Headline: Researchers say LLMs can be good at natively reading and writing neural network weights; GPT-6 Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights to make it better at math (Rikiya Takehi)
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MIT CSAIL, Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, published findings on November 2, 2026, saying frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights. They call this Weight-Space Programming. In their experiments, GPT-6 Astra read the raw weights of small networks and named the game each was trained on, and it identified what diffusion models generate and which language small language models learned, even with the first and last layers removed. Astra also wrote small game-playing networks from scratch that outplayed networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps, all without being allowed to write training loops.

Asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra found an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen's own model card warns about, and fixed it by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, that correction raised MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and raised IFEval by 3x, generalizing out of the box to instruction following. In another experiment, Astra edited 3.5% of a trained policy's weights in one shot, taking success from 0% to 100% at getting a car over a strip. Astra read 17,253 weights with no tools and named Breakout with 99% confidence, and it found every copying head in three small language models, matching the measured ones.

The authors say the work could matter for both optimization and interpretability. They argue that throughout deep learning's history, simple inductive biases were encoded into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon, and that this is changing, with weights soon to be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about them. They describe the results as early and exciting, covering reading, fixing and writing weights, first on small networks and then on real language models. They note Astra uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly.

The articles describe the work as a blog post published on rikiyat.github.io, with Techmeme linking to it under the same headline and author. The experiments include reading weights to identify games, shapes and languages, fixing a failing control network, and writing networks for three MinAtar games and for Go. The authors frame the approach as reasoning-driven optimization coming even for differentiable neural networks. The articles do not say what happens next beyond presenting these early results.

stories.Headline: Oracle’s New Lakehouse Tools Target a Blind Spot in Enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced several additions to its Autonomous AI Lakehouse at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas during the week of November 4, 2026. The additions include a new business semantic layer, expanded support for Apache Iceberg, an AI Data Catalog and tools for running business simulations. Oracle said the goal is to help companies work with data spread across different systems while giving AI agents a clearer understanding of what that data means. Not everything is available yet, and some capabilities are expected over the next year.

The updated Business Semantic Layer lets companies define business terms, metrics and calculations in one place so applications and AI agents use the same definitions. The AI Data Catalog helps users and agents search for information across Oracle and other platforms and provides details such as where datasets came from and how they are used. Oracle Data Studio brings SQL, Python and natural-language tools into one workspace, connects to more than 100 data sources and does not require users to set up a database first. Oracle expects the Business Semantic Layer and AI Data Catalog to become available within the next 12 months.

Oracle also added the ability to create and update Iceberg tables using SQL and to access earlier versions of data. Rhett Rowan, vice president of IT at Liberty Energy, said the lakehouse gives decision-makers real-time visibility into field revenue, inventory usage, costs and profitability. He said it brings together Apache Iceberg tables with data from Amazon S3, Amazon databases, Microsoft SQL Server on Azure, MongoDB and PostgreSQL, making it easy to add new data sources. Oracle claims its updated Data Lake Accelerator ran queries up to three times faster on a 100 TB TPC-DS dataset, though those are Oracle's own test results.

It says a semantic layer can help an AI agent understand what a metric means but cannot guarantee the agent will use it correctly. Several pieces of the announcement are still on the way, and the article says the ultimate test will be whether the tools make life easier for data teams and produce more reliable results from AI systems.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] PATEO Advances In-Vehicle AI via NVIDIA Thor
stories.Summary:
PATEO announced on November 3, 2026, that it is advancing in-vehicle AI by deploying NVIDIA Nemotron and the 35-billion-parameter ByteDance Doubao language model in its AI Box, which is built on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. The solution combines local AI inference with PATEO's AI Agent platform to support multilingual interaction, understand cabin context and coordinate vehicle functions. At Auto China 2026 in Beijing, PATEO announced joint development of the solution with ByteDance and a leading new energy vehicle automaker. PATEO has also secured a project nomination for a new-generation vehicle from a leading new energy vehicle automaker, with mass production for that program expected in the second quarter of 2027.

PATEO has integrated NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR for speech recognition into its in-vehicle model suite, and with ByteDance it has integrated Doubao, a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts language model. The suite also includes text-to-speech synthesis and a 2-billion-parameter language model for semantic classification and request rejection. The integrated suite can run inference locally without a cloud connection, supporting multilingual voice interaction and real-time streaming speech recognition. This keeps core AI functions available when connectivity is limited, while connected services and cloud updates extend the system's capabilities. The AI Agent platform combines voice, visual and sensor inputs to interpret user requests and cabin conditions, and within vehicle safety permissions it can invoke cabin controls and online services, coordinate concurrent tasks and manage longer-running requests.

The AI Box supports scenarios such as Sentinel AI alerts for risks including parking violations, flooding and fire, and separate driver and passenger climate settings by voice or gesture. During extended highway driving, the agent can detect driver fatigue and ask whether the driver would like to open a window or activate seat massage, and in areas with poor air quality it can suggest closing windows and switching to recirculation. Built on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, the AI Box connects perception, reasoning, execution and learning, and sustaining these experiences requires memory bandwidth alongside peak compute measured in TOPS. By adding dedicated AI computing capacity without replacing the original main control chip, it offers an upgrade path for existing vehicles whose processors cannot support larger models through software updates alone.

PATEO is building on the AI Box to expand from one-time hardware delivery into ongoing AI services, and its in-vehicle Tokenomics strategy aims to create recurring revenue around the deployment and use of AI capabilities. In June 2026, PATEO formed partnerships with Mininglamp Technology, Xunce Technology and Saimo Technology to jointly develop a token-based physical AI world model and TokenOS. The company is also extending its expertise into robotics and reports a project nomination from a leading domestic robotics computing provider. PATEO says its focus on reusable technology, deployment across vehicle programs and ongoing AI services supports its evolution from a smart cockpit supplier into an AI platform company.

stories.Headline: Florida Learjet crash victims identified: 20-year-old copilot, tech entrepreneur and his family among those killed
stories.Summary:
A private Learjet flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas crashed and exploded near West Palm Beach, Florida, on Sunday. The victims were identified as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, and caregiver Anita Maria Cetina. Passengers Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr also died, along with copilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. The identity of the pilot, who was also killed, has not been made public. Robinson, 45, was the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com and the CEO of Moltsets, and he previously worked at Lehman Brothers and Barclays.

He told the ProfitLed podcast that he and his family lived in Aspen, Colorado, and that he felt like he was living the dream. Filgueiras was 20 years old and had held a pilot's license since 2023, when she was a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School. Her license showed she had the rating to fly the jet but not to be in command of the flight, and the Palm Beach County School District paid for her license through the school's aviation academy. A statement from the families of the seven passengers identified the victims. The family of Reed and Fehr said the couple was full of joy and adventure, loved each other fiercely and were building a life together.

It was not immediately clear what their relationship was with Robinson and Sharp. Thom Singer, CEO of the Austin Technology Council, told the AP that Robinson was part of the entrepreneurial fabric of Austin. Robinson was known in Austin, where Retention.com was based, and his death is the second this year of an Austin tech entrepreneur in a plane crash, after Joshua Baer died in June. Filgueiras told WPEC-TV in 2023 that some people think it is weird that she can fly planes but cannot drive a car, and that she finds it funny. The articles do not say what happens next.

Geographic diversification is another focus, given significant operations in China and the goal of winning share at global foundries. The article does not quote company officials directly.

stories.Headline: St. Louis County, Mo., Council Turns to AI for Budget Cuts
stories.Summary:
The St. Louis County Council in Missouri approved a yearlong contract in September 2026 for an AI budget tool from Plano, Texas-based Tyler Technologies. The council is paying $273,300 for the company's Priority Based Budgeting solution, according to St. Louis Magazine, while the Post-Dispatch reported the cost as $273,000. The tool has already produced reports with ideas such as trimming jail overtime, charging vendors at events and cutting some holiday programming. The county is facing a $53 million deficit this year.

The software works by taking a government's line-item budget data and searching a database Tyler built from budget information from governments across the country. It then produces reports with ideas and case studies, including brief seven-page reports a council member could use in a department budget hearing. One parks report suggested charging separate fees for commercial vendors and private rentals during seasonal and holiday programming, which it said could raise $14,000 to $29,000 a year. Another idea, using building-energy monitoring to find after-hours waste as Boise did, could save $19,000 to $29,000 a year. Tyler's Chris Fabian said the tool uses traditional machine learning rather than generative AI.

The council's budget director, Chris Grahn-Howard, said he is hopeful the tool will brainstorm directions nobody else has thought of. He said the real outcome will come when the council digs into the details next year, and that the annual cost will drop to roughly $250,000 in Year 2. A spokesperson for County Executive Sam Page, Elizabeth Eisele, said the county is already doing most of the suggested things, citing LED lighting, online permitting and an online reservation system as examples. She said filling corrections jobs is hard because St. Charles County and St. Louis city raise pay too. Doug Linkhart of the National Civic League said AI could be part of the mix but should not be relied on, and that asking people for ideas would be better.

The council and Page have been locked in a bitter budget fight for years, and the lone no vote on the purchase was Councilwoman Lisa Clancy, Page's only council ally. Eisele noted that the AI has suggested some of the same ideas Page previously offered, including updated fees and bringing in sponsors to share costs, and that legislation for the Parks Department has been prepared but not acted on. Grahn-Howard said conversations with Tyler began nearly a year ago and the mid-September signing came too late to help much with this year's process. Some ideas could be incorporated into this year's budget, but the council will look at the reports in more detail next year. Tyler has drawn bad headlines elsewhere, including in Kansas City over property assessments and in Kirkwood over a $15 million deficit, though Grahn-Howard said those are different products.

stories.Headline: Africa must build AI systems that preserve its languages, culture – Sam George
stories.Summary:
Sam George, Ghana’s Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovation, called for the development of national language models to preserve African languages as artificial intelligence becomes more influential in the digital world. He spoke at the 15th Africa Internet Governance Forum on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. He said Africa’s role in the global technology revolution must go beyond adopting new tools and include systems that recognise the continent’s languages, cultures and social realities. He identified national language models that preserve African languages as one of the key issues the continent must address.

Mr George said African countries must ensure their languages remain part of the digital environment as artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies reshape communication and access to information. He said language has a dual character, serving as both a means of communication and a carrier of culture. He argued that African language models were necessary so the continent’s cultural identity is not left behind as digital technologies advance. He also called for African countries to develop digital solutions based on their own realities rather than rely entirely on systems designed elsewhere, saying African problems demand African solutions designed by Africans, for Africans, and grounded in African realities.

He further argued that Africa must have a greater role in shaping the global digital environment, including the standards and technologies that influence what people see, buy and believe. He warned that powerful interests were already shaping the digital world and said African countries could not afford to remain on the margins of those decisions. Separately, Ghana has begun work on a national AI computing centre to provide advanced computing, storage and cloud services for government and the country’s technology ecosystem. Mr George announced this at the Africa Virtual Assets Summit 2026 in Accra on Monday, November 2.

He described the proposed facility as a sovereign AI-enabled nerve centre that will provide world-class digital infrastructure while ensuring Ghana maintains control over its critical technology systems. According to Mr George, the centre will serve both government institutions and the wider technology industry, providing computing power, storage capacity and cloud services to support innovation and digital transformation. He said the initiative would complement the government’s G-Cloud platform, which provides secure local hosting for government, financial and educational institutions. He stressed that sovereign digital infrastructure was essential to Ghana’s ambitions in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, blockchain, Web3 and tokenization, and said the country needed secure, reliable and locally controlled infrastructure to support digital products and services.

stories.Headline: SUSE to cut 10 per cent of global workforce, cites AI and automation
stories.Summary:
SUSE plans to cut about 10 per cent of its global workforce, which could affect around 190 employees from a reported 1,900-strong workforce. CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen cited artificial intelligence and automation in an internal memo sent on Monday. Affected employees are expected to be informed by November 4. Employee representatives are scheduled to be nominated the following day, and individual meetings are expected to begin early next week.

The memo said automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate. It said modern tooling is already changing daily workflows, letting teams move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished, and other roles will evolve over the next few years. The company has not disclosed which roles or geographical regions will be affected, and the impact on its Indian workforce remains unclear.

Van Leeuwen described the decision as painful for employees, the company's culture and its open-source community, but necessary to adapt and build a sustainable SUSE for the long term. He said the existing organizational design and cost base would not carry the company forward successfully. He said the cuts reflect shifting organizational needs, not the talent or commitment of the staff. He added that any organization would be fortunate to have their expertise.

SUSE had previously offered voluntary exits to long-serving employees in September, but the offer reportedly did not attract enough volunteers. The company increased investment in AI in 2025 and announced agentic AI capabilities for its Linux management tools on October 27. The memo did not quantify the productivity improvements attributed to AI. SUSE is expected to brief remaining employees on its fiscal year 2027 strategy on November 16.

More than 137,000 technology workers across 340 companies have lost their jobs in 2026, according to Layoffs.fyi. Microsoft, Amazon, Innodata and Dropbox have also undertaken workforce reductions or voluntary exit programmes in recent weeks. EQT bought SUSE from Micro Focus for $2.5 billion in 2018 and floated it on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 2021. EQT took the company private again in 2023, and in March EQT was reportedly considering selling it off again.

stories.Headline: KLAC Q1 Earnings Call Highlights AI Demand and 2027 Growth Outlook
stories.Summary:
KLA Corporation reported results for its first quarter of fiscal 2027 on its earnings call, with revenues of $4.14 billion beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.05 billion, and adjusted earnings of $1.22 per share topping the consensus estimate of $1.18. CEO Rick Wallace pointed to accelerating investments in leading-edge foundry and logic manufacturing, high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging as the main demand drivers. CFO Bren Higgins raised KLA's calendar 2026 wafer fabrication equipment market expectation to the mid-$150 billion range, including advanced packaging, and management expects the market to exceed $200 billion in calendar 2027. The company reported a 62.7% non-GAAP gross margin and a record operating margin of 46.1% in the September quarter.

For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, KLA expects revenues of $4.7 billion, plus or minus $200 million, and non-GAAP earnings of $1.44 per share, plus or minus 11 cents. Higgins expects December-quarter operating expenses of approximately $710 million. Wallace said advanced packaging process control systems revenue remains on track to reach approximately $1.1 billion in calendar 2026, representing more than 70% year-over-year growth, which is nearly twice the expected growth rate of the advanced packaging market. Management expects advanced packaging to keep outgrowing its underlying market in 2027, and it expects greater investment in 2-nanometer and emerging 1.4-nanometer logic technologies during 2027.

Higgins said elevated memory component costs remain a profitability headwind, and he discussed product cost reductions, memory optimization and pricing initiatives, expecting improvement toward the company's 63% to 64% gross margin target in the latter part of 2027 and into 2028. He said equipment lead times average approximately 12 months, with certain advanced systems requiring longer, and that KLA continues expanding manufacturing capacity and coordinating investments with critical suppliers. Wallace emphasized maintaining technological leadership and supporting customer manufacturing roadmaps, and executives acknowledged that customer facility readiness and infrastructure constraints can influence equipment delivery schedules. Higgins projected sequential revenue growth over the next several quarters, supported by expanding backlog and improving customer visibility, with a more consistent growth trajectory throughout 2027.

The articles note that KLA faces competition in advanced packaging, with Onto Innovation raising its 2026 advanced packaging growth outlook to approximately 80% from 50% and Applied Materials expecting its packaging revenues to grow more than 70% in 2026. KLA shares have risen 37.8% year to date compared with 17.4% growth for the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector, and the stock trades at a forward 12-month price/earnings of 28.68X versus 19.39X for the sector. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for KLA's fiscal 2027 earnings is $5.44 per share, up 2 cents over the past 30 days and suggesting 44.7% growth. KLA currently has a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) in one article and a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) in the other, and the articles say the company will need to manage supply constraints and increase production capacity to meet customer requirements.

stories.Headline: Press Release dated November 4, 2026: ACHETER-LOUER.FR Invests USD 250,000 in Lucid Computing, a Specialist in Trusted Infrastructure for Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
ACHETER-LOUER.FR announced on November 4, 2026 that it had invested USD 250,000 in Lucid Computing, a specialist in trusted infrastructure for artificial intelligence. The investment was made through the company's wholly owned subsidiary SOL Treasury Corp and was funded from the Group's own resources. It involved a direct subscription for 28,550 newly issued Series Seed Preferred shares at USD 8.756298 per share, for a total of USD 249,992.31. The transaction was the first completed step in the Group's technology diversification strategy and was part of a funding round of approximately USD 13 million.

The shares represent 0.24% of Lucid Computing's share capital on a fully diluted basis, assuming the funding round is completed in full. The preferred shares carry rights including priority over common shares in distributions upon liquidation or certain deemed liquidation events, a right to convert into common shares, and collective governance rights. These rights do not guarantee repayment of the invested capital or any return on the investment. Taking the cash outflow into account, the Group said it now estimates it has sufficient resources to fund its requirements through the end of October 2027, subject to drawdown of the remaining tranches under a bond financing arrangement established with Digital Ventures I in January 2026. Without those drawdowns, the Group said its cash runway would be limited to six months.

Laurent Campagnolo, Chairman of the Management Board of ACHETER-LOUER.FR, said the investment was a first concrete step in the company's diversification into artificial intelligence. He said the ability to verify where and how AI systems operate addresses a growing need among organisations, and that the Group intends to identify promising technologies selectively, with a long-term perspective and careful risk management. Kristian Rönn, Co-founder and CEO of Lucid Computing, said trust in AI can no longer rely on promises alone as AI becomes critical infrastructure. He said organisations need proof of where their AI runs, what it does and who controls it, and that Lucid makes this verifiable at the hardware level.

Lucid Computing was incorporated in the State of Delaware in December 2024 and has a core team of approximately 15 people, supported by specialist contractors and advisers. It is co-founded and led by Rönn, previously a co-founder of Normative and a former member of the Future of Humanity Institute at the University of Oxford. Its specialist investors include Juniper Ventures, Lionheart Ventures, Safe Artificial Intelligence Fund (SAIF) and Halcyon Futures, and SAIF was founded by Geoff Ralston, former President of Y Combinator. The proceeds of the funding round are primarily intended to finance engineering and product development, delivery of existing customer projects, business development and working capital, and the Group said it intends to continue selectively identifying new investment and diversification opportunities, though no such transaction is currently underway.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike to Acquire 2 Firms to Secure Enterprise AI Agents
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike said on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, that it plans to make two acquisitions that will add artificial intelligence observability and automated AI security testing to its Falcon platform. The company signed a definitive agreement to acquire Fiddler, whose pre-deployment evaluation and continuous behavioral monitoring will become part of the platform. It also signed a definitive agreement to acquire Dreadnode, which provides automated AI security testing that lets companies validate the security of AI systems before they go into product. CrowdStrike expects both proposed transactions to close during its fourth quarter of fiscal year 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that CrowdStrike will pay about $400 million for Fiddler and about $95 million for Dreadnode, a combined purchase price of $495 million. Shares of the cybersecurity company gained more than 2% in early trading. CrowdStrike also announced the AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian, which gives security teams control over AI agents. If an agent deviates from its intended behavior, a defender can terminate it wherever it runs, prevent it from launching again, and cut off its enterprise network access.

CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas said AI observability provides a lens into agent behavior before and after they ship, and that AI explainability shows why agents made their decisions and where their actions may have gone awry. He said Fiddler delivers both. He also said businesses are integrating AI models, agents and applications into daily operations faster than security teams can validate them, and that traditional software security testing is not built to capture the risks these technologies can present. He said that with Dreadnode, CrowdStrike will extend the Falcon platform to give enterprises a fast, repeatable way to test their AI systems before they are deployed. George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike, said AI safety is how you get the full benefit of AI, and that when you deploy agents with a kill switch, you stay in control.

CrowdStrike announced in June that it added a new security control plane for AI agents that provides continuous, risk-aware enforcement. This Continuous Identity for AI agents, which joined the Falcon platform, authorizes every agent action based on who owns it, who is calling it and real-time risk, the company said. The articles say cybersecurity companies have benefited from the rise of agentic AI, which is driving increased demand for verification and authentication, despite concerns earlier this year that AI would disrupt traditional business models. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the expected closing of both transactions in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2027.

stories.Headline: Roderick Lucas, Co-Founder and CEO of Moonlit – Interview Series
stories.Summary:
Roderick Lucas is co-founder and CEO of Moonlit, a company that provides legal data infrastructure and research tools. Moonlit began as an internal project at Deloitte, where Lucas worked for nearly a decade and served as Artificial Intelligence Lead, and it became an independent company in 2024. Lucas has also taught technology courses at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and Tilburg University. The company connects official legislation, court decisions, and regulatory information across European jurisdictions through its platform, Data API, and MCP server.

Moonlit's Commentaries library offers article-by-article legal analysis that is generated by AI models from primary sources and vetted by named legal specialists before publication. Each commentary is accessible with a free Moonlit account, every citation is verified and links to the official government or court record, and readers can suggest edits for editorial review. At launch the commentaries focus on indirect tax (VAT), with commentaries on data protection in the works. Lucas said a commentary subscription from commercial publishers runs to hundreds of euros per user per month, and he argued the public effectively pays twice for law it must follow. He said one launch commentary links to 165 verified sources, and that editors are academics and practitioner-authors who are paid and whose names appear on the page.

Lucas said language models struggle with law because they treat case numbers and statutory citations as probabilistic text patterns rather than verified records, and because their knowledge stops at a training cutoff while tax rulings and appellate decisions update every week. He said there have been over 2,100 recorded court decisions involving AI hallucinations, more than 800 of which directly involved legal practitioners. He said Moonlit's model retrieves the law from official records instead of recalling it from memory, so a citation either points to an authentic document in its repository or does not appear, and a named legal expert still stands between the draft and the reader. He said the reference graph contains hundreds of millions of links, that source documents are not translated and searches run in the original language, and that the MCP server makes nine read-only tools available to external AI assistants.

stories.Headline: Setting guidelines for using AI in the classroom
stories.Summary:
Before the start of this school year, New York City officials banned generative AI for public preschools through eighth grade, and Los Angeles educators banned access to generative AI platforms on school devices for all grade levels. In recent polls, 75% of parents reported supporting pausing AI in schools, while 73% of respondents said children already use AI for schoolwork. Alphabet, Google's parent company, has offered discounted Chromebooks to schools since at least 2011, and Gemini is included in Google's Chrome web browser. Because Google does not allow its AI summaries or chatbot to be turned off, Fairfax County Public Schools developed its own plug-in to block Google AI search results.

The article calls for clear guidelines rather than temporary pauses, since AI is embedded in many online platforms. It says state lawmakers must define academic standards and adopt appropriate guardrails for responsible use of AI in classrooms. The Heritage Foundation developed model legislation for AI in schools that prioritizes human-centered learning and oversight, transparency, safety and data security. The model says schools should not be required to adopt AI into lesson plans, but for those that do, educators should help students tell the difference between getting help with homework questions and plagiarism.

The authors say state lawmakers should respect parent rights and require schools to obtain parent consent for AI use, and educators should offer alternatives when families opt out. They say AI vendors should not gather student data for targeted advertising or sell or rent this information, and educators must follow state and federal privacy laws such as the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. They say teachers should prohibit AI companions that mimic personal relationships, since romantic conversations or simulated friendships have no academic use and interfere with children's social skills and healthy development. Florida recently adopted rules for AI in schools that are consistent with many of these provisions.

The article says state officials recognize that teachers and students can use AI effectively, and that banning AI will not eliminate the use of large language models but will cause the activity to go unmonitored. It warns that if AI use goes underground, the potential for cheating increases, with potentially disastrous consequences for student learning. It says lawmakers should use lessons already available in research and in the media on effective and ineffective uses of technology to advance policy ideas dedicated to protecting student privacy and promoting student learning. It says state officials should adopt thoughtfully designed boundaries for student and teacher use of AI, including restrictions on non-academic uses, so teachers can blend AI into instructional guidance and help prepare students for the future.

He received briefings on advanced semiconductor packaging research from local researchers, including Hiroichi Kawahira, head of Samsung's DS Research Japan, and Takashi Kariya, head of the APL. Lee also discussed plans to work with Japanese materials, parts and equipment suppliers.

Samsung is investing 40 billion yen, or about $253.53 million and around 350 billion won, over five years starting in 2024. The Japanese government is providing 22.5 billion yen in subsidies, equivalent to roughly 190 billion won. Samsung set up a local entity in Yokohama in 2023 and plans to increase the local research workforce to more than 100 by 2027. The lab will develop and verify core packaging technologies, including wafer bonding and glass substrates, and research new packaging structures for low-power, high-performance AI chips.

Lee urged the team to secure core advanced packaging technology and called for stronger global technology partnerships. Samsung said it will actively use Yokohama's talent pool and its industry, academic and research infrastructure. The company said it will develop the APL into a research collaboration hub connecting Japanese materials and equipment companies with Samsung's semiconductor technology capabilities. The APL operates separately from the packaging research team at Samsung's semiconductor research institute in Korea, but the two organizations will work closely together.

Advanced packaging now helps determine chip performance and power efficiency, as gains from miniaturization alone become more limited. The APL links Samsung's design and manufacturing capabilities with Japan's supplier network, which includes companies such as Uemura, Disco and Resonac. Samsung plans to maximize research synergies through cooperation among the APL and its domestic facilities in Giheung, Hwaseong and Cheonan. Lee has recently stepped up visits to semiconductor sites, including a June visit to the Cheonan plant to review HBM production and advanced packaging.

Efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in courts have stalled, the ABA Journal reported on November 4, 2026. The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years. Its efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy. Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, including one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360 that she was not hopeful at this point. The article gives no other named individuals and no dates for the setbacks beyond the November 4, 2026 publication date. It also gives no specific numbers, such as counts of comments or votes. The concerns center on the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules is the body responsible for developing the proposals, and it advises the Judicial Conference of the United States. stories.Headline: Source: Meta has decided to stop using fruit for its AI model codenames, as they didn't suit its lofty AI ambitions; its latest model was named "Watermelon" (Charles Rollet/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Meta has decided internally to stop naming its artificial intelligence models after fruit, a person familiar with the matter said. The change is largely a branding decision, because fruit-based codenames do not fit Meta's lofty AI ambitions, the person added. The company's latest model, Wonder Full, which Meta described as its first cutting-edge frontier model, carried the internal codename Watermelon. Meta teased that launch by posting photos of the fruit, and it declined to comment on the naming change.

Meta had dubbed its previous language and image models Avocado and Mango. On the Cheeky Pint podcast last month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg and AI chief Alexandr Wang joked that they had run out of fruit names. Zuckerberg said they were out of fruits and would have to switch to a new convention. Wang said the only fruit technically larger is the durian, and you do not want to go to the durian.

Meta is not the only tech company to name AI products after grocery store items. In 2025, OpenAI internally dubbed one model Garlic, according to The Information, and Google released its Nano Banana image generator that same year. More recently, as AI models grow more powerful, it has become trendy to give them more awe-inspiring names, such as Anthropic's Mythos or OpenAI's Astra. The articles do not say what naming convention Meta will use next.

Separately, Yahoo Finance video host Ejaaz Ahamadeen said AI is breaking the traditional search business because people no longer go to Google and scroll through links. He said they outsource searching to AI, which does not carry monetizable search revenue and belongs to Anthropic, OpenAI and other chatbot competitors. He cited Reddit, which reported record earnings yet saw its stock fall around 26% in opening trading hours, after noting that search ad revenue was not driving enough traffic to its site. Ahamadeen said Reddit is building walls around its service, requiring users to create an account and log on, because it fears AI will replace its company and moat by training on its data without paying.

stories.Headline: New AI Architecture Could Help Medtech Firms Stay Ahead of AI-Powered FDA Reviews - Medical Device and Diagnostic industry
stories.Summary:
Enlil rolled out a new governed artificial intelligence framework built into its platform, the company announced on November 3, 2026. The framework is meant to help medical device manufacturers produce regulatory evidence that holds up when AI reviews submissions on the agency side as well as on the company side. The backdrop is the FDA's own use of generative AI, including its internal tool Elsa, which gives review and compliance staff faster and deeper ways to examine submissions. Enlil says evidence that used to be compiled manually near the end of a development program must now withstand automated, cross-referenced and rapid scrutiny.

The architecture is built on a unified system of record with governance and traceability enforced across four layers. A secure cloud-based execution layer routes tasks to different AI models based on factors like accuracy and cost while keeping data inside Enlil's governed environment. A shared services layer grounds AI interactions in each customer's own regulated content and terminology, and a read-only analysis layer can surface patterns and inconsistencies across connected quality, product lifecycle, risk and manufacturing data without altering operational records. A fourth layer of narrowly scoped agents performs specific tasks within strict boundaries and routes compliance-sensitive decisions to human reviewers. A connected data model links quality, product lifecycle, requirements, risk, procurement, manufacturing and post-market records by design, and the platform supports standard integrations with tools such as CAD, ERP and testing systems.

Enlil's leadership argues that adding AI features to existing systems is not enough in a regulated environment. The company says bolt-on AI introduces three structural vulnerabilities: sensitive data potentially leaving its governed environment for outside AI services, outputs built from disconnected documents rather than verified records, and autonomous agents operating without clear limits on what they can access, modify or approve. Enlil frames the architecture as keeping AI operations in a controlled environment, grounding outputs in verified records, enforcing boundaries on what AI can access or change, and producing documentation ready for audits or submissions. Separately, the FDA received more than 500 comments by mid-October on its August discussion paper on generative AI in medical devices. AdvaMed, the Medical Device Manufacturers Association and GE Healthcare called for building on the existing framework, while physicians and patients sought more postmarket monitoring and stronger safeguards, and hospitals and provider groups said developers, not doctors, should be responsible for device safety and performance.

The FDA's discussion paper proposed evaluating generative AI-enabled devices using a framework inspired by physician credentialing and emphasized postmarket monitoring. AdvaMed asked the FDA to keep existing premarket expectations, saying generative AI in a device should not automatically trigger a competency assessment, and to broaden its predetermined change control plan mechanism, which it called possibly too restrictive for generative AI. It also backed continued risk-based postmarket monitoring and said manufacturers should bear that responsibility. Dr. Afnan Tariq and Dr. Islam Abudayyeh of SCAI's AI task force said it is important to clarify when generative AI tools support decisions versus make them, with Abudayyeh noting the line is fine because output can look like a decision. Oura Chief Medical Officer Dr. Ricky Bloomfield asked the FDA not to treat informational, non-directive functions as devices or to place them under enforcement discretion.

stories.Headline: Moms for Liberty/JOCO testing A.I. program to detect DEI content in school board agendas
stories.Summary:
Moms for Liberty has developed an artificial intelligence program called M4L AWARE, which stands for Agenda Watch, Alert, Response, and Engage. The national organization designed it to detect Diversity, Equity and Inclusion content in some 13,000 school board agendas nationwide. The Moms for Liberty chapter in Johnson County, Kansas, is among those volunteering for pilot projects of the technology. The program scans school board agendas every 12 hours for issues including DEI, gender policies, curriculum changes and Title IX, according to the parental rights organization.

When the system flags a high-priority item, it sends local Moms for Liberty chapters a plain-language summary and a ready-to-share alert. That alert is designed to help parents organize before a school board meeting. Moms for Liberty CEO Tina Descovich said the technology promises to give parents a heads-up before school board meetings that decide district policy. She also said the program will save parents time and act as a more efficient watchdog on school board agendas.

Descovich said Moms for Liberty is harnessing AI to increase oversight of school boards across the nation and empower parents. She said the group has asked parents for five years to show up at school board meetings, and they have. She said sifting through thousands of pages of agendas each week is incredibly time-consuming, and school districts count on that. Johnson County Chapter Chair Erika Sheets said her chapter is utilizing the M4L AWARE school board alert tool quite successfully and volunteered to be part of the testing pilot program.

Sheets said the tool will help parents and community members in Kansas and across the nation demystify what school boards are doing. She said it will show how decisions are made and where and how taxpayer dollars are prioritized. She said it will generally make it much easier to be knowledgeable and engaged regarding your public school district. Sheets also said there are absolutely districts still utilizing DEI in Johnson County and likely around the state.

stories.Headline: Brutal artificial intelligence sell-off stirs recession fears
stories.Summary:
A sell-off in artificial intelligence and Big Tech shares has stirred fears that a global slowdown could deepen into recession, Jamie McGeever wrote in a Reuters column published on Wednesday, 4 November 2026. The S&P 500 is down only 4% from its recent peak, while the Nasdaq is down 10%. Over the past four years the S&P 500 had only one downturn of more than 10%, the plunge after US President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariff announcement in April 2025, and that was short-lived. The article says it remains to be seen whether the current sell-off snowballs into something more serious.

The column cites estimates on how much AI has propped up growth. Adam Slater of Oxford Economics estimated that AI-related effects in 2025 to 2026 added an average of 0.2 percentage point to GDP growth across a sample of six advanced economies, without which underlying growth was only around 0.5% to 1% a year. US growth over the same period was 2.4%, and around a third of that was related to AI, he estimated. Stocks now make up almost 47% of US households’ financial assets and 34% of total assets, both record shares. Economists at Goldman Sachs estimated the AI boost to US consumer spending growth from positive wealth effects was worth 0.4 percentage point, or 0.25% of GDP, over the past year.

Slater wrote last week that the weakness of underlying growth across advanced economies meant the risk of recession would be substantial if the AI boom slowed seriously. Pimco’s Tiffany Wilding and Andrew Balls noted that a downward repricing of AI-related equities could generate a meaningful negative wealth effect, especially at the top of the income spectrum. The article says a total AI capital expenditure bust and complete market meltdown are both unlikely, since the infrastructure build-out and the AI revolution are still in their infancy. It adds that the AI market narrative and sentiment are clearly shifting.

The column describes a cooling global backdrop. Domestic demand in China remains weak as a five-year property slump continues, and Beijing could struggle to post annual growth next year of 4.5% to 5%. It says the outlook looks shaky in many of Europe’s largest economies, with political unrest and budget gridlock in France, Germany expected to grow at around 1%, and Britain’s 2027 outlook just slashed. Brent crude closed last Friday at its highest level in six months, European gas prices are the highest in four years, US mortgage rates are well above 7%, and corporate borrowing spreads are widening notably. The article says that if investor discomfort turns into a rout, global growth could be hit hard.
