stories.Headline: ICAIR 2026: Africa Risks Economic Dependence Without Home-grown AI Technologies, Experts Warn
stories.Summary:
Academic leaders and technology experts warned at a conference that Africa risks permanent economic dependence on advanced nations unless it shifts from importing artificial intelligence technologies to building its own. They spoke at the 6th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, known as ICAIR 2026, which ran from November 3 to 5, 2026, at the University of Lagos in Nigeria. The event was organised by the Machine Intelligence Research Group at the University of Lagos and carried the theme Artificial Intelligence for Africa's Sustainable Economic Growth. It brought together academic leaders, researchers and technology experts to examine how the continent could use AI for sustainable development.

The experts said Africa's economic future and technological sovereignty depend on developing home-grown AI models, building indigenous digital infrastructure and equipping its young population with relevant skills. Dr. Oladipupo Sennaike, who heads the local organising committee and chairs the planning committee, said Africa cannot remain a passive spectator in the latest technological revolution. He noted that the agricultural and industrial revolutions created new economic powers and that the digital revolution transformed the global economy, adding that Africa must position itself to benefit from the AI revolution. He urged African countries to move from importing AI solutions to developing technologies that address their own challenges.

In his keynote, Prof. Kanshukan Rajaratnam, director of the School for Data Science and Computational Thinking at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, said the defining challenge of the AI era is who will shape the technology and benefit from its economic opportunities. Sennaike wrote that the conference aimed to go beyond presenting research papers and to create an environment where people exchange ideas and find opportunities to work together. He named other confirmed keynote speakers as Dr. Sunday Oladejo of Stellenbosch University and Mr. Opeyemi Folorunsho, vice president of research and development at Moniepoint. He said the different backgrounds of the speakers would bring valuable perspectives on the link between research, innovation and industry application.

Sennaike said the conference was not only for computer scientists, listing software developers, data scientists, entrepreneurs, investors, lecturers, students, policymakers and journalists among those who should take part. He said physical and virtual participation were both provided because not everyone could travel to Lagos. He stressed that Africa has considerable talent and no shortage of ideas, but must keep building research capacity, institutional support, investment and collaboration to turn those ideas into solutions. He added that the responsibility of shaping Africa's AI future cannot be left to other parts of the world.

HD Hyundai Robotics said on Nov. 1 that it delivered a keynote presentation at Palantir's Sovereignty Bootcamp in New York, an event focused on protecting corporate data while exploring ways to strengthen competitiveness through AI. The keynote was given by Ahn Sung-hwan, the company's chief technology officer, who outlined its physical AI adoption strategy and shared progress from its collaboration with Palantir. The two companies have been working together to transform workflows and redefine the role of on-site engineers in industrial operations. AI agents analyze existing robot programs and identify possible improvements, which on-site engineers then refine using their experience. On-site engineers will be trained as field solution specialists who define problems and use AI to implement optimal solutions. The companies will hold regular steering committee meetings with senior executives to discuss the direction and priorities of their collaboration.

Ahn said the company will identify opportunities to solve on-site problems quickly and effectively and will expand the scope of business applications. Ryan Taylor, chief revenue officer of Palantir, said the collaboration is focused on projects that can deliver measurable results in a short period, and that Palantir will help HD Hyundai Robotics use its accumulated experience to secure a competitive advantage. Palantir has expanded its work with HD Hyundai affiliates since making a 24 billion won equity investment in HD Hyundai Oilbank in 2021. stories.Headline: Together AI Beats OpenRouter, Fireworks: $0.88/M [2026]
stories.Summary:
On November 4, 2026, shattered.io published a comparison of Together AI, Fireworks AI and OpenRouter, written by Tom Vance. It reported that Together AI and Fireworks AI sell tokens directly from their own GPU fleets, while OpenRouter is a routing layer that bills each request at the underlying provider's list price and collects a fee when customers buy credits. On the open models both clouds host, the standard rates match to the decimal, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens at either one. Meta's Muse Spark Open landed on Together AI on October 15 and on Fireworks AI on October 20, and OpenRouter rebuilt its default provider routing on October 28.

OpenRouter charges 5.5% on credit purchases under its Standard plan and 8% under Business, with a $0.80 minimum per purchase, and crypto payments carry a flat 5% fee. Its first $25,000 per month of list-price inference through a customer's own provider keys carries no fee, and usage above that costs 5%. Together AI charges no fee on serverless usage and has no minimums, with entry pricing per token, and its US endpoint multiplies input, cached input and output rates by 1.25. Fireworks AI advertises pay-per-token usage from $0.05 per million input tokens, with Priority adding 25% on Ember-1, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 20% on GPT-OSS 120B and 50% on Muse Spark Open and Qwen 3.8 Max, while Spot cuts 30% and Batch cuts 50% off input and output. Fireworks applies a 50% premium on US-only serverless for select models, waived on Muse Spark Open, and its fine-tuning starts at $0.50 per million training tokens.

Together AI's Post-Training, launched October 19, bills reserved GPU time, and its example of four trainer and four generator GPUs on B200-SXM at $11 per GPU-hour comes to $88 per hour, with a promotional rate valid until December 14, 2026. Together's dedicated H100 80GB runs $5.49 per hour, and Fireworks' On-Demand pricing is reportedly $13 per hour. OpenRouter's Auto Exacto re-evaluates providers every 5 minutes for tool-calling requests and is on by default, and on October 30 the company added Private Endpoints for Enterprise customers. A separate Quasa.io article from November 2, 2026 reported InferenceBench measurements: on GLM-5.2, Together's median time to first token was 291 ms against OpenRouter's 413 ms, with reported reliability of 93.5% against 99.1%, and on DeepSeek V4 Flash, OpenRouter led on output throughput, 101 against 67 tokens per second, and reliability, 100% against 91.9%.

The articles say the choice depends on the workload. Quasa.io said to choose Together AI when a fixed model on its inference service meets latency and reliability needs, and OpenRouter when an application benefits from selecting among providers, controlling a route's price or keeping another provider if one fails. Shattered.io said that if cost predictability matters, customers should pin a specific provider in the request rather than accept the default, because the 5.5% fee is a known quantity while an unpinned router is not. It also noted that OpenRouter's secondary coverage reportedly puts the cost increase from the routing change near 6%, though that figure does not come from OpenRouter and the sources checked could not confirm it.

stories.Headline: Y Combinator CEO spends ₹1.8 crore on AI tokens annually
stories.Summary:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan spends up to ₹1.8 crore, or $200,000, a year on AI tokens, he said on Walter Isaacson's podcast The Builders, which was set to publish on Tuesday. He uses AI agents for work projects, coding tasks and preparing for conversations. The agents can read his entire email history, his Dropbox files, his Apple Notes and even his therapy notes going back 20 years. Tan has also shared 23 Claude Code skills on GitHub under the name gstack to teach others what agents can do. Tan described the experience as having a Jiminy Cricket on his shoulder at all times, one that knows him and helps him see around corners.

Y Combinator also uses an internal AI agent called Stray Light, which holds the context of every founder the firm has backed, anyone who has emailed it and all applications. Tan said he has learned not to treat AI agents like traditional software, because some people trade away the best parts of working with them over worries about repeatability and safety. He believes personal AI agents will become mainstream only if costs come down, and he called his own spending a crazy privilege that not everyone can do. In a related case, Cisco gave a 27-year-old employee, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, unlimited AI tokens for a project to rewrite a large portion of the company's legacy code. Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel said the goal is to refactor 98 per cent of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months.

Patel believes giving young, AI-native employees ambitious engineering projects can help companies innovate their work processes. Tan said he knows his spending level is not something everyone can afford. Tan also warned about free agents controlled by Big Tech, saying Meta controls the algorithm and people wish it did not at some level. He suggested people could imagine a personal AI that they control and program themselves. The articles do not say what Tan or Cisco will do next beyond these plans and views.

stories.Headline: QX TaxReady combines AI and humans to manage tax prep for firms
stories.Summary:
QX Global Group launched QX TaxReady in the United States on November 3, 2026, according to a GlobeNewswire release, and Accounting Today reported the news on November 4, 2026. The service is a fully managed tax preparation offering that combines agentic AI with more than 500 tax specialists. QX's AI tax agents had already been available and had prepared and delivered thousands of returns for some US CPA firms, but this is the first time they have been combined with human experts. The US launch follows the debut of QX TaxReady for UK accounting and tax firms in September 2026.

Under the service, a firm sends QX its client documents, and the ROBO1040 AI handles repeatable preparation work such as document intake, data extraction and working paper population. A human QX preparer then validates the information, handles exceptions and prepares the return, and a senior reviewer checks every return before it goes back to the firm for its own final review and signature. The service covers simple, complex and business tax returns, including all federal returns for all individual taxpayers, and it requires no separate software license. QX said the AI agent's first pass has been more than 95% accurate in early deployments, average handling time per return has been 40 to 50% lower than with manual preparation, and preparation costs are more than 50% lower than with traditional outsourcing models. There is one negotiated price per return, with no hourly billing, and QX said the price stays the same in October and on April 15.

CEO Vijay Pahuja said firms kept telling QX they did not want another tool to manage during busy season and wanted the work done right. He said US firms have been stuck with three imperfect options: in-house work means burnt-out staff and capacity that runs out when needed, traditional outsourcing brings prices that creep up and billing that is hard to follow, and a pure AI tool is fast but nobody is accountable when it gets something wrong. Vishal Kurani, vice president of brand communications and marketing, said traditional outsourcing runs on people and hours, so costs rise with volume and prices spike when demand peaks, while QX starts from the outcome of a ready and accurate return and prices that. Kurani said the results come from the combination of AI and human expertise, not either one alone, and that a qualified senior reviewer checks every return so the efficiency does not cost the firm accountability.

QX said the service was developed in response to three industry challenges: not enough staff, with many firms turning away work because they cannot staff for the season, rising costs when outsourcing demand spikes, and AI that can make mistakes but cannot be held accountable for them. The company said its data handling is SOC 2 compliant and certified to ISO 27001, with data privacy under ISO 27701 and quality management under ISO 9001. The US business is led by Rahul Bhalla, executive vice president and business head for the Americas, and Steve House, previously in senior growth roles at EisnerAmper and Baker Tilly, leads Accounting Services growth. QX said state coverage is a work in progress, starting with some major states, and the service is available now to US accounting and tax firms ahead of the 2027 filing season.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI models trail US rivals in new AI rankings
stories.Summary:
Artificial Analysis, an independent firm that measures AI performance, overhauled its testing system and published new rankings on November 3 and 4, 2026. The change made many tests secret so that AI companies could not train their models specifically for them. Under the new system, Chinese and other open-weight AI models fell sharply behind American rivals. The gap between the best open-weight models and the overall leader widened from three points to 12 points.

The rankings gave Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 a score of 58 points, while the leaders among models with publicly released weights scored only 32 points. That group included Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro. Even Anthropic's smaller Claude Haiku 5.5 model outperformed every publicly released open-weight model. The articles say the results suggest American companies have a bigger lead than previously believed, particularly in complex scientific tasks.

Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO of Snowflake and a former Google executive, wrote on X that the day benchmarks went private, the open-model gap went from 3 points to 12. He asked whether open models were catching up or the test was leaking. Nathan Lambert, cofounder of Trillium Labs, said the previous index was likely flattering open-weight models too strongly. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other experts have called training models for known tests benchmark hacking.

The articles say the findings could affect the billions of dollars investors are pouring into AI, and could strengthen the case for Anthropic's planned IPO and a possible future OpenAI listing. Dax Raad, cofounder of OpenCode, estimated that almost all of the previous day's DeepSeek traffic through OpenRouter could be handled by a single rack of Nvidia computers costing $6 million to $7 million. OpenRouter covers only a slice of the market, but the articles say the figures raise questions about how much demand open-weight models really have, compared with ChatGPT's more than one billion monthly users. Lambert said open-weight models remain competitive in areas such as software development.

stories.Headline: Tencent Launches Upgraded Hy4 AI Model With Visual Understanding
stories.Summary:
Tencent Holdings launched its next-generation large language model, Hunyuan Hy4, on Wednesday, Nov. 4, according to Caixin Global. The model adds visual understanding and the ability to operate computers, as Tencent seeks to narrow the gap with leading AI developers. The release is part of Tencent's push to embed advanced AI in enterprise software and turn technical improvements into commercial value. Tencent's Hong Kong-listed shares closed up 1.1% at HK$401.6, giving it a market capitalization of about HK$3.65 trillion.

Hy4 is an open-source model with 770 billion parameters, up from its predecessor. It cut hallucination to 7.2% from 12.95% and guessing errors to 5.6% from 23.1%, and it is priced at 6 yuan per million input tokens. Separately, Moonshot AI launched an upgraded Kimi model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, which China Daily said debuted fourth on independent evaluator Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index with 55 points, up 11 from its predecessor. The model has 2.8 trillion parameters, with about 104 billion activated for each token processed, and a one-million-token context window. Moonshot plans to release its full weights by Nov. 4.

Moonshot said the upgrade was built through further training of Kimi K3, with improvements aimed at practical tasks such as building software, creating 3D assets and analyzing financial documents. The company said it removed cybersecurity-related data from parts of its training pipeline, including reinforcement-learning environments, while keeping general programming tasks. It said it aims not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. On its internal test of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, K3.1 Pro scored 81.0%, compared with 90.5% for a comparable version without such safeguards, figures the company reported itself. In its Terminal-Bench 4.0 evaluation, K3.1 Pro scored 65.7%, ahead of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 58.2% and just behind Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4%.

The launches come as Moonshot prepares to tap public markets. Bloomberg reported that the Beijing-based firm had completed a private funding round valuing it at about $50 billion and was targeting a Hong Kong debut in the first quarter of 2027. Bloomberg Intelligence said China's top AI models have narrowed the performance gap with US rivals to around 3%, the lowest on record, and senior analyst Robert Lea said the speed of the catching-up raises questions over how long the US can maintain its technological lead. Stanford's 2026 AI Index said the gap had effectively closed, with the best US model ahead by only 2.7% as of March. Zhang Yaqin of Tsinghua University's Institute for AI Industry Research said Chinese models have entered the global top tier, while professor Tang Jie said China still needs to catch up in high-end computing chips, fundamental AI architecture and the broader technology ecosystem.

stories.Headline: Smugglers Melt Solder to Strip Korean HBM for Huawei
stories.Summary:
Smugglers are diverting high-bandwidth memory made by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix into China by packaging it with low-end server processors, The Information reported on November 2, 2026. The combined package is classified as a low-end server processor rather than a standalone HBM product, so it slips past U.S. export limits. Once the packages reach China, technicians heat them to melt the solder, pry off the HBM and discard the server processors. The work needs precision and failure rates are high, because too much heat warps or cracks the memory stacks. Smugglers accept the risk because the profit is large even after ruined units are counted.

The HBM obtained this way flows mainly to Huawei's customers, and Huawei has told some customers that its next-generation Ascend 960DT AI chip will contain substantial amounts of Samsung and SK hynix memory. Huawei has said the chip will deliver twice the performance of its existing products. Unable to buy memory directly from the Korean suppliers, Huawei has told some customers ordering its AI chips to source the memory themselves. Samsung and SK hynix together control more than 80% of the HBM market, and Chinese domestic output is minimal. A broker in their 20s who arranges smuggled memory deals in China told The Information the work is about contributing to the motherland.

According to that broker, the price of a single HBM3E unit has jumped to about $4,000 from several hundred dollars a year ago. Because one AI chip package requires six to eight memory units, the memory alone adds $24,000 to $32,000 on top of the cost of the AI chip, servers and power. SK hynix said it strictly complies with all applicable laws and regulations, including U.S. and Korean export controls, and has not supplied products to Huawei since Washington imposed export restrictions in 2020. One smuggler who has been ordering memory chips from Korea said the routes are now being used by other dealers, and that crackdowns in Korea and the U.S. will only get tougher.

That smuggler said they plan to sell most of their stake in the company next year. The situation is awkward for the two Korean suppliers, which could come under U.S. government scrutiny if their memory is found inside Chinese-made AI chips. Taiwan's TSMC faced a U.S. investigation in 2024 after one of its chips turned up in a Huawei product, and was later ordered to halt all AI chip exports to China. HBM is a critical component that lifts AI chip performance by moving data at very high speed, and the shortage limits the ability of Chinese firms such as DeepSeek and Moonshot to keep training and deploying large models.

stories.Headline: Siri AI opens to third-party apps in iOS 27.3 beta
stories.Summary:
Apple began beta testing iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3 and other updates on November 3, 2026, after iOS 27.2 reached customers on October 26. A highlight of the beta is that Apple now allows all developers to connect their apps to Siri AI using App Intents. The betas also bring two Audio Intelligence features to the latest Apple Watch models, Live Rewind and Siri Recap, and they bring back Apple's redesigned Health app. Apple Intelligence tools also arrive in China with this update, though Siri AI does not.

Apple said the preview lets any app bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness and natural language. Users will be able to check a delivery, book a reservation or place an order without opening an app, and developers can teach Siri to combine several actions for more complicated requests. The new capabilities are available for testing in the betas, with apps expected to begin reaching customers in 2027. Submissions to the App Store using the new capabilities are open until spring, and Apple says iOS 27.3 will reach the public in December.

On Apple's earnings call on November 2, chief financial officer Kevan Parekh said AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch, and that there are opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities. He did not elaborate on what those opportunities might be, and Reuters reported that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue. Parekh said App Store performance in the September quarter was similar to the prior year, with a record number of paid subscriptions and double-digit growth for third-party apps, but he noted headwinds in mobile gaming. He said services growth is expected to be between 8 and 9 percent in the December quarter.

Apple has been talking up third-party access to Siri AI since WWDC26 in June, and the beta is the first step toward it. The first beta is available to registered developers through Software Update in Settings, and a public beta should follow the developer release. The Audio Intelligence features work only on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 because they depend on a hardware-isolated Secure Exclave in the new S11 processor. The redesigned Health app adds an Insights tab with personalized recommendations and a Longevity section with a Health Age estimate, and it had been pulled from later iOS 27.2 betas before the public release.

stories.Headline: The AI sell-off saved Apple from a sell-off of its own
stories.Summary:
Apple reported its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share, with iPhone revenue up 17.5% to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion and Mac revenue up 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest in four years. Despite the results, Apple shares fell 2% on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as investors focused on slowing services growth and lower projected margins, and the stock dropped further in premarket trading after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze holiday quarter margins. The wider AI sell-off a few trading days earlier may have cushioned Apple's fall, since investors fleeing Google, Amazon and Microsoft moved money toward Apple as a safer bet. AI was mentioned 45 times on the earnings call, a record according to AlphaSense, and CFO Kevan Parekh cited a wide range of ways AI can add to revenue over time.

Apple's approach relies on on-device processing, its own servers and outside AI technology rather than heavy infrastructure spending. Siri AI uses models built with Google's Gemini technology, and Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features like writing tools and image generation. Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon's $77.3 billion and Alphabet's $51.4 billion, while operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as research and development spending, including on AI, increased. The revamped Siri AI launched in beta for US English users in September and expanded to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in October, and Apple plans to charge for expanded access to server-based features in the future.

CEO John Ternus, on his first earnings call as CEO, said he sees tremendous opportunity in AI, and Parekh said AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch to get the latest capabilities. HSBC analyst Nicolas Cote-Colisson wrote in a note on Tuesday that Apple is in a better position than many of its tech peers and keeps delivering record operational and financial results quarter after quarter. Ternus said Mac Mini and Mac Studio are pushing the boundaries of local, private AI, and he cited Gap running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores and Christie's running local models on Mac Studio computers for tasks including pricing estimates. Former CEO Tim Cook said earlier this year that demand for the Mac Mini and Mac Studio for AI and agentic tools was higher than Apple had predicted.

Apple has more than 2.5 billion active devices, giving it a large audience for whatever AI services emerge, and it can collect fees on subscriptions to AI apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from AI subscriptions. Parekh said it is too early to predict how many Siri AI requests will need servers rather than on-device processing, and those cloud costs will appear in services cost of sales and could grow with usage. Ternus said customers who need more capacity will be able to purchase expanded access in the future, comparing it to how iCloud tiers began largely as storage and gained more features over time.

stories.Headline: Global AI protein design challenge seeks participants worldwide
stories.Summary:
The Changjiang Cup 2026 Global AI Protein Design Challenge announced its competition topics and full rules on Sunday, with registration open worldwide until the end of November. The contest is guided by the Shanghai Municipal Commission of Economy and Informatization and the Shanghai Municipal Science and Technology Commission. It is jointly initiated and hosted by Shanghai Jiao Tong University, the Beijing-based Changping Laboratory and the Shanghai-based Lin Gang Laboratory. The challenge aims to gather global innovation power in AI for science through an open contest.

The competition features seven protein design targets and focuses on the de novo design of VHH nanobodies or minibinders. The organizing committee will carry out wet lab validation on no fewer than 7,000 selected candidate proteins, exploring the research cycle from AI design to automated experimental validation. It is open to universities, research institutions, companies and interdisciplinary innovation teams worldwide, and it encourages researchers in AI, computational biology, structural biology and protein engineering to work across disciplines. More than 1,900 teams have already registered, including nearly all of the global top 50 universities and more than 50 global innovative pharmaceutical companies, a record in scale and level for similar events.

Separately, scientists led by a team at Westlake University in China developed a large-scale AI model called Pinal that can generate candidate proteins from natural language prompts alone, as detailed in a paper in the journal Nature. A user enters a written description of the job they want the protein to do, and Pinal uses two modules, T2struct and SaProt-T, to build a structural blueprint and then a matching amino acid sequence. The study authors wrote that Pinal translates high-level functional descriptions into candidate protein sequences, reducing reliance on manually specified structural templates or geometric constraints. Training used 135 million protein sequences, which became a library of 1.7 billion protein-text pairs, with predicted 3D structures from an existing AlphaFold database.

In tests, Pinal designed four proteins: a fluorescent protein, a plastic-breaking enzyme, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein. For the glowing protein it created 50,000 sequences, filtered them to 29 for testing, and only one actually fluoresced, and the researchers acknowledged that controlling specific properties is still difficult. The system did better with the metabolic H-protein shuttle, where five of 20 candidates worked and the best one boosted the output of a key carbon-capturing process to 1.7 times that achieved using the natural E. coli protein. The article says Pinal still has limitations and that further work is needed before it becomes a routine lab tool.

stories.Headline: '30 Days of Work in One': Public Servant Builds AI Safety Platform
stories.Summary:
Shin Hae-seop, an administrative officer at the Construction Headquarters of Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, developed a facility safety management platform himself beginning in January 2026. The project grew out of the difficulties he faced managing hundreds of road facilities such as bridges, tunnels, underpasses and retaining walls, which deteriorate as they age. As the number of facilities kept growing, officials had to check inspection schedules and targets one by one, and legal standards differ by facility type. Staff also had to draw up design specification documents by hand each time a safety inspection contract went out to bid. No outside contractor was hired and no separate budget was allocated, and Shin used artificial intelligence as a development tool.

The platform automatically classifies inspection targets based on the legal standards for each facility type, analyzes whether higher-level inspections have been carried out, and determines whether lower-level inspections can be skipped. Damage, cracks and repair and reinforcement records that had been scattered across individual reports are now consolidated by facility, so users can check whether a crack in the same location is widening or whether a repair is coming due. Work that previously took more than 30 days for safety inspection and diagnostic contracts now takes less than a day. The platform automates data verification, the application of calculation standards and document preparation, which cuts repetitive administrative work and speeds up contract awards.

Records are no longer lost when staff change, according to the article. Son Du-yeong, head of the Construction Headquarters, said administrative innovation using AI and digital technology improves work efficiency and contributes to public safety. He added that the city will continue to upgrade its facility safety management system and expand administrative services that employees and residents can feel in practice. Officials said the system is highly usable because it was created by a public servant who knows the field best, in the language of the field.

Separately, Fraunhofer researchers are developing an AI-driven civil protection dashboard with partners in the RegioGuard-PRO project, which runs from March 2026 through March 2028 and is funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space. The project builds on two earlier projects, AKRIMA and HERAKLION, and a ready-to-use demonstrator is planned within two years. Research scientist Kai Fischer said municipalities often have vast amounts of data during crises but it is scattered across sources and not interconnected, and that the platform consolidates and analyzes large data sets to enable early detection of hazards. Demonstration centers are being established in Trier, Mainz and Wildau to test the dashboard under realistic field conditions, with the aim of eventually deploying it in other regions.

stories.Headline: Legal system must keep pace with AI growth
stories.Summary:
At the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Zhejiang province, cyberspace experts spoke on Wednesday at the Cyberspace Rule of Law Forum, which was held on the sidelines of the event under the theme "Law and AI for Good: World's Landscape and China's Practice." Renata Mielli, special adviser to Brazil's minister of state for science, technology and innovation, said AI adoption is moving much faster than society's ability to understand its consequences and regulate it. Keovisouk Solaphom, deputy minister of technology and communications of the Lao People's Democratic Republic, said his country attaches great importance to improving its legal system for AI. Liu Taizong, director of the economic crime prosecution department of the Supreme People's Procuratorate, said new AI issues such as the "algorithm black box," "data poisoning" and "AI hallucinations" have emerged one after another.

Mielli said existing data protection, consumer protection and constitutional safeguards in Brazil remain essential but are insufficient for the specific challenges of AI. She called for clear obligations on algorithmic impact assessments, nondiscrimination, human oversight and accountability throughout the AI value chain, and said regulation should not be seen as an obstacle to innovation. She said appropriate rules can create trust, legal certainty and better conditions for responsible technological development. She added that Brazil faces the challenge of accelerating its national AI strategy, strengthening domestic technological capabilities and establishing an effective regulatory framework.

Solaphom said Laos is moving step by step on a legal foundation that includes laws on cybersecurity and personal data protection, the amended law on digital technology and the decree on digital government. He said the first task is to review these instruments to see whether they address AI issues and then to determine where new ones are needed. He said no country can address these challenges alone and that they require extensive consultation, joint contributions and shared benefits. He added that countries should share legislative experience, safety standards and testing methods to improve compatibility among regulatory frameworks and better prevent misuse of AI in fraud and scams.

Liu said criminals are increasingly using deepfakes and generative large language models for illegal activities, threatening cybersecurity and social stability. He said the rapid development of AI and the upgrading of industry models require continuous updates to governance rules. He said prosecutorial agencies will work with legislative and administrative bodies to advance legal frameworks in the AI field, such as the AI law. He said whether AI serves humanity as a trustworthy, reliable and controllable tool or becomes a source of risks depends on using the rule of law to establish safeguards, guide technology toward positive uses and regulate its applications.

stories.Headline: AI agent autonomy remains an elusive work in progress
stories.Summary:
A KPMG survey conducted in July and August found that 62% of IT leaders were building, deploying, or developing AI agents, up from 53% in the previous quarter, according to an article by Grant Gross published by CIO on November 5, 2026. Despite that growth, many IT leaders remain uncomfortable with turning internal processes over to agents, with exceptions for basic, low-risk functions such as tier 1 IT support. Jim Olsen, CTO of the AI lifecycle management and governance vendor ModelOp, said agent autonomy is making inroads in limited cases, for example to process customer refunds or credits without human intervention. He pointed to the wide adoption of Clawdbot and OpenClaw by individuals who gave the tools full access to their email and full autonomy, saying it worked out well for some people but carried a large risk exposure.

Olsen recommended confining autonomous bots to a strict sandbox with well-defined policies that limit their autonomy, and he said he does not see enterprises allowing agents full and complete autonomy in the near future, though restricted autonomy is already in use. He predicted that activities that are not mission critical and lack access to sensitive information will be where IT leaders first grant agents full autonomy, and that trust will improve along with the breadth of use cases. The article also notes concerns about autonomy creep, when agents quietly take more authority than they are given, and warnings from AI and security experts that human-in-the-loop guardrails do not always give employees the authority or time to fix agent errors. Olsen said IT leaders can enforce runtime policies through API gateways, OS-level enforcement, and credential management, tying clear policies to the specific agent and use case, though he added that a more cohesive strategy is needed to reach a minimal level of trust.

Siroui Mushegian, CIO of the cybersecurity vendor Barracuda Networks, has about 2,000 agents deployed in her enterprise and still has human employees checking bot actions. She said many of her ticketing automations fall in a trust-but-verify category, and that while success brings greater comfort, she is still not fully certain she wants zero human accountability, especially for auditable processes. She said the consequences of a mistake should determine how much evidence is needed before giving an agent more authority, and she named routine internal support requests with well-documented answers, limited actions, and easy corrections as reasonable candidates for autonomy, while agents that can change access permissions or production systems are less likely candidates. Joshua Rowe, co-founder and CTO of the household bills app provider Taupia, said he would draw the line at the action rather than the agent, since the same agent can act alone on one step and need sign-off on the next. He said Taupia is testing agent functionality that compares energy deals and lets customers switch providers without employees approving each step, though the customer still reviews and confirms the change before it takes effect.

Rowe said autonomous authority for irreversible actions depends not on smarter AI models but on how quickly an organization can make each action reversible or bounded, with spending limits, cooling-off periods, rollback, and an audit trail good enough to undo a mistake. He said he would keep a person approving actions that cannot be undone, such as signing a contract or moving money out of an account, for the foreseeable future. Maciej Walaszczyk, CTO at the AI customer service platform provider Text, said agents in customer service can answer inquiries without constant supervision because they learn from knowledge provided by humans, and that the scope of autonomy depends on permissions and the consequences of an action. He said he would not hand entire departments over to agents, and instead recommended delegating specific processes where leaders can define the goal, set boundaries, and verify outcomes. He added that an agent acting on his behalf cannot have more authority than he does, that oversight must be real and means more than clicking approve, and that irreversible actions or those with major consequences require human review.

stories.Headline: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training
stories.Summary:
Qitan Lv, Ke Fan, Hong Wang, Wen Wu, Yilin Wang, Bowen Zhou, Feng Wu and Chao Zhang posted a paper to arXiv on 5 November 2026 describing a post-training method for Video Large Language Models called OWLET. The method is built on an observation from their experiments: the same model reasons more accurately when its video view combines global temporal context with question-relevant details. Comparing the same student-generated response under that view and under uniform sampling showed changes in token likelihoods and internal representations, which the authors treat as a training signal for evidence use. The paper is listed under the identifier 2610.13272. The authors say existing post-training methods follow two main paradigms, reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation, and that neither fully exploits visual evidence.

Reinforcement learning, in their account, supervises the policy with a single trajectory-level reward, which they call too coarse-grained for video reasoning because the same response-level advantage is applied to every generated token. On-policy distillation gives token-level supervision through output-distribution matching but lacks direct supervision of the spatiotemporal representations that produce those outputs. OWLET is described as an evidence-privileged reinforcement learning method that derives training signals from a richer teacher view, which couples uniform global context with question-conditioned local windows and provides visual evidence without requiring a larger model. To exploit this privileged visual evidence, OWLET introduces two components. The first is evidence-aware credit redistribution, which compares token likelihoods across the two views and redistributes positive response-level advantages according to their relative evidence support.

The second is spatiotemporal state alignment, which aligns the two views' hidden states on responses accepted by a verifier. The paper presents these as its contributions for better using visual evidence during post-training. The abstract frames post-training as a key stage for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Video Large Language Models. It states that the authors observed the reasoning difference across extensive experiments. The article does not say what happens next, such as whether code or models will be released or where the work will be published.

stories.Headline: Netflix's AI-powered search lets you search by your mood
stories.Summary:
Netflix announced on November 3, 2026, that it is launching a new AI-powered search feature called AI Discover. The feature appears as a new tab on the Netflix TV app, where users can say what they are in the mood for and get TV and movie suggestions from the catalog. Netflix had tested the idea last year before announcing the launch. The company said the tool is beginning to roll out to U.S. users who watch in English.

Users pick a theme such as Something Light or Scare Me, and they can also choose by how much time they have or who they are watching with. Netflix then matches them with recommendations, and if they are not satisfied they can search more specific themes that pop up. A Tune Your Recommendations option lets them keep or toss each suggested title. The Hollywood Reporter said the first version is built around a carousel of themes and initially includes only TV shows, not movies.

A Netflix spokesperson said AI Discover is powered by a new intelligence layer that responds to what members say in real time and keeps learning. The spokesperson said the company can understand what subscribers are in the mood for right now and open up new paths to discovery beyond the predefined ones. Etay Teller, an engineering director at Netflix, said the goal is to reimagine Discover so that every member's experience feels more personal, effortless and in tune with what they want. A representative also said user feedback from the feature will not be used to help executives make programming decisions.

Netflix described AI Discover as a test kitchen where it tries out new recipes for discovery, and it said some may make their way into the main Netflix experience. The feature was developed in-house and is described as a completely different, more expansive use of the technology than the company's earlier OpenAI partnership for its basic search field. Mashable reported that the search engine is powered by OpenAI, though Netflix's blog post did not clarify this. Netflix plans to expand the feature in the coming weeks and will keep testing how it works.

He said the offering combines HCLTech's mainframe expertise with AI-driven capabilities to help clients simplify operations, reduce risk and get more value from their mainframe investments. Raghu Kidambi, Corporate Vice President and Head of AI Ecosystems at HCLTech, said AI is changing how enterprises manage and derive value from their technology platforms. He said the platform would help organisations shift from reactive management to proactive, insight-driven operations while preserving security, resilience and governance.

Mainframes continue to underpin critical enterprise workloads even as companies look to modernise legacy infrastructure. HCLTech said organisations operating these systems face increasing pressure to modernise without compromising reliability or control. The company said the offering is designed to support enterprise operations while maintaining human oversight and the security, resilience and governance that mission-critical systems require. stories.Headline: OpenAI considers rebranding data centers to 'AI compute campuses" as data center backlash intensifies
stories.Summary:
OpenAI is considering rebranding its data centers as "AI compute campuses," according to reports from Axios cited by TechCrunch and Tom's Hardware. The company is preparing a public relations campaign for after the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as Democrats seemed likely to win back the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, told Axios that the midterms would be "a bit of a movie trailer" for what he expects in 2028, when he believes AI will be the issue in the presidential election. The proposed terminology change has reportedly been ongoing since August.

The rebrand is part of a broader push that includes several proposals, such as developing AI "speed limits," helping people see AI as empowering in their daily lives, and pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards. A company spokesperson said "compute campuses" better describes the role of the infrastructure OpenAI is rebuilding for AI, calling the projects long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled jobs. Alongside the rebrand, OpenAI this week launched the "Grid Protectors Program," a non-binding pledge to reduce data center electricity demand when the U.S. grid is under strain, working with utilities, regulators, and policymakers. Lehane said OpenAI's policy priorities and urgency, especially on frontier safety, are about meeting the moment in response to rapidly advancing capabilities.

Lehane described the conversation around data centers as "good and healthy" and said communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they truly get a transformative benefit from these projects. The articles note that data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, and nearby communities have raised concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills, and limited public consultation. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed opposed having a new data center built in their community, and an August report described negotiations between developers and local authorities frequently taking place behind non-disclosure agreements. Amazon and Microsoft have said they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments.

The resistance has affected construction plans. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle's $16 billion Stargate project went ahead in Saline township despite local opposition, and Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback. Other companies have also tried to reshape AI language: President Donald Trump directed federal agencies in late September to replace "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence," Nvidia CEO Huang has referred to data centers as "superintelligence factories," and Meta established Meta superintelligence labs in 2025. The articles say OpenAI's proposed terminology will face a harder test than finding a name, since communities will still want answers about the raised issues.

stories.Headline: Europe's Biggest Tech Startup Cuts AI Coding Costs by 90% Using Chinese Model
stories.Summary:
Revolut, the British fintech company, cut its costs for AI coding tasks to about one-tenth of what it had been spending on Anthropic and OpenAI by self-hosting the open-weight GLM model from the Chinese AI lab Z.ai on dedicated NVIDIA GPUs. David Abitbol, who leads AI operations at Revolut, revealed this at a technical session at the AI Engineering conference. The company began experimenting with AI tools in January 2025, first introducing Gemini for internal data access and then testing Anthropic's Claude Code. Concerned about commercial AI costs, with some engineers spending $1,000 to $10,000 monthly without clear returns, Revolut imposed strict usage budgets before it began self-hosting open-source models in April 2026 and settled on the GLM family for coding work.

The deployment improved engineering lead times by 70% and coding time by 60% across a sample of 2,000 engineers. Abitbol said self-hosting GLM brings the blended cost of tokens to 30 cents per million. The infrastructure consists of 56 NVIDIA B200 GPUs serving about 2,000 engineers running GLM-5.3, with a target time to first token below three seconds and interactive workloads served at around 200 tokens per second, rising to 800 tokens per second after 5 pm when GPU demand is lower. Between April and August, requests per second rose from about three to more than seven while time to first token fell from over 10 seconds to around 1.6 seconds, an 88% performance improvement despite a 76% increase in demand. Revolut still uses frontier tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini for specialised workloads including image recognition, while its internally hosted GLM models handle most coding tasks.

Abitbol said Revolut downloads model weights and runs inference on US-based infrastructure rather than sending requests to Chinese-hosted endpoints. He said open source is now a priority at Revolut, the economics are favourable, the billing is flat and there is no bill shock at the end of the month. He attributed the performance gains to inference optimisation rather than simply adding computing capacity. In October, CEO Nik Storonsky said Revolut was developing proprietary AI models trained on customer transaction data, citing the company's 30 million to 40 million daily transactions as a source of training data.

Revolut was valued at $115 billion in a secondary share sale in July, up from $75 billion last November and $45 billion in 2024, reinforcing its position as Europe's most valuable private technology company. Chinese open-weight models from labs including DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.AI, Alibaba and Tencent have won over users with lower costs and strong capabilities, and the top Chinese models lag the leading closed US systems by just 3% on benchmark scores. Some Western enterprises fear the models are too aligned with the Chinese Communist Party, and startups such as Hirundo and Lazarus AI edit the models to realign their values and remove censorship for Western markets. In October, the Trump administration barred civilian government agencies from using products or services from DeepSeek, citing a potential threat to national security. Graham Webster of Stanford's DigiChina Project said most users of Chinese models do not care about their alignment, and Stu Clott, a developer in San Diego, said he has not had a single situation where censorship got in his way.

stories.Headline: Lee vows bold investment in AI, future growth engines for 'growth for all'
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung pledged bold investment in artificial intelligence and other future growth engine industries in a speech at the National Assembly on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. He used the speech to call for bipartisan support for passage of the 2027 budget bill. The government submitted the bill to the National Assembly in September. It proposes 820.9 trillion won, or US$614.5 billion, in total government spending next year. The bill is the largest-ever budget and represents a 12.8 percent increase, which Lee called the biggest annual growth on record.

The government plans a 160 trillion-won Future Fund to support younger generations, promote economic growth engines and boost regional development. Under three megaprojects, 21.3 trillion won will go to a semiconductor manufacturing hub, data centers, physical AI and AI promotion. A separate 4.6 trillion won is for a sovereign AI model, and 13.8 trillion won is for competitiveness in 10 strategic technology sectors. Lee said the bill would make South Korea a leader and secure its dominance in the future while turning national growth into growth for the people. He said it would lay the foundation for a great leap forward and let all people share in the opportunities and fruits of growth by narrowing gaps.

He described the Future Fund as a strategic investment platform that would buttress a rebound in growth potential and help reduce deep social gaps. He said the expanded spending reflects higher living standards South Koreans deserve and the need to strengthen the country's future capabilities. The budget increase comes amid expectations of higher tax revenue from a semiconductor boom. Lee said the government would boldly invest in AI and future growth engines to boost growth potential, which he called the basic physical strength of the economy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the call for bipartisan support for the bill's passage.

stories.Headline: Shield AI cofounder teases ‘snowball’ of X-BAT fighter drone announcements in Europe
stories.Summary:
Shield AI announced on November 3, 2026, that its first full-scale X-BAT prototype, called X-BAT 001, has completed assembly in Frisco, Texas. The company released a video showing the autonomous, tail-sitting fighter drone in a hangar, with digital camouflage, markings reading "X-BAT 001" and "Powered by Hivemind," and what appears to be GE F110 propulsion hardware installed. Shield AI has not confirmed the aircraft's configuration or readiness. The next step is testing at the company's facility in Newton, Kansas, with initial vertical takeoff and landing tests targeted before the end of 2026.

The X-BAT is a vertical takeoff and landing aircraft with no cockpit, and Shield AI and the US Navy are jointly investing $400 million in it. Ryan Tseng, Shield AI's cofounder and chief strategy officer, said a per-aircraft cost could reach $25 million, with an extra $10 million for a higher-end sensor configuration, which he said is about a quarter the cost of a Eurofighter or an F-35 in Europe. Production is planned to begin in 2029 at a designated site in Des Moines, Washington, with full rate in the early 2030s. In June, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reportedly said Shield AI plans local X-BAT production with Poland, and the firm recently announced a strategic agreement with Greece's GEK TERNA on possible parts production, aircraft integration and long-term sustainment in Greece.

Tseng, speaking at the International Fighter Conference in Munich, said a "snowball of activities" covering European orders and regional partnership agreements would be announced soon, when the company is ready, and declined to comment on aircraft quantities. He said Europe can and should be a critical part of the X-BAT supply chain, arguing a European sovereign supply chain makes the region stronger at a warfighting level and makes the US more capable. Andrew Hawkes, X-BAT director for Europe at Shield AI, said the company is involved in several active sales campaigns across the continent but declined to name individual customers. Armor Harris, the aircraft chief, told Defense One in October that two full-scale prototypes were being built and described an early operational capability around 2029 as the goal of a potential later development phase.

The planned European export business builds on the Polish and Greek developments. In July, Shield AI and GE announced successful integration, actuation and engine light-off testing of the F110-GE-129E engine with GE's Axisymmetric Vectoring Exhaust Nozzle at GE's Peebles facility in Ohio. Shield AI's October update said flight-test aircraft were under construction and weapons-bay aerodynamics had been evaluated in low- and high-speed wind-tunnel tests. The next milestone will be demonstrating that the aircraft can lift off, remain controlled in vertical flight and land safely.

stories.Headline: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References
stories.Summary:
A team of fifteen researchers led by Xinyu Fang released a benchmark called BlenderWorld on November 5, 2026, according to a paper posted on arXiv. The benchmark is described as the first comprehensive test for evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. It contains 223 tasks covering architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, and the tasks are driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. The work was posted under the identifier 2610.23986.

The benchmark sets up a unified evaluation protocol, rendering submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and scoring them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics along with holistic visual quality scores. The authors tested thirteen frontier models. GPT-6-Astra received the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 at 73.0 and GPT-5.6-Sol at 67.7. The paper reports that current models can parse broad instructions but still struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender.

Separately, Loova AI launched Loova MCP, a Model Context Protocol integration, on November 3, 2026, according to a company announcement carried by GlobeNewswire. The integration brings AI image generation, AI video generation, and creative workflows directly to compatible AI agents. It runs on two layers, a foundational layer powered by premium models including Seedance, Kling, and Wan AI, and a second layer of creative workflows that orchestrate multiple production steps. The initial release includes nine specialized workflows across four production categories, including Product Photoshoot, Product Listing Images, UGC Ad Creator, Product Video Maker, Character Swap, Mimic Motion, and a Viral Video Clone workflow that accepts a reference video and lets creators review and revise an adaptation script before production begins.

Anbang Xu, founder at Loova, said professional creators need more ways to develop an idea and make it their own, and that with Loova MCP they can bring existing assets to the agent they prefer and choose the workflow that fits the project. The company says a single source asset can become a studio photograph, a listing image set, or a promotional video without rebuilding context or switching tools. Loova plans to expand into animation, short-form drama production, script development, storyboard generation, and video assembly tools. The BlenderWorld authors conclude that substantial headroom remains for future 3D-native agentics.

stories.Headline: Your car's AI assistant could be a privacy nightmare
stories.Summary:
New AI assistants built into cars and wearables are raising privacy concerns, according to Axios and research firm GlobalData. Automakers including GM, Ford, Rivian, Mercedes-Benz and BMW are introducing assistants that can control car functions, check vehicle health, coordinate family activities like child pickups, reschedule meetings and learn routines such as favorite destinations and restaurants. GM's new OnStar assistant lets drivers talk to their cars naturally. Rivian offers an optional memory function. The Axios report was published on November 4, 2026, and the GlobalData research was reported by IT-Online on November 3, 2026.

The systems need access to sensitive personal information to work, which raises questions about who controls it and how it is protected. Today's connected cars already collect data on where people go and how they drive, and the new assistants could know why someone is going somewhere and whom they are meeting. On the wearable side, GlobalData says new AI-capable devices are launching almost weekly, including smart glasses, rings, clip-ons and watches, and they can book flights, shop for groceries, capture conversations and give health coaching. Smart glasses can record people who may not know they are being captured, and other devices can tap into microphones, health information, email, calendars and conversations.

GM recently agreed to pay $220 million to settle allegations that it improperly shared drivers' behavior and location data with brokers, which passed it to insurers, and consumer class-action cases over its handling of driving data continue. Researchers at Northeastern University, working with Consumer Reports, found that 19 of 21 vehicles tested connected to third-party servers over WiFi, and many companion apps shared information such as vehicle IDs, email addresses, phone numbers or precise locations with advertising and tracking companies. GM has simplified its privacy disclosures, added controls over data sharing and pledged not to sell identifiable vehicle data to third parties, and Michael Wahlstrom, an executive director of software product management, said most voice commands will be processed inside the vehicle. Ford unveiled a Privacy Promise and pledged never to sell customers' driving data to brokers, and its chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said the pledge does not change the company's underlying practices and is simply a straightforward statement of them.

GlobalData senior analyst Amanda Mitchell said the convenience raises a harder question about privacy and that the industry appears to be moving faster to launch new devices than to make them less invasive. Meta made the recording light on its smart glasses more tamper-resistant after consumer pressure. In October, the European Data Protection Board called for recording cues that are difficult to miss and said manufacturers cannot simply shift privacy obligations onto wearers, while bans and restrictions are emerging in countries such as Norway and Australia. Automakers' protections do not necessarily extend to the technology companies whose services and apps are integrated into their vehicles, and consumers will ultimately have to decide whether always-available assistance is worth giving AI that much access to their lives.

She said AI has come to stay, comparing it to the earlier advent of the Internet and describing it as a sort of repeat of the Y2K advent. She said the educational system is being revamped as well, so learners need to know how to be future-ready. He said there are about 31 million small businesses in the country and 22 million of them are one-man mom-and-pop shops. He said AI can take mundane tasks like billing, legal work and design off their plates so owners can focus on what they started the business for. He said people who totally depend on a tool without a human touch are being lazy, and he called AI a tool. He said what used to take him a year now takes somebody a month, and an ad that once took three months can now come out in 30 seconds.

John has been on Shark Tank since it began airing in 2009, and he said the show is a true reflection of what changes in the economy. He said this year will show a lot of health and wellness businesses, and non-alcoholic beverages because the kids are not drinking anymore. He said he did not know whether he would have wanted AI when he started FUBU, because everything happened for a reason. stories.Headline: The AI Readiness Gap Almost No One’s Auditing
stories.Summary:
A November 4, 2026 article by Sumanth Kumar Gadde on govtech.com describes a gap in how public agencies prepare for artificial intelligence. Agencies check vendors, security and staff skills before launching an AI tool, but far fewer audit the data the system will learn from. Gadde points to an internal state review of Michigan's automated unemployment fraud system, which examined more than 20,000 determinations and found a 93 percent error rate. That system was not today's AI, but he says the lesson carries over because speed and scale turn hidden assumptions into public harm.

Gadde proposes three audits before go-live, each answering one plain question. The source audit asks where the data came from and who answers for it, including which source wins when two conflict and who approved that rule. The target audit asks what the system is really learning, whether the data reflects the people it will act on, and whether inputs are protected characteristics such as race, age or disability or close proxies like ZIP code, first name or employment gaps. The safeguard audit asks what catches the system when it is wrong, including whether a reviewer with real authority checks high-stakes decisions and whether residents can contest outcomes. He gives the example of a county using a model trained on past violation records to send inspectors to buildings likely to have code violations, which keeps sending inspectors to the same neighborhoods while problems elsewhere stay invisible.

Gadde says guidance nobody owns gets skipped under deadline pressure, so the fix is structural. He recommends adding a data readiness gate to every AI project plan the same way a security review is added, starting with the use case where a wrong answer would hurt someone most. A named data owner should sign off and the findings should be written down, and "we don't know" should be treated as a finding rather than a failure. He says an unanswered question found before launch is cheap, while the same question found afterward costs money, public trust and sometimes someone's benefits or livelihood.

A separate report from Dun & Bradstreet, published by ET CIO on November 2, 2026, found that 69 percent of Indian businesses plan to increase AI spending over the next 12 months. Only 3 percent described their enterprise data as fully ready to support AI at scale, compared with 8 percent globally, while 42 percent said mostly ready and 44 percent partially ready. More than 60 percent of respondents had moved beyond planning, with 35 percent scaling pilots into production and 26 percent reporting AI embedded across multiple core business processes. Julian Prower, Executive Vice President at Dun & Bradstreet and Managing Director and CEO for India and Taiwan, said India has reached an inflection point and that the next chapter will be about moving from AI adoption to AI advantage. The report said businesses with fully AI-ready data were 6.3 times more likely to report broad or strong returns than those with partially ready data.

stories.Headline: China plans AI safety rules spanning development and deployment
stories.Summary:
China plans to introduce wide-ranging artificial intelligence safety standards that would cover both the development and deployment of AI models, Bloomberg reported. Wang Ruomeng, a senior official with the National Development and Reform Commission, announced the plan at a briefing in Beijing on Tuesday. The framework would cover the entire life cycle of AI systems, including data, computing resources and algorithms. The measures would affect developers such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba, whose models are central to China's efforts to compete with American companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Authorities would speed up legislation on the foundations of AI and its use in important sectors, and would introduce ethical guidelines and safety standards. Officials would regularly assess how the rules are implemented and revise those that no longer reflect technological developments. Beijing also plans a transition period, whose length was not specified, and guidance meant to reduce the burden of compliance. Sector-specific regulatory sandboxes would let developers test applications and learn from failures under supervision. Developers and operators would be expected to strengthen their own risk management and to disclose safety threats, incidents and vulnerabilities.

Wang said AI safety is not a problem one company, industry or country can tackle alone and called it a global challenge requiring international cooperation. He urged governments to strengthen cooperation on safety governance, coordinate the disclosure of vulnerabilities and responses to risks, and build greater confidence in one another's systems. The proposals also address employment: authorities will monitor how AI changes the labor market and displaces workers, and will provide broad protections for those affected. The initiative reflects Beijing's attempt to balance technological ambition with concerns that increasingly capable systems could escape human control or make cyberattacks more damaging.

The announcement comes amid discussions between Washington and Beijing about managing the technology's risks. China and the United States agreed in September to pursue a shared understanding of AI's benefits and threats, ahead of a Washington summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at which AI featured prominently. Despite the planned safeguards, China will continue encouraging open AI development during its 15th five-year plan, which runs through 2030. That commitment preserves an approach that has helped Chinese models gain users internationally, Bloomberg reported.

stories.Headline: North Carolina To Receive $7.6 Million in GM Data Privacy Settlement
stories.Summary:
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson and a bipartisan coalition of 36 states reached a $220 million settlement with General Motors, according to WHKY. The settlement resolves allegations that the company improperly collected and sold drivers' personal driving and location data. The investigation centered on the OnStar Smart Driver program, which tracked driving habits between 2016 and 2024. The program gathered information about hard braking, rapid acceleration, speeding over 80 miles per hour and late-night driving.

North Carolina will receive approximately $7.66 million as part of the settlement. State investigators alleged that some drivers were enrolled without their consent, while more than 370,000 others were incorrectly told through the OnStar app that they were not enrolled. The coalition also alleged that GM sold driving and location information to third-party data brokers, which then provided it to insurance companies. Insurers used the data to help determine customer premiums based on driving behavior.

The settlement requires General Motors to obtain express consent before collecting or sharing driving and location data. The company must also limit the information it collects, strengthen consumer privacy protections and provide additional oversight and training at dealerships. Jackson said GM promised drivers their information would remain private and would not be shared with insurers without their permission. General Motors discontinued the Smart Driver program following reporting by The New York Times about the data-sharing practices.

Separately, CNBC reports that GoodRx agreed to a $32 million settlement over claims it unlawfully shared user data with third parties, including Meta, Google and the advertising firm Criteo. A 2023 complaint claimed that tracking technology on the GoodRx site and app sent information about users' health conditions and medications to advertising partners without consent. According to court filings, roughly 54.8 million people's information was shared through GoodRx's tracking tools. GoodRx has not admitted any wrongdoing but agreed to the settlement to resolve the allegations.

Anyone who used the GoodRx website, app or service before April 20, 2024, may be eligible for a payout. Claims must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 29, 2026, and the estimated per-person amount has not yet been established. The chief plaintiffs' attorneys are seeking $10.67 million, or roughly one-third of the total settlement fund, for fees and legal expenses. A final approval hearing is scheduled for Feb. 11, 2027, and payments would be issued after that if the court approves, though appeals may slow the process.

Kinetic announced a partnership with SKYOVI on November 2, 2026, to bring an artificial intelligence design platform to its fiber-installation operations. The platform helps Kinetic plan and build the final fiber connection, known as a drop, to each home and business. stories.Headline: Qualcomm HBC Compared to HBM
stories.Summary:
Qualcomm announced on November 2, 2026, that it has validated first-generation silicon for its high-bandwidth computing (HBC) architecture in the lab. The company said its engineers used industry-standard automated test equipment to confirm the complete memory read-write path and near-memory computations at production levels. Qualcomm first introduced the HBC architecture in July 2026 as a way to address the memory wall in AI inference. The validation comes ahead of sampling for the Dragonfly AI250, which Qualcomm says is due for release next year.

The testing found that HBC can deliver as much as 18 times the memory bandwidth of LPDDR and an energy-efficiency measurement of five times the terabit-per-second-per-watt compared to HBM4, the sixth generation of high-bandwidth memory. In HBC, a stack of LPDDR-based memory sits in the package with a compute die underneath it, so data moves across micrometers rather than millimeters. Qualcomm says this gives the AI model faster access to data and reduces the time, energy and cost of moving it. The AI250 is expected to start sampling in the first half of 2027, with Dragonfly C1000 CPUs also set for next year and Dragonfly AI300 samples coming in 2028.

Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, said traditional architectures have plenty of DDR capacity but a narrow link that moves data slowly, while HBM increases lanes and speed at a premium in cost, power and complex packaging. He described HBC as a co-processor where most decode operations happen inside the package, so the slower link to the AI250 does not affect end-to-end performance because only results are sent back. He said the solution gives the bandwidth needed at the lowest energy, with at least an order of magnitude less energy spent moving data. He also said the validation is important because HBC is a clear differentiator, since the compute sits under the memory stack, and that it should erase doubts about high-yield manufacturing of the AI250 next year.

Qualcomm has for more than a year been working to become a larger player in the AI datacenter space and an alternative to Nvidia. HBC will be integrated into the Dragonfly AI250 to create what executives call a full AI inference accelerator platform, which will be foundational to the Qualcomm Dragonfly Rack for inference workloads. Giaretta said Qualcomm is working with various partners on different ways HBC can be used and that the AI250 is not the only product where it will appear. He said the company usually does not do a blog or pre-briefing for a chip bring-up, but did so because the technology is completely new.

stories.Headline: EU rules on Artificial intelligence devices will apply in NI
stories.Summary:
The UK government said on 4 November 2026 that some EU rules on Artificial Intelligence will apply in Northern Ireland. The EU's AI Act was passed in 2024, and in 2025 the European Commission proposed that the parts concerning goods should apply in NI. That has been under negotiation with the UK since then. The rules will apply because of the Windsor Framework, the Brexit deal which keeps NI inside the EU's single market for goods.

The EU rules will only apply to physical goods which have an embedded AI system. They will not affect an NI business simply because it uses online or downloadable AI tools to manage work, analyse data, or carry out business functions. They will also not place obligations on the developers of those tools for their use in NI, unless the AI is closely integrated into a physical product placed on the NI market. Examples of covered products include a smart speaker with a built-in AI voice assistant or a smart watch requiring a manufacturer's AI health monitoring app.

The regulation of AI in NI will largely be a matter for the UK government and Stormont. The government said the EU AI Act does not apply to NI in full. It said the Act applies only where an AI system is closely integrated with a tangible physical product that is placed on the NI market. The main idea of the EU law is to regulate AI based on its capacity to cause harm to society.

The higher the risk, the stricter the rules, with some AI applications being banned. The government's examples of physical products which could be banned include a connected toy embedding AI that encourages children to undertake increasingly risky activities in exchange for reward or praise, or an AI-connected camera with voice recognition that detects employee emotions. In general terms, when the EU's rules on the regulation of goods are updated, the UK government has to agree which of them should apply in NI. In some circumstances the NI Assembly also has a vote on the matter.
