stories.Headline: Jobplanet, LinkedIn leadership discuss AI-driven future of hiring
stories.Summary:
Jobplanet, an online recruitment platform run by Worxphere, said on Wednesday that it had exchanged views with LinkedIn executives on Korea's hiring market and the role of artificial intelligence in recruitment. The meeting took place at Jobplanet's headquarters in Seoul on Oct. 19. Hari Srinivasan, LinkedIn's Ecosystem Chief Product Officer, led a delegation of vice presidents. Jobplanet explained what sets the Korean market apart. Jobplanet said companies in Korea handle open, rolling and performance-based hiring at the same time, and an aging workforce has employers caring more about the right candidates than wide job-posting reach.

Worxphere said it trains its engine on years of job seeker data from its JobKorea and Albamon services to sharpen personalized recommendations. It also envisions services that align what applicants and employers expect from each other. The company valued the meeting for uniting a Korean platform with more than 10 million company reviews and Microsoft-owned LinkedIn, which has more than 1 billion members. Jobplanet CEO Joon Lee said it was meaningful to exchange views with the leadership of a global HR platform on what makes Korea's hiring market different and where it is heading. He said the company will continue to innovate its hiring services to connect job seekers and employers more precisely in the AI era.

The gathering coincides with Jobplanet's transformation into an AI-powered career platform covering everything from career exploration to hiring. It draws on its archive of company, salary and interview reviews. Partnerships with about 90 universities extend Jobplanet's reach to early-career users. Ties to Worxphere's hiring services help it support workers across their careers, the company said. The article does not say what was agreed at the meeting or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Jobplanet, LinkedIn leadership discuss AI-driven future of hiring

stories.Headline: Costs above competition? Why US voters aren’t buying Trump’s China AI pitch
stories.Summary:
Voters in the 2026 US midterm elections turned against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, according to the South China Morning Post. The article, published on 5 November 2026, reports strong backlash at the polls and Democratic victories. Analysts said framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans. The piece was reported by Nayan Seth in Washington and Lucy Quaggin in New York.

The article says the results underscore the need to address local concerns about power bills, water use and the impact on local communities. It gives no specific vote counts, project figures or dates beyond the 2026 midterms and the 5 November 2026 publication. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution's John L. Thornton China Centre, said the argument that more data centres are needed to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the resonance it did before, if it ever did. Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.

The analysts quoted in the article place the responsibility for the message on those making the China competition case for AI investment. Chan questioned whether that argument ever resonated with voters. Lee said the lesson is that invoking China is becoming less effective. Both spoke to the Post about why the pitch did not land.

The article presents the midterm backlash as a sign that the China framing failed and that local concerns need addressing. It does not say what policy changes, if any, will follow the elections. It also does not say what happens next for the data centre projects themselves. The article offers no further details on the outcome beyond the Democratic victories it mentions.

Articles.Title: Costs above competition? Why US voters aren’t buying Trump’s China AI pitch

stories.Headline: Trump's "Use SI, Not AI" Pressure One Month In: 91% of S&P 500 Companies Still Stick With "AI"
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump began pressuring companies in late September to use the term "Super Intelligence (SI)" instead of "AI," arguing in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly that AI makes the technology seem fake. Days later he signed an executive order changing the AI designation in government documents, and last month he warned that those who do not use SI would be regarded as "enemies" of the White House. Elon Musk renamed SpaceX's AI business unit SpaceXSI and had Tesla specify SI in a securities filing, while Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said the company would rebrand its AIForce platform as SIForce. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he would keep the company's name, and Anthropic used AI throughout its 335-page IPO filing.

An analysis of 206 S&P 500 companies that used the relevant terms in earnings releases, securities filings and press releases between September 29 and November 2 found that 188, or 91.3%, used AI in at least 90% of references. Eleven companies mixed the two terms, and only seven, or 3.4%, used SI in at least 90% of references. Of 119 companies that mentioned the technology in just the past week, only five used the term superintelligence. Spelling was inconsistent, with some writing it as one word and others as two, and capitalization varied.

Microsoft president Brad Smith caught himself mid-sentence during a podcast last month, saying "AI safety, no, SI safety," and Microsoft said it uses multiple terms in parallel. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang mentioned "the future of superintelligence" on X the day after signing a technology safety pledge at the White House, but weeks later at a Berlin conference he said "every company in Europe will be an AI company." Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the nonprofit Alliance for Safe AI, said companies are trying to keep their existing terminology while avoiding an outright confrontation with the White House, and his organization said it would not change its name. Even First Lady Melania Trump's Facebook account recently promoted a student computing competition and used the term AI as is.

Superintelligence originally refers to a hypothetical AI with cognitive abilities surpassing the most brilliant humans, and Trump is seeking to use this specialized concept as a general label encompassing all of AI. The issue is not one that will rattle near-term financial statements, but it poses a judgment burden for tech companies facing U.S. government procurement and regulatory compliance. If SI designations are required in government documents and contracts, companies may have to run dual product-name and description systems, while AI remains the standard in consumer-facing channels and investor communications. Given that a terminology change could affect brand value, search visibility and even regulatory interpretation, Silicon Valley's word choices are expected to continue for the time being.

Articles.Title: Trump's "Use SI, Not AI" Pressure One Month In: 91% of S&P 500 Companies Still Stick With "AI" - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Trump Pushes Tech to Say SI Instead of AI, Leaving Big Tech Scrambling
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump is pressuring companies to stop calling artificial intelligence AI and use SI, short for super intelligence, instead. The Wall Street Journal reported on November 4 that Trump argued at the U.N. General Assembly in late September that the term AI makes the technology sound fake. Days later, he signed an executive order changing AI terminology in government documents. Last month, he also warned that people who refuse to use SI would be treated as enemies of the White House.

Some companies have changed names to match the White House. Elon Musk announced that SpaceX would rename its AI division SpaceXSI, and Tesla said in a securities filing that SI refers to its existing AI technologies and activities. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said the company would rename its AIForce platform SIForce. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the company would keep its name because brands do not change easily. Microsoft President Brad Smith referred on a podcast to AI safety, or rather, SI safety, and Microsoft said it uses several terms for the technology.

Corporate documents still overwhelmingly favor AI. Among S&P 500 companies that used related terms in earnings releases, securities filings and press releases from September 29 to November 2, 188 of 206 used AI more than 90% of the time. Eleven companies used both terms, while seven used SI more than 90% of the time. Even in the most recent week, only five of 119 companies that referred to the technology used super intelligence.

Super intelligence already has a distinct technical meaning, referring to hypothetical AI with cognitive abilities that exceed those of the most capable humans. Trump is trying to use the term as a label for the whole field, which leaves companies trying to satisfy the president while describing the technology accurately and protecting their brands. Brendan Steinhauser, chief executive of the nonprofit Alliance for Safe AI, said companies are trying to avoid appearing to oppose the White House while keeping the existing terminology. The group also said it would not change its name. Mixed usage continues even around the White House, where first lady Melania Trump’s Facebook account recently used AI in a post introducing a student computing competition.

Articles.Title: Trump Pushes Tech to Say SI Instead of AI, Leaving Big Tech Scrambling - bloomingbit

stories.Headline: Will Democrats stop Trump's 'flourishing' AI and data centre policies?
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, according to The National. The result ends a period in which President Donald Trump's administration promoted AI development with limited regulation. Trump had promised to support AI rooted in free speech and human flourishing, and he often claimed his actions drew trillions of dollars in investment from global tech companies. The Democrats will take control of key congressional committees overseeing technology, cyber security and commerce in January.

Trump keeps veto power, so sweeping regulatory legislation is unlikely, and analysts expect political gridlock rather than immediate reversals. Michael Strobaek of Lombard Odier said Democrats may push to scale back tax incentives, shift more grid costs onto developers and introduce early safety regulations. Charu Chanana of Saxo Bank said the more likely outcome is two years of political confrontation, greater congressional oversight and legislative gridlock. Mark MacCarthy of Georgetown University said a stalled Senate bill with mandatory ratepayer protection for new data centres could be reintroduced as a free-standing bill and serve as a starting point for action.

Timothy Kneeland, a political scientist at Nazareth University, said the days of wine and roses for AI and data centres without regulation are over. Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, posted that people should always be in control of the future and should not cede control to superintelligence. Elon Musk joked that data centres in space look appealing now, and he later joked that his election-interfering space lasers did not work this time. Lisa Su, chief executive of AMD, told CNBC that the election results do not change her outlook on AI and that demand for more compute is intense worldwide.

Analysts warned before the elections that AI-linked shares could be the most exposed to risk if Democrats won. Manjeet Markanda of Lunaro Markets said investors now see tougher scrutiny of Big Tech and data centres as more likely. David Meier of Julius Baer said greater regulatory scrutiny of AI would weigh on capital expenditures and related inflows, an important source of US dollar support this year. Nvidia's Jensen Huang has not made any statement on the shift in power.

Articles.Title: Will Democrats stop Trump's 'flourishing' AI and data centre policies? - The National

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence and intellectual property rights: the situation in Thailand - International Bar Association | IBA
stories.Summary:
Thailand has no AI-specific intellectual property laws, according to an article published on 3 November 2026 by the International Bar Association. The piece was written by Suebsiri Taweepon of the law firm Tilleke & Gibbins in Bangkok. It says the country's existing IP framework predates modern AI and gives limited guidance on AI-generated works, AI training practices and AI-generated inventions. The article reviews the current legal framework, the key IP issues arising from AI and practical considerations and future developments.

The article states that existing legal principles generally apply to AI-related activities, but there is limited guidance on AI model training, no text and data-mining exceptions and little judicial precedent. It notes that Thailand's Civil Court issued a regulation, effective since 17 November 2025, on the use of AI in preparing pleadings and other documents submitted to the court. The rule requires parties and their counsel to disclose any AI-generated content submitted to the Civil Court and to verify and certify its accuracy. The article adds that the Civil Court's rule is consistent with guidance issued by the President of the Supreme Court in September 2025, and that the Central IP and International Trade Court, where IP cases must be filed, has not announced similar rules as of the date of the article.

On copyright, the article says Thai law is founded on human authorship and does not expressly address works generated autonomously by AI systems. It notes that the US Copyright Office has confirmed that copyright protection generally requires human authorship, while acknowledging that AI-assisted works may qualify where sufficient human creative contribution exists. It points to Section 9 of the Thai Copyright Act B.E. 2537 (1994), under which the default rule is that an employee owns the copyright in a work created in the course of employment unless the parties have agreed otherwise in writing. The article also says that, unlike Singapore and Japan, Thailand does not provide a broad text- and data-mining exception permitting the use of copyrighted works for AI training.

The article says the Patent Act B.E. 2522 (1979) provides no clear mechanism for recognising an AI system as an inventor, and that mathematical methods and abstract ideas are generally not patentable. It notes that Thailand's Trade Secrets Act B.E. 2545 (2002) provides the statutory framework for trade secret protection, and that the Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 256 is also relevant to AI datasets containing personal data. It advises businesses to rely on contractual arrangements to allocate ownership, liability and risk, and to consider legal protections early in the AI adoption process rather than waiting for regulatory certainty. It adds that the IP&IT Court is likely to issue similar rules on AI use, but no such announcement has been made.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence and intellectual property rights: the situation in Thailand - International Bar Association | IBA

stories.Headline: Education chief dismisses push for final-year university internships amid AI threat
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong’s education minister has rejected a suggestion to turn the final year of undergraduate degrees into an internship period. Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin spoke on Wednesday, 4 November 2026, in response to a question from lawmaker Priscilla Leung Mei-fun. Leung had asked whether authorities would reform four-year bachelor’s programmes by converting the final year into an internship year. The proposal was raised amid a fall in entry-level jobs caused by the rise of artificial intelligence.

Choi said university courses should not be changed solely to meet manpower needs. She also warned against basing such decisions on single indicators, such as labour market supply and demand data. She said university education should not be turned into vocational training solely to meet short-term job market needs. The article does not say what specific changes, if any, the government will make to degree programmes.

Choi is the Secretary for Education and gave the response. Leung is the lawmaker who asked the question about reforming the four-year programmes. Choi said courses should not be altered just to match manpower needs or single indicators like labour market data. She warned against turning university education into vocational training for short-term job market needs.

The push comes as entry-level jobs have fallen due to the rise of AI. The article does not say what happens next or whether the proposal will be raised again. It also does not give any further dates or numbers beyond the four-year programme length and the 4 November 2026 date. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Education chief dismisses push for final-year university internships amid AI threat

stories.Headline: Tokyo police to introduce AI-based accident reconstruction system
stories.Summary:
Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department plans to introduce a system that uses artificial intelligence to reconstruct traffic accidents, it was learned on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. The system will combine AI with 3D spatial data from accident sites and footage from nearby security cameras. It is meant to reduce the need for lengthy on-site inspections, which require traffic restrictions and often cause congestion and economic losses. The department plans to test the system from June 2027 and launch full-scale operations in January 2028.

Currently, fatal accidents and hit-and-run incidents are investigated through on-site inspections, in which vehicles are positioned as they were at the time of the crash and measurements are taken to produce reports and diagrams. Such inspections sometimes require traffic restrictions lasting two to three hours, resulting in congestion. In some cases, more than 20 personnel are mobilized, including traffic controllers. The new system will use an existing mobile mapping system in which camera-equipped vehicles capture surroundings to generate 3D spatial data.

The system will let investigators extract necessary information, such as vehicle speed, distance and positional relationships, on a screen. It will also enable simulations from multiple perspectives, including overhead views of collisions and the viewpoints of drivers and pedestrians. This is expected to make it easier to prepare investigative reports and diagrams. Related expenses have been included in the police department’s budget request for the next fiscal year.

Articles.Title: Tokyo police to introduce AI-based accident reconstruction system

stories.Headline: The best is yet to come: Asia's chance to reimagine AI
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Jaime Valles, managing director for Asia Pacific, Japan, and China at Amazon Web Services, published by Nikkei Asia on November 4, 2026. It argues that companies in Asia have a chance to reimagine how they use artificial intelligence. The piece says businesses should pick one place to start experimenting and see where AI could genuinely change how they operate. It also says companies that rethink processes and empower teams can turn AI gains into new products.

The article does not report a specific event, date, or set of figures beyond its publication details. It names no companies other than AWS, where the author works, and gives no numbers about investment or adoption. Its central suggestion is that firms begin with a single area of experimentation rather than spreading effort widely. The stated payoff is that rethinking processes and giving teams more responsibility can lead to new products.

Responsibility for acting on this rests with businesses, in the author's view, and the article presents the advice as his own argument rather than a report of decisions already taken. Valles writes that companies should choose one place to start experimenting. He says they should then see where AI could genuinely change how they operate. The article does not say whether any company has followed this advice.

The context is the wider AI boom covered elsewhere on the same site, including stories on chip exports, data centers, and hardware costs. The article itself gives no timeline for what happens next and makes no predictions with dates. It closes on the idea that the best is yet to come for Asia. No follow-up steps or announcements are described.

Articles.Title: The best is yet to come: Asia's chance to reimagine AI

stories.Headline: Connecticut’s AI Rules Take Shape: What Employers and Developers Need to Know
stories.Summary:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont signed SB 5, Public Act No. 26-15, on May 27, 2026. The law sets new obligations for employers that use AI in employment decisions and for the developers who build those tools. It covers automated employment-related decision technology, known as AEDT, which processes personal data and produces an output that is a substantial factor in an employment-related decision. The law also covers developers that build or substantially modify such tools for use in employment decisions.

The employer disclosure and notice duties begin October 1, 2027. Employers must tell employees and applicants in plain language when they are interacting with an AEDT, unless that is obvious to a reasonable person. Before using an AEDT in a decision, employers must give written notice of the tool's purpose, its trade name, the personal data it will analyze, the data's sources and the employer's contact information. Developers must give employers the information needed to meet these duties, and the parties may allocate obligations by binding contract. The use of an AEDT is not a defense to a discrimination claim under an amendment effective October 1, 2026, and employers serving federal WARN Act notices on the Connecticut Department of Labor must disclose whether layoffs relate to AI or another technological change.

The requirements are enforceable solely by the Connecticut attorney general under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act, with no private right of action. For violations through December 31, 2027, the attorney general may give notice and a 60-day cure period if the violation is curable. Frontier developers may not retaliate against employees for protected whistleblowing, and large frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual gross revenues must set up an anonymous internal reporting process by January 1, 2027. The commissioner of economic and community development must develop a plan for an AI regulatory sandbox effective July 1, 2027, with legislative recommendations due by January 1, 2028.

The law adds Connecticut to a growing list of jurisdictions regulating AI in employment, with requirements that overlap with but differ from those in California, Colorado, Illinois and New York City. The article advises employers to inventory their AI tools, review vendor contracts, prepare disclosure and notice templates, and review anti-bias testing. It also advises updating WARN notice procedures and training internal teams. The article says it will continue to monitor developments in this area.

Articles.Title: Connecticut’s AI Rules Take Shape: What Employers and Developers Need to Know - JD Supra

stories.Headline: ChatGPT creator OpenAI loses bid to block Singapore start-up’s GemGPT trademark
stories.Summary:
OpenAI lost its bid to stop Singapore start-up Porolis Technologies from registering the name GemGPT. The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore ruled on Oct 28 that the name could proceed. Porolis, part of the B.P. de Silva group, was also awarded $10,000 in costs, including disbursements. All five of OpenAI's objections to the trademark application were rejected.

Porolis applied to register GemGPT on May 22, 2023, for AI-powered gemstone authentication and related software services. The company, founded in 2022, said it chose "Gem" for gemstones and "GPT" to describe its use of generative AI models, and its service is neither built on nor powered by OpenAI's models. OpenAI argued that GemGPT conflicted with its earlier trademarks, including ChatGPT and numbered GPT marks such as GPT-3 and GPT-4, and alleged confusion, harm to its well-known logos and bad faith. Principal assistant registrar Gabriel Ong found that as at the application date, less than six months after ChatGPT's launch on Nov 30, 2022, OpenAI had not established that the three letters alone identified its business, and that the names had to be considered as whole names.

Ong said the public would see GemGPT as an unrelated AI or technology product for gemstones and would not mistake it for OpenAI's marks simply because both contain "GPT". He compared the case to Gmail, saying that being well-known would not by itself stop another business from using the non-distinctive element "mail". On bad faith, he accepted that Porolis knew of OpenAI and ChatGPT but said this did not mean its conduct fell below acceptable commercial standards. He also said the ruling did not mean OpenAI could never establish that GPT was distinctive, and that at a future date, based on other evidence, it could be possible.

Articles.Title: ChatGPT creator OpenAI loses bid to block Singapore start-up’s GemGPT trademark

stories.Headline: New GovTech-Google DeepMind app flags potential scams by analysing incoming messages
stories.Summary:
A new app called AntiScam Pango was launched on Nov 4 to help users spot potential scams by analysing and flagging suspicious conversations, including those involving numbers that have not previously been reported. It was developed by the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) and Google DeepMind, and unveiled by Acting Minister for Manpower Jasmin Lau at GovTech's biennial STACK Conference 2026 at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre. News of the on-device scam detection model was first announced in October on the sidelines of the Singapore International Cyber Week. The app uses artificial intelligence to analyse all messages and flag suspicious conversations as they unfold.

For a start, Android users can download the beta app from the Google Play Store. Once users grant the necessary permissions, AntiScam Pango runs in the background and checks messages on WhatsApp, Telegram and SMS, warning users in real time before they take further actions. When it flags a potentially suspicious conversation, it explains the indicators that suggest it could be a scam, so users can recognise social engineering tactics, and users can then decide whether to continue the exchange, report it or take precautions such as independently verifying the sender's identity. The app does not automatically block or delete messages, and message content is not sent to external servers unless the user chooses to report it. GovTech said neither the agency nor its partners can access users' personal information or private messages through the app.

Lau said the analysis happens on the phone itself, so messages stay private. GovTech's director of trust and safety Mark Chen said the aim is to show people they do not have to choose between protection from scams and keeping their personal messages private, and that the collaboration with Google DeepMind is pushing the boundaries of what small AI models can do. The AI model was trained on scam patterns and scenarios to recognise manipulation tactics and characteristics commonly found in scams targeting people here, with training data from ScamShield, developed by GovTech's Open Government Products unit, the police and the National Crime Prevention Council, and from an in-house AI-powered classifier tool that evaluates suspicious web links. ScamShield's enhanced app has recorded 1.61 million installations since August 2024.

AntiScam Pango adds to the existing protections offered by ScamShield, which helps users block scam calls, filter suspicious SMS messages, and check or report potentially fraudulent messages, phone numbers and links. Unlike ScamShield, AntiScam Pango proactively assesses conversations as messages arrive across supported messaging platforms, rather than relying on users to submit them for checking, and it can flag suspicious exchanges involving numbers not previously identified as risky. GovTech said it is exploring the integration of AntiScam Pango into ScamShield, but no timeline has been provided, and it is assessing other messaging platforms to expand coverage beyond WhatsApp, Telegram and SMS. For now the app is available only on Android because the operating system allows apps to request access to incoming notifications from messaging services, and GovTech is exploring ways to offer similar protection on other operating systems, including Apple's iOS, while retaining on-device analysis and the same privacy and security standards.

Articles.Title: New GovTech-Google DeepMind app flags potential scams by analysing incoming messages

stories.Headline: As Canva restructures, how is AI reshaping creative businesses? | Explained
stories.Summary:
Canva announced a reorganisation of its workforce on November 4, 2026, and said 1,271 jobs are affected. The design platform described the move as a response to slowing growth and rapid technological change. The article was published by The Hindu and updated the same day. It was written by Balasubramanyam C.P. from Chennai.

The reorganisation comes as generative AI changes how visual content is designed, produced and sold. The article says AI is changing the economics and competitive landscape for businesses that make creative software and sell visual content. It names Adobe, Figma and Getty Images as examples of companies where generative AI is reshaping products, costs and business models. Canva is described as one of the companies navigating this shift.

The article does not give direct comments from Canva or the other companies about the restructuring. It says Canva is reorganising its workforce amid slowing growth and rapid technological change. It also says the move comes as other companies in the creative industry grapple with the opportunities and challenges posed by generative AI. No individual is named as responsible for the decision.

The article frames the change as part of a wider shift across industries, businesses and geographies. It says AI is upending the rules of the game and touching almost every aspect of the economy. The creative industry is no exception, according to the article. It does not say what happens next for Canva or the affected workers.

Articles.Title: As Canva restructures, how is AI reshaping creative businesses? | Explained

stories.Headline: The AI Resilience map: Where’s your organisation Now?
stories.Summary:
A Dell Technologies article published on 4 November 2026 sets out a way for organisations to judge how ready they are for AI failures. It was written by Venkat Sitaram, Senior Director and Country Head of the Infrastructure Solutions Group at Dell Technologies India. He argues that there is plenty of guidance on AI resilience, but organisations must first understand their own starting point. He compares this to sailing, where a good map was useless without knowing your own position. The article cites the Dell Technologies Modern Enterprise Readiness Study 2026, conducted by Vanson Bourne.

It found that 61% of Indian organisations surveyed said security and compliance concerns had slowed or paused AI adoption. It also found that 26% reported well-established AI or generative AI solutions in production, up from 20% a year earlier. Sitaram says ambition and deployment do not automatically mean readiness. Sitaram describes two maturity curves, one for cyber resilience and one for AI adoption, which move independently. Together they create four positions: Clean Slate, Fortified Newcomer, Exposed Frontrunner and Proving Ground.

He says each position needs different priorities, such as listing dependencies, extending recovery practices to AI-specific assets, prioritising critical workloads or testing recovery under realistic conditions. He says resilience must evolve with the technology and the business processes it supports. Sitaram is responsible for the argument, and the study figures come from Vanson Bourne. He says the first step is an honest view of where an organisation stands, and that a uniform approach risks directing resources away from the most immediate vulnerabilities. The article does not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: The AI Resilience map: Where’s your organisation Now?

stories.Headline: Ricursive AI Releases Ripple-65B Preview: A 65B Dense Open-Weight Model Scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1
stories.Summary:
Ricursive AI released Ripple-65B Preview on November 4, 2026. It is a 65B dense open-weight model pretrained from scratch for agentic coding, and it is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive's AI chip design platform. Ricursive reports a score of 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which it calls the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. The release includes three checkpoints under Apache 2.0: an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version, and a BF16 base model.

The model was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context. Ricursive says the full R&D cost was $32M, which it estimates at one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. The model runs in BF16 on datacenter GPUs at 250 tokens per second on 2x B200, and an experimental NVFP4 build targets NVIDIA DGX Spark. Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity, and training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization.

The architecture is thin and deep, with a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. Ricursive says it built its post-training recipe without buying any post-training data, using its own synthetic pipelines. Its mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering and a linear length penalty, and it reached 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts, which Ricursive puts at roughly 70x fewer than Beam. On other benchmarks it scored 79.1 on SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard, 76.5 on SWE-bench Verified, 98.3 on AIME 2025 and 90.5 on HMMT Feb 2026.

Its weak spots include SciCode at 39.4, DeepSWE 1.1 at 44.3, MCP Atlas at 71.67 and GPQA Diamond at 85.2. Ricursive compares Ripple with larger MoE rivals: Reflection Beam at 501B total parameters scored 80.1, Meta Muse Spark Open at 816B scored 76.4, Thinking Machines Inkling at 975B scored 63.8 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra at 550B scored 56.4. In a rerun of Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K, most rivals dropped, with Beam falling to 70.8 and Muse Spark Open rising to 78.7, still below Ripple's 80.5. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud and OpenRouter, and Fireworks goes live later today.

Articles.Title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding

stories.Headline: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
stories.Summary:
Kino AI launched on Hacker News on November 4, 2026, posted by Luke Igel, who goes by lukeigel on the site. The company, part of Y Combinator's S23 batch, describes itself as an AI media manager and video editor that lets agents and teammates work on the same timeline. The post says storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are bundled into one product. Igel wrote that colleagues and tools like Codex and Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place.

The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration, and MCP access for a user's own agent. Pro costs $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside a team. Kino is code-first, built on Remotion, and everything in it has a URL, including projects, clips, footage, comments, replies, a single frame, and the line of code that draws it. The company says it built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, and R3D, and that a 250GB ProRes clip can be dragged straight into a Kino timeline. Kino is available as an Electron download for now, and a pure web browser version has not been released.

Igel said he grew up making YouTube videos and co-directed a 3.5 hour archival documentary during his undergrad at MIT. He said the first launch in 2023 was more like Palantir for Hollywood, with bespoke on-prem deployments on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef, and that in 2025 the team rebuilt Kino as a true editor and bet on coding-as-editing. In the comments he told one user about a workflow button that indexes footage from an iPhone or SD cards and lays out a quick stringout, and he pointed another user to templates at kino.ai/templates. He also said an eye contact feature had shipped and could be found by right-clicking a timeline item.

Igel described his launch video as made entirely with Kino, with more than five agents editing the timeline at once while a friend ran a separate swarm a few minutes further down. He said one agent was rotoscoping, an LLM was color grading all media through LUT support, and both he and his friend made small tweaks along the way. Commenters raised questions about templates, the choice of Remotion over other options, and whether the proxy scrub and final render stay consistent, and Igel replied that Kino renders locally and lets users scrub original footage. The post says teams are using Kino to manage a whole company's media and spin up agents to make new videos every day, and it invites people with ProRes media or legacy editor projects to try the tool and share feedback.

Articles.Title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor

stories.Headline: Verizon AI-RAN work rides nationwide Ericsson Intelligent Controller deployment
stories.Summary:
Verizon is working with Ericsson to integrate AI into radio access network automation, and the effort includes a nationwide rollout of Ericsson's Intelligent Controller by the end of 2026. The platform will run AI-native rApps, which are microservices-based applications that operate in non-real time and give an operator more control over open RAN environments. Verizon pointed to an already implemented method for handing over fixed-wireless access devices from its 4G LTE network to its 5G standalone network, which it says removes the need for manual intervention when handovers fail. The news was reported on November 4, 2026.

Matt Butz, Verizon's vice president of network planning, said in a statement that the work has already shown measurable results. He cited AI control of massive MIMO antennas and traffic steering that produced a near nine percent improvement in downlink data radio bearer throughput and up to an eight percent improvement in uplink user equipment throughput. The companies also plan to test and deploy new rApps, including a cell anomaly detector, a root cause explainer and an anomaly general optimizer, which Verizon said will speed its move toward level-four network autonomy. Verizon CTO Yago Tenorio said earlier this year that early work had cut tasks that once took hours down to 90 seconds, and he wanted that in production before the end of the year, starting with the radio and later moving to transport and core.

The controller is part of Ericsson's Intelligent Automation Platform, which is meant to support multi-vendor and multi-technology systems running 4G and 5G RAN, and it is also used in rival AT&T's $14 billion network overhaul. The work builds on earlier efforts between the two companies, including a pre-standard 6G field call in the 7 GHz band at a California site and Verizon Business using Ericsson for international private 5G services. Ericsson is also part of the Verizon-led 6G Innovation Forum that launched last year. Verizon has previously used Samsung and Qualcomm in a multi-vendor deployment of AI-RAN management applications on a RAN intelligent controller, including a Samsung-developed network-efficiency rApp.

Articles.Title: Verizon AI-RAN work rides nationwide Ericsson Intelligent Controller deployment

stories.Headline: Modular AI Data Centers Gain Ground as Crusoe Debuts Unit
stories.Summary:
Crusoe announced a new modular data center unit called Spark Liquid on November 4, 2026, according to Data Center Knowledge. The company said the unit supports up to 3.5 MW of compute capacity per unit. It is designed for Nvidia GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks. Crusoe said Spark Liquid delivers five times the compute density of earlier Spark generations. Production will join the existing Spark line in Brighton, Colorado, in 2027.

The unit uses a closed-loop direct liquid cooling system, which Crusoe said needs minimal ongoing water and has no evaporative loss. Crusoe said the platform is aligned with Nvidia's DSX POD, a blueprint for modular infrastructure for the Vera Rubin platform. Nvidia validates the reference design, and partners manufacture, integrate, and service it. Crusoe is one of eight container solution providers on Nvidia's list, which includes Eaton, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv. Customers still need a prepared site with power, water, and network connections.

Bryan Schramm, head of Spark at Crusoe, said three constraints are converging: power, predictability, and time to token. He said modular helps with all three, because large grid interconnects can take years while a factory-built unit can use power available now. He said building in a factory can make delivery dates more reliable and can bring capacity online in as little as a few months from a ready site. He said direct liquid cooling is necessary at the power density Spark Liquid is built for, because air cannot remove that much heat. He said efficiency at any site will vary with climate, so each deployment is designed with local conditions in mind.

Crusoe has been developing this approach for nearly a decade, and Spark Liquid is its sixth-generation modular platform. The company acquired electrical manufacturer Easter-Owens Electric in 2022 to bring manufacturing in-house, and it builds Spark units at its 352,000-square-foot factory in Brighton. Schramm said Nvidia standardizing on modular reinforces the approach Crusoe has taken for nearly a decade. He said deployments will move closer to demand, including sites near data sources such as a robot fleet, sites within sovereign boundaries, and sites built in the tens of megawatts.

Articles.Title: Modular AI Data Centers Gain Ground as Crusoe Debuts Unit

stories.Headline: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
stories.Summary:
A user posted an Ask HN thread on Hacker News on 4 November 2026 asking how people use AI day to day. The poster, eggbrain, said the thread had 161 points and 184 comments 13 hours after it went up. The post listed five questions about subscriptions, other models, coding harnesses, orchestration tools and broader agent platforms. The poster said no one needed to answer every question and that the aim was a gut feel for current use.

Commenters described a wide range of setups. One said they self-host Qwen and Gemma 4 variants and use their own harness, having moved away from Cline and VS Code to focus on review. Another pays for Claude Ultra at 200 and ChatGPT at 20, runs local models on an M4 MacBook Pro with 128GB of RAM, and drives Claude Code through Telegram with scheduled jobs and containers. A third said they dropped Cursor and Codex for the Claude IDE after Opus 5.5 arrived, set it to medium and removed their skills. Others reported using Muse and Cursor, local models on an M1 Max, Claude Opus 5.5 on a Pro plan, and Google Ultra at 100 a month with DeepSeek pay-as-you-go tokens.

Several commenters said the default tools are good enough. One argued that people using out-of-the-box Claude Code or Codex likely get the newest agent features anyway. Another said Claude and Codex desktop are innovating fast and that built-in code review has made many AI code review startups obsolete. A third said they ask Claude Code to review a pull request and it spawns a sub-agent, though it almost always finds something wrong even after fixes. One solopreneur said they avoid agent swarms because they like to do QA on what the tools generate.

Some commenters described how much work they run at once. One said five things concurrently lasts about a day, three lasts all week and leaves weekends for untangling, and two or three a day feels manageable. Another said they have paid for a 200 plan since March 2026, cycle between four or five work projects and two or three personal ones, and tell their agents at night to keep going without asking questions. One reply said that person was doing everything right. The thread gives no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?

stories.Headline: A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout
stories.Summary:
Docusign announced on Tuesday that it has acquired Suplari, an AI-powered spending analysis company based in Seattle. The deal comes five years after Microsoft bought the startup and nearly three years after Microsoft spun it back out to its founders. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari's technology into its contract management platform.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh Parekh, Jeff Gerber and Brian White. By 2021 it had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures. Microsoft acquired the company in July 2021, when it had about 40 employees, and said it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft keeping a minority stake, and Gerber became CEO. Suplari now has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Docusign said it will pair Suplari's analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with its Iris AI engine. The goal is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms. Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said joining Docusign allows the company to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company's spending. Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari's technology and talent will help Docusign connect what supplier agreements say with actual spending.

Parekh wrote in a blog post earlier this year that after ChatGPT arrived in November 2022, Microsoft redirected new-product investment to Copilot. He said succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers. Microsoft concluded, and the founders agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again. Parekh, who stayed at Microsoft before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn, remains a Suplari shareholder and advisor and said he is ecstatic about the second exit.

Articles.Title: A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

stories.Headline: Did IBM Just Tell the Truth About AI?
stories.Summary:
IBM reported higher revenue but its stock fell, according to a Motley Fool podcast recorded on Oct. 22, 2026 and published on Nov. 4, 2026. Host Jon Quast and contributors Matt Frankel and Lou Whiteman discussed the results alongside Lam Research's quarterly report. Lam's revenue rose 22%, with a 40% operating margin, and its service business posted $2.5 billion in sales, up 40%. The podcast did not give IBM's specific figures or explain its unique take on AI spending in the transcript provided.

The discussion covered several numbers tied to Lam and the wider chip industry. Lam expects its service business to grow about 30% this year and advanced packaging sales to grow about 70%. Equipment spending could rise from around $150 billion to more than $200 billion next year, and Lam's stock trades at about 35 times earnings, or roughly 22 times forward earnings. Frankel described advanced packaging as stacking and connecting multiple chips instead of making one giant chip. Helium matters to chipmaking because fabrication facilities blow it across the back of silicon wafers to keep temperatures precise during etching, and spot prices have cleared $100 per thousand cubic feet.

Frankel said the service side works like a razor and blades model, where every tool sold creates years of service revenue. Whiteman compared it to aerospace and said the services side helps investors see past a possible bubble. He said management's guidance suggests the up cycle is safe at least into 2028, though he still sees cyclicality and limits on how fast the company can grow. Frankel said he would nibble on the dip but would not call the stock a value stock, and Whiteman said he would wait for a better deal.

Quast said the market was down as the podcast was taped, citing comments from President Trump implying the Iran conflict would intensify after the midterm elections. Frankel said South Korea gets about 65% of its helium from Qatar, where Samsung and SK Hynix make chips, and that there is no good substitute for helium. The transcript provided does not say what IBM requires or changes, and it does not give IBM's own statements beyond the panel's discussion of its AI spending. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Did IBM Just Tell the Truth About AI?

stories.Headline: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle returned just 9.3% of cash to shareholders in the first three quarters of 2026, a 15-year low amid AI spending (Patturaja Murugaboopathy/Reuters)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle returned just 9.3% of their cash to shareholders in the first three quarters of 2026, according to Reuters. That figure marked a 15-year low for the five companies. The report was published on October 30, 2026, and was written by Patturaja Murugaboopathy. The low share of returned cash came amid heavy spending on artificial intelligence.

The same five companies have collective AI spending commitments of more than $3 trillion over the coming years, according to Bloomberg. Alphabet alone accounts for $1 trillion of that total, and Meta accounts for $800 billion. The spending figures were reported by Brody Ford of Bloomberg. The commitments cover the years ahead and sit alongside the reduced cash returns to shareholders.

The shareholder return figure and the spending commitments were reported by Reuters and Bloomberg respectively. Murugaboopathy wrote the Reuters report, and Ford wrote the Bloomberg report. Both reports were carried on Techmeme on October 30, 2026. The articles do not say who at the companies is responsible for the spending plans or what executives said about them.

The articles do not describe any next steps or future plans beyond the spending commitments already listed. They give no timetable for when the AI spending will be completed. They also do not say whether the low rate of cash returned to shareholders is expected to continue. No further context on the companies' plans appears in the two reports.

Articles.Title: The 13 AI Giants, from Alphabet to Oracle, Sit on $1.13 Trillion in Cash. They Can Keep Spending on AI even if Markets Get Ugly

stories.Headline: Economy Is Running Hot on Strong Consumer Spending Growth & Massive AI Investment Boom
stories.Summary:
The US economy grew at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026, adjusted for inflation, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis figures reported on October 29, 2026. A narrower measure covering private domestic demand rose 4.9%, the fastest since the second quarter of 2021, after 4.6% in the second quarter. Consumer spending grew 3.8% for a second straight quarter and added 2.5 percentage points to growth. Gross private domestic investment jumped 19.4% and added 3.7 points, while a surge in imports subtracted 3.32 points.

Current-dollar GDP rose 5.6% to $33.0 trillion, and the gap with real growth put inflation at 2.2%. Private fixed investment rose 9.4%, with nonresidential investment up 12.7% and intellectual property products up 8.4%, while residential investment fell 3.3%. Federal spending rose 15.8% and added 0.91 points, and state and local spending dipped 0.1%. Imports of goods rose 26.4%, exports fell 5.7%, and the trade deficit widened to $1.32 trillion.

Treasury debt rose 1.8% to $40.2 trillion while GDP rose 1.37%, lifting the debt-to-GDP ratio to 121.7%, down from 122.4% a year earlier. The article attributes the debt situation to Congress, saying lawmakers have created it and refuse to acknowledge it, and that they are already talking about tax cuts again. It says they are addicted to buying votes with promises until the bond market forces them to act. The article presents these as the author's own remarks.

The article says the third-quarter growth was far above the 2.5% average between the Great Recession and the pandemic. It says the import spike came from high-dollar AI data-center equipment, including semiconductors, and that the investment boom was driven at least in part by AI. It says the housing market faces a glut of new homes, with builders applying prudence. It does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Economy Is Running Hot on Strong Consumer Spending Growth & Massive AI Investment Boom

stories.Headline: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
stories.Summary:
In 2025 Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, devised a way to test introspection in large language models by injecting “thoughts” directly into their neural networks, a technique he described as targeted digital neurosurgery. He dialed up activation patterns linked to concepts such as denim, secrecy or vegetables in some copies of a model, while other copies served as controls, and then asked all of them whether they detected an injected thought and what it was about. In 20% of trials with the most powerful version of Claude, the models correctly flagged the injection and described the concept, while control models never reported one. The work followed a public demo in May 2024 in which users could interact with a version of Claude steered toward the Golden Gate Bridge.

The experiment asked each model two questions, whether it could detect an injection and whether it could describe the injected concept, and counted a trial as a success only when both answers were correct. Kyle Mahowald, a computational linguist at the University of Texas, Austin, and the philosopher Harvey Lederman, then his colleague there, repeated the experiment on large open-source models and studied the two questions separately. They found that models which flagged an injection but failed to name the concept often guessed something completely unrelated, saying “apple” rather than a related word such as “shirts” or “shoes.” They also showed they could degrade the models’ ability to name injected concepts without making them any worse at detecting injections, which suggested the two processes were entirely separate.

Lindsey said that given a theoretical landscape where no one agrees on anything, the best path forward is to do a lot of empirical science. He said that when the steered model wrote “Whoops, let me start over,” you cannot infer that it has some awareness of what is going on in its internals, because it can just read what it is writing and notice that it is weird. Mahowald said Lindsey’s findings seemed super compelling but that striking behavior in language models often turns out to have a simpler explanation, and that if it is somehow less real than it seems, that is super interesting to understand. Lederman said that bizarrely, the models say “apple” all the time.

The articles say that in the year since Lindsey’s paper, which was deliberately limited in scope and did not imply that language models have subjective first-person experiences, researchers have rushed to replicate the study with other models. Some aspects of what Lindsey observed have simpler explanations unrelated to introspection, while others have proved harder to explain away, and whether they should count as introspection remains hotly contested. Shauli Ravfogel, a language model researcher at New York University, noted that models are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time, which is why researchers want tests that cannot be gamed using outside information. Lederman and Mahowald suspected that the answers to Lindsey’s first question might also have a more mundane origin, but the articles do not say what they concluded after subjecting the models to a battery of tests.

Articles.Title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts

stories.Headline: I Asked AI Tools How To Build Wealth on Middle-Class Income
stories.Summary:
MoneyLion asked three AI tools, ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, how someone could build wealth on a $75,000 salary, and published the answers on November 5, 2026. The article was written by Martin Dasko and edited by Brendan McGinley. It cited a TD Bank U.S. survey finding that 69% of Americans would let bank-provided AI tools complete a financial task for them, and that 49% had used some form of AI assistant for a personal finance decision in the past year. The piece was created with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by the editorial team.

ChatGPT said a $75,000 salary can be enough for a strong financial future with strategic money management. It advised spending less than you earn, investing 15% to 20% of gross income, buying diversified low-cost index ETFs, affordable real estate and career investments, raising income through skills and negotiated raises, avoiding lifestyle inflation and building an emergency fund. Gemini recommended a conscious spending plan that sets fixed costs, savings goals and guilt-free spending in advance, automating contributions so money moves into investments before it can be spent, using employer matches and low-cost index funds, and guarding against lifestyle creep. Claude said investing about $940 a month, which is 15% of $75,000, at an average 7% a year grows to roughly $1 million in 30 years, and put after-tax pay at roughly $4,700 to $4,900 a month.

The article said chatbots will not always be accurate on personal finance, but called some tips universally accepted as excellent advice. These were setting a clear budget, automating savings and investments, choosing simple investments because time in the market beats timing it, avoiding lifestyle inflation by raising savings, and staying patient. It said following these general tips can build wealth on any salary. For detailed numbers it recommended working with a financial advisor, and it noted that AI-generated content may be inaccurate, incomplete or outdated and should be checked against reliable sources.

Articles.Title: I Asked AI Tools How To Build Wealth on Middle-Class Income

stories.Headline: Gavel to Gavel: AI training data – Don’t run with scissors
stories.Summary:
A technology attorney, Robin M. Meyer of McAfee & Taft, wrote an opinion piece published on November 4, 2026, in The Journal Record about legal risks in AI training data. She noted that building products with AI models is now common for both industry experts and non-experts. She cited David Friedberg of the All-In podcast, who predicts a future billionaire will come from nowhere. Meyer said the need for speed is constant, but speed while running with scissors is not. Meyer wrote that the United States has no overarching AI law, but existing intellectual property laws still apply when AI models are used.

She listed steps for companies, including avoiding subscriptions to competitive products just to get data. Companies should confirm that co-founders, partners or employees with knowledge of a competitive product are not restricted from sharing it. She also said contractors providing training data should be covered by contracts with liability, indemnity, and representations and warranties, and that the process of obtaining training data should be documented upfront. Meyer said a business may already hold data ideal for training but must still analyze limits on its use. She warned against assuming that data already in the business's possession can be used for training.

She said customer contracts should be reviewed for language prohibiting use of data beyond providing services, and for restrictions on continued use after a contract ends. She also said businesses should review sector-specific laws and data and technology laws for prohibitions or requirements. Meyer said AI-driven innovation can be life-changing but urged companies to focus on legal aspects central to development. She said businesses should proactively ensure that data used for training is truly available. The article appeared in the Gavel to Gavel opinion column, which covers business and legal topics.

Articles.Title: Gavel to Gavel: AI training data – Don’t run with scissors

stories.Headline: Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape
stories.Summary:
Canva announced its first major round of layoffs in its 13-year history on November 3, 2026. The company said 1,271 people, around 22% of its overall staff, will be laid off, reassigned to new roles, or relocated to its headquarters in Sydney, Australia. The news came in a press release from cofounder and CEO Melanie Perkins. Perkins said the layoffs are part of a larger plan to make Canva's teams more agile and less siloed.

The restructuring folds product, growth, and platform teams into one unit and reduces the number of subspecialties at the company. Perkins said she had come to the difficult conclusion that small changes would not be enough. She said Canva needs to refound itself and get back to its roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions and take ownership. Canva did not give a broader business reason for the layoffs.

Perkins is responsible for the changes and explained them in her letter to staff. In an August interview with Fortune, she said demand for new AI features had significantly exceeded the company's expectations. She said this validated the demand but also showed Canva needed to reduce the cost of completing an AI task. She said Canva decided to slow the rollout while it rebuilt the architecture and strengthened the business model.

The layoffs come as Canva works through growing pains and questions about the timing of a potential IPO. In early August, Canva told investors it was downgrading its revenue growth forecast for 2026 from 30% to 20%. By the end of 2025, Canva had more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users. Perkins told Fortune that since launching Canva 2.0 in April, cost per task had dropped by 90%, and Canva said its October launch of Canva Brush cut cost per task by 46% compared with the previous design agent.

Articles.Title: Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape

stories.Headline: Steve Weiss Says the Midterms Just Put a Lid on AI Spending. Here’s Who Could Get Hurt
stories.Summary:
Democrats won sweeping midterm victories on November 4, 2026, taking control of both chambers of Congress, according to the article. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott after promising a moratorium on data center construction and an end to subsidies and tax breaks for major developers. Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms and Ohio's Amy Acton made similar assurances, and voters had approved 37 ballot measures limiting data centers as of Wednesday afternoon, CBS News reported, citing Redbud Consulting. Steve Weiss, a regular on CNBC's Halftime Report, said the market was treating the Democratic victory as forced control on capital spending.

Weiss said companies won't be able to spend what they committed if there is a moratorium on new data centers, particularly in Texas, where he said 30% of all projects are. GLJ Research's Gordon Johnson told CBS the Texas result could delay 13 gigawatts of planned data center power. The article reports that Vistra, a Texas-based power producer, closed at $120.29, down 13.83%, and Vertiv, which sells power and cooling systems for data centers, closed at $205.55, down 12.89%. NVIDIA fell 3.17% to $200.13 and Broadcom fell 2.00% to $325.48, a smaller drop the article attributes to chipmakers selling into data centers worldwide.

Rob Sechan said on the program that less data center build-out means pressure on the chips. Ariana Salvatore of Morgan Stanley said on the firm's Thoughts on the Market podcast that in Texas the incoming Democratic governor would still face a Republican controlled state legislature, limiting the scope for some of the more ambitious changes. Johnson said Abbott himself halted new grid connection approvals for data centers in August pending an audit, and that the new governor only has to keep it in place. The article says both views can hold at once, because a legislature can block new taxes and repeal of incentives while an existing executive pause rolls forward.

The article says broad index funds carry large positions in chipmakers and the cloud providers funding the expansion, so a capital spending slowdown would reach 401(k) balances even for investors who never bought an AI stock directly. It lists signals to watch, including whether Hinojosa continues Abbott's permit pause by executive action after taking office and whether Bottoms signs an executive order to pause construction. It also lists whether cloud companies trim spending plans or shift projects to friendlier states on their next earnings calls. The article says the next few months of permits and guidance will show whether the cap on spending holds or the money moves elsewhere.

Articles.Title: Steve Weiss Says the Midterms Just Put a Lid on AI Spending. Here’s Who Could Get Hurt

stories.Headline: Voters rejected Trump’s ‘booming’ economy narrative and the AI that underpins it
stories.Summary:
Voters handed Democrats sweeping gains in Congress and in statehouses on Tuesday night, according to NBC News. The result delivered a stark message to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans about the economy. Exit polling showed Americans' negative outlook on the economy was the clearest through line of the night. The article was reported by Allie Canal, Kayla Steinberg and Rob Wile.

The article gives no vote counts, seat totals or specific dates beyond the Tuesday night of the election and the Nov. 4, 2026 publication time. It says voters judged that the economy is what matters most and that it is not working. It describes the outcome as a rejection of Trump's "booming" economy narrative and of the AI that underpins it. It does not list specific policy changes the results require.

The article does not quote Trump or other officials directly, and it names no individual as responsible for the outcome. It reports that Republicans have begun grappling with how they lost so badly. It also says Democrats plan to use their House majority to investigate Trump and tackle affordability. The article does not give paraphrased remarks from those responsible.

The article describes the result as a midterms rout and says the Trump coalition imploded. It also reports that the midterms are over and that Trump is over the midterms. It says Iran described the result as Americans rejecting Trump's war. It does not say what happens next beyond the Democratic plans for the House majority.

Articles.Title: Voters rejected Trump’s ‘booming’ economy narrative and the AI that underpins it

stories.Headline: Should Your Firm Adopt an AI and Cybersecurity Policy Statement?
stories.Summary:
A commentary published on November 4, 2026, in wealthmanagement.com argues that professional advisory firms, including law firms and estate-planning practices, should consider adopting a formal written policy statement governing artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. The article says AI is becoming more common in everyday life and is reshaping the daily operations of advisory firms. It says writing these policies down gives professional and administrative staff clarity, creates a framework for training and shows a firm has acted deliberately in meeting its responsibilities. A written policy can also help when firms fill out insurance carrier cybersecurity applications, because some carriers ask whether a formal policy exists.

The article says the policy should be tailored to a firm's actual workflow, since an unmodified generic form offers less protection and may raise exposure if staff cannot follow it. It says the policy should identify the systems used for storage, communication, collaboration and AI work, define who is covered and specify categories of highly sensitive information such as Social Security numbers, tax IDs, signed instruments and meeting recordings. It should also address client-specific requests, such as a refusal to be recorded or insistence on a particular portal, and distinguish among confidentiality, privilege and attorney work product. The article says firms should reassess and update their policies periodically because of the rate of change, and that annual or more frequent reviews are warranted.

The article says attorneys are obligated to stay current on the benefits and risks of relevant technology, and that reasonableness, rather than perfection, is the governing standard. It says an AI policy cannot merely state that professional review of AI output is required, and should address how the firm decides which AI systems are approved, what uses are permitted, how prompts are handled and how outputs are validated. It says firms might mandate certain standard prompt components to reduce the risk of hallucinations, and might require both AI and manual conflict checks until confidence in the tool is established. The article also says fraud and impersonation are major risks, perhaps as significant as data breaches, and that controls may include dual approval for significant transfers, an escalation process for unusual instructions and a written information-security program.

The article says technology should not be treated as a separate silo but integrated into broader considerations of competency, confidentiality, communication and supervision. It says the underlying policy question is not whether AI should be used, but how it is selected, what tasks may be delegated to it, what data may be entered, what review follows and when its use must be disclosed. It says the strongest policies tend to be practical rather than aspirational, identifying the tools used, classifying the information handled and defining who may do what. The article says such a document may assist with training, improve consistency, support insurance presentations and reduce ad hoc technology decisions that become informal policy.

Articles.Title: Should Your Firm Adopt an AI and Cybersecurity Policy Statement?

stories.Headline: Tech, AI Stocks Split After Democratic Sweep: Microsoft Jumps, Tesla and Nvidia Tank
stories.Summary:
Technology stocks delivered a mixed performance on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after Democrats swept the U.S. midterm elections. The Nasdaq-100 climbed 1.14% to 28,500, recovering from an overnight selloff that briefly pushed index futures down more than 2%. Microsoft jumped 6.01% to $552.32, and Google parent Alphabet rose 4.63% to $292.99. Meanwhile, Nvidia fell 2.19% to $202.17, Tesla dropped 3.61% to $384.10, and Intel lost 5.80% to $57.04. Trump Media & Technology Group plunged 14.29% to $5.10.

The conflicting moves reflect uncertainty over what Democratic control of Congress will mean for technology companies that benefited from the Trump administration's approach to deregulation. According to Reuters, investors are particularly concerned about greater scrutiny of AI data centers following Democratic victories in states such as Texas and Georgia, where large infrastructure projects have become politically contentious. The AI sector was already facing questions over enormous infrastructure spending and whether those investments would generate adequate returns. Trump Media had already lost approximately 55% of its value year-to-date before Tuesday's vote. The stock has been in a technical pattern traders call a "death cross" since March 2025 and has lost nearly 90% of its market cap since its 2024 cap.

The article attributes the market moves to investors weighing the prospect of tougher artificial intelligence regulation against expectations that a divided government could limit major policy changes. It cites Reuters for the concern about AI data center scrutiny. The Nasdaq-100 remains well below its October highs above 31,000, with the 28,000 area as immediate support and a move back above 29,000 strengthening the short-term recovery. Bitcoin recovered strongly, trading around $80,512, up 4.12% in the day, after an initial election-related selloff. The article says Wednesday's split between technology winners and losers suggests investors are becoming increasingly selective about their exposure to the AI boom and the political risks surrounding it.

Articles.Title: Tech, AI Stocks Split After Democratic Sweep: Microsoft Jumps, Tesla and Nvidia Tank

stories.Headline: Sovereign AI at Texas A&M cuts research compute costs
stories.Summary:
Texas A&M is building a state-funded AI and high-performance computing platform called IGNITE, short for Innovative Growth in Next Generation AI Technology Ecosystem. The Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station, known as TEES, leads the project, and Dell Technologies is building the system with Advanced Micro Devices graphics processing units inside an Equinix data center in Dallas. Vince Kellen, chief information officer of the Texas A&M University System, and Casey Bryan, chief information officer of TEES, discussed the work during theCUBE's coverage of the AI Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit. The effort is meant to give research teams computing power their existing systems lack.

Bryan said existing resources are severely underpowered, and that research is getting done but could be helped by capacity and scale. Kellen said taking the same science to a classic neocloud provider today would cost 5 to 10 times as much. He said controlling the assets significantly reduces costs and strengthens security, and that sovereignty spans four pillars: data, infrastructure, capability and model, and governance. As a state agency, TEES follows National Institute of Standards and Technology frameworks 800-53 and 800-171, as well as Texas Administrative Code 202, and it wants IGNITE to be ready for Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Level 2.

Bryan said researchers should not have to think about the many controls TEES must inherit, and that using the capabilities should be seamless. He said security came first when TEES met with Dell's implementation team to schedule workshops, and that the project's architecture review board has since affirmed that direction. He said the idea was to build a security foundation that all other operational components could be built on and referenced back to. His advice to institutions starting their own sovereign AI projects was to start with security early and embed it in the process from the beginning.

Articles.Title: Sovereign AI at Texas A&M cuts research compute costs

stories.Headline: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
stories.Summary:
Researchers have developed an AI-native experimental laboratory called AutoDNA for autonomous biomolecular operations, according to a study published in Nature on November 4, 2026. The system was created by a team including researchers with ORCID identifiers and authors such as Jiabin Wang, Zhiyuan Dong, Jingkai Yang, Qingting Li and Tianyu Huang. AutoDNA is designed to carry out multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments with minimal human intervention. The work was published as an article in Nature with supporting data, code and supplementary information.

The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to perform core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing. Human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields and accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold. It also completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation.

The authors say AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing applications in synthetic biology and information storage. They describe the system as realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework through co-design of models, experiments and instruments. The paper frames the work as addressing a long-standing goal of AI-native laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention. The authors note that existing autonomous experimental systems remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation.

The study positions AutoDNA against an add-on architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than giving it a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. The data supporting the findings are available in the article and its supplementary information, with sequencing data and agent-related outputs available at Zenodo. The code is available on GitHub, and the version used in the study is also available at Zenodo. Reference genome hg38 was downloaded from the National Center for Biotechnology Information, and further data are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

Articles.Title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations

stories.Headline: Is The AI Bubble Really Popping Now?
stories.Summary:
The article, published on November 4, 2026, by mindmatters.ai, examines whether the AI bubble is now popping. The author says he has focused on the economics of AI, its applications, and what makes a bubble. He notes that almost every bubble is different, and that the AI bubble involves a small number of companies in a simple value chain. End users only get value if AI models improve corporate or individual productivity.

The article says the AI labs, such as Anthropic and OpenAI, have mostly set prices far below their costs. It says there were a few months in early to mid-2026 when the labs raised prices, but then Chinese models increased their market share and the labs cut prices again. Jim Cavello of Goldman Sachs started the public side of this argument in 2024, and the calculations assume 50% margins.
