The article says almost $1 trillion in revenues are now needed, or $2.5 trillion by 2031, while the AI labs have only about $100 to $200 billion.

The author says he and many AI skeptics have pushed this argument for years, and he wrongly believed investors would eventually sell shares. He cites Nobel Laureate Robert Shiller, who claims a narrative emerges to explain a bubble's growth and later its deflation. The author says determining that AI is a bubble and determining when it pops are two different questions. He admits he probably still lacks the skill of reading movements in stock and bond prices.

The article says the bond market identifies over-valued companies and bubble risk long before the stock market does, because it is concerned with the risk of default. Over the last year, it says, the bond market raised interest rates for many AI-related companies, particularly Oracle, Softbank, and the neo-clouds, and less so for the hyperscalers. Oracle operates data centers, Softbank has been a big investor in OpenAI, and CoreWeave and Nebius are neo-clouds that rent out GPU time. Those interest rates spiked in the last few months and again in the last few weeks, sparking a recent decline in stock prices for Oracle, Softbank, CoreWeave, and Nebius.

Articles.Title: Is The AI Bubble Really Popping Now?

stories.Headline: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
stories.Summary:
In elections on November 3, 2026, voters backed candidates and ballot measures that would restrict AI and data centers. Redbud Consulting tracked 44 measures in 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, and 38 passed so far, including dozens of moratoriums and bans. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed, in a North Dakota city, and it still requires developers to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings. Voters also elected anti-AI candidates in key states, most notably Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governor race.

Analysts said the measures will not affect data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, and will mainly hit projects planned for 2028. Texas was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028, and Bloomberg reported that about 13 gigawatts of data center capacity is now exposed. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research said projects with power, permits and steel keep going, but those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months, and some projects may leave the state, perhaps for Louisiana or Georgia. Hinojosa plans to delay projects until laws pass tackling impacts on water, electricity, air and property rights, and Johnson said she would impose a moratorium until legislation gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills and ends tax incentives for data centers. Democrats also won governor races in Arizona, Georgia and Ohio, and Axios projected that nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity could face similar delays, while Bloomberg estimated that half the data centers in the US are now more vulnerable to scrutiny.

Adam Kovacevich, a former Google executive and CEO of the trade group Chamber of Progress, said the results offer little evidence of a voter mandate to crack down on AI or data centers. He said Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed data center bans won at a higher rate than those who supported them, and that people should not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate. Alejandra Montoya-Boyer, vice president of The Leadership Conference's Center for Civil Rights and Technology, disagreed, calling the 2026 midterms the first true AI election in the US. She cited NBC News exit polls showing 3 in 4 voters opposed to data centers and more than half saying AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Brad Carson of Americans for Responsible Innovation told Axios that voters sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers.

Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, told the South China Morning Post that a slowdown in the US could be a win for China, with new constraints on US computing capacity keeping AI token prices high and giving China an opportunity to export cost-effective inference services. Michael Strobaek of Lombard Odier noted that Trump can still veto federal laws, and Time reported that Democrats would likely need substantial Republican support to pass laws over a veto. Trump did not directly mention AI in his Truth Social posts reacting to the results. Elon Musk, who gave almost half a billion dollars to Republican candidates as of October, saw SpaceX and Tesla shares drop as votes came in, and according to SemiAnalysis, SpaceX raised its goal for data center capacity in 2027 from 10 gigawatts to about 13GW.

Articles.Title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”

stories.Headline: AI a threat to news organizations
stories.Summary:
Meta's new terms for businesses that use Facebook have alarmed newspapers and media outlets, according to a report in the Pine County News. The terms say media companies must allow web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents into their websites so Meta can collect news content for its use. Businesses that use Facebook have no opt out option and would be forced to agree to the new terms. Newspapers and other media outlets are joining together in possible litigation against Meta unless the terms are revised to protect intellectual property.

The policy says Meta may periodically pull updates from domains, web pages or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products. Meta says the update only applies to its ads and business products. The terms first said the content would be used to train AI, and Meta changed the word train to develop on October 16. The new terms take effect on November 20, after Meta delayed the original October 30 date to consult with publishers and advertisers.

Sen. Martha Blackburn, a Republican, and Sen. Adam Schiff, a Democrat, are getting involved. Schiff reached out to Mark Zuckerberg directly and insisted the company withdraw the terms as written. The Norwegian Media Businesses' Association filed the first lawsuit against Meta over the terms, and the European Publishers Council signed a joint letter arguing the terms violate the Digital Markets Act. Editor & Publisher magazine argues that if Meta can build models on local journalism and use them to generate competing summaries, publishers can argue Meta is using their property to undercut them.

Editor & Publisher also states that Google pays roughly 100 publishers for AI sourced answers, while Meta is offering nothing. The article says that if outlets agree to the terms, AI could put more newspaper companies out of business, and Meta would then have nothing to draw content from. Management at the paper has said that if the terms stand, it may deliver the news the old way, through the printed paper and website, and potentially through email or other social media platforms. Traci LeBrun is the editor of the Pine City Pioneer.

Articles.Title: AI a threat to news organizations

stories.Headline: Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change
stories.Summary:
Google is giving Seattle's Allen Institute for AI about $5 million, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model from Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades ahead. The grant was announced on a Wednesday morning and comes from Google.org, the company's philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. The three-year project will build an open-source model called NeuralGCM+, which builds on Google's NeuralGCM, a model that mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team.

The money is meant to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years. Ai2 will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, aiming for stable simulations that span decades, and will build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against traditional climate models. The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google's internal systems, so other researchers can train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google's chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2's director of research for AI climate modeling, said Google's model work centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most, and that the company has less interest and expertise in projections that run decades out. He said climate modeling is more of a public good, information people need to know, and that government agencies are often the ones thinking about it. Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, said in a statement that Ai2 is uniquely positioned to extend NeuralGCM into the next generation of long-term climate projections, citing its climate science expertise and commitment to open research. Watt-Meyer said making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part and could take longer than three years, and that "we don't know if it'll work necessarily."

The team's origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who started a climate modeling effort around 2016 at what was then known as Vulcan, his Seattle-based holding company. The group moved to Ai2 in 2021, about two and a half years after his death; Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014. The original plan was to combine physics and AI, but the group set that aside because the AI couldn't be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language, and Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem. Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE, which rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM, but versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn't experienced yet. Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM's design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won't change, and he said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time.

Articles.Title: Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

stories.Headline: Jeanette Winterson’s point about AI brings to mind an Isaac Asimov story | Letters
stories.Summary:
The Guardian published two letters on 4 November 2026 responding to an interview with Jeanette Winterson about AI and the future of humanity. The interview had appeared on 28 October. Ed Kelsey wrote that he enjoyed the interview, especially her quotation from Jill Lepore that we are living out the sci-fi books tech leaders read when they were 13. He said he was one of those 13-year-olds and that his favourite author was Isaac Asimov. Kelsey said many Asimov stories predicted the modern world, from mobile technology to AI through the fictional supercomputer Multivac.

He singled out Winterson's closing point that we need doctors and chemists but also well-rounded people. He said this brought to mind Asimov's story Profession, published in Nine Tomorrows in 1959, which depicts highly specialised automated worlds and the need for some specialists to be well-rounded. He encouraged Winterson to read it and said he did not grow up to be a tech-bro but did become a computer programmer. Arthur Gould thanked Winterson for making readers think about the possible benefits of AI and repeated her line that there is no inevitable dystopia. He asked whether AI, if it shows intelligence superior to Homo sapiens, might be a force for good in the future.

He suggested it might see a way out of the climate catastrophe and the senselessness of bombing cities. He said important decisions will be removed from humans and made by a superior intelligence, which might not always be palatable but might serve the planet's long-term interests. The letters respond to Winterson's interview and do not report any new event or decision. They give no dates beyond the interview and the 1959 story, and no names beyond Winterson, Lepore, Asimov, Kelsey and Gould. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Jeanette Winterson’s point about AI brings to mind an Isaac Asimov story | Letters

stories.Headline: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
stories.Summary:
Kehan Lu, Tianhao Chu, AIERSI TUERHONG, Yiwen Sun, Huan Luo, Fang Fang and SI WU posted a preprint on bioRxiv on 5 November 2026. They trained recurrent neural networks with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, oscillatory phase coding emerged in the networks on its own. In this pattern, memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm.

The amplitude of the oscillation encodes item identity, and its phase encodes serial order. Ablation studies found three elements required for the coding: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis showed content cells and time cells emerging in the trained network, handling item identity and sequence order separately. Connectivity analysis showed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups.

The authors say the coding arises from network structures and task demands. They propose a neural circuit model that reproduces it through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. They state that the work offers insights into how the coding is implemented and computed in biological systems. They also say it can inspire computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

The authors declared no competing interests. The preprint is published under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 International license. The copyright holder has granted bioRxiv a license to display it in perpetuity. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory

stories.Headline: Pliant Raises $80 Million to Open B2B Payments to AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Pliant raised $80 million in a Series C funding round, the Berlin-headquartered company said in a Wednesday, Nov. 4 press release. The round was led by Seaya Nova and Speedinvest. The company said it will use the money to deepen its B2B payment infrastructure around agentic payments and workflows. It will also use the funding to support expansion in the United States and Canada and to prepare entry into additional international markets.

The round follows an April 2025 Series B round in which Pliant raised $40 million and brought its total funding to more than $100 million. At that time, Pliant was readying its expansion to the U.S. Pliant's modular platform provides commercial card issuing, payment accounts, foreign exchange and spend management for businesses and artificial intelligence agents. Businesses use it to manage complex payment workflows, and FinTechs, software platforms and banks use it to build and operate their own commercial payment offerings. The platform includes its own AI agents that help customers automate recurring finance work, and it lets third-party agents connect via Model Context Protocol.

CEO and Co-Founder Malte Rau said the platform has been API-first from day one and that Pliant has adopted AI in its platform and its own operations. He said the company is built for established businesses that want AI to automate payments with the right guardrails, and for AI-native companies that need a licensed partner that moves as fast as they do. He said the investment will help Pliant open more of its infrastructure directly to AI agents and expand into new markets. Seaya Nova General Partner Vinoth Jayakumar said AI has made infrastructure more valuable, as in past waves of software. He said that when agents move money, someone still has to be licensed, auditable and liable, and that this is the layer Pliant owns.

Articles.Title: Pliant Raises $80 Million to Open B2B Payments to AI Agents

stories.Headline: Nothing CEO says company’s mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Nothing CEO Carl Pei posted on X that the company’s first AI-native product ships in December. Nothing is the smartphone startup behind the distinctive Nothing Phone. Pei said the device is a tool built with the personality and care that define a Nothing product. He said it has no new screen and could not have been an app.

No firm release date has been announced. Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time, and the company has also said it plans to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses and earbuds with AI integrations. He called the product a productivity tool. He seemed to downplay any link to AI wearables, writing that the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment with the pendant, the pin, the glasses and the companion.

He said he admires the boldness but reads this moment differently. Nothing fans should know soon enough what the company has in store. Pei is the CEO of Nothing and made the announcement in his post on X. He described the device as a tool built with personality and care. He said it has no new screen and could not have been an app.

He also said he reads the industry’s hunt for a magical consumer AI device differently. The articles do not say what the device is, and they give no price or further specifications. They say only that it ships in December and that no firm release date has been announced. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: Nothing CEO says company’s mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month

stories.Headline: Nice CEO links 500 job cuts to AI productivity gains, including in R&D
stories.Summary:
Nice CEO Scott Russell explained on the company's third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that the Israeli-founded software company is cutting approximately 500 jobs worldwide, about 5% of its roughly 10,000 employees. He said the restructuring goes beyond slower-growing business lines and also includes research and development, where teams are using AI tools to raise productivity. CFO Beth Gaspich said the cuts would be concentrated mainly in product development, go-to-market operations, customer support and services. The company expects restructuring charges of $15 million to $20 million, mostly in the fourth quarter.

The reduction supports Nice's shift toward its CXAI platform and its faster-growing businesses, with more reliance on global systems integrators and other partners to help customers deploy its products. In the third quarter, revenue rose 8% to $791 million, while AI annual recurring revenue increased 46% to $392 million. Cloud revenue growth remained below what management wants, and profitability weakened on a GAAP basis. Russell said cloud growth was not where it needs to be, though he expressed confidence that investments in AI, sales capacity and partnerships would eventually bring faster growth.

Russell said Nice had looked at slower-growing parts of the business to find efficiency gains, and that R&D teams are leveraging AI tools to increase productivity materially. He added that the company is simplifying its organization by removing layers of management and span of control. In July he had told CTech that the plan was to grow, not shrink, and that there were no plans to reduce headcount. He also said then that Nice had no plans to reduce its workforce in Israel, where it employed approximately 1,000 people, around 10% of its global workforce.

The announcement does not establish how the 500 cuts will be distributed across countries, and Nice has not disclosed how many employees in Israel, if any, will be affected. The company said the reductions would be global, with the main areas targeted including product development and customer-facing functions. Nice develops software that helps large companies manage customer service operations, increasingly using AI agents to automate interactions previously handled by human representatives. It is now applying a similar productivity argument internally, saying AI tools can help its own development teams produce more with fewer resources.

Articles.Title: Nice CEO links 500 job cuts to AI productivity gains, including in R&D

stories.Headline: AI Multiplies Advisor Expertise: A Computer Nerd Comes Clean
stories.Summary:
Mark Tennenbaum, who describes himself as a computer nerd, wrote in Advisor Perspectives on November 4, 2026 about building an AI-assisted platform called FlightDeck. He began using new AI reasoning models in 2025 to turn his ideas into working code. Since February 2026 he has built FlightDeck, a market intelligence platform with live portfolio monitors, a market weather system, replays of historical crises, a regime classification history going back to 2000, and a publishing system for his firm's research. He is the chief engineer for his firm's information systems as well as its chief portfolio and investment model designer.

Tennenbaum estimates that building the platform the way he would have in 2019 would have taken roughly 3,800 hours of senior financial engineering. At the $150 to $200 an hour he would expect to pay experienced U.S. contract fintech engineers, that comes to well over half a million dollars before the first support ticket. The actual cost was a handful of AI subscriptions, cloud hosting, and his own design and engineering expertise. He says 40-plus years of knowing where data comes from, how it flows, and when a number is wrong made the design work.

He describes three cases where the AI gave confident wrong answers that he caught because he knew what the right answer should be. In one, the AI overruled his architecture and gave monitors their own calculations, which produced screens that disagreed about the same portfolio. In another, it proposed rebalancing triggers built on a research framework meant only to judge whether alpha can be measured. In a third, it misread tickers and declared a catastrophic concentration in a single issuer, then heaped praise on the same process after he corrected it. He says none of these was a classic hallucination but a failure of comprehension and context at the prompt level.

He cites research showing AI helps novices most on tasks inside its competence and can hurt users outside it. Among 5,179 customer support agents, AI raised productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices, with little gain for the most skilled. Among 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants, those using AI on a task outside its competence were 19 percentage points less likely to get it right. In an Advisor360° survey of 300 advisors released in January 2026, just 3% said they rely on AI-generated financial recommendations while 93% called retaining control over decisions and advice non-negotiable. He urges advisors to keep one source of truth, know what each tool is for, distrust both alarm and applause, and make the AI show its assumptions.

Articles.Title: AI Multiplies Advisor Expertise: A Computer Nerd Comes Clean

stories.Headline: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says
stories.Summary:
On Uber’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the company said very few people are using personal AI agents to order rides or food. During its busiest week in October, the week of Halloween, only four rides were ordered through an AI agent. Uber handled around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats that week, but only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by an AI agent. Chief financial officer Balaji Krishnamurthy gave the figures to Wall Street analysts on the call.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the traction was very, very early and very limited so far, and added that the company hopes there will be more. He pointed out that booking a ride in the Uber app takes only 50 seconds on average, and re-ordering a favorite food takes 90 seconds, which suggests an AI agent is not necessarily saving anyone time. He also said he sees agents as another opportunity to reach the platform and expects them to be a net positive for demand. He noted there are around eight major AI assistants on the market now, and he expects that number to grow to more than 10, adding that every single AI system company is talking to Uber.

The low numbers come amid growing hype for AI agents that handle tasks on users’ behalf. Instinct, a personal AI startup founded last year, raised its most recent funding round at a $10 billion valuation, and Meta’s Muse became the No. 1 app in Apple’s U.S. App Store last month, topping 10 million users per Meta’s own reporting. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and SpaceXAI (Grok) also offer their own AI agents, as do numerous smaller startups. DoorDash said on its earnings call last week that it has received only a few hundred orders from AI agents so far, as most customers still order through its app.

Articles.Title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says

stories.Headline: Professional services reinvented: Certinia’s Veda AI agents
stories.Summary:
Certinia Inc. has expanded Veda, its suite of AI agents for professional services businesses, with a new offering called System of Action, which the company unveiled in September 2026. The company launched Veda in April 2026 with 10 package agents and has since grown that number to 24, with plans to finish the year with more than 40. In July 2026, Certinia acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform built for the professional services sector. Certinia, which launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc. and rebranded in 2023, says its platform facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month.

The System of Action more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135 and uses a three-tier architecture to bring agents into services workflows. The first tier combines structured records with unstructured project data, the second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia's services experience, and the third lets agents act inside existing workflows. The Moonnox acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review.

Robert Cesafsky, Certinia's chief operating officer, said the services industry has probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry, and that clients need the right tools and control over their services business. Mimi Spier, the chief marketing officer, said AI can take away administrative tasks so customers deliver outcomes faster at a lower cost to serve, and can identify expansion opportunities and at-risk customers. Raju Malhotra, the chief product and technology officer, said the package agents are persona based and help customers, and that Certinia wants to accelerate delivery rather than just hand over a project plan. Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research, said Veda offers a glimpse of enterprise AI working alongside humans in consequential workflows, grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.

Certinia has a long-standing relationship with Salesforce, having built its platform natively on Salesforce and being featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce's AgentExchange. Hebner said professional services is a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability. He said that if Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Certinia's plan to finish the year with more than 40 package agents.

Articles.Title: Professional services reinvented: Certinia’s Veda AI agents

stories.Headline: Dance, engineering professors awarded grant for dance AI model
stories.Summary:
Two assistant professors at the University of Texas at Austin have been awarded more than $600,000 from a science nonprofit, according to an Oct. 21 news release. Sinclair Emoghene teaches in the Department of Theatre and Dance, and Lillian Chin teaches in the Department of Electrical and Chemical Engineering. The two met during a faculty orientation two years ago and began exploring how their fields could merge. Chin said they happened to sit next to each other, and that Emoghene had been really interested in how technology can inform dance.

The grant comes from the Humanities and AI Virtual Institute at the nonprofit Schmidt Sciences. It will let the team develop its sensor technology through August 2029 and add to its database of dance recordings from different countries and cultures. So far the team has recorded and processed 155 dance recordings from 33 countries and built an online platform to explore how the dances are organized. Dancers wear motion sensor pads that collect data as they move, and that data trains an AI model linking each dance to its cultural origins. The model is meant to help preserve traditions as knowledge of the dances' history fades.

Emoghene said in the news release that documenting and codifying these dance movements helps preserve them as traditions change and the knowledge they carry disappears. The research is supported by the Department of Arts and Technologies and the Lab for Immersive Media in the College of Fine Arts. Michael Baker, the departmental chair for Arts and Entertainment and founding director of the lab, said the lab is about combining technologies. He said it brings together people and technologies from very different disciplines and unlocks new possibilities. The team includes undergraduate and graduate researchers.

Articles.Title: Dance, engineering professors awarded grant for dance AI model

stories.Headline: AI Makes Its Way Into Agriculture
stories.Summary:
Preston Schrader, a Monmouth native, created a tool called Clevis AI to help grain farmers manage their operations and farm data, according to a report from 977wmoi.com dated November 4, 2026. The report says technology has become more integrated into everyday life over the last few years, and agriculture is no exception. It says artificial intelligence is playing a growing role in shifting modern agriculture from manual labor toward data-driven, automated systems. These technologies range from precision irrigation and weed and pest control to autonomous machinery.

Schrader said he had the thought that eventually technology would reach a place where a farmer could manage all this stuff without having to acquire headcount, meaning the full-time staff that would require extra time. He described himself as always having been a technology guy and said that after AI tools came out he had the idea of starting Clevis. He explained that only a farmer knows what Clevis means, since a clevis is the connector that connects a tractor to an implement. In the same way, he said, Clevis is designed to connect every aspect of a farm so the AI has contextual knowledge of the operation and can give recommendations and advice based on that specific data.

The report says Clevis is currently a grain-focused AI system with a Midwest base. It says Schrader is looking to expand to more southern-based crop data and livestock operations. The same site also carried other items, including a National Ag Day announcement of a 2027 video essay contest theme asking how technology will help agriculture strengthen rural America. It also listed a land auction of Jacobson Family farmland shares hosted by Tharp Auction Service on Thursday, November 12th, with auctioneer Thad Tharp.

Articles.Title: AI Makes Its Way Into Agriculture

stories.Headline: AI Liability: Lagging in Time, Leading in Importance
stories.Summary:
In late 2025, several large US insurers asked regulators for approval to exclude AI-related liabilities from corporate policies, according to the article. Their main worry was correlation, since the industry can absorb a single $400 million loss but not thousands of simultaneous claims from one AI provider's error. On October 15, 2026, the CEO of Marsh, a leading insurance broker, warned that broad AI exclusions could create real confusion and uncertainty. Harbor, a San Francisco company, came out of stealth on October 13, 2026 with a $10 million seed round led by Base10, Abstract and 8VC. It says its first customers are banks and insurers in the US, Europe and Latin America.

The article describes AI insurance and AI policy as the trailing edge of the AI cycle, meaning the frameworks that come last. It says insurers have built this kind of layer before, citing boiler insurance and inspection in 1866, Underwriters Laboratories in 1894, the first car insurance policy in 1897 and the first compulsory insurance law in Massachusetts in 1925. Cyber insurance reached $15.3 billion in global premiums in 2024, under 1 percent of global property and casualty premiums, about 30 years on and still not fully developed. Deloitte projects about $4.7 billion in annual AI insurance premiums by 2032 at roughly 80 percent annual growth, while cyber insurance reached an estimated $16.3 billion in 2025.

The article says the lag is real and often longer than expected, and that insurers also wrote the rules through their business model. It says early boiler and electrical safety standards were private policy, written by insurers years before governments acted. It adds that the trailing edge can stay small for a long time, as cyber insurance shows three decades after the commercial internet rose. The author, Nora Panholzer, argues that AI risk is unusually correlated because an AI agent acts autonomously and its mistakes can repeat across countless transactions before anyone notices. She says attribution, knowing what the system did and why, is part of the trailing edge itself.

The article says the gap is opening from two directions, with incumbent insurers pulling back while the law has not settled whether liability falls on the companies that build AI or those that deploy it. It says Harbor's model follows the historical template: measure the risk, reduce it, insure what is left. It argues the market will probably not be winner-take-all, because correlated risk has to be spread across many balance sheets, which is why Lloyd's syndicates and reinsurers stand behind most new entrants. It also cites Aldrich and Fiol, who argued in 1994 that new industries lack legitimacy and founders win it collectively. The author says the next decade will reward those who build the insurance, standards and rules that make AI safe to use.

Articles.Title: AI Liability: Lagging in Time, Leading in Importance

stories.Headline: VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds
stories.Summary:
Broadcom Inc. announced on November 4, 2026 that it is expanding its VMware portfolio with new capabilities for deploying artificial intelligence workloads, strengthening infrastructure security and simplifying disaster recovery. The company also introduced a lower-cost virtualization platform for smaller customers that do not need a full private cloud platform. The updates span VMware Cloud Foundation, the company's flagship private cloud platform, and a set of optional advanced services. Several capabilities are already available in VCF 9.1.1, which was released in September, while others are scheduled for the first quarter of Broadcom's 2027 fiscal year, which began on Monday.

Broadcom is introducing AI Infrastructure Quickstart, an automated deployment capability that combines vCenter cluster deployment, vSphere Supervisor activation and VMware Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning into a single workflow. Another enhancement, multitenant model sharing, lets multiple business units use centrally deployed AI models while keeping separate security boundaries and data privacy controls, and it is already available in VCF 9.1.1. Broadcom is also adding native S3-compatible object storage through VMware vSAN, expected to become generally available in the upcoming VCF release. On security, the company is building capabilities directly into VCF, including confidential computing support for Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. processors, which was already available in VCF 9.1.1, plus planned policy-based virtual private cloud connectivity and automated infrastructure configuration compliance.

Broadcom is also moving disaster recovery functionality into the core VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation platforms, providing orchestrated recovery across thousands of workloads, including recovery from outages, equipment failures and natural disasters. Additional protection will come through VMware HyperArmor, a previously announced service that provides hypervisor-level defenses including virtual patching, continuous monitoring and multifactor authentication. At the lower end, the company is adding VMware vSphere Express, a new offering for environments containing up to 128 processor cores that is based on vSphere 9 and includes live virtual machine migration, high availability, distributed networking, security and simplified patching. Prashanth Shenoy, Broadcom's chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions, said the product is intended for customers that need basic virtualization without buying the more comprehensive and costly VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF platforms, and that they do not need a whole cloud in their two-server environment.

More than 2,600 customers had deployed VCF 9 as of September, representing more than 24 million allocated cores, according to Shenoy. The changes are part of a broader Broadcom effort to position VCF as a common infrastructure platform for traditional virtual machines, containers and increasingly demanding AI workloads. Customers can upgrade to the larger platforms as their requirements grow. Broadcom did not disclose pricing, although Shenoy indicated Express would be substantially less expensive than its higher-end offerings.

Articles.Title: VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds

stories.Headline: AI and Medicine: Who’s the Doctor?
stories.Summary:
A November 4, 2026 HPCwire interview with Dr. Frederick H. Hausheer, a medical oncologist and clinical pharmacologist who heads Hausheer BioMed, examined AI's role in medicine. The interview was conducted by HPCwire contributor Steve Conway as the first of three parts. Hausheer described AI's potential in earlier and more accurate diagnosis, better selection of tests and treatments, fewer avoidable adverse effects and drug interactions, and more effective use of physicians' and patients' time. He said a quick answer is useful only if it is accurate, relevant and actionable for the decision being made.

Hausheer said three levels of evidence must be kept apart: a model performs well on a defined task, clinicians using it make better decisions, and its use improves patient outcomes. He said evidence for one does not establish the next. He noted that AI and high-performance computing are not new to medical research, recalling that in 1986 at the National Cancer Institute possible AI applications were being considered. He pointed to a September 30, 2026 joint statement by physician organizations, reported by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, that raised concern about broad claims of AI superiority over physicians. He said a demonstrated advantage on a particular task should be acknowledged without becoming an unsupported conclusion about all of medicine.

Hausheer said the authority given an AI system should depend on prior performance and safety evidence for its specific function, the likelihood and clinical consequences of error, and the controls governing its use, not on computational capability alone. In a hypothetical case of cancer that progressed after several treatments, he said a useful system would reconstruct the therapy sequence, distinguish progression from delays or discontinuation due to toxicity, and organize treatment options by supporting evidence while identifying missing information. He said options should distinguish FDA-approved uses, evidence-supported off-label uses and investigational treatments. He described ASCO's Guidelines Assistant as helping clinicians find guidelines, not as an autonomous treatment selector, and said performance should be tracked by task and system version.

Hausheer traced his views to high-performance computing work beginning in 1986 at the National Cancer Institute's Advanced Scientific Computing Laboratory and later at BioNumerik Pharmaceuticals, where computational predictions were followed by laboratory testing. He said that approach, though not today's generative AI, remains relevant: form a hypothesis, predict with a model, test it experimentally and let the result guide the next step. He said integrating physics-based simulation with modern AI and experimental science offers an important opportunity in drug research, with the goal of better medicines and patient outcomes rather than substituting computational confidence for evidence. He said safety should start from the principle of first, do no harm, with foreseeable hazards identified before deployment and remaining risks monitored.

Articles.Title: AI and Medicine: Who’s the Doctor?

stories.Headline: Jordi Visser on AI, Rates, Eli Lilly and Micron
stories.Summary:
Jordi Visser, head of AI Macro Nexus Research at 22V Research and a former president and CIO of Weiss Multi-Strategy Advisers, spoke to Phil Rosen on Full Signal in an interview published on November 4, 2026. He said AI is the only macro story that matters and that this year's rise in Treasury yields reflects higher nominal GDP plus the debt and capital needs of the data center build-out. He said bank credit desks are worried about concentration, not collapse, because the biggest borrowers are also the biggest equity holdings, and that this does not mean the AI bubble is blowing up. He expects next year to look different, citing Goldman Sachs's view that investment-grade bond issuance growth is set to peak, with more financing moving to private credit and special purpose vehicles.

Visser said Microsoft has offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, which he said is 27% of the company's workforce, and he estimated the savings at about $24 billion if all 60,000 left. He sees pressure building on governments to support workers because companies are thriving, and he expects a redistribution of profits from capital to labor rather than universal basic income, possibly through higher corporate tax rates on the largest companies. He rejected the idea that AI has not boosted productivity, saying it has shown up in corporate profit margins, with profits growing while companies barely hire. He said he is still cautious on the hyperscalers despite calling their balance sheets pristine, and he expects S&P 500 earnings to rise about 30% this year while the index was up only about 11% when they spoke.

On Eli Lilly, Visser said the stock has compounded more than 30% a year for 10 years and that he has said publicly it will be the biggest stock in the S&P 500 by 2030. He called obesity and diabetes drugs a non-cyclical, regulated business that AI cannot easily disrupt, with only about 10% of the 100 million obese Americans on treatment. On Micron, he said he sold out around May and June and has been buying back in, seeing downside of maybe 10% to 20% while the upside is 60 to 80%. His advice to investors is to stop extrapolating today and find the decade-long story, echoing Adam Parker's view that the AI trade is still in its early innings, and he said longevity is a major theme, adding he would rather be long travel and recreation than McDonald's.

Articles.Title: Jordi Visser on AI, Rates, Eli Lilly and Micron

stories.Headline: Advertisers weigh AI cost savings against consumer skepticism
stories.Summary:
A 2026 survey from the Interactive Advertising Bureau found a wide gap between how advertising executives and young consumers see AI-generated ads. Of the executives surveyed, 82% thought Gen Z and millennial consumers felt positively about such ads, while only 45% of the consumers surveyed said they did. The survey was based on more than 500 Gen Z and millennial consumers and 100 advertising executives. Shane Ginsberg, founder of Street Poller Media, said the distinction partly comes down to what an ad asks viewers to believe. His company produces street-interview advertising built around filmed interactions with people in public settings.

The survey also found that disclosure could support acceptance. Seventy-three percent of consumer respondents said knowing an ad used AI would either increase or make no difference to their likelihood of purchasing. Ginsberg argues that content explaining a product serves a different purpose from content presenting someone's personal experience with it, and that an apparent customer reaction carries expectations about whether that experience actually occurred. The article notes that filming a real person does not establish that an encounter was spontaneous or that editing preserved its meaning. It also says the Federal Trade Commission's guidance on consumer reviews and testimonials addresses fake or false testimonials, including misrepresentations about a person's existence or experience.

Ginsberg expects automation to put pressure on advertising formats that compete mainly through production speed and volume, and he argues that credible human participation could become a more important differentiator as generated content becomes more common. The article describes this as a business thesis, not an established pricing trend. It says production cost is only one part of a campaign's economics, since media placement, distribution, editing and performance measurement still affect the final result. It adds that a cheaper video is not necessarily less expensive per customer acquired, and a costlier human-led production does not automatically justify its price.

The article says consumer attitudes complicate the idea that audiences universally reject AI-made advertising, and that the findings do not establish how every audience will respond. It says no advertising format is automatically protected from technological change, and credibility alone does not guarantee commercial performance. For advertisers allocating budgets, it says the practical challenge is to separate savings in content production from results in the marketplace. It concludes that AI can change how an ad is made, while whether audiences believe it and whether it produces worthwhile business outcomes remain separate questions.

Articles.Title: Advertisers weigh AI cost savings against consumer skepticism

stories.Headline: Rhys Williams on the AI Boom, Health Care and Energy
stories.Summary:
Rhys Williams, chief investment officer at Wayve Capital Management, spoke with Phil Rosen on Full Signal in an interview published on November 4, 2026. He said the current AI boom is not a repeat of the 1999 dot-com bubble. He pointed out that Cisco traded at about 120 times earnings in 1999, when the 10-year Treasury yield ended the year above 6%, while Nvidia now trades at about 15 to 16 times earnings and Micron at about six times. He said sentiment is awful even though fundamentals are very strong, and he blamed political backlash against data centers, saying power and water concerns have largely been addressed.

Williams laid out a barbell strategy for 2027 that pairs AI infrastructure stocks with health care and energy. In health care, he named Ligand Pharmaceuticals and Eton Pharmaceuticals as smaller companies with a lot of shots on goal, and said he would inch into Ligand after its run rather than take a full position. He called Takeda, the large Japanese drugmaker, a value pick that pays a nice dividend and a good sleep at night stock. In energy, he named Exxon and Chevron as the conservative way to play rising oil prices if the wars involving Russia and Iran drag on, and he also likes refiner Phillips 66 because diesel and jet fuel prices are high, along with the Alerian MLP ETF, whose dividend he put at around 7%.

On AI stocks, Williams said Astera Labs gets about 75% of its business from Amazon, which he said makes it nearly a pure play on AWS, and he called Amazon the less risky way to play that trend while Astera may offer more upside. He flagged one risk: whether Astera keeps its content in Amazon's Trainium 4 chip, which he said arrives at the end of 2027. He also said he was impressed by how little cash Anthropic has used, based on its S-1, which showed $131.6 billion in cash and short-term investments as of June 30, after the company raised $141.1 billion. He compared today to the internet era, when the semiconductor index rose 850% from 1994 to 2000 despite two 50% corrections, and said he doesn't see cracks like the December 1999 order cut at Broadcom now, calling this just a buying opportunity. His base case is no recession, and he thinks health care will be a big winner.

Separately, Adipec opened on Monday in Abu Dhabi, and The National published an editorial on November 2, 2026, saying AI is transforming the energy industry while its growing appetite for electricity demands urgent attention. The four-day gathering, held annually in Abu Dhabi since 1984, has 2,260 exhibitors, 181,000 pre-registered visitors, 40 government ministers and 12,000 conference delegates. Research jointly conducted by Adnoc, XRG and Microsoft shows that 62% of surveyed energy leaders now rank the technology among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42% last year, and almost nine in 10 increased spending on it, while 63% expect returns on existing investments to cover or exceed costs. According to the survey, nearly three quarters of respondents expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030, while only 52% believe existing infrastructure can meet the additional demand, and a separate Adipec survey found that 81% of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts. The editorial said ramping up energy production can only partially meet this surging demand, and that investment must be made to modernise grids, expand storage and accelerate cleaner generation, too.

Articles.Title: Rhys Williams on the AI Boom, Health Care and Energy

stories.Headline: Pittsburgh experts weigh in on who is responsible when AI makes medical mistakes
stories.Summary:
The article is a Pittsburgh discussion of who is responsible when AI makes medical mistakes, published on November 4, 2026. It does not name any patient, doctor, hospital or company involved in a specific incident. It also gives no date or place for any particular error. The piece is about the question of responsibility in general, not about one event.

The article does not list any new rule, law or requirement that would change how AI is used in medicine. It gives no numbers on how often AI makes mistakes or how many cases exist. It names no regulator or agency taking action. The only date it gives is its own publication date.

The article says Pittsburgh experts weighed in on the responsibility question. It does not name those experts or say what each of them said. It does not quote anyone directly. Because of that, there is no way to say who is responsible or what they said, beyond the fact that the experts discussed it.

The article does not describe the wider context or say what happens next. It carries no information on upcoming hearings, lawsuits or policy changes. It also does not say whether any of the experts called for new rules. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bloom Energy Sinks 8%, Lumentum Down 11% as AI Power Stocks Fade After Democrat Sweep
stories.Summary:
Bloom Energy shares fell 8% on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after Democrats swept the elections held the day before. The drop gave back part of the stock's gain from a Barclays upgrade on Tuesday. Lumentum fell 11% with no news of its own, and MARA Holdings dropped 4% along with other bitcoin miners. The contractors Quanta Services fell 13% and Comfort Systems USA fell 17%.

The wider selling followed reports that tied the slide to the risk of tighter rules on AI infrastructure. Keefe Bruyette downgraded two bitcoin mining peers after Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat Greg Abbott in Texas. Quanta's backlog reached a record $63.7 billion at September 30, and Comfort Systems' backlog nearly doubled in a year, from $9.38 billion to $17.81 billion. Both companies reported before the vote, so their fourth-quarter reports will show whether customers start pausing.

Analysts expect Bloom's normalized earnings per share to rise from $0.76 in 2025 to $8.24 in 2028. Customer deposits were $661.4 million at September 30, up from $78.2 million at the end of 2025. Bloom trades at roughly 40 times forward earnings, below the 76 times it averaged over the past three years. Its free cash flow was negative $180.6 million in the third quarter.

The article's author, Bobby Sankhagowit, called the drop an overreaction, since Bloom fell with the group on no news of its own while estimates and deposits keep rising. He wrote that an election does not cancel anyone's order. He also noted that if a Democratic Congress tightens rules on data centers, every campus slows down, Bloom's included. Bloom's fourth-quarter report in early 2027 will show whether orders held up.

Articles.Title: Bloom Energy Sinks 8%, Lumentum Down 11% as AI Power Stocks Fade After Democrat Sweep

stories.Headline: The Security Companies Trying to Get AI Agents Under Control
stories.Summary:
The Information published a story on November 4, 2026 about security companies trying to get AI agents under control. The article is an exclusive from theinformation.com.
