stories.Headline: UK agency alleges China AI cyberattack threat; expert views move to keep attack edge, deny deterrence
stories.Summary:
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre, part of the GCHQ spy agency, published its annual review on Tuesday, 3 November 2026. The report claimed that AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. It also alleged that China is best placed to launch AI-powered cyberattacks on Britain. The Guardian reported that the UK's definition of critical national infrastructure covers sectors including energy, transport, defense, food, health and finance.

The report alleged that countries including China will start using AI routinely in cyberattacks, according to the Guardian. The Independent claimed that Chinese cyber activity is the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK. The articles give no further details of what the report requires or changes. They also note that the UK sanctioned two China-based companies in December 2025 over alleged cyberattacks.

Xiao Xinguang, chief software architect at the Chinese cybersecurity company Antiy, said the UK's mudslinging against China is merely grandstanding. He told the Global Times that professionals know it is Western countries, not China, that have pushed hardest to weaponize super intelligent AI. He said Western institutions first identified these capabilities themselves and then slung mud at China, which he called logically incoherent. He added that their aim is to keep Western capacity to launch AI attacks while denying targeted countries the right to build deterrent and countermeasure capabilities.

The articles cite the Financial Times reporting in June that Anthropic is helping the US National Security Agency deploy its Mythos AI model for offensive cyber operations. Reuters reported in August that the UK's AI Security Institute caught an AI agent creating fake online identities to gain unauthorized access during tests of models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China stands against hacking and fights such activities in accordance with the law. He said China strongly rejects the UK's political manipulation under the pretext of cybersecurity and has lodged serious protests in Beijing and London.

Articles.Title: UK agency alleges China AI cyberattack threat; expert views move to keep attack edge, deny deterrence - Global Times

stories.Headline: Not buying lipsticks but tokens? A top Chinese commercial livestreamer sells 2 trillion AI units in 30 minutes on Monday
stories.Summary:
On Monday night, Chinese livestreaming e-commerce influencer Li Jiaqi, known as China's "Lipstick King," sold tokens during his show for the Double 11 shopping festival. He hosted the livestream with Chen Yusen, Vice President of Alibaba Group and CEO of QwenWork. Within half an hour, they sold 100,000 monthly personal membership cards for QwenWork, equivalent to about 2 trillion tokens, according to the Global Times. The article describes this as the first time a top Chinese livestreamer has sold AI computing power as merchandise.

A token is the unit used to measure how much information a large AI model processes and generates, so buyers are essentially purchasing a quota for model calls. The monthly personal membership was offered at 0.01 yuan and gives unlimited use in standard mode for office tasks such as document writing, data processing and making PowerPoint presentations. Li and Chen also demonstrated live how AI agents can cover office work, daily life, education and entertainment. Li shared how his livestream business uses AI and big data to generate shopping rankings in real time.

Li and Chen are the people named in the articles as running the sale. The articles do not include direct statements from them beyond the demonstration and the description of the membership card. The articles say the livestream chat filled with comments such as "3-2-1, drop the tokens!" as netizens chased the comments.

The listing comes as competition among AI model developers grows intense. Major e-commerce platforms like Tmall and JD.com have rolled out sales entries for tokens, with Zhipu, MiniMax, Alibaba Cloud Bailian, QwenWork, Moonshot and StepFun among the vendors that have settled on the platform. According to data Alibaba sent to the Global Times, on October 20, the first day of Double 11 early sales, Taobao's token category gross merchandise volume jumped 450 percent from a month earlier. After Zhipu opened an official flagship store on Tmall, brand searches rose 50 times within 48 hours, and sales of AI token subscription products climbed more than 160 percent month on month.

Articles.Title: Not buying lipsticks but tokens? A top Chinese commercial livestreamer sells 2 trillion AI units in 30 minutes on Monday - Global Times

stories.Headline: Smart healthcare, transformed into wearable AI devices, moves into daily life at 140th Canton Fair
stories.Summary:
The 140th Canton Fair opened its third phase on Saturday in Guangzhou under the theme "Better Life," and its smart healthcare zone drew attention for devices moving from hospitals into daily life. The zone has 46 exhibitors across 168 booths. At the fair, a staffer walked down a simulated slope on a carbon-fiber bionic lower-leg prosthesis made by Zhejiang Zeanso Technology. Li Zhe, the company's general manager, said the knee senses the thigh's posture in real time and locks the joint when it detects a stumbling risk.

Li said the prosthesis weighs about 1,350 grams and offers roughly 60 hours of use on a four-hour charge, and that stumble recovery is completed within 20 milliseconds. He said the product is already sold in Europe, the Americas and Asia. Zhejiang-based Fubao Robot showed an AI mental-health booth called "happy cabin," where a Mexican buyer sat facing a camera for 30 seconds and got an assessment about 15 seconds later. Mei Chao, a vice president at Fubao Robot, said the cabin combines a multimodal AI mental-health model, voice interaction and micro-expression recognition, and is mainly designed for campus screening.

Guangzhou Retion International showed a CPR training robot that guides users with voice prompts, screen demonstrations and motion correction. Kong Xiangna, a manager at Retion, said its AI CPR evaluation system, described as a world first, analyzes performance videos and gives instant feedback. Hangzhou-based Deep Informatics showed the DPS 750 digital pathology scanner, which loads 750 slides at once and supports 24-hour unattended batch scanning. Deng Lusha, an AI solution manager at the company, said this can shorten waits for pathology reports at large hospitals.

Other products included a "magic mirror" that generates a skin-age report from a 30-second facial video and a contactless electrocardiogram machine using millimeter-wave radar and AI. A suitcase-sized portable bath machine weighing seven kilograms can handle washing, showering and hair-washing in bed. China's smart wearable health device market stands at about 82.6 billion yuan, or $12.4 billion, according to an industry report. In January, China's National Healthcare Security Administration launched pilot programs for a "personal medical insurance cloud" designed to connect data from wearables and home monitoring devices into individual health records.

Articles.Title: Smart healthcare, transformed into wearable AI devices, moves into daily life at 140th Canton Fair - Global Times

stories.Headline: AI-generated pet videos win over young Chinese viewers
stories.Summary:
AI-generated pet videos have become popular on Chinese social media platforms including Douyin, Xiaohongshu and Bilibili. On Douyin, some pet-themed videos have attracted hundreds of thousands of likes. The videos show cats running street stalls, cooking meals, traveling with friends and going to work. One creator, known on Douyin as "Orange Cat Pang Dundun," began making AI cat videos in June 2025.

The creator is 29 years old and is based in Shandong Province in East China. Her Douyin account has attracted around 154,000 followers, and her videos have received more than 60 million likes in total. She first made cartoon-style videos and later shifted to a more realistic vlog format. She chose orange cats for their broad appeal and chubby, endearing appearance, which suited the food, travel and leisure themes of her videos.

The creator said the theme of her videos is friendship and the interactions between close friends. She said viewers can enjoy the cute and healing aspects of cats while also seeing something of themselves in the characters. She described AI pets as a kind of "cyber immortality," through which owners can imagine their beloved animals living happily after they are gone. Wang Tong of Beijing, who has cats, told the Global Times that she knows the AI pets are fake but finds them cute and watches them every day.

Bu Xiting, an associate research fellow at the Communication University of China, said using AI products for emotional companionship is likely to become increasingly common. He said excessive reliance on virtual pets could make it harder for people to cope with real-world relationships or develop a sense of responsibility. He said AI should supplement human emotions, not replace them, and called on creators to consider their influence on younger audiences. The creator said tools are just a medium and that building an IP, designing stories and coming up with creative ideas matter most.

Articles.Title: AI-generated pet videos win over young Chinese viewers - Global Times

stories.Headline: South Korea’s dream of AI autonomy lays bare contradiction within the alliance with the US
stories.Summary:
South Korea's President Lee Jae-myung plans to build a major semiconductor cluster in southwestern South Korea, part of what the article describes as a $1 trillion chip bet. The United States wants more of Seoul's AI expansion to happen on American soil, according to media reports cited by Global Times. The article says the two countries disagree not on whether to develop semiconductors but on who will control advanced manufacturing and share the benefits of the AI era. Samsung has already built an advanced foundry in Texas, and SK Hynix is investing in a high-bandwidth memory packaging fab in Indiana.

The article says Washington wants South Korean companies to move more capital, technology and production capacity to the US to support manufacturing reshoring and supply-chain localization. It also says the US has not adequately resolved problems involving skilled technical personnel and cross-border labor. In September 2025, US law enforcement detained more than 300 South Korean nationals at a Korean-invested factory project in Georgia, which the article says shocked South Korean society. South Korea wants to keep more of the technological, financial and employment benefits of AI development at home rather than relying only on chip exports to the US.

The article says the Gwangju project shows the tension, because South Korea plans to relocate an existing military airfield tied to joint US-South Korean operations and build the cluster on the vacated land. It says the US military is still carrying out construction at the airfield, so Seoul cannot fully set the timetable alone. The article states there is currently insufficient evidence to conclude that Washington is deliberately using the relocation to obstruct South Korea's chip development. It adds that the US AI industry remains highly dependent on advanced memory chips from Samsung and SK Hynix, which cannot be fully replaced in the short term.

The article says the two countries are more likely to keep adjusting the distribution of benefits through cooperation and competition than to enter outright confrontation. It says South Korea's fundamental dilemma remains unresolved, since greater investment in the US may ease trade pressure but does not necessarily secure greater strategic autonomy. The author is the director and professor of the Center for Korean Peninsula Studies at the Shanghai University of International Business and Economics. The article does not say what specific next steps either government will take.

Articles.Title: South Korea’s dream of AI autonomy lays bare contradiction within the alliance with the US - Global Times

stories.Headline: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
stories.Summary:
OpenAI launched Image 2.0 earlier this year, and the model surprised many people by producing well-designed documents with long passages of text in multiple languages while keeping a high degree of accuracy. The work was not as good as that of professional type designers, but for a layperson making a poster or a brochure it was just fine. Before this, AI-generated fonts and layouts had always looked clunky, inconsistent or error-ridden, and designers had hoped AI would never replace them. The article, by Liu Yuli and published by Sixth Tone on Nov 2, 2026, says typography had been the last stronghold of graphic design still firmly controlled by professional designers.

Chinese typeface design has always been extremely labor-intensive because of the huge number of characters. Studies show 3,500 characters account for 99.5% of character usage, but the industry often sets 7,000 characters as the target size for a typeface, and some larger projects cover 27,000 or even 87,000 characters. Advertisers who need to print a 20-character slogan may have to buy a license for a typeface containing 7,000 characters, and many users are reluctant to pay type foundries. Chinese printers largely stuck with carving entire texts onto woodblocks for centuries, and only gigantic projects such as state-backed archives used movable-type printing.

Chinese type foundries have used internal AI tools to assist typeface production for years. Traditionally a lead designer creates several hundred characters to set the design direction, and a team produces the remaining thousands along those lines, but an AI model can learn the style from those characters and apply it to others, with human adjustment increasing productivity. Since the early 2020s, open-source AI tools have let independent designers produce usable typefaces on their own, and designer Wang Tingrui has used AI tools to develop typefaces reminiscent of classic lead-type printing. The article says AI could expand a design concept across thousands of additional characters, making the long tail of less common characters far less of a burden.

The article says AI may also help with new Chinese characters, which are mostly made by combining components, as Chinese chemists did in the 19th century when naming newly discovered elements. Traditional typeface design records whole characters rather than components, so new characters would not appear in existing typefaces, but AI should allow users to render new characters in the style of an existing typeface. Leading models including Qwen, Seedream, ChatGPT and DALL-E are moving toward generating text directly onto posters, videos and Douyin cover images in a style the user specifies, bypassing typefaces entirely. The article notes problems with inconsistency and copyright, and says professionals will no longer monopolize the creation of stylistic Chinese characters but will keep pushing the boundaries of design as gatekeepers of taste and judgment.

Articles.Title: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography - Sixth Tone

stories.Headline: Meituan Unveils New AI Model Trained on Homegrown Chips
stories.Summary:
Meituan unveiled a new artificial intelligence model called LongCat-2.5 on Monday, November 3, 2026, according to Caixin Global. The on-demand service giant said the model was trained entirely on homegrown chips. It is a native multimodal model trained with 1.6 trillion parameters. Meituan plans to use it to improve efficiency across its core businesses.

The model is designed to handle long-range agent tasks and supports merchant-focused work such as commercial analysis and software development. Benchmark scores place LongCat-2.5 between Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5, though a developer described the real-world experience as average. Meituan's research and development spending rose 22.5% year on year to 7.7 billion yuan, or about $1.1 billion, in the second quarter of 2026. The company aims its AI at merchant tools rather than selling raw computing power.

CEO Wang Xing said Meituan prioritizes using AI to strengthen its core business instead of selling computing power, according to the article. The report says Meituan's launch shows Chinese tech companies increasingly relying on homegrown chips to advance AI despite hardware limits. It also points to a strategic focus on making money from AI through existing business ecosystems. Other firms are making similar moves, with iFlytek testing domestic chips for model training and Z.AI partly running a 1-gigawatt data center on domestically made chips.

A separate article in The Hindu examines privacy risks in AI training. It says the Supreme Court upheld the right to privacy in 2017, but current legal tools seem inadequate. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023, and its rules were notified in November 2025, with some consent and safety provisions taking effect only in 2027. Before that law, the Information Technology Act of 2000 and its 2011 rules governed personal data, capping penalties for unauthorized disclosure at three years' imprisonment or a fine of 5 lakh rupees.

Articles.Title: Meituan Unveils New AI Model Trained on Homegrown Chips - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack
stories.Summary:
A 3AM ransomware affiliate attacked a school estate in the UK, then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools, according to research Bitdefender published on November 3, 2026. The attackers stole backup credentials, created rogue domain-admin accounts, established trusts between previously separate Active Directory domains, moved between schools, stole data, and deployed 3AM ransomware. Bitdefender said the attack did not fit neatly into existing buckets for AI-generated, AI-assisted, or AI-operated attacks. Instead, the vendor argued that an AI system appeared to handle repetitive command generation and troubleshooting while a human operator made high-level decisions.

Bitdefender pointed to signs of an agentic loop, the control structure that makes an AI agent work. The commands showed a call to the Veeam backup software web interface on a port and with a login method that did not match the vendor's documentation, along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script. The time between PowerShell command attempts was shorter than a human would take by hand but longer than an LLM working alone, and even the quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. Bitdefender said it could not access the machine the attacker worked from, so it could not document anything tangible involving the AI model itself.

Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, told Dark Reading that a hybrid model is more reasonable for financially motivated cybercriminals, technically and economically, than a fully autonomous attack. He said an agentic loop does not make an attack quiet but makes it repetitive, with the same command re-run, small tweaks, numbered scripts and probe files left on disk. He added that speed is not the giveaway and repetition is. The vendor recommended keeping admin credentials of different domains separate, treating backups as a possible target, restricting remote execution and administrative shares to known management hosts, blocking interpreters and shells on machines that never use them, and putting endpoint security tooling on every machine.

Bitdefender said the attack largely followed a familiar ransomware playbook, so the defender recommendations that stop regular ransomware would also stop it. The report stops short of showing AI-enabled capabilities the attacker otherwise lacked, though it suggests the affiliate may have used an AI agent to scale the attack by handling repetitive troubleshooting and command generation. The research noted that from a domain controller the attacker enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL for the names and subnets of other schools. The vendor said defenders should prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed, because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth.

Articles.Title: 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: NATO’s Crossed Swords Exercise Brings AI Agents Into Cyber Operations Training
stories.Summary:
NATO’s Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence began Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, on Monday, and the exercise’s execution phase is set to run through Friday. More than 250 people from over 40 countries, including both NATO members and non-members, are taking part. Participants include military cyber operators, threat hunters and digital forensics experts from national cyber forces and the units that support them. The drill is also tied into a training event for special operations forces.

The exercise practices planning cyber operations and timing them with kinetic military action, at both the command level and the hands-on tactical level. New this year is a dedicated track on AI agents, in which participants build, deploy and assess agents and work alongside them. The environment runs on locally hosted AI and, for the first time at Crossed Swords, also uses OpenAI’s Daybreak cyber defense offering. Over 20 organizations from industry, academia and the NGO sector support the event, among them Bitdefender, ESET, Elastic, Mandiant, OpenAI, Stamus Networks, TryHackMe and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Exercise Director Jozef Kostelansky said the core operational challenge being tested is synchronisation. He said cyber effects must hit at the right moment to support a kinetic or special operations action, in sequence rather than in parallel, with timing measured in minutes and not hours. He said this year that gets harder because AI is now in the loop on both sides. He also said that by bringing AI agents into the operational workflow, the exercise addresses a major shift in the cyber threat landscape, and that participants are trained to use AI while keeping the human oversight complex missions require.

Crossed Swords traces its roots to a 2014 red teaming workshop and has since expanded to include command-level training and combined cyber and kinetic operations. Participation has roughly doubled since 2022, when around 120 people from 24 countries took part, and last year’s edition had 240 participants from about 40 nations. The drill also pairs national cyber forces with civilian partners so that critical infrastructure protection is built into their plans. The CCDCOE’s larger Locked Shields exercise involved more than 4,000 participants from 41 nations in 2026.

Articles.Title: NATO’s Crossed Swords Exercise Brings AI Agents Into Cyber Operations Training - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: NTT to help Japanese companies update at-risk aging IT with AI
stories.Summary:
NTT will offer a service that uses artificial intelligence to modernize corporate IT systems, Nikkei has learned. The company aims to help the roughly 60% of Japanese businesses that still rely on aging technology. The report was published by Nikkei Asia on November 4, 2026, with a dateline of Tokyo. The article was written by Natsuki Yamamoto, Kosuke Shimizu and Uta Tokuda.

The service is meant to improve cybersecurity for companies using obsolete software, which the article says leaves them vulnerable to cyberattacks. NTT will use AI to shorten development times on the new systems it builds by 40%. The article gives no other figures on pricing, availability or the number of companies expected to sign up. It also does not name any specific clients or partner firms.

NTT is the company responsible for the service, according to the report. The article does not include direct statements from NTT executives or other officials about the plan. It presents the 60% figure and the 40% time saving as what Nikkei has learned. No one else is named as taking part or commenting.

The context is that about 60% of Japanese companies are described as saddled with aging technology, which the article links to cybersecurity risk. The report does not say when the service will launch or what it will cost. It also does not say what happens next beyond NTT providing the service. No further steps or timelines are given in the article.

Articles.Title: NTT to help Japanese companies update at-risk aging IT with AI - Nikkei Asia

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Rises 7.16% as AI-Linked Stocks Advance at Close
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares rose 7.16% at the U.S. close on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as several AI-linked stocks advanced, TokenPost reported. Oracle gained 5.85%, Dell rose 3.98%, Advanced Micro Devices added 3.65% and onsemi advanced 3.55%. The Nasdaq rose 0.83% and the S&P 500 finished up 0.36%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.38%, while the VIX declined 1.51%.

The article gives no details on what caused the moves or what they change for any of the companies. It lists only the closing percentages for CoreWeave and the other AI-linked stocks. It also gives the closing levels for the three main indexes and the VIX. No figures beyond those percentages and no dates beyond the close are provided.

The report is by Enna Lee, who covers investing and digital-asset markets for TokenPost. The article carries no statements from CoreWeave or any other company named. It also includes no comment from officials or analysts on the day's trading. TokenPost lists a contact address for corrections and tips.

The piece is a short market report of about one minute's reading, published on November 3, 2026, at 8:08 PM EST. It describes the session as one in which AI-linked stocks advanced while the Dow declined. It does not say what happens next for CoreWeave or the wider market. No further context on the moves is given.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave Rises 7.16% as AI-Linked Stocks Advance at Close - www.tokenpost.com

stories.Headline: A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission.
stories.Summary:
A developer opened Postman on November 3, 2026, and two AI coding agents changed without their permission, according to The New Stack. The article was written by Amanda Caswell and published at 06:00:00Z that day. The story is labeled under AI Agents, Developer tools and Security. The articles do not name the developer or the two agents. The articles give no further numbers, dates or names about the incident.

They do not say what the agents changed or what the change requires. They do not describe any fix, patch or update tied to the event. The articles also do not say whether the developer reported the change to anyone. The articles do not say who is responsible for the change. They do not include any statement from the developer, the agents' makers or anyone else.

No one is quoted saying anything about what happened. The articles give no explanation for why the agents acted. The articles give no context beyond the headline and the section labels. They do not say what happens next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission. - The New Stack

stories.Headline: MathWorks R2026b adds AI tools for engineering teams
stories.Summary:
MathWorks released R2026b of MATLAB and Simulink on 3 November 2026, adding new products and expanding existing tools. The release introduces Simulink Variant Manager, Visual Inspection Toolbox and Polyspace Test Server. It also extends capabilities across aerospace, embedded software, artificial intelligence, perception, audio engineering and statistical analysis. The changes are aimed at engineering teams working on systems that combine software, electronics and AI.

Simulink Variant Manager is designed to help developers manage multiple product configurations across models and system architectures. Visual Inspection Toolbox combines AI and image-processing methods for visual inspection in manufacturing and industrial settings. MathWorks also added Point Cloud Toolbox to broaden workflows for lidar, camera, radar and SLAM-based applications. For embedded software teams, Polyspace Test Server focuses on automated testing and code coverage analysis for C and C++ software in continuous integration environments.

In MATLAB, the changes cover project management, source-control workflows, interoperability and data access, including TOML-based project files, package management through File Exchange and Google Sheets integration. In Simulink, MathWorks added published models that can be reused without rebuilding, JSON-based data dictionaries and AI-assisted profiling insights through Simulink Copilot. Aerospace Toolbox now supports high-fidelity orbit propagation, manoeuvre modelling, constellation design and lunar mission work. Deep Learning Toolbox now includes a Time Series Modeler app and support for co-execution of PyTorch models in MATLAB and Simulink.

MathWorks, founded in 1984 and based in Natick, Massachusetts, employs more than 6,500 people across 34 offices worldwide. Avinash Nehemiah, Head of Product Management and Marketing for Design Automation at MathWorks, said engineering organisations are being challenged to deliver sophisticated products that blend software, AI, electronics and connected systems while maintaining quality, compliance and development speed. He said R2026b helps teams connect design, simulation, testing and deployment workflows so they can spend less time managing complexity and move from concept to production more quickly. The release reflects a wider push by software suppliers to support engineering teams working across mechanical systems, software development, electronics and AI in a single workflow.

Articles.Title: MathWorks R2026b adds AI tools for engineering teams - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Australian energy retailers turn to AI to cut costs
stories.Summary:
Australian energy retailers are increasing their use of artificial intelligence and automation in customer service as the sector faces pressure to cut costs and compete more aggressively on price, according to an article published by IT Brief Australia on 4 November 2026. Richard Valente, Vice President of Customer Experience Strategy at TP in Australia, said energy companies were moving faster on AI than other industries because of pressure from governments and consumers to reduce costs. He said the central question for retailers was what customers were prepared to trade off in return for a cheaper energy deal. Households have faced higher electricity costs despite falls in regulated prices, as retailers lifted daily usage and supply charges in response to higher underlying costs, which has sharpened the focus on operating expenses including call centres and customer support. Valente said retailers were looking at automation to lower the cost to serve without removing access to human help when customers need it most.

Routine billing queries and simple requests can be handled more quickly by automated systems, while more difficult cases can be directed to trained staff. Across TP's energy and utilities operations, 82% of supported interactions take place through voice channels, with 16% handled through back-office channels and 2% through social media assistance. Valente said there was little sign that customer service in the sector would become entirely digital, and in his view the more likely model is a blended system in which automated tools manage simple, repeatable tasks and staff focus on interactions that require judgement or empathy. Valente said reducing the cost of operations can give retailers greater flexibility to compete on price and potentially pass those efficiencies on to consumers, but customers shouldn't have to choose between a cheap energy plan and a good customer experience. He said customers will accept speed and automation for a straightforward problem, but expect a person to step in when an issue becomes complex.

He also said retailers were assessing hybrid workforce models that combine Australian-based teams with offshore or nearshore operations, matching the level of support to the complexity of the task. He said the choice doesn't have to be between a person or a machine, and that the best customer experience is likely to be both. As competition in the Australian energy market intensifies, retailers are likely to face closer scrutiny over the economics of the entire customer journey, from billing and onboarding to complaints and account changes. Pressure to offer lower prices without undermining service standards means back-office efficiency and frontline support models are becoming a more significant part of retail strategy. Valente said retailers are seeing that they can use AI to remove unnecessary costs and make everyday interactions easier, and everyone can benefit.

Articles.Title: Australian energy retailers turn to AI to cut costs - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Snowflake adds always-on AI bots for CoCo & CoWork
stories.Summary:
Snowflake introduced new features for its CoCo and CoWork AI agents, adding always-on bots that can carry out recurring tasks in the background, IT Brief Australia reported on 4 November 2026. CoCo is Snowflake's coding agent for data teams, while CoWork is aimed at knowledge workers. The bots can operate continuously, use a customer's existing permissions and role settings, and seek approval only when a decision or sign-off is required. Snowflake is also adding automation so teams can schedule repeated workflows, including automated CoCo runs with an audit trail and task history, and CoWork scheduling for recurring analysis and reports.

The tools will work across software employees already use, including Slack, Excel, Sheets and mobile devices. Snowflake is introducing an asynchronous application programming interface for CoWork so longer, multi-step tasks can continue in the background and resume if interrupted. Usage figures released by Snowflake show CoWork is used by more than 5,800 accounts and CoCo by more than 9,100, and the company said it serves more than 14,500 enterprise customers globally. Users will be able to share workflows and plug-ins across organisations, set role-based profiles, and use memory functions that retain previous context and decisions while allowing teams to review or delete stored information.

Christian Kleinerman, Executive Vice President of Product at Snowflake, said the wider issue for businesses is whether AI agents have enough access to reliable internal context to avoid confident but inaccurate answers. He said agents that guess differ from agents that know because of data, and that Snowflake already holds the data, context and governance controls enterprises run on. Snowflake pointed to Cisco, Docusign and United Rentals as customers using the software for data migration, account research and operational analysis. Srini Namineni, Senior Vice President and Chief Automation Officer at Cisco, said its customer experience teams use specialised agents built in Snowflake to identify upsell and renewal opportunities, while CoCo helps engineers migrate core corporate data and convert legacy code.

Bala Sahejpal, Chief Data Officer at Docusign, said CoCo and CoWork have cut the data team's time to deliver value dramatically and power its conversational data agents, letting go-to-market teams research accounts without SQL expertise. Tony Leopold, Senior Vice President and Chief Technology and Strategy Officer at United Rentals, said work that once took days can now be done in minutes using natural language. Snowflake said it is bringing in the Mora team to strengthen business intelligence features, and it is launching an AI data package with more than 60 curated industry datasets, semantic views and a ready-to-use CoWork agent. New model routing options for CoCo will let teams assign simpler background jobs to lighter models and reserve advanced reasoning models for harder tasks, and Cortex Training lets organisations tailor open-weight models to their own data inside Snowflake's environment.

Articles.Title: Snowflake adds always-on AI bots for CoCo & CoWork - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: AI success takes more than a promising pilot project
stories.Summary:
Thoughtworks CIO Jessie Xia said organisations are launching AI projects faster than ever, but governance is lagging behind. She said the nature of AI lets it move faster than earlier technologies, and that about 88 percent of AI adoption is happening faster than a governance structure can keep up. She explained that AI is more distributed than other technologies, with security, data, legal and risk teams all involved in decisions, and many organisations lack clear decision-making arrangements. Xia said many organisations put policies on paper but need to build them into architecture and process controls, with traceability and clear accountabilities.

Xia said moving from a trial to production is a challenge even with good governance, and the typical obstacles are security, data quality and integration with existing systems. She said a business department may build something quickly but then struggle to reach production, and a Thoughtworks survey found about a third of respondents reported data quality and integration as issues. She said a pilot can work in controlled settings, but integrating with other systems in large organisations requires looking at how new applications fit the current infrastructure. She also said ROI and ownership economics need careful consideration, and Thoughtworks has a Chief AI Officer on its leadership team to coordinate software development, governance, infrastructure and security.

Xia said AI literacy will become increasingly important, but critical thinking and judgement will become more valuable as people's roles change. She said people will need to challenge what AI is doing, check for biased responses and define how AI and humans should interact. She said Australian organisations are doing well but most show qualified maturity on AI governance, with 55 percent embedding dedicated technology leads in business units, 48 percent establishing formal AI governance and operating models, and 38 percent standardising software and digital transformation across business units. Her advice was to establish clear accountability before scaling, put identity, data access, monitoring and traceability into systems and automate them where possible, and measure value while investing in workforce capability.

Separately, Siemens CEO Roland Busch and Naver CEO Choi Soo-yeon spoke at APK 2026 in Seoul on Saturday, urging companies to move beyond AI pilot projects toward measurable productivity gains. Choi said businesses must first organise information scattered across paper records, employee computers and departmental systems into formats AI can use, and ensure it is accurate, up to date and accessible. She said generating reports with AI does not automatically raise productivity, and companies should measure whether it reduces waiting times, improves efficiency or removes repetitive tasks. Busch said adoption has to come from the top, and cited a Japanese automaker that deployed Siemens technology across 10,000 machines with a payback period of less than three months.

Choi highlighted Naver's experience running more than 200 delivery robots at its 1784 headquarters for over four years, showing the challenges of reliable AI services in spaces shared with people. In an audience poll, 41 percent of respondents named data sharing and interoperability as the biggest barrier to scaling industrial AI across regions. Busch called for clear data-sharing policies and specialised expertise, noting customer data could train industrial AI models without leaving company premises. Busch warned that repetitive, rules-based jobs would face displacement and called for reforms in education and workforce training, while Choi said Naver keeps hiring each year but would need new business models to offset rising AI costs.

Articles.Title: AI success takes more than a promising pilot project - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Snowflake launches free AI data training for users
stories.Summary:
Snowflake launched a free foundational training course called Snowflake Practitioner for its customers and partners worldwide, the company announced. The programme is offered in instructor-led and on-demand formats, including public and private live sessions and a self-paced version. It is built around a two-day curriculum, and learners get 30 days of access to hands-on labs. The course is organised around three user groups: Data Analysts, Data Engineers and Platform Administrators.

Each group starts with a shared lecture before moving into role-specific labs. The labs cover querying, reporting and visualisation for analysts, pipelines, data loading and transformation for engineers, and security, roles, access control, cost management and monitoring for administrators. The course also includes Snowflake CoCo, the company's coding agent for data teams, in all three tracks. After the foundational course, users can go on to more specialised role-based learning, and SnowPro Certification is a further step, though exam fees still apply.

Denise Persson, Chief Marketing Officer at Snowflake, said world-class platform education should be the starting point for every customer and partner relationship. She said the course reflects the company's commitment to democratising AI fluency by making essential training accessible from day one. She added that opening access to foundational data and AI skills creates a shared language for the agentic enterprise, helping organisations move faster from insight to action. Snowflake said its broader education programmes have already reached hundreds of thousands of learners globally.

Snowflake said the training follows a model of learning together and applying separately, with mixed groups receiving common instruction before splitting into role-based sessions. The company presented the programme as part of its response to a wider skills shortage in AI and data work, and said it could help organisations standardise baseline knowledge as data platforms spread beyond specialist staff. Swedbank is among the organisations cited as already using the training. Jelena Korotõtš, Data and Platform Engineering Lead at Swedbank, said the course delivered immediate, role-tailored fluency and that regular sessions have been scheduled through 2027.

Articles.Title: Snowflake launches free AI data training for users - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Appliers.ai acquires Prevail to boost enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
Appliers.ai, a Melbourne-based company, has acquired the AI strategy and platform specialist Prevail. The deal was announced on 4 November 2026, and the terms were not disclosed. Pete Gatt, who founded Prevail, has joined Appliers.ai's founding team as Chief Technology Officer, and Ben Ashby has been appointed Chief Solutions Officer. Prevail's entire team will move to Appliers.ai, and the two businesses say they have together worked with more than 600 companies.

The acquisition does not include Emanda Ventures or the Emanda app, which were specifically excluded from the transaction. Appliers.ai said the deal builds on a shared approach centred on business strategy and technology delivery. The buyer has also expanded through partnerships, becoming EOS Worldwide's global AI Transformation Partner. The deal comes as AI companies globally use acquisitions to expand, with Crunchbase counting 195 AI startup deals by venture-backed companies to the end of September, 14% higher than the total for all of 2025. Figures cited by Appliers.ai show 12% of Australian businesses use AI.

Rob Pisano, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Appliers.ai, led the transaction and said the rationale was clear, describing the fit as written in the stars and saying clients would get platforms built faster with decades of enterprise experience behind every build. David Comande, Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer, said the two teams lined up on values and direction from the first conversation. Gatt said he and Pisano had moved in the same corporate circles for years and the fit was obvious, and that joining Appliers.ai gives Prevail's approach more scale. Ashby said every good build starts with how a business really works and that clients now get a bigger team behind them.

Gatt founded Vibrato, an early Australian cloud and DevOps consultancy later acquired by Servian, now part of Cognizant, and has worked on model-agnostic large language model architecture for large organisations. Ashby has led product, technology and transformation teams across startups and large companies, including transformation programs for Telstra, Optus and Bunnings. Pisano is a five-time founder who previously helped scale a startup acquired by Salesforce. The deal reflects a broader shift in the AI services market, where companies are combining advisory work with software delivery to win larger transformation projects, and providers are increasingly expected to link AI systems to operating models, workflows and commercial outcomes.

Articles.Title: Appliers.ai acquires Prevail to boost enterprise AI - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: The AI literacy gap between Indian CEOs and their teams is hurting adoption - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Raj Goodman Anand, founder and director of AI-First Mindset, wrote in an ETCIO article published on November 3, 2026, that an AI literacy gap between Indian CEOs and their teams is slowing adoption. He based this on his workshops with owners and senior leaders of mid to large companies in India. He described the gap as running in both directions. Some CEOs ask for AI without having used it hands-on, while in other companies junior staff have used ChatGPT quietly for months while leadership assumes nothing has started.

Anand said the gap where the boss does not use AI does more damage, because teams read it as optional and adoption follows what leaders do rather than what they announce. He said leaders who hand AI to the IT head leave business decisions unmade, since IT can buy tools but cannot decide how sales writes proposals or how finance closes the month. He added that a CEO who cannot judge AI output cannot set a standard, and that middle managers often stay neutral, which is where adoption stalls. He also warned that teams hide their AI use, which starts shadow AI, and that under the DPDP Act an employee pasting customer details into a free tool can create exposure the company does not know about.

Anand said the fix starts with CEOs using AI on their own work, such as drafting emails, preparing board notes or reviewing contracts. He said leaders should then ask which processes can be redesigned and which tasks can be automated, and that a CEO does not need to become an AI engineer but must understand enough to lead adoption. He said the junior person using AI on the side is usually the company's best internal teacher and should be brought into the open rather than banned. He recommended a short policy of about one page naming approved tools and data that must never go into them, training leaders and staff together on the same tools, and asking each team head for one named task to be done differently within a month.

Anand said none of this is expensive and usually takes a few hours from a busy person, which is probably why it gets postponed. He said that when a company tells him its AI effort has stalled, the cause is rarely the budget or the choice of tool. More often, he said, the person at the top has not tried it yet and everyone below has noticed. The article carried a disclaimer that the views are solely the author's and that ETCIO does not necessarily subscribe to them.

Articles.Title: The AI literacy gap between Indian CEOs and their teams is hurting adoption - ET CIO

stories.Headline: The AI-First Employee is Not What You Think
stories.Summary:
Mastech has launched an internal program called the Autonomous Enterprise initiative, and the company says it has achieved 67% productivity gains from its AI-first operations. The company began by identifying areas where employees spend time on manual, repetitive and low-value activities, then rethought those processes using AI. AI agents now support work across Finance, HR, IT, Security and operations, with the aim of accelerating cycle times, reducing manual touchpoints and improving the employee experience. The article was published by Analytics India Magazine on 3 November 2026.

The initiative is meant to change how the organisation operates rather than treat AI as another technology rollout, and Mastech says it is using the lessons from its own transformation to help clients with their AI journeys. Kannan Sugantharaman, Chief Finance and Operations Officer, said credibility starts with practicing what you preach, and that the lessons learned internally are the same insights the company can bring to clients. Sandhya Ramesh, Chief People Officer, said the company looks for people with unlimited curiosity and the drive to experiment, innovate and help customers win with AI. She said they should have a mindset to build the organisation, technology, solutions and culture, and to reinvent themselves along the way.

Mastech is looking beyond AI specialists to technology experts, domain specialists, functional professionals and emerging talent, and its people strategy emphasises inclusion, collaboration and continuous learning. Debasis Satpathy, Chief Revenue Officer, said the next decade will reward value created and measured, and that engineers are becoming architects of decision systems while analysts are becoming designers of the logic those systems reason with. He said AI only amplifies the quality of the thinking behind it. The article says the IT services industry is entering a period in which access to skilled people and technology alone may no longer differentiate a company, and that customers increasingly want partners who can redesign work, apply AI to real business problems and deliver measurable outcomes.

The article says Mastech's customer-zero approach is an attempt to build that capability through its own transformation, testing AI across internal functions and carrying the lessons into customer engagements. It says autonomy does not mean removing people from every process, but determining which tasks AI can handle, where human judgement remains essential and how employees can focus on work that creates greater value. The article says the next generation of AI-first services companies will need to do more than deploy agents, and will have to rethink operations, develop employees who can build with AI and show the technology delivers outcomes beyond individual productivity. It says that for Mastech the transformation begins at home, with its own people and processes, before extending to the customers it helps to win with AI.

Articles.Title: The AI-First Employee is Not What You Think - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Coforge Is Outgrowing Its Larger Rivals. Is AI the Reason?
stories.Summary:
Coforge reported revenue of ₹6,170 crores for Q2 FY27, up 53.6% year on year, or 40.1% in dollar terms, according to its results reported in the article. The company completed its acquisition of digital engineering firm Encora on April 23, making Q2 its first full quarter with the business included. Of the 10.9% sequential growth in constant currency, 3.8% was organic and Encora supplied the rest. Coforge also reported order intake of $1.04 billion and raised its FY27 EBIT margin guidance to 16% from 15.5%. It signed eight large deals in the quarter, the most in its history, contributing almost $500 million of intake, and all eight came from existing clients.

The company says it is moving from selling engineering hours to selling outcomes. Its offerings include Nuuron, an enterprise autonomy suite, Momentuum Blue, a unit of forward-deployed engineers launched in July, and Mod Squads, hybrid pods launched in April in which agents do the work and humans approve key decisions. Coforge reports more than 520 AI engagements across more than 225 clients, with over 260 agents in live operations, but management gave no figures on the size and margin of those engagements when asked on the call. Its newest launch, an Autonomous Software Factory, comes with no disclosed customers or quantified gains. The repeat-business ratio stood at 95.5%, against 94% in Q3 FY26, and a second client has crossed an annualised run rate of $100 million.

CEO Sudhir Singh called the quarter a tipping point for AI adoption inside Coforge and tied the margin upgrade to AI, arguing it is breaking the link between scale and margin. CFO Saurabh Goel said Encora's revenue was largely flat, and that AI-led efficiencies in existing fixed-price contracts will show from Q4, with the uplift coming from those contracts rather than better pricing on future AI projects. Singh said most large deals are sole-sourced and driven by proactive solutioning, and that some deals pass part of the efficiency gain to the client and others do not. Yugal Joshi of Everest Group said AI is making modernisation and software development more accessible, a headwind for specialists, and that client-specific context will matter more.

Coforge's consolidated EBIT margin was 16% in Q2, matching Q1, and management expects 17% in Q4. General and administrative expenses fell to 6.3% of revenue from 6.6% in Q1. Rivals are adopting similar models: TCS is targeting up to 8,900 forward-deployed engineers and Infosys about 6,000, while HCLTech reported advanced AI revenue of $219 million and Infosys put AI at 10.5% of revenue. On margins Coforge trails, with HCLTech at 18.2% and Infosys at 21%. Anmol Garg of DAM Capital Advisors said AI-led deflation still exceeds the revenue AI brings in across Indian IT, and the article says Q4 will show whether Coforge keeps the value its AI capability creates.

Articles.Title: Coforge Is Outgrowing Its Larger Rivals. Is AI the Reason? - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Can India’s AI Boom Reach Bharat?
stories.Summary:
India’s push to become an AI-powered economy risks leaving students in smaller towns behind because they lack infrastructure and opportunities, according to an Analytics India Magazine report published on 3 November 2026. In Rajasthan’s Dholpur district, where nearly 97,000 students attend around 501 schools in the block, only about 68% of schools have internet connectivity and 53% have computers. The report says the challenge goes beyond getting students online and includes access to computers, reliable power, AI labs, trained teachers, industry mentors and hands-on projects. Dholpur already has some building blocks: Engineering College Dholpur offers a B.Tech programme focused on computer science and AI, Government Polytechnic College Dholpur offers a 60-seat computer science diploma, and Rajasthan’s iStart programme has set up a launchpad at Government College, Dholpur.

The report cites the IAMAI, Kantar 2025 report, which says rural areas account for 57% of India’s 958 million active internet users, yet computing resources and specialised talent remain concentrated in major cities. Nivrutti Avhad, Additional CEO of the Rajasthan Institute for Transformation and Innovation, said the challenge now is to connect these foundations with AI labs, industry mentors, real-world projects, cloud and GPU access, internships and local employment opportunities. He said a student in Dholpur should not have to move to Jaipur or Delhi to get their first meaningful opportunity to learn, experiment and build with AI. Shailendra Bhadauria, Chancellor of Pratap University in Jaipur, said a student in a metro might have a fully equipped computer lab while a student in a rural area often relies entirely on a basic smartphone screen, and he called for colleges to provide real-world projects and technology companies to offer remote internships and local partnerships.

Policy analyst Vikas Lohchab highlighted the importance of affordable tools and AI systems that work in Indian languages, particularly for people who may not be comfortable using English-language interfaces. Avhad said the Digital Samvidhan Ghar project seeks to bridge the divide between rural and urban India, including unequal access to technology and digital skills, and includes training in cybersecurity and financial literacy aimed at helping women use technology and exercise greater agency. The report says Dholpur’s AI programmes offer a starting point, but the central problem remains whether students can progress from basic digital access to practical AI skills and paid opportunities. It says that calls for reliable connectivity, affordable computers, trained teachers, access to computing resources, industry-linked projects and routes into employment.

Articles.Title: Can India’s AI Boom Reach Bharat? - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Dispatch Network Raises ₹5 Cr Pre-Seed Led by Antler India to Build AI-Powered Delivery Network
stories.Summary:
Dispatch Network, a Pune-based last-mile delivery startup, raised ₹5 crore in a pre-seed funding round led by Antler India. The round also included angel investors Krishi Fagwani, founder of Thrive, Yashin Mahadevia and Parth Modwadhia. This was the company's first public funding announcement. Dispatch was founded by Rajit Arya and Navneeth Kannan. The company will use the capital to expand its AI team and develop its Large Logistics Spatio-Temporal Model, which it uses to improve delivery allocation and reduce idle time for riders.

Dispatch assigns orders to riders across multiple platforms, and its AI model decides which order a rider should take next and where they should wait. The company says riders on its network earn around 55% more per month than the industry average, with two-thirds fewer empty kilometres and rider retention 80% better than the industry average. It has completed more than 1,00,000 deliveries since launching in Pune in June, and monthly volume rose from 3,014 in June to 55,000 in October, with about 3,500 deliveries a day now. Arya, co-founder and CEO, said riders need more orders but more importantly the right next order, and that every idle minute removed goes back into a rider's earnings. Kannan, co-founder and head of product and AI, said most of the world's deliveries still run on rules someone wrote by hand, and that Dispatch is building the decision layer for last-mile delivery.

Nitin Sharma, partner at Antler India, said most of last-mile delivery has been optimised for the platform, while Arya and Kannan started from the rider. Dispatch works with food delivery and quick-commerce platforms including Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto, Instamart and BigBasket, and also serves restaurants and stores through direct APIs and the Open Network for Digital Commerce. According to the company, riders can spend up to 50% of their kilometres travelling without an order. Dispatch plans to expand to Mumbai in November, with a next target of 50,000 orders a day across five cities.

Articles.Title: Dispatch Network Raises ₹5 Cr Pre-Seed Led by Antler India to Build AI-Powered Delivery Network - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Tokenomics: How to control your firm's AI spending
stories.Summary:
AI spending at accounting firms has risen sharply over the past year, according to an article published November 3, 2026 by Chris Gaetano in Accounting Today. The article attributes much of the increase to model providers moving from subscription to consumption-based pricing. Other factors it names are more people using AI for more complex tasks and software vendors raising prices as they add AI features. The article reports that firm leaders are not pulling back and are spending more than ever.

The article says firms are now watching how tokens are used rather than simply using fewer of them. It describes user segregation, in which people get token budgets based on their needs and skill. Charlie Apigan of LBMC is described as setting a $25 per month soft limit and a $500 hard limit for people in his department. The article also says firms limit which models people use, because a simple task can cost far more on an advanced model.

Marc Staut of Boomer said in an email that he is not seeing a meaningful slowdown and that firms want value from what they already pay for. Philip Comerford of PKF O'Connor Davies said the firm put guardrails in place to limit excess use but does not want to discourage AI use. Hrishikesh Pippadipally of Wiss and Co. said most cost controls are behavioral and governance-related at their root. Cheryl M. Burke, also of PKF O'Connor Davies, said people are taught to write efficient prompts and pick a simpler model for simple tasks.

The article says firms track who uses which AI tools, how much they use them and in some cases what prompts they enter. Pippadipally said heavy users with little impact get an email asking them to explain their processes, with a possible follow-up meeting. Staut said one CIO in his community saw a single user run up $600 in AI costs in one day. The article says the firms getting this right pair caps with training and monitoring.

Articles.Title: Tokenomics: How to control your firm's AI spending - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: Advanced Packaging Outlook 2027: Five Trends Reshaping CoWoS, HBM and Chiplets
stories.Summary:
TechInsights published an advanced packaging outlook on November 3, 2026, written by Ray Fontaine, Cameron McKnight-MacNeil and Stephen Russell. The report says advanced packaging will cap semiconductor growth in 2027. It states that AI accelerators and HBM4 both depend on packaging, and that the packages being built are far harder to make. NVIDIA's Rubin Ultra puts two GPUs and 16 HBM stacks in one socket, and TSMC's CoWoS roadmap reaches 9 reticles of interposer area.

The report gives several numbers. Only four 9-reticle interposers fit on a 300 mm wafer, against 12 to 18 today. A 16-high stack reaches about 72% yield at 98% per-layer assembly yield. CoWoS demand grew 35.7% in 2026, against 3.4% for 5 nm wafer capacity. TSMC now targets a 9.5 reticle equivalent area for CoWoS-L packaging in 2027.

The report names five trends for 2027. Memory has become the main cost and performance variable in AI compute, and HBM is now the most expensive component on a leading accelerator, ahead of the GPU die. Capacity in wafers per month stops being a useful measure of packaging supply. Hyperscalers such as Google, AWS, Meta and Microsoft set 2027 package specifications through partners such as Broadcom and Marvell, and they decide reticle count, HBM stacks and optical integration.

The report also covers carbon and supply chains. AI GPUs accounted for about 1.8 million tonnes of CO₂e in 2024, or 0.9% of semiconductor manufacturing emissions, and emissions per GPU are rising. Packaging has become a source of resilience, leverage and differentiation, but only for companies that design for multiple sources from the start, and the report calls the Baidu Kunlunxin P800 the clearest proof. TechInsights plans three webinars, on November 18, December 2 and December 9, 2026, and the full report is available through registration on its Platform.

Articles.Title: Advanced Packaging Outlook 2027: Five Trends Reshaping CoWoS, HBM and Chiplets - TechInsights

stories.Headline: Smugglers Reportedly Pair Top-Tier HBM With Throwaway Server Chips To Dodge U.S. Export Controls, Then Melt Them Apart In China
stories.Summary:
A report from The Information, summarized by Wccftech and TechRadar on November 3, 2026, describes how smugglers are moving high-bandwidth memory (HBM) made by Samsung and SK hynix into China despite U.S. export controls. The scheme is run by a man in his 40s who is fluent in Chinese and Korean and has experience in the Korean semiconductor industry. His company is on paper an ordinary chip design firm, but it deliberately designs processors so cheap and weak that no data center would buy them, which gives it a reason to order top-tier HBM. Packaging firms in Taiwan, South Korea and Southeast Asia bond the memory to the processors, and the packages are declared under the processor's classification code and shipped to Hong Kong.

The trick exploits a gap in the December 2024 U.S. rules, which exempted HBM already integrated into logic chip products. Because the package's computing capability is judged by the processor rather than the memory, it falls below the restricted threshold. From Hong Kong the packages are reportedly carried into mainland China in luggage, car trunks, and the bags of toll couriers and daily commuters. Once in China, workshops run by accomplices heat the packages until the solder melts, detach the memory stacks, and discard the processors. The process is delicate, since heating too quickly or too slowly can warp or crack the stacks, but smugglers accept the failure rate because of the profits.

The separated memory goes to a chip broker in Shenzhen who is in his early 20s and has three years in the trade. He reportedly got his start at a chip company, where he built contacts who know how to extract memory from legitimate Samsung and SK hynix supply chains. He said HBM3E that sold for a few hundred dollars a year ago now costs about $4,000 a stack. Since one AI chip package needs six to eight stacks, the memory alone would cost $24,000 to $32,000 before the chip, server and power are added. He does not accept that he is a smuggler and believes he is contributing to his country.

The report says China's own HBM development is progressing slowly, so smuggled memory is currently the best alternative. It also notes that NVIDIA's top-tier B300, which is on the U.S. export control list, has somehow ended up in China. Chinese tech commentator AB Kuai.Dong summarized the report for his followers on X, describing the decoy chips as clunky processors and calling the arrangement a compliant export. Wccftech rated the report 55% plausible, citing strong sourcing but limited corroboration.

stories.Headline: [News] China Reportedly Obtains Smuggled HBM via Server Packages; Huawei 960DT Faces Domestic HBM Shortage
stories.Summary:
Smugglers have recently been bringing high-bandwidth memory chips into China by packaging them with lower-performance server processors, according to The Information, which cited sources. The rules assess a package's computing power based on the processors rather than the memory, so the packages get through. Once the packages reach China, technicians heat them to soften the solder, remove the HBM stacks and discard the processors. The process carries a high risk of damaging the memory, but the potential profits make it worthwhile for smugglers.

The smuggled memory reportedly often ends up with customers of Huawei Technologies. Huawei's next-generation Ascend 960DT AI accelerator, expected in the first quarter of 2027, is set to rely heavily on HBM from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix and to double the memory bandwidth and capacity of Huawei's current AI processor. With U.S. export restrictions blocking direct supplies from the South Korean chipmakers, Huawei has reportedly asked some AI chip customers to source the memory themselves. Huawei is also working with DeepSeek to optimize the chip for AI model pre-training, a task DeepSeek previously handled exclusively on NVIDIA chips.

China's domestic memory suppliers remain unable to fill the gap, according to the report. Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit, a U.S.-sanctioned memory maker that has supplied Huawei for years, trails its South Korean competitors technologically and lacks the capacity to meet demand. Reuters reports, citing sources, that CXMT's HBM3E yields remain at just 20% to 30%, well below the roughly 70% achieved by SK hynix. HBM shortages are also pushing up Huawei's chip prices, and Huawei recently told some customers it was raising the suggested price of its Ascend 950DT to more than RMB 250,000, approximately US$37,000.

According to Reuters, citing sources, Cambricon has raised its indicative pricing for its next-generation 690 chip by 20% to 30%, while MetaX and Iluvatar CoreX have reportedly made similar increases. Beyond HBM shortages, Chinese companies could face additional hurdles in accessing advanced AI computing resources. According to Financial Times, citing sources, NVIDIA has told cloud computing customers that at least 51% of their services must be sold to non-Chinese companies, requiring its data center partners to reduce their exposure to Chinese customers. The move could further complicate China's AI ambitions as Washington seeks to restrict access to advanced U.S. chips through overseas cloud computing services.

Articles.Title: [News] China Reportedly Obtains Smuggled HBM via Server Packages; Huawei 960DT Faces Domestic HBM Shortage - TrendForce

stories.Headline: KLAC Q3 deep dive: AI and advanced packaging drive growth, supply chain remains in focus
stories.Summary:
KLA Corporation reported results for calendar Q3 2026, its fiscal Q1 2027, on November 3, 2026. Revenue rose 28.9% from a year earlier to $4.14 billion, beating analyst estimates of $4.04 billion. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $1.22, above the $1.18 analysts expected. The company also guided next quarter's revenue to $4.7 billion at the midpoint, 4.8% above analyst estimates of $4.49 billion, and guided adjusted earnings per share to $1.44 at the midpoint, above the $1.36 estimate.

Operating margin was 45%, up from 41.7% a year earlier, and management said operating margins exceeded 46% for the first time. Inventory days outstanding were 236, in line with the previous quarter, and market capitalization stood at $207.2 billion. Revenue from advanced packaging process control systems is on track to reach $1.1 billion for the year, with over 70% growth. The services segment grew 14% year over year.

CEO Richard Wallace said the quarter was supported by strength in leading edge foundry logic tied to AI infrastructure investments and by increasing process control intensity across leading edge devices and advanced packaging. CFO Bren D. Higgins said supply chain investments have positioned KLA to support sequential growth for the next several quarters, and he pointed to new fab projects and greenfield facilities as further opportunities. Management said demand for AI, high bandwidth memory and advanced packaging is accelerating. It also said improvements in product mix and pricing should help margins.

Management expects AI infrastructure and advanced packaging demand to drive sequential revenue growth, with new fab investments and technology transitions expanding the market through 2027. The company plans to keep expense growth below revenue gains and to offset input cost headwinds through cost optimization, especially in memory usage. Management cautioned that long lead times for components and possible customer delays in facility readiness could affect the timing of revenue recognition. KLA stock traded at $164.00, up from $158.53 just before the earnings.

Articles.Title: KLAC Q3 deep dive: AI and advanced packaging drive growth, supply chain remains in focus - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: After SK Hynix's 57% Plunge, iM Securities Says HBM Alone Justifies Market Cap, Sets Target at approximately $1,700
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix shares have fallen 57% from their June 2026 peak to their October low, and iM Securities issued a Buy rating and a target price of 2.3 million won, about $1,700, in a report on November 4. The target implies 64.5% upside from the closing price of 1.398 million won on the 29th of last month. Analyst Ko Eui-young wrote that the decline exceeds the 51% average of past downturns and that a correction that previously took 8 to 13 months has played out in just four months. The report argues the market has excessively priced in concerns about an earnings collapse after 2028.

iM Securities estimates HBM revenue will grow from 43 trillion won in 2026 to 183 trillion won in 2028. Applying TSMC's price-to-earnings ratios gives an HBM business value of about 946 trillion won in 2027, or 93% of current market capitalization, rising to about 1,372 trillion won, or 135%, in 2028. The report forecasts 2026 revenue of 364.37 trillion won and operating profit of 283.745 trillion won, with revenue up 56.9% to 571.665 trillion won next year and operating profit up 59.6% to 452.846 trillion won. It puts 2028 operating profit at 541.959 trillion won.

Ko said HBM alone already explains the current market capitalization by 2027, and that even a 10x multiple gives a similar result. He said the shift to customized HBM locks in volumes and prices before production and that the company is at the forefront of this transition. The report assumes SK Hynix returns 50% of free cash flow to shareholders after 2028, with 70% of that going to buybacks and cancellations, giving total shareholder return of 17-24% annually in 2028-2030. Ko said the per-share value effect of buybacks grows as the P/E falls, and that per-share earnings will keep growing even if earnings stagnate after 2028.

The target price applies a target price-to-book ratio of 2.3x to estimated 2027 book value per share, a level more than two standard deviations above the average since listing. An upside scenario of 3.6 million won is presented if the market's focus shifts to 2028 earnings. The report notes that the post-2028 free cash flow return ratio and dividend proportion are the brokerage's own assumptions, not confirmed company policies, and that uncertainty over HBM pricing and the strength of long-term supply agreements may remain a discount factor. It forecasts the stock will trade in a range in the first half of next year, with a re-rating in the second half if long-term contract extensions and 2028 earnings stability are confirmed in the numbers.

Articles.Title: After SK Hynix's 57% Plunge, iM Securities Says HBM Alone Justifies Market Cap, Sets Target at approximately $1,700 - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Huawei tells customers to find their own AI chip memory, effectively outsourcing procurement to the black market
stories.Summary:
Huawei has told some customers to source the memory for its AI chips themselves, according to The Information, as reported on November 3, 2026. The company plans to launch the Ascend 960DT early next year and says it will double the performance of its current chips. Huawei's Chinese suppliers cannot produce enough High-Bandwidth Memory, and U.S. export rules block direct purchases from Samsung and SK Hynix. Those two companies together control more than 80 percent of the global market.

Smugglers bundle HBM with cheap server processors whose performance falls below the export threshold, then ship the packages to China through Hong Kong. Workshops there separate the memory chips from the processors, a fragile process with a high error rate that the margins still make worthwhile. Prices for smuggled HBM3E memory have jumped from a few hundred dollars to around $4,000 per unit in just one year, according to a broker in Shenzhen. Each AI chip needs six to eight units, so the memory alone can cost up to $32,000.

The black market also draws on older Nvidia GPUs stripped for parts and on excess inventory from chip designers who scrapped projects or cut orders. South Korea's customs authority had uncovered trade violations worth $560 million by May, already surpassing the previous full-year record. A third of that total involved strategic goods like chips exported without proper authorization or with false declarations. The articles do not say what Huawei or the authorities will do next.

Articles.Title: Huawei tells customers to find their own AI chip memory, effectively outsourcing procurement to the black market - The Decoder

stories.Headline: Global AI Expo 'MARS 2026' Opens in Seoul
stories.Summary:
MARS 2026, a global AI expo organized by Hwaseong City, opened on November 3 at an auditorium on the third floor of COEX in Seoul. The three-day official program runs through November 5 under the slogan "AI City in Action." Sessions are held at COEX Hall D, the auditorium and Conference Room E. About 1,000 people attended the opening ceremony, including Hwaseong Mayor Chung Myoung-keun, Hwaseong City Council Chairman Lee Kye-chul, current and former lawmakers from both ruling and opposition parties, business executives, AI industry officials and residents. The ceremony began with a performance by Walker C1, a humanoid robot built with physical AI technology, which performed ballet movements. A children's choir then sang a song about hope.

In his opening address, Mayor Chung said Hwaseong Special City last year became the first local government to hold the MARS AI expo, and that this year the city will turn that vision into action. He said Hwaseong is home to Samsung Electronics, the Namyang research centers of Hyundai Motor and Kia, and more than 26,000 manufacturers, and that the city will apply AI to manufacturing, aerospace, health care, transportation, safety and care services. The keynote address was delivered by Sam Richards, a professor at Pennsylvania State University, on the theme "The Future of AI: Can Korea Lead the World?" Richards praised Korea's sense of community and Hwaseong's industrial capacity, saying Korea has the strength to have solved problems by thinking of "we" before "I" even in times of crisis. The opening ceremony also featured the launch of the 2026 MARS Alliance, with participants including Samsung Life Insurance, Hyundai Motor Group, Kia, Daewoong Pharmaceutical, Shinsegae Property, Innospace, Dongtan City Hospital, JM Robotics, Voltline, Abiman Robotics and Zeus.

The participants declared action-oriented AI cooperation through a touchscreen performance and issued a launch statement centered on AI technology demonstration, industrial innovation, technology commercialization and expanded data and research cooperation. Specialized sessions continue during the event, including a "Mobility AI" session on future vehicles and autonomous driving, a "Real Life AI" session on health care and smart homes, and an "Industry AI" session on the AI transformation of manufacturing. At the auditorium, the launch ceremony for Hwaseong Special City's aerospace industry task force and the Space AI Forum discussed plans to build a Hwaseong-style aerospace cluster. Sixty-two companies and institutions are taking part in the exhibition at COEX Hall D2, organized around five themes: future mobility, autonomous driving and UAM; manufacturing AI and robotics; health care and smart homes; transportation, safety and urban data; and aerospace and satellite data. Hwaseong City said it plans to use the event to begin full implementation of a city strategy that applies AI technology to industry and residents' daily lives.

Articles.Title: Global AI Expo 'MARS 2026' Opens in Seoul - Seoul Economic Daily
