An autoscaling engine adjusts hardware based on user traffic, and an online RL feature periodically fine-tunes weights using the prompts a model receives. The company also offers a model router called Shift-1 that sends each request to the most cost-efficient model and can split complex tasks among multiple models.

Applied Compute said its annualized recurring revenue has topped $100 million, and it counts Microsoft Corp., DoorDash Inc. and other major tech firms as customers. The company launched less than 18 months ago and will use the new capital to grow its market presence and buy more infrastructure. In a blog post, founders Rhythm Garg, Yash Patil and Linden Li wrote that training, inference and routing are the first pieces of a much larger stack. They said they are building the AI infrastructure every company will need to fully own its intelligence, from the models themselves to the systems that run, monitor and secure them.

Articles.Title: AI cloud startup Applied Compute raises $350M after reaching key revenue milestone

stories.Headline: University of Toledo to launch online master’s degree in data science and AI in spring 2027
stories.Summary:
The University of Toledo will launch an online master's degree program in data science and AI in spring 2027, according to an article published by 13abc on November 3, 2026. Bill Kulies, director of UToledo's School of Interdisciplinary Data Science, developed the program. He said it is fully online and can be taken full time or part time. Kulies said it is open to recent graduates or professionals who want to increase their skills in data science or AI.

Kulies said the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates that data science related jobs will grow by 34% nationally and 28% in the northwest Ohio region over the next 10 years. He said these are high-paying jobs with salaries over $100,000. According to UToledo, graduates will be prepared for jobs that use advanced analytics, machine learning and AI to drive better decisions, inform strategy and advance innovation. Those jobs include data scientists, machine learning engineers, AI engineers and data analysts.

Kulies said AI will automate some routine data science related tasks, so it becomes much more important to upskill workers so they know how to make good judgments about how to use AI responsibly and ethically. He said manufacturing systems are now very sophisticated and can measure all sorts of things, and there needs to be a way to analyze that data and understand how to improve efficiency. He said AI is being used in all industries, including the auto industry and other manufacturing, the financial industry and health care, and that working professionals are needed who know how to use it responsibly. The article does not say what happens next beyond the spring 2027 launch.

Articles.Title: University of Toledo to launch online master’s degree in data science and AI in spring 2027

stories.Headline: AI may help tailor treatment for childhood brain tumors
stories.Summary:
An international team led by researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute developed an artificial intelligence model that may help doctors choose treatment for children with malignant brain tumors. The findings were published in Nature Genetics on November 3, 2026. The model is called MANTIS, short for Methylation profiling and Artificial Neural networks for Time-dependent Individualized Survival predictions. It uses DNA methylation profiling, a test already used to help diagnose brain tumors, to make personalized survival predictions for children with medulloblastoma and ependymoma.

The researchers found that MANTIS outperformed current risk-prediction approaches for many patients across several large validation cohorts. Instead of placing patients in broad risk groups, the model estimates how survival probability changes over time based on the biology of each child's tumor. When the researchers adapted MANTIS to estimate the likely effects of different radiation doses, the model suggested that more than half of children with average-risk medulloblastoma may be candidates for lower-dose craniospinal irradiation. In the data analyzed, lower-dose radiation was linked to better cognitive outcomes, and the researchers did not detect a significant survival disadvantage in this group.

Volker Hovestadt, a computational biologist at Dana-Farber and senior author of the study, said the goal is to move beyond broad risk categories toward a more individualized understanding of each child's tumor. He said that for children with brain tumors, this could help match treatment intensity to the biology of the disease and ultimately reduce long-term side effects for some patients. Sabina Stefan, a postdoctoral researcher at Dana-Farber and first author of the study, said one exciting aspect of the work is that it shows how artificial intelligence can learn from molecular tests that are already part of care. She said that with further clinical study, this type of approach could help support more personalized treatment decisions not only for pediatric brain tumors but potentially for many other cancers as well.

Current methods for predicting risk combine clinical and molecular features to help guide treatment, but children within the same risk group can still have very different outcomes. MANTIS was designed to capture that variation by combining genome-wide molecular data, including DNA methylation patterns and copy number changes, with long-term patient follow-up. The researchers first developed the model for medulloblastoma, one of the most common malignant brain tumors in children, and then extended the same framework to ependymoma, another pediatric brain tumor in which outcomes can vary widely. The findings suggest that similar AI-based methods could eventually be applied to other pediatric and adult cancers in which patients with the same diagnosis can have very different clinical courses.

Articles.Title: AI may help tailor treatment for childhood brain tumors

stories.Headline: Responsible AI Adoption Requires Clear Policies, Ongoing Oversight
stories.Summary:
Leanna Baker, PharmD, MS, digital solutions lead at Cencora, spoke in an interview at the Academy of Managed Care Pharmacy Nexus 2026 meeting about what responsible artificial intelligence adoption requires. The interview followed her October 27 session, "Is Your Organization Ready for AI? A Managed Care Playbook," which presented primary research on AI adoption trends, perceived value, barriers, and gaps across managed care. The article was published on November 3, 2026.

Baker said costs go beyond a model's token usage to include the time teams spend developing processes, getting approval from IT or governance teams, and assigning someone to monitor each system. Because policies and internal processes change, that person must continually confirm each tool delivers the expected value and update it as needed. She said AI governance spans internal and external considerations, with organizations needing to judge whether a tool is accurate and trustworthy and whether it protects internal information, while state and federal legislation can restrict how AI is used. She gave the example that if a law prohibits using AI for automatic approvals, organizations need a way to recognize that change and update their systems.

Baker described ongoing cost and governance review as a job in itself that helps ensure organizations are not put at risk. She said responsible adoption depends on considering everyone a tool affects, including patients and staff, and that employees should understand what a tool can and cannot do. Organizations should keep a clear use policy without gaps and a way to communicate updates, and a policy prohibiting AI use with personally identifiable information should specify whether it applies to names, dates of birth, or anonymized data. She said it is not just having a policy but also being able to communicate it so no one feels scared about using the technology that has been rolled out.

Articles.Title: Responsible AI Adoption Requires Clear Policies, Ongoing Oversight

stories.Headline: Q&A: Can AI-Driven OCT Reduce Breast-Conserving Surgery Reoperations?
stories.Summary:
In March 2026, the FDA granted premarket approval to the Claire OCT System, the first optical coherence tomography imaging platform with integrated AI software for adjunctive detection of breast cancer. The approval was reported in a Q&A published by Physicians Weekly on November 3, 2026. The article says about one in five commercially insured women in the US need reoperation after initial breast-conserving surgery because malignant cells remain at the surgical margins. Sommer Gunia, DO, a breast surgical oncologist at HonorHealth Cancer Care's Comprehensive Breast Center of Arizona, is slated to integrate the system into her surgical workflow.

The system works alongside clinician review and provides real-time, volumetric cross-sectional depth visualization. Its AI-driven computer-aided detection algorithm isolates and annotates focal areas suggestive of mammary malignancy. The approval includes an authorized predetermined change control plan, a preapproved regulatory pathway for updating the AI as more clinical data become available. The article states the system is an adjunctive tool that does not replace standard tissue histopathology or provide a diagnosis, and it is not available for sale outside the US.

Gunia said her practice focuses on treating breast cancer while preserving as much healthy breast tissue as possible. She said a second operation can mean another procedure, another recovery, and more time away from work and family, and may affect when patients move on to radiation or other recommended care. She said what she finds most promising is the chance to act on additional information while the patient is still in the operating room. She said final pathology remains essential, and the potential is to make more informed decisions during the initial procedure. The article lists her as a clinical speaker and educator for Perimeter Medical Imaging AI.

The article says breast cancer can extend beyond what surgeons can see or feel, and microscopic disease may extend into surrounding tissue or along ducts. It says surgeons ultimately rely on postoperative pathology to determine margin status, so some information needed to assess whether more surgery is necessary comes only after the initial procedure. Gunia said she expects AI-assisted imaging to become more integrated into surgical workflows over the next 5 to 10 years. She said these tools need to be practical for the operating room team and fit into the procedure without adding unnecessary complexity.

Articles.Title: Q&A: Can AI-Driven OCT Reduce Breast-Conserving Surgery Reoperations?

stories.Headline: ID-Pal deal arms ThirdEye against AI-fuelled financial crime
stories.Summary:
ThirdEye, an anti-money-laundering platform provider, has chosen ID-Pal to supply the identity and business verification functions within its offering across Australia and New Zealand. Under the partnership, ID-Pal’s verification technology will sit inside ThirdEye’s AML platform. The deal is designed to address mounting pressure on banks and other regulated firms in the region to tackle fraud, tighten compliance and build trust from the moment a customer signs up. It also extends ID-Pal’s presence in overseas markets. Organisations in Australia, New Zealand and the UK will now be able to use ID-Pal’s document authentication, biometric checks and address verification alongside ThirdEye’s current modules.

The combined service aims to give firms in these markets a more streamlined option that can scale as their needs grow. ID-Pal applies AI to confirm that identity documents are genuine, verify both people and companies, and help detect fraud. The company says it takes a privacy-preserving approach, shielding sensitive customer data while returning verification outcomes in real time. ThirdEye pairs automation with in-market knowledge to give banks, financial institutions and other heavily regulated businesses a secure tool for countering financial crime. Its adaptable models cover customer screening, transaction monitoring, case management and regulatory reporting, helping clients protect customers, control risk and keep pace with compliance obligations.

ThirdEye general manager Hamish Shaw identified progress in AI as a major driver behind the agreement. He said the financial crime landscape has never been static and that bad actors keep evolving new techniques, and that with AI accelerating the threats it is crucial for those on the right side to work together to stay ahead. ID-Pal CEO and founder Colum Lyons said fraud and financial crime know no borders, and increasingly neither does the technology used to commit them. He said ThirdEye has built a strong AML proposition across Australia, New Zealand and the UK, and that ID-Pal is delighted to have been chosen to power identity and business verification within it. He said the two companies can together help organisations establish trust at onboarding and manage fraud and compliance risk throughout the customer lifecycle.

Articles.Title: ID-Pal deal arms ThirdEye against AI-fuelled financial crime

stories.Headline: AI Insights: Did AI Almost Break the Internet?
stories.Summary:
In 2024, developers working on PHP, the scripting language that runs much of the web, noticed a problem when the software ran out of memory, according to the PHP Foundation. They suspected it could be used to break into a server but had no concrete attack. This summer, researchers using AI tools demonstrated working attacks involving that problem and related flaws. On October 21, PHP released emergency fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell, that could let an attacker run code on a vulnerable server without credentials. The article says the issue affected 70% of all websites.

The vulnerabilities sat inside PHP's engine, which processes instructions for sites built with it, including WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software behind Wikipedia. In the first flaw, reaching the memory limit at the wrong moment could interrupt PHP while it was setting up internal data, corrupting memory and possibly exposing that data to a visitor. The second involved references to memory that were no longer valid, so a later request could use a stale reference and reach earlier memory. By arranging memory contents and triggering the errors under suitable conditions, researchers could turn these failures into remote code execution. The attacker did not need an account or a password.

Calif, a security research firm in OpenAI's Patch the Planet program, began its PHP audit on July 30. Researcher Ryan Austin reported the first vulnerability to PHP on August 11 and shared a working exploit days later, and OpenAI says Calif used GPT-5.6 Sol in the research. Wiz independently found the vulnerabilities using its Wiz Atlas system, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, and it describes AI as helping with the repeated analysis, testing and debugging needed to make an exploit work across different applications and memory layouts. The PHP Foundation cites compatibility concerns, performance trade-offs and a small team with competing responsibilities as reasons earlier work had stalled. Once remote attacks were demonstrated, fixing the problem became its security team's top priority.

The coordinated release was planned for October 22, but on October 20 the vulnerability identifiers began circulating online, followed by a mistakenly published Calif demonstration video. PHP brought the release forward to October 21, giving distributors some time to finish packaging updates while shortening the wait for a public fix. The project published patched releases for PHP's 8.2, 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5 branches. The fixes changed how PHP handles memory exhaustion and clears its internal state between requests, addressing the underlying failures the researchers had exploited. The article says the best way to defend against AI-enabled attacks is to use AI to find and detect vulnerabilities, and it notes that quantum computing could bring a new set of cybersecurity challenges.

Articles.Title: AI Insights: Did AI Almost Break the Internet?

stories.Headline: Shoppers will let AI browse, but they still want their hand on the wallet
stories.Summary:
Nuvei published research on November 5, 2026, on how U.S. shoppers feel about AI-assisted commerce. The study found that 58% of consumers find AI useful for researching products and comparing prices, and 39% say they are using it more while shopping than three months earlier. But 56% say they would never allow AI to spend money without their approval, and only 1% want the shopping process fully automated from start to finish. Shoppers have accepted AI as a research assistant but not as a wallet.

The research gives specific numbers on what worries consumers and what would reassure them. Seventy six percent named fraud or unauthorized charges as their biggest concern, more than double the 33% who worried about the AI buying the wrong item. Eighty four percent said the ability to cancel or reverse an AI-initiated purchase after checkout is extremely or very important, with 64% calling it extremely important. Sixty one percent pointed to spending limits and 59% pointed to a required human approval checkpoint before checkout. Fifty eight percent would still prefer to complete an AI-assisted purchase on the retailer's own site or app, compared with 12% comfortable finishing inside the AI platform itself, and 62% are not comfortable letting AI complete a purchase without a traditional checkout page at all.

The article says businesses should build visible controls into the front of the experience, such as spend caps, category limits and a checkpoint before money moves, rather than burying them in settings menus. It says reversibility should be treated as core to the experience, the way free returns became a baseline expectation in e-commerce. It also says retailers have reason to build first-party AI shopping tools on their own properties rather than ceding the checkout moment and the customer relationship to third-party agent ecosystems. The article compares this to contactless cards and mobile wallets, which earned trust gradually as issuers added visible security cues like tokenization and biometric confirmation at payment.

The research points to where agentic commerce is likely to take hold earliest: purchases that are repetitive, predictable and already low-stakes. Consumer packaged goods and household replenishment are named as a natural starting point, along with subscriptions and recurring services, and food and beverage such as grocery and restaurant reorders. Travel and booking may follow once trust in reversibility catches up, but higher price points likely mean it lags the more routine categories. The article says agentic commerce gains ground fastest wherever the financial risk is small, the decision is familiar, and the shopper can see and control the guardrails around it.

Articles.Title: Shoppers will let AI browse, but they still want their hand on the wallet

stories.Headline: There Are Now Growing Signs That AI Is Hurting Employment in the Job Market
stories.Summary:
New reporting by the Financial Times describes two new sources of data that point to AI's impact on the labor market. The first is an analysis by US-based financial researcher Eric Basmajian, who wrote in a social media post that AI productivity gains are showing up in jobs data. He said only about 15 percent of jobs seem to be impacted so far. Basmajian said the three heaviest AI adopters, information, professional services and finance, went from a 2.2 percent productivity trend to 5.0 percent since 2022.

The day after Basmajian's post, what appears to be an internal Goldman Sachs report began circulating on social media. It warned that the AI labor market impact has been spreading beyond tech work, a field already hit hard as generative AI becomes a common tool for writing software code. The report shows a rising trend between an industry's AI exposure and unemployment around non-tech professional sectors like finance, telecomms, technical services and administration. This seems to reinforce Basmajian's assertion.

The Financial Times adds several disclaimers to the findings. It says the productivity metrics are not necessarily reflective of quality, meaning the data may reflect lower headcount rather than skyrocketing output and revenue. The data is also specifically about the US, pointing to broader post-Pandemic economic woes rather than a global AI jobpocalypse. The FT says the link visible in the US between AI usage, productivity growth and falling employment is conspicuously absent elsewhere.

The article does not say who is responsible beyond the researchers and reports named, and it gives no further statements from Basmajian or Goldman Sachs. It says the AI doomers finally have something to write home about as far as the labor market is concerned. It adds that anyone preparing for a hypothetical AI labor revolution will have to keep waiting. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: There Are Now Growing Signs That AI Is Hurting Employment in the Job Market

stories.Headline: Weta FX and TAICCA Partner to Turn Taiwan Into an AI Screen Production Hub for Asia (EXCLUSIVE)
stories.Summary:
Weta FX, the New Zealand visual effects studio known for "The Lord of the Rings" and "Avatar," is partnering with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) to make Taiwan a center for AI-driven screen production in Asia. The partnership will be formally launched on Nov. 6 at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei. The launch will take place on the festival's main stage right after the opening ceremony. The partnership will have three strands: joint investment, AI research and development, and training new talent.

Specifics of the arrangement are being held back until the launch. TAICCA chair Sue Wang will appear at the event alongside three Weta FX executives: CEO Daniel Seah, chief technology officer Kimball Thurston and VFX supervisor Sheldon Stopsack. The pact pairs Taiwan's AI and advanced-tech capabilities and its pool of creative talent with Weta FX's VFX know-how, its track record on international productions and its global network. The aim is to plug Taiwanese technologists and creatives into work across the worldwide screen business.

Seah grew up in Taiwan, which gives the deal a personal angle for him. The studio has also been building ties on the island, appearing at the Taoyuan International Film & Technology Forum in August. The tie-up fits within TAICCA's wider brief, which includes the use of new technologies to make content. Taiwan's Ministry of Culture set up TAICCA in 2019, and the agency backs Taiwanese content from development through production, distribution and overseas marketing across film, TV, animation, publishing, comics, music, gaming and the performing arts.

Weta FX is based in Wellington, with outposts in Vancouver and Melbourne. It has won eight Oscars for visual effects, 17 Academy Science & Technology Awards, eight BAFTAs for special visual effects, 10 VES Awards in the photoreal feature category and five Emmys. Its latest work on the "Avatar" franchise was 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash." Titles in production at the studio include "The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum," Marvel Studios' "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Children of Blood and Bone."

Articles.Title: Weta FX and TAICCA Partner to Turn Taiwan Into an AI Screen Production Hub for Asia (EXCLUSIVE)

stories.Headline: In an AI world, cybersecurity requires human judgment
stories.Summary:
Madeline Pumariega, the president of Miami Dade College, wrote an opinion article published on November 3, 2026, in Miami's Community Newspapers. The article argues that cybersecurity in an age of artificial intelligence depends on human judgment. It describes how a cyberattack can disrupt a hospital, harm a small business, or expose a family's financial information. Pumariega says such damage goes beyond technology because it interrupts care, threatens livelihoods, and undermines trust.

The article says AI can help professionals analyze information and identify threats, but it can also help criminals craft convincing deceptions and exploit vulnerabilities. Pumariega writes that familiarity with the latest tools is only the beginning and that professionals need knowledge, investigative skills, and judgment. She says a person must decide whether unusual activity flagged by a system is an attack and whether an automated response would interrupt an essential service. The article notes that the National Security Agency has designated Miami Dade College a National Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense. It says the college became the first in Florida with both associate and bachelor's degree programs in cybersecurity.

Pumariega says the college's responsibility is to prepare graduates who can understand complex systems, evaluate risk, and respond under pressure. She writes that students need to know how networks operate, how information moves, and how vulnerabilities arise. At the college's Cybersecurity Center of the Americas, students use a Cyber Range to detect, investigate, and respond to realistic attacks in a simulated environment. She says this practice builds communication, teamwork, critical thinking, and ethical judgment. She also calls on employers to offer internships, realistic training scenarios, and sustained engagement with faculty.

The article says educators should assess whether students can apply knowledge in unfamiliar situations, justify decisions, and explain consequences. Pumariega writes that hiring practices should let candidates demonstrate what they know and can do. She says working adults, veterans, and first-generation college students bring experience the cybersecurity workforce needs, and that certificates and degrees offer multiple entry points. The article ties local talent development to economic opportunity and community resilience in Miami. It ends by saying Cybersecurity Awareness Month should prompt consideration of the people behind digital defenses.

Articles.Title: In an AI world, cybersecurity requires human judgment

stories.Headline: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Stock Fair Value Edges Higher On AI Optimism And Valuation Debate
stories.Summary:
Simply Wall St published an article on November 3, 2026, saying the fair value estimate for Advanced Micro Devices had moved from about US$629.21 to about US$646.74. The update reflects how analysts are framing the stock, with debate over how quickly AMD can turn its data center and AI ambitions into earnings and how much optimism is already in the share price. The assumed revenue growth rate rose from about 51.02% to about 51.37%, and the assumed future P/E multiple went from about 34.86x to about 36.17x. The assumed net profit margin slipped from about 28.76% to about 28.29%, and the discount rate moved from about 11.27% to about 11.26%.

Several firms, including Goldman Sachs, Citi, Mizuho, Stifel, BofA, Argus and Raymond James, raised price targets on AMD. Goldman Sachs pointed to stronger Q3 results and guidance, with attention on data center strength, gross margin performance and controlled operating expenses. Susquehanna, BMO Capital and Piper Sandler pointed to AMD's position in AI infrastructure, including Helios racks and MI450 GPUs, as central to their growth assumptions. Morgan Stanley kept an Equal Weight rating despite a higher US$510 price target, signaling a view that the current valuation already embeds much of the expected growth, and Truist framed attractive entry points as occurring mainly on meaningful sell offs.

The article links AMD's story to expectations for a full AI infrastructure offering across Instinct GPUs, EPYC server CPUs and Helios rack systems in a high performance and AI computing market it sizes at about US$2t by 2030. It cites large Helios rack and AI system commitments from customers such as OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, plus ROCm software adoption, as central to analyst expectations for higher data center revenue and margins. It says risks include tight supply of advanced components, lower margins on MI450 accelerators, fast moving sentiment around AI spending and any slowdown in customer AI infrastructure rollouts. The article states it is general in nature and not financial advice.

Articles.Title: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Stock Fair Value Edges Higher On AI Optimism And Valuation Debate

stories.Headline: Ted Schlein's Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom
stories.Summary:
Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein, is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds. The San Francisco firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week, TechCrunch learned through regulatory filings. It plans to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing. The $360 million flagship target matches the size of the firm's previous fund raised in 2024.

Ballistic announced a $300 million debut fund in 2022 and raised $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, according to PitchBook data, and the new Fund B is targeting a similar amount. Founded in late 2021, the firm's founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded Fortify Software and AlienVault. Ballistic Ventures declined to comment on its fundraising plans.

A cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch that Ballistic's ties to Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals. The person said its investment strategy is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures. The firm has backed companies including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks, and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike, alongside startups such as Armadin, GetReal, Nudge Security, and Oligo Security. The fundraising plans come as growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks.

The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them. U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent JPMorgan Chase report said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said. Separately, Microsoft warned in its annual Digital Defense Report last month that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development.

Articles.Title: Ted Schlein's Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom

stories.Headline: Hedgeness CEO: Fit AI to the workflow, not the other way around
stories.Summary:
Jay Singh, co-founder and CEO of Hedgeness, said artificial intelligence and automation offer many possibilities, but new technology alone does not guarantee adoption or business value. He said technology should create value for the people using it rather than add another layer of complexity. His key insight was that AI should be fitted to the workflow, not the other way around. The article was published by Digital Insurance on November 5, 2026, and was written by Grace Crane. The article gives no further numbers, dates or names beyond Singh, Hedgeness, Crane and the publication date.

It sets out no specific requirements, policy changes or new rules. It does not describe any product, funding round or deal. The piece is a short interview item in the outlet's Meet the Insurtech series. Singh is the person responsible for the view expressed, as co-founder and CEO of Hedgeness. He said technology should create value for the people using it, not introduce another layer of complexity.

He framed the point as a key insight about AI and automation. The article presents his comments without further attribution or response. The context is the outlet's Meet the Insurtech series, which runs short profiles and interviews with insurtech leaders. The same page links to other recent items on AI in insurance, including one on insurtechs getting AI past the pilot stage and one on insurers raising AI budgets before seeing returns. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Hedgeness CEO: Fit AI to the workflow, not the other way around

stories.Headline: Government uses open-weight AI to control costs and meet mission needs
stories.Summary:
At the Red Hat Government Symposium in Washington, D.C. in October 2026, public sector and cybersecurity leaders discussed how federal agencies are using open-weight AI models to control costs while still meeting mission needs. The discussion was reported by TechTarget on Nov. 5, 2026. Open-weight models have trained parameters that users can download, deploy and, depending on the license, modify or fine-tune, unlike proprietary models that are typically accessed through a vendor's hosted platform or API. Examples include models from Meta's Llama family, Alibaba's Qwen and DeepSeek. Agencies are weighing the capabilities of frontier models against the economics of open-weight alternatives.

The article describes a hybrid approach that combines frontier models for complex analysis and mission-critical reasoning with smaller, less expensive models for routine tasks. The Department of Homeland Security's January 2025 Playbook for Public Sector Generative AI Deployment recommends that agencies evaluate commercial, open-source and open-weight models, including the possibility of using multiple model types. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has sought access to open-weight model hosting and inference services for its Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The General Services Administration has pursued discounted AI agreements through its OneGov initiative, and in October 2026 it announced an expanded agreement with Anthropic providing a 40% discount on token-based usage across Claude models for government customers.

Ben Cushing, Red Hat's chief architect for health and life sciences, said a hybrid approach lets agencies control costs without sacrificing access to top-tier AI capabilities, and he described running open-weight models locally on infrastructure the agency controls as the safest way to take advantage of frontier lab capabilities. He recalled that CIOs in the federal health space told him last year they had gone through their cloud credits on tokens within a month despite planning for the whole year. Lance Jenkinson, CIO and deputy assistant inspector general for management administration at the Department of Veterans Affairs, said his agency has created 42,000 patches over the last several months, primarily using open-weight models, and that about 300 AI-driven processes exist with 85% of them today using open-weight models rather than frontier models. He said answers can be just as accurate, more often than not, at a far lower cost, and he said each agency needs to weigh whether a tool is secured and supported.

The article says open-weight models are not the only way government organizations control spending, since purpose-built proprietary AI services, government-specific pricing agreements and consumption-based contracts can also reduce costs. It notes that open-weight AI can introduce infrastructure and maintenance expenses that offset some of its apparent savings. Cushing said there is absolutely not one model that rules them all, and that every model is better at certain things than others, with cost and accuracy elements to consider. Panelists recommended that decision-makers evaluate models based on the work they need to perform.

Articles.Title: Government uses open-weight AI to control costs and meet mission needs

stories.Headline: Google puts new limits on AI agents that hunt threats and fix vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud added new controls to CodeMender, its AI tool for finding and fixing software vulnerabilities, on November 5, 2026. The updates let businesses verify vulnerabilities and simulate exploits in an operating system-level sandbox or an isolated virtual machine. They also add human checks for local writes and command execution to keep testing within defined limits. Businesses can scan an entire code repository, a specific folder, or only files modified since the last scan, which gives them more control over scanning speed and costs. CodeMender remains in preview.

Google Cloud is also extending security and governance controls across environments where AI agents run, including Gemini, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run, and the new Agent Compute Engine. Auth Manager is now generally available and centralizes credential management in a Google-managed vault governed by IAM. Agent Identity JWT support, in preview, lets agents authenticate across services including AWS, Azure, on-premises backends, and Model Context Protocol servers without static, long-lived API keys. VPC Service Controls ingress and egress rules now support IAM roles, and Workload Identity Federation for GKE is in preview. A new Model Armor custom topic detector, also in preview, lets businesses define prompt-based rules to check whether agent conversations stay within approved topics.

Ivan Fontarensky, CTO of Cybersecurity Services at Thales Group, said adversaries attack at machine speed and the Fairwind Program helps keep pace with application security. He said early evaluation of CodeMender shows the potential to reduce vulnerability discovery time by over 95%, while keeping expert validation and remediation under human oversight. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, said Wiz and Google Cloud are combining deep autonomous application understanding, connected security context, and threat intelligence to help organizations innovate securely and stay ahead of emerging threats. Google says its approach to countering autonomous, multi-agent threats combines continuous workload monitoring, threat intelligence, and automated investigations, with agents presenting mitigation actions for human approval.

Google Threat Intelligence telemetry is incorporated into defensive models to trigger automated threat hunts that reconstruct process trees and isolate threats in real time, according to the company. Wiz AI Static Application Security Testing is now in preview and correlates code weaknesses with infrastructure context in the Wiz Security Graph. A shared data model now connects Wiz Defend and Google Security Operations, and analysts can access Wiz Blue Agent's investigation findings within Google Security Operations. Google DeepMind and Wiz also launched Scan for Good, which Google says used Gemini 4 Argon to help more than 50 public service organizations and critical infrastructure providers identify and address critical security exposures during its first month.

Articles.Title: Google puts new limits on AI agents that hunt threats and fix vulnerabilities

stories.Headline: Anthropic releases FlashProve, an open-source prototype that cryptographically verifies an AI response came from a given model, not one that a router swapped in (Anthropic)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released FlashProve on November 2, 2026, an open-source prototype that uses cryptography to prove an AI response came from a specific model rather than one swapped in by a routing service or an attacker. The work was done by Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, including Roy Rinberg and Alex Allain, with outside researchers from EPFL, MIT, StarkWare, Succinct and RESI. For a 400B-parameter Llama 4 Maverick model in 4-bit quantization, a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens per second, with a proof size of about 19 MB per 1,024-token request. That is roughly 70 to 95 times the GPU time needed to run the model itself on vLLM, and prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower.

The system relies on a cryptographic proof called a zkSNARK, which lets a provider commit to a model and prove each response came from it without revealing the weights. Anthropic released five artifacts: the blog post, a technical report, a protocol specification, executable code with a prover and two verifiers, and Lean proofs of the top-level security statements. The code, Lean proofs and documentation are under the Apache 2.0 license. The proofs hide the model's weights but not its architecture, and the team says the work is intermediate progress meant for others to take and improve.

Anthropic says the tool could help regulators check that hardware is serving the claimed model, help companies detect tampered servers, and let users verify which model answered them. The team notes that Claude is good at optimization but can make decisions that are hard to evaluate in large complex systems, so they included auditable Lean statements for the claimed security guarantees. Anthropic also says the system does not establish that hardware is not training on the side. The company had set a public goal of a provable inference prototype by September 30, 2026, and says it met that goal through a separate project that signs inference traffic and recomputes it on a trusted server.

The release is framed as a step toward provable inference, which Anthropic links to customer trust, independent evaluation and AI pacing requirements. The post says the certificates could support auditors and regulators and could help providers show they meet commitments and legal obligations. Anthropic is sharing the work openly so others can examine and improve it. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: Anthropic releases FlashProve, an open-source prototype that cryptographically verifies an AI response came from a given model, not one that a router swapped in (Anthropic)

stories.Headline: New to The Street Launches "The PureCipher Series," a Multi-Part Look at Trusted AI for the Physical World, Airing on Bloomberg Television and Fox Business
stories.Summary:
New to The Street announced on November 3, 2026, that it has launched The PureCipher Series, a multi-part sponsored program about PureCipher Inc., an AI safety company. The series was filmed at New to The Street's New York City studios and will air monthly on Bloomberg Television and FOX Business Network. Broadcasts will reach the United States, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa, and Southeast Asia. Each episode will also be distributed across New to The Street's YouTube network of more than 6.6 million subscribers, including the New to The Street TV and NewsOut channels.

Planned episodes cover PureCipher's guiding principle that security creates trust and trust creates safety, its AFWERX Direct-to-Phase-II SBIR award for Noise-Based Communications for secure camera control and protected video transmission, and a demonstration of Secure Operation for Advanced Readiness, or SOAR, shown during Northern Strike in August 2026. Other episodes explain Physical AI for drones, robots and autonomous systems, demonstrate OmniSeal cryptographic seals that make data tampering detectable and provenance verifiable, show Zero-Exposure AI running real-time AI inference over quantum-safe encrypted data, and cover Intent Preservation, which keeps AI decisions and actions aligned with human intent and detects deviations before unauthorized actions occur. The series is supported by national and international commercials on Bloomberg and FOX Business, New York market TV commercials, Times Square billboards, anchor-recorded NewsOut video press releases, Wall Street New York Magazine coverage, daily social media distribution, and accredited-investor events at New to The Street's Hudson Yards penthouse. Air dates and episode links will be announced as each installment premieres.

Wendy Chin, Founder and CEO of PureCipher, said AI is changing the world and PureCipher is making it safer. She said that as AI takes on greater autonomy, safeguards must protect the integrity of its data, preserve human intent and keep its actions within authorized boundaries, and that these safeguards have real-world consequences when AI controls physical systems. Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street, said Wendy and her team are building something every company deploying AI needs, and that trust is the next frontier for artificial intelligence. He said the series lets the audience see the technology working and hear directly from the people building it.

PureCipher is headquartered in Boca Raton, Florida, and describes its mission as ensuring AI remains on the side of humanity. Chin is a former Fortune 100 technology executive and serial entrepreneur with an MBA from the Wharton School and MEng and BS degrees in Electrical Engineering from Cornell University. New to The Street says its sponsored programming reaches more than 225 million homes on Bloomberg Television on Saturdays at 6:30 p.m. ET and on FOX Business on Mondays at 10:30 p.m. ET, and that it has aired more than 778 episodes and worked with more than 200 public companies, including more than 30 listed on the NYSE.

Articles.Title: New to The Street Launches "The PureCipher Series," a Multi-Part Look at Trusted AI for the Physical World, Airing on Bloomberg Television and Fox Business

stories.Headline: Vodafone Business UK Selects Amdocs to Drive Agentic Transformation of B2B Operations with aOS
stories.Summary:
Amdocs announced on November 3, 2026, that Vodafone Business UK, the enterprise arm of VodafoneThree, has selected it to lead the agentic transformation of its B2B operations. The program will consolidate and upgrade multiple legacy business support systems onto a unified agentic platform built on Amdocs' BSS capabilities and powered by Amdocs aOS, its agentic operating system specialized for telecommunications. Amdocs will act as Lead Systems Integrator and long-term technology partner, overseeing implementation and supporting the platform's ongoing operation and evolution. The companies say the work is meant to create simpler customer journeys, accelerate the launch of new products and services, and lay the foundation for an agentic operating model.

For Vodafone Business customers, the transformation is designed to make services easier to buy, manage and support, while giving Vodafone greater flexibility to respond to changing business needs and introduce new offerings. Amdocs aOS will bring agentic capabilities across implementation and ongoing operations, supporting a move toward more intelligent, automated workflows that can continuously evolve. Amdocs is listed on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the ticker DOX and reported revenue of $4.53 billion in fiscal 2025. VodafoneThree is investing £11 billion in its network and services over 10 years.

Jon Ryan, Business Enablement Director at VodafoneThree, said the ambition is to give every business customer a simpler, faster and more consistent experience, backed by the UK's best network and the right digital foundations. He said the companies are consolidating B2B systems and transforming how Vodafone operates, introducing agentic capabilities that can automate workflows, continuously evolve and respond to changing customer needs. Anthony Goonetilleke, Group President, Growth Horizons at Amdocs, said communications service providers are moving beyond experimentation with AI and focusing on embedding agentic intelligence into the core of their operations at scale. He said the combination of aOS, proven BSS capabilities and deep telecom expertise is meant to help Vodafone Business build a more agile, intelligent operating model that can accelerate time to market, simplify the end-to-end customer journey and respond faster to changing business needs.

Amdocs describes itself as having more than 40 years of experience serving the world's leading communications companies, combining proprietary technology, deep industry expertise and end-to-end accountability from transformation through ongoing operations and evolution. The company says it runs billions of transactions daily and brings industry-specific AI into core business processes, advancing customers toward intelligent, increasingly autonomous operations across business, IT and network domains. VodafoneThree is a UK communications business serving consumers, businesses and public-sector organisations with mobile, broadband and digital services, and Vodafone Business helps organisations connect people, places and things through connectivity, cloud, cybersecurity and Internet of Things solutions. The press release did not say when the transformation is scheduled to be completed.

Articles.Title: Vodafone Business UK Selects Amdocs to Drive Agentic Transformation of B2B Operations with aOS
