stories.Headline: AT&T and Amdocs Expand Collaboration, Bringing Together Amdocs aOS and AT&T's AI-Enabled Framework to Simplify Operations and Improve Customer Experiences
stories.Summary:
AT&T and Amdocs announced on November 3, 2026 that they are expanding their longstanding collaboration through an eight-year agreement to modernize AT&T's business and customer operations using AI. The deal pairs Amdocs aOS, the company's agentic operating system for telecommunications, with AT&T's AI-enabled delivery framework. The companies said they will work as one delivery team, combining AT&T's technology environment and business priorities with Amdocs' telecom and engineering expertise. The goal is to simplify operations, improve efficiency, deliver new products and services faster, and enhance customer experiences.

Under the agreement, the two companies will share responsibility for delivering projects faster while reducing the total cost of modernizing and operating critical systems. Amdocs, which is listed on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol DOX, reported revenue of $4.53 billion in fiscal 2025. AT&T says it serves more than 100 million U.S. families, friends and neighbors, plus nearly 2.5 million businesses. Amdocs has more than 40 years of experience serving communications companies.

Jeremy Legg, Chief Technology Officer at AT&T, said the company is changing how it builds and operates technology so it can move faster and deliver more for customers. He said AI delivers the greatest value when it is grounded in the business, technology and people it supports, and that bringing together shared expertise can simplify complex work and bring new products and experiences to customers faster. Shimie Hortig, President and Chief Executive Officer of Amdocs, said the real test of AI in telecom is whether it can transform mission-critical systems and fundamentally change how communications companies operate. She said AT&T's approach to AI and its ambition to rethink technology delivery reflect its leadership in the industry.

The companies described the agreement as building on decades of trust between them. Amdocs said its aOS brings industry-specific AI into core business processes, advancing customers toward intelligent, increasingly autonomous operations across business, IT and network domains. Amdocs also included a forward-looking statement noting risks and uncertainties that could cause future results to differ from expectations, including macroeconomic conditions, trade policies and tariffs, competition, security incidents and the potential loss of a major customer. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the terms of the agreement.

Articles.Title: AT&T and Amdocs Expand Collaboration, Bringing Together Amdocs aOS and AT&T's AI-Enabled Framework to Simplify Operations and Improve Customer Experiences

stories.Headline: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
stories.Summary:
Fujifilm announced on Thursday that it will invest roughly 10 billion yen, about $63 million, to increase its production capacity for magnetic tape fivefold. The company said the spread of generative AI is producing exponential growth in data needs worldwide, which is driving demand for archiving. The 5x increase will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels. The investment covers the Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site, and Fujifilm called it the largest investment it has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.

The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel. The extra capacity is primarily meant to produce the latest-generation FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10 tape. Fujifilm's history with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000 the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011 it was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls fine hybrid magnetic particles by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech.

Fujifilm said major cloud service and data center operators have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. The company highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data. Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, Fujifilm said, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.

Articles.Title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand

stories.Headline: DataMEDS AI Signs MOU to Deploy Health Lives Here GLP-1 Patient Management Program with Florida-Based HMO
stories.Summary:
DataMEDS AI, Inc. signed a Memorandum of Understanding with a Florida-based health maintenance organization whose name is being withheld at its request, the company announced on November 5, 2026. The agreement covers deployment of the Health Lives Here mobile application, initially focused on helping members on GLP-1 receptor agonist medications manage their treatment. The HMO expects to have between 25,000 and 30,000 members for 2027 following open enrollment, which closes on December 8, 2026. NFL Alumni Health, a strategic marketing partner of Health Lives Here, expects to support member engagement efforts.

The program aims to improve medication adherence and HEDIS and CMS star ratings, initially in obesity and diabetes members. The HMO serves Medicare Advantage members, including Chronic Special Needs Plan and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan beneficiaries. DataMEDS would earn revenue on a per member per month model for use of the app by all HMO members, with additional revenue from an add-on GLP-1 drug patient management program. Further opportunities may arise in pharmacy dispensing, diagnostic lab testing and medical food products, and the companies expect to execute definitive agreements in the fourth quarter of 2026 to begin rolling out the app in the first quarter of 2027. The MOU is non-binding and subject to definitive agreements.

Gerald Commissiong, Interim Co-CEO of DataMEDS, said HMOs represent a significant opportunity for the company and Health Lives Here. He said the company has been adding technologies to its platform while making sure it markets the app not only direct-to-consumer but also to organizations that manage patients. He said the agreement positions DataMEDS to add its first corporate customer and to fine-tune its offering for payors. He said the framework opens the door to giving payor groups a platform they can easily implement to improve efficiency and encourage member engagement.

DataMEDS, formerly Wellgistics Health, Inc., is headquartered in Tampa, Florida, and trades on Nasdaq under the symbol MEDS. Its retail pharmacy, Corexa Pharmacy, is in-network with the HMO's pharmacy benefits manager and Medicare, and its diagnostic laboratory, Helomics, is in-network with Medicare. The press release lists forward-looking statements covering the timing of the rollout, pricing, member uptake, NFL Alumni Health's participation and related compliance matters, among other risks. It says actual results may differ materially and that the company undertakes no obligation to update its statements except as required by law.

Articles.Title: DataMEDS AI Signs MOU to Deploy Health Lives Here GLP-1 Patient Management Program with Florida-Based HMO

stories.Headline: AI Security | Automated AI Security Testing
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 3, 2026, that it plans to acquire Dreadnode, a company whose work supports automated AI security testing. The announcement came from CrowdStrike and was tied to its Fal.Con Europe event, where the company presented its latest innovations. The deal is meant to advance AI trust and to deliver automated AI security testing for what CrowdStrike calls the agentic enterprise. CrowdStrike also published a press release and a blog post about the acquisition alongside the announcement. The articles describe the problem the acquisition targets rather than the deal's price or closing terms.

They say AI models and agents are probabilistic, meaning they can be jailbroken, manipulated through prompt injection, and can fail in ways conventional software testing was never built to catch. Those weaknesses sit inside the model and the agent's reasoning loop, a layer traditional security testing never reaches, and most enterprises have no way to find them before deployment. Conventional testing, such as pentests, probes code rather than cognition, so it misses prompt injection and model-specific flaws. CrowdStrike frames the acquisition as a way to test every AI model, application, and agent for security weaknesses before deployment. The stated goal is to find AI weaknesses before attackers do, using real techniques to find what breaks and what to fix before deployment.

The company presents the deal as advancing AI trust for the agentic enterprise. No individual executive is named or quoted in the articles, so responsibility is attributed to CrowdStrike as a company. The context is CrowdStrike's broader push into AI security, which includes AI detection and response, agent security, and services such as frontier AI readiness and resilience. The articles do not give the acquisition price, a closing date, or other deal terms. They also do not say what happens next beyond the stated plan to acquire Dreadnode and deliver automated AI security testing.

Articles.Title: AI Security | Automated AI Security Testing

stories.Headline: AI debt is hitting record levels at the worst possible time
stories.Summary:
Wall Street is facing a growing challenge to the AI investment boom, which has delivered most of the S&P 500's gains since the bull market began four years ago. The flood of AI investment has shifted this year from cash generated by the biggest tech companies to borrowing. Tech sector debt issuance has reached around $623 billion this year, according to Wells Fargo data, a record share of borrowing from nonbank companies. Wells Fargo analysts estimate that around a third of this year's AI capital spending has been financed in the bond market.

The four largest hyperscalers, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta Platforms, need $730 billion in capital spending this year, with another $1 trillion-plus expected in 2027. Adding lower-credit-quality borrowing from companies such as Oracle and neocloud spending from the likes of CoreWeave takes the 2027 tally to around $1.6 trillion. The cost of that debt is rising: the investment-grade spread has risen to around 95 basis points from around 74 a year earlier, and spreads on AI related high-yield debt are nearing 350 basis points, the most since May 2025. Oracle raised $10 billion in debt this week plus $10 billion in stock, Microsoft closed a $25 billion bond deal last week, Alphabet sold a $6.7 billion euro-denominated deal and Meta is reportedly preparing another $20 billion in debt after a $97 billion equity raising last month.

Lawrence Gillium of LPL Financial says the divergence in spreads reflects a rational assessment that is likely to continue. He says the investment-grade gap should narrow if the buildout slows and supply eases, while the high-yield gap reflects real exposure to the buildout itself. He adds that losses would show up first at the leveraged end of AI credit if spending slows. S&P Global revised the outlook on Meta's AA credit rating to negative last week, citing a dramatic increase in leverage and a free cash flow outlook likely to remain negative beyond 2028.

Investors' main question has shifted from who is gaining the most ground in the AI buildout to who is ready to generate the best return on capital already committed. S&P 500 profits are expected to rise around 36% this year, with 2027 growth expected at less than half that pace. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise its benchmark rate for a second time this year in December, and next year's deficit is expected to pass $2 trillion. Henry Allen of Deutsche Bank says wider spreads raise the cost of capital and tighten financial conditions, making investment harder to justify.

Articles.Title: AI debt is hitting record levels at the worst possible time

stories.Headline: Copper Falls as Traders Assess AI Trade, US-Iran Diplomacy Hopes
stories.Summary:
Copper fell to a seven-week low on Tuesday as traders weighed the artificial-intelligence trade and the chances of diplomacy in the Middle East conflict. The metal dropped 2.2% on the London Metal Exchange to settle at $14,036 a metric ton, the lowest since Sept. 14. Comex copper fell 2.5% to settle at $6.4020 a pound. A drop in oil on unconfirmed reports of progress in peace talks in the US-Iran conflict pushed bond yields and the dollar higher, which weighed on metals priced in the US currency.

Concerns about the rollout of artificial-intelligence spending have hit equities in recent weeks, feeding fears about global growth and metals demand. South Korea's tech-heavy stock market came under pressure Tuesday, while a rebound in a gauge of chipmakers sent US equities higher. RBC Capital Markets analysts wrote that the selloff has put the AI demand narrative behind copper's rally under renewed scrutiny. Copper is still up about 13% this year, but Tuesday's decline threatens to push prices out of a range held over the past two months.

The 2026 rally was largely driven by expectations that the US would impose import tariffs on refined metals, and uncertainty over Washington's plans is now weighing on prices. Metals broadly can benefit from demand tied to spending on AI-linked infrastructure, but copper has stood out as a potential major winner. Tin, used in soldering electric circuitry, also fell 4.5% to the lowest since April. All other base metals on the LME declined.

Articles.Title: Copper Falls as Traders Assess AI Trade, US-Iran Diplomacy Hopes

stories.Headline: India's new AI-training framework is a repeat of old mistakes
stories.Summary:
India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology released a new framework last week aimed at breaking the data deadlock and widening access to data for building artificial intelligence models. The framework is called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI Training, and it is meant to allow responsible data sharing while ensuring privacy, transparency and trust. The article, published on 3 November 2026, was written by Rahul Matthan, a partner at Trilegal and the author of a book on India's approach to data governance. He argues that the framework is not a new architecture and that it undercuts much of what India's original DEPA was designed to achieve.

Under the original DEPA, decisions about what can be done with personal data sat with the data principal, but the new handbook moves that power to training data providers such as hospitals and banks. The handbook starts from the premise that individual consent is impractical at scale, and it makes those providers responsible for sourcing, curating and preparing datasets for AI training. It offers data principals little beyond a suggestion that providers could get priority access to the resulting models and a promise to explore royalties for them. Matthan writes that direct benefits will go only to model developers and the institutions that hold personal data, not to the people whose data was used.

Electronics and information technology minister Ashwini Vaishnaw says in his foreword that the framework is consent-based and user-controlled, which Matthan says the rest of the document contradicts. The principal scientific advisor calls it an elegant, India-specific solution in his foreword, but Matthan notes that secure data environments are not new. He points to Finland's 2019 law on secondary use of health and social data and the UK's 2022 Data Saves Lives strategy, which made secure data environments the default for National Health Service data. He also cites a 2022 project in which 71 institutions led by Penn Medicine trained a brain tumour model using federated learning in a confidential clean room.

Matthan traces part of the problem to an earlier mistake, when DEPA was called a consent management framework instead of a portability solution, and the term consent managers then entered the Digital Personal Data Protection Act with a different meaning. He describes the 40-page handbook as a word salad of technological jargon and regulatory buzzwords that promises more than it can deliver. He says the failings in it exceed anything he has seen before. The article does not say what the government or the ministry plans to do next.

Articles.Title: India's new AI-training framework is a repeat of old mistakes

stories.Headline: AI is disrupting the art of campaigning
stories.Summary:
At least 220 campaign ads in the current US election cycle have used AI-generated content, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising. More than $137m has been spent airing these ads. Two examples involve James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan. One ad shows Talarico wearing a dress and singing about transgender children, while another shows El-Sayed laughing at cards reading “Death to America” and “Celebrate 9/11”.

A recent survey by the American Association of Political Consultants found that 83% of campaign strategists and political consultants regularly use AI for their work. El-Sayed paid $170,000 to Daisychain, a company offering an AI-powered platform that holds personalised conversations with voters over text messages. The progressive group Swing Left has volunteers record voice memos of conversations with voters, and AI software analyses hundreds of these recordings to help campaigns tailor their messages. Saikat Chakrabarti, an unsuccessful Democratic House candidate in California, had three staffers use AI to code replacements for virtually all the campaign’s paid software.

Yasmin Radjy, Swing Left’s executive director, said AI gives campaigns a much better ability to understand the idiosyncrasies of a voter. Eric Wilson of the Centre for Campaign Innovation argued that the core of a campaign, connecting with voters, is still a people business, and that AI lets campaigns do more of that than the boring, busy work. He also said concerns about AI attack ads are overblown, likening them to political parody. The AAPC found that at least 38% of voters had received election information from an AI search summary.

A study by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a think-tank in London, found that leading chatbots gave wrong, incomplete or outdated answers to over a quarter of basic questions about the midterms. VisionHeight, a cyber-security firm, recently uncovered dozens of apparently AI-generated websites masquerading as local newspapers, designed to trick chatbots into pumping out favourable coverage of certain congressional candidates. A Russian disinformation network is thought to be behind videos in which a supposed former student falsely accuses Talarico of sex crimes. Of the $137m spent on AI ads, 88% has come from Republican campaigns and aligned groups.

Articles.Title: AI is disrupting the art of campaigning

stories.Headline: Shivamogga SP appeals to students to use social media, AI tools responsibly
stories.Summary:
Shivamogga Superintendent of Police B. Nikhil spoke to students on Tuesday at the 40th foundation day of Kuvempu University in Shankaraghatta. He appealed to them to use social media and artificial intelligence tools responsibly. He warned that careless use can harm students' careers and futures. He said unethical activities that start on social media are on the rise.

Mr. Nikhil said posts and comments that break the law, whether made while hiding one's identity or by mistake, can ruin a student's career. He said digital footprints cannot be erased once a person logs in and uses digital media. He said AI is spreading into every field, including education, and should be used to supplement studies rather than relied on entirely. He also urged students not to feel dejected if they do not land high-ranking posts, saying that doing any chosen job with sincerity is the real achievement.

Vice-Chancellor Sharath Ananthamurthy said students should not confine themselves to textbooks and should take an active part in art, literature and cultural activities. He said the university would provide more opportunities for distinctive learning experiences in the coming days. Registrar (Evaluation) Prof. R. Thimmarayappa, Dean of Student Welfare Prof. G. Prashanth Naik, deans Prof. S.K. Narasimhamurthy and Prof. Gajanana Prabhu, and extracurricular activities coordinator Dr. Talawar Venkatesh were present. Faculty members, non-teaching staff and students also attended.

Articles.Title: Shivamogga SP appeals to students to use social media, AI tools responsibly

stories.Headline: Friday's jobs report could be a tiebreaker for Wall Street's AI trade as inflation worries linger
stories.Summary:
The October jobs report is due on Friday, and it could act as a tiebreaker for Wall Street's AI trade, according to a Business Insider article by Joe Ciolli published on November 5, 2026. The market has been torn between worries about AI spending and valuations and relief from falling oil prices and inflation expectations. Oil's decline continued on Wednesday after a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, with Brent crude falling below $100 per barrel for the first time in months. All major US stock indexes soared as investors embraced the low-oil and moderating-inflation narrative.

Economists expect about 65,000 payroll additions in Friday's report, a number that could signal a healthy cooldown, growth headwinds, or renewed inflation trouble. The best case for stocks would be a modest payroll number, steady unemployment, and tame wage growth, which could keep Treasury yields falling and give expensive AI growth stocks breathing room. A weak payroll number would raise fears that recent AI wobbles are part of a broader slowdown, while a surprisingly strong number could rekindle inflation fears and send yields back up. That would put fresh pressure on the AI trade, especially companies that have leaned more heavily on debt financing.

The article says the report won't answer whether AI will deliver on all its promises. It could answer the more immediate question of whether markets have enough macro breathing room to stay patient while they wait. Investors are already asking tougher questions about financing, which firms want to avoid. The article does not say what happens next beyond Friday's report.

Articles.Title: Friday's jobs report could be a tiebreaker for Wall Street's AI trade as inflation worries linger

stories.Headline: AI disruption, geopolitics and partnerships in focus at Hong Kong business summit
stories.Summary:
About 100 business owners, executives and academics attended the fourth edition of the Family Business Summit in Hong Kong. The event was co-hosted by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital, with UBS as the presenting partner. It took place on Wednesday and Thursday, with the article published on 5 November 2026. Technology-driven disruptions, superpower rivalry and global partnerships dominated the closed-door discussions.

Attendees came from the United States, mainland China, Hong Kong, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. At a welcome dinner on Wednesday, Singapore's Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo spoke about her country's approach to AI. She discussed how the city state aims to capitalise on the technology while ensuring no one is left behind. The summit's focus reflected efforts by countries and tech giants to boost growth and lead the race in artificial intelligence.

The gathering was the fourth edition of the event, which brings together family business owners, executives and academics. Josephine Teo is the minister responsible for digital development and information in Singapore, and she addressed the dinner on Wednesday. The article paraphrases her remarks as covering how Singapore seeks to benefit from AI while making sure no one is excluded. The summit was co-hosted by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital, with UBS as presenting partner.

These organisations organised the event, which drew about 100 participants. The context is a global push by countries and technology companies to drive growth and compete for leadership in artificial intelligence. Superpower rivalry and technology-driven disruption shaped the agenda alongside global partnerships. The article does not say what follows the summit or any planned outcomes.

Articles.Title: AI disruption, geopolitics and partnerships in focus at Hong Kong business summit

stories.Headline: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute starts operations with AI focus; names interim CEO
stories.Summary:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore launched the Future of Finance Institute on Nov 3, and it began operations that day with a focus on AI in finance. The institute was first announced in June, with the aim of speeding up the adoption of new financial technologies and encouraging innovation in the financial sector. Alan Lim, who heads the financial infrastructure and AI office at MAS, is serving as interim CEO of the FFI at the same time as his existing role. MAS said he will lead the institute’s strategy and operations as it builds out its programmes and deepens partnerships in the financial and technology ecosystems.

The FFI will bring financial institutions together to share practical experience in implementing AI, develop good practices for deploying agentic AI, and strengthen the management of risks from AI use. To start, it will work through three pillars, PathFin.ai, BuildFin.ai and SafeFin.ai. Under PathFin.ai it will build on the existing programme and widen the range of solutions available through its knowledge hub, and it will also gather industry practitioners to discuss common challenges and practical approaches to AI adoption. Under BuildFin.ai it will work with industry players on guidance, good practices, industry standards, and common tools and infrastructure for deploying AI, with a focus on the safe use of AI agents in financial services.

Under SafeFin.ai it will promote sound AI risk management practices. MAS managing director Chia Der Jiun said the FFI will seek to anchor key capabilities in Singapore and connect the ecosystem to speed up innovation and support safe adoption of new technologies. The launch comes as banks and regulators become increasingly concerned about the risks that rapid AI adoption may bring to the financial industry. MAS said the FFI will progressively expand into other areas of financial innovation, including tokenisation.

Articles.Title: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute starts operations with AI focus; names interim CEO

stories.Headline: ‘At some point it’s going to be too much’: global financiers grapple with AI risks
stories.Summary:
Global financiers warned at a Hong Kong summit that the artificial intelligence boom is creating unprecedented demand for capital and infrastructure. They spoke on a panel at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit on 3 November 2026. The executives questioned whether debt markets, power grids and corporate productivity can keep pace with the technology's expansion. Emmanuel Roman, CEO of Pimco, said investment in AI infrastructure could reach US$10 trillion over the next five years.

Roman noted that this figure approaches the size of the US$12 trillion US bond market. He said that at some point it is going to be too much. He compared the transformation to the Industrial Revolution in Britain in 1760. He also pointed out that rising interest rates or intensifying geopolitical tensions could trigger a downturn.

The warnings came from executives of global asset management firms and investment banks. Roman, as CEO of Pimco, gave the specific figures on AI infrastructure investment and the US bond market. He described the scale of the boom as a possible burden at some point. The panel discussion took place during the Hong Kong summit.

The articles do not say what specific measures or policies the executives proposed. They do not name any next steps or decisions from the summit. The context given is the unprecedented demand for capital and infrastructure created by the AI boom. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the warnings raised at the panel.

Articles.Title: ‘At some point it’s going to be too much’: global financiers grapple with AI risks

stories.Headline: Grab eyes more AI investment after Taiwan deal blocked
stories.Summary:
Grab Holdings tried to buy rival Foodpanda's Taiwan business, and the deal was blocked, Nikkei Asia reported on November 3, 2026. The company is now looking to put more money into artificial intelligence and into support for its drivers and merchant partners, according to its chief financial officer. The report gave no date for when the Taiwan deal was blocked and did not say who blocked it. Grab's ride-hailing revenue grew 10% year on year in the July-September quarter of 2026, the article said.

The chief financial officer said Grab has no other deals "on the horizon" outside Southeast Asia, according to the report. The article did not name the CFO or give any figure for how much Grab might invest in AI. It also did not say how much Grab had offered for the Taiwan business. The report did not give a timeline for the new investment plans.

Grab is based in Singapore and runs ride-hailing and delivery services across Southeast Asia. The article mentions a prior report that SoftBank and Grab would develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia's Sarawak, and that SoftBank plans a $50bn AI investment in Malaysia, according to the country's prime minister. The report did not say whether the blocked Taiwan deal and the AI plans are directly connected. It gave no further detail on what happens next with the Taiwan business or with Grab's investment plans.

Articles.Title: Grab eyes more AI investment after Taiwan deal blocked

stories.Headline: As global AI sell-offs rattle investors, Goldman Sachs touts ‘enormous opportunities’
stories.Summary:
A sell-off in artificial intelligence technology stocks in China rattled investors around the world, the South China Morning Post reported on 3 November 2026. The report was published at 2:39pm and updated at 5:47pm that day, and was written by Zhang Shidong in Shanghai. Despite the pullback, two large Wall Street firms said they still expect the technology to deliver productivity gains and lower costs. The article described the AI boom as a possible super-long cycle.

The article names David Solomon, chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs, and Ted Pick, chairman and CEO of Morgan Stanley. Both spoke on Tuesday at the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. They touted the prospects of the technology and the demand for it. They also pointed to the resilience of the US economy, which the article says withstood global headwinds including an oil shock caused by prolonged military conflicts in the Middle East.

The article says the two men suggested the current pullback in technology stocks could be a temporary speed bump. It does not give any figures, dates beyond the publication and summit timing, or specific commitments from the firms. The report frames the sell-off as having unnerved many investors, while the two executives maintain that the productivity and cost benefits of AI will win out. No further details on the scale of the sell-off are provided.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the executives’ remarks at the summit. It offers no timeline for a recovery or any policy response. The context given is the global AI sell-off and the Middle East conflicts affecting oil. More to follow.

Articles.Title: As global AI sell-offs rattle investors, Goldman Sachs touts ‘enormous opportunities’

stories.Headline: Why Chinese AI stars like Z.ai, MiniMax struggle to match Anthropic’s profit margin
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed an IPO prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission last week, and the filing showed a large profitability gap with Chinese AI developers Z.ai and MiniMax. Anthropic reported a gross profit margin of 85.4 per cent in the first half of 2026. Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, reported 26.4 per cent for the same period. MiniMax reported 17.9 per cent, according to Anthropic's S-1 prospectus and the two Hong Kong-listed companies' latest financial disclosures.

The figures compare the Claude developer with its most direct Chinese counterparts. The comparison comes despite continued advances in model capabilities by the Chinese companies. The article says the US giant's massive revenue advantage highlights the struggle Chinese AI developers face. It also says the gap shows the challenges China's AI model developers face in turning technological advances into sustainable businesses.

Anthropic is the company behind Claude, and it made the filing with the SEC. Z.ai is also known as Zhipu AI, and it is listed in Hong Kong along with MiniMax. Analysts said the filing revealed a significant financial advantage for Anthropic over the Chinese firms. The article does not give direct comments from the companies.

The article frames the gap as a test for China's AI model developers. It says they have made technical gains but still struggle to match Anthropic's profit margin. The article does not say what steps the companies plan to take next. It also does not say when further financial results will be released.

Articles.Title: Why Chinese AI stars like Z.ai, MiniMax struggle to match Anthropic’s profit margin

stories.Headline: Open-source AI is the ‘only’ sustainable way forward, says Alibaba’s Joe Tsai
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Group chairman Joe Tsai said on Tuesday that open source is the only viable path to a sustainable artificial intelligence industry. He spoke at the opening ceremony of the annual World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Zhejiang province, eastern China. Tsai pointed to growing agreement on open ecosystems among domestic tech companies. He said this comes as rising AI demand runs into continuing shortages of computing power.

Tsai said that only through open source can AI become popularised, and only through popularisation can a sustainable and inclusive intelligent era be created. He described open-source systems as the only way to build a sustainable, inclusive AI industry. The event was backed by the Cyberspace Administration of China and the Zhejiang provincial government. The article was published by the South China Morning Post on 3 November 2026.

Tsai is the co-founder and chairman of Alibaba, and he made the remarks as the company doubles down on its open-source AI strategy. The article says his comments came amid pushback from the United States. It gives no further details on that pushback. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Open-source AI is the ‘only’ sustainable way forward, says Alibaba’s Joe Tsai

stories.Headline: US tech giants' hidden AI debt swells 90% to $3.2tn in 6 months
stories.Summary:
US tech giants' hidden debt tied to artificial intelligence rose about 90% in six months, reaching roughly $3.2 trillion, Nikkei Asia reported on November 4, 2026. The report said the off-balance-sheet debt comes from AI-related commitments and obligations. It said these obligations equal about 80% of the companies' assets. The article named Google and Meta among the companies involved.

The report said investors are increasingly alarmed by spending that appears to have no end. It described the companies as pouring money into AI infrastructure, including data centers. The figures cover off-balance-sheet debt, meaning obligations kept off the companies' balance sheets. The article did not give a full list of the companies beyond naming Google and Meta.

The article did not say who is responsible beyond the tech giants themselves, and it gave no direct statements from company officials. It did not say what the companies plan to do about the debt. It also did not say what regulators or investors will do next. The report gave no timeline for future disclosures.

The article appeared in Nikkei Asia and was dated November 4, 2026, Japan time. It was filed from Palo Alto, California, and written by Kohei Yamada. The report linked the debt growth to the AI boom and heavy spending on AI infrastructure. It did not say what happens next beyond noting investor concern.

Articles.Title: US tech giants' hidden AI debt swells 90% to $3.2tn in 6 months

stories.Headline: The Wait Is Over: 2 Historic Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Splits Were Just Announced
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms announced its first-ever stock split on Oct. 21, 2026, through its quarterly report, and Sandisk announced its first split since being spun off from Western Digital in February 2025 just eight days later. Meta's move creates a new class of stock, with current Class A shareholders receiving a one-for-one Class C non-voting stock dividend after the Jan. 19 effective date. That structure effectively acts as a 2-for-1 split of Meta's Class A shares. Meta had been the only member of the Magnificent Seven that had not split its stock, and its shares had oscillated between $500 and $750 for more than two years.

Sandisk's board of directors approved an aggressive 8-for-1 forward split, which becomes effective after the close of trading on Nov. 19. The company said the split is designed to make its shares more accessible to retail investors and employees. Sandisk shares had skyrocketed more than 6,000% at one point since its public debut. Over the last 14 months, Sandisk's 2027 projected earnings per share jumped from less than $10 to nearly $228, and its gross margin reached almost 85%.

Meta said the unorthodox new share class was meant to make its shares more accessible to retail investors who cannot purchase fractional shares through their broker. Sandisk attributed the need for its split to overwhelming demand for memory and storage solutions in AI-accelerated data centers, a combination of strong demand and persistent supply shortages. The article notes that history shows memory and storage products are highly cyclical, with premium pricing power rarely having staying power. Sandisk has reduced near-term risk by locking in orders more than a year in advance, though the prospect of an AI bubble-bursting event still looms large.

The article frames both splits against investor enthusiasm for high-profile stock splits alongside the AI trend. A stock split lets a public company alter its share price and outstanding share count by the same factor without affecting its market cap or operating performance. Meta generates most of its revenue from advertising on its family apps, including Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads, and is integrating generative AI into its ad platforms. Meta also recently introduced Muse, its agentic personal AI tool capable of multitasking on users' behalf.

Articles.Title: The Wait Is Over: 2 Historic Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Splits Were Just Announced

stories.Headline: [ROUNDTABLE] Korea must navigate US-China AI rivalry with strategic clarity: experts - The Korea Times
stories.Summary:
The Korea Times hosted a roundtable titled “Beyond U.S.-China AI race: Korea’s strategic edge” in Seoul on Oct. 28, with the article published Nov. 4, 2026. Participants included Kim Sung-han, former national security adviser and Korea University professor emeritus, Reform Party of Korea Rep. Lee Jun-seok, Lim Jong-in, former presidential cybersecurity adviser and Soongsil University AI committee chair, and Bone AI CEO Lee Do-kyung. Korea Times President-Publisher Oh Young-jin moderated the discussion. The roundtable examined how Korea should navigate competition between the United States and China over artificial intelligence.

Lim Jong-in estimated that the United States accounts for 50 percent of frontier AI model development capabilities, China 40 percent and the rest of the world 10 percent. He said China had reached about 90 percent of the U.S. level with models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, while U.S. equipment restrictions and sluggish domestic demand constrained China’s AI development and deployment. He identified memory chips, power infrastructure and energy storage systems as areas where Korea could benefit from U.S. efforts to exclude China from supply chains, while warning of possible Chinese retaliation. Participants cited the Maven Smart System, developed by Palantir Technologies, as a U.S. military AI platform that helped U.S. forces identify, prioritize and strike more than 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of the campaign against Iran.

Kim Sung-han called for high-level consultations between Cheong Wa Dae and the White House to define the scope of cooperation with China, saying Korea can cooperate with China outside narrowly defined areas involving critical technologies. He said Seoul realistically needs to consult Washington to ensure such cooperation does not violate U.S. export controls. Rep. Lee Jun-seok warned against excluding China, noting that Chinese AI models offer overwhelming cost advantages, particularly in inference, and said areas not involving core national interests or critical technology leaks should be opened. Lee Do-kyung stressed that Korea should find areas where it can build its own competitive advantages, pointing to manufacturing capabilities and industry-specific operational knowledge.

Participants warned that Korea should draw clear boundaries between areas open to cooperation with China and those involving critical security interests. Kim said Korea should account for military technology gaps when discussing the transfer of wartime operational control from the U.S., arguing that Seoul should use its integration with U.S. military systems and standards to learn from American technology and strengthen its own capabilities before the transfer. Rep. Lee raised similar concerns, warning that Korea’s existing defense posture could become vulnerable if North Korea develops an effective AI-powered command system ahead of Seoul or acquires such technology from China or Russia. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title:
[ROUNDTABLE]
Korea must navigate US-China AI rivalry with strategic clarity: experts - The Korea Times

stories.Headline: Kospi slides at open 3.36% on concerns over AI infrastructure spending
stories.Summary:
Korean stocks opened sharply lower on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as concerns about massive spending on AI infrastructure weighed on the market ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The Kospi fell 196.71 points, or 3.36 percent, to 5,662.37 as of 9:15 a.m. Overnight, U.S. stocks closed mixed, with the Nasdaq Composite down 1.07 percent and the S&P 500 down 0.51 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.41 percent. Oil prices fell on optimism about a potential U.S.-Iran peace agreement.

In Seoul, most shares opened in negative territory. Samsung Electronics tumbled 4.59 percent, and chipmaker SK hynix slumped 5.1 percent. Carmaker Hyundai Motor decreased 1.57 percent, and energy firm Doosan Enerbility sank 3.77 percent. Shipbuilder HD Hyundai Heavy Industries fell 2.26 percent, and defense company Hanwha Aerospace declined 0.81 percent. The local currency rose 3.95 won from the previous session's close to trade at 1,342.05 against the greenback as of 9:15 a.m.

The article attributes the decline to lingering concerns over massive spending on AI infrastructure, with tech and AI shares remaining shaky in U.S. trading. It does not name any official who commented on the drop. The report also notes that investors were focused on the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday. It gives no further statements from companies or authorities.

The article provides no additional context beyond the opening numbers and does not say what happens next. It does not include any forecasts or plans from regulators or officials. No further details on the cause of the AI spending concerns are given. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Kospi slides at open 3.36% on concerns over AI infrastructure spending

stories.Headline: Pentagon Task Force Plans Public Inventory of Rules Governing US AI Labs
stories.Summary:
Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael said on November 4, 2026, that the U.S. federal government plans to publish an overview of the laws and regulations that apply to domestic AI companies later this month, according to a Reuters report. Michael, who is vice chair of the government's Super Intelligence Task Force, made the announcement at a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California. He said the group expects to make the regulatory overview public within one or two weeks. The task force is an intergovernmental agency established by President Donald Trump to shape federal AI policy, and it intends to lay out the existing regulatory landscape for domestic AI labs.

Michael said the goal is to create a framework that gives Americans confidence that AI companies will act responsibly, according to the report. He warned that, without a coordinated approach, Congress could produce fragmented regulation that could harm the industry. Michael did not provide details about the document's scope, the agencies involved or how it would be used. The announcement signals an effort to map existing rules rather than introduce new legal requirements, and the scope, level of detail and intended use of the forthcoming document remain unclear.

For chief data officers, a clearer picture of the federal regulatory landscape could help organizations assess how existing obligations apply to their AI initiatives, particularly where data privacy, security, intellectual property and accountability intersect. However, an overview of existing laws will not replace the internal structures organizations and AI governance need to manage AI systems. Companies still need clear ownership of AI-related risks, documented approval processes, controls over data access and mechanisms for monitoring systems after deployment. As organizations align internal policies with evolving requirements, allocating responsibility across technology, legal, risk and data teams will remain important. The task force's forthcoming publication should provide a clearer indication of how the administration intends to describe the rules governing the U.S. AI companies.

Articles.Title: Pentagon Task Force Plans Public Inventory of Rules Governing US AI Labs

stories.Headline: European Enterprises Face Growing Pressure to Turn AI Investment into Business Value, ISG Says
stories.Summary:
Information Services Group, a technology research and advisory firm, published new research finding that European enterprises are under growing pressure to turn AI adoption into measurable business value. The research found that AI performance and adoption are exceeding expectations, but business and financial returns are lagging. ISG announced the findings in a press release on November 5, 2026. The firm said strategies for moving AI beyond isolated experiments will be explored at the 2026 ISG AI Impact Summit Paris.

The summit will take place November 9 to 10 at the Pullman Paris Tour Eiffel. Leaders from the Adecco Group, ArianeGroup, Cigref, Lagardère Travel Retail, Linxens, Pfizer, Philip Morris International, Thales and WPP will join the event. The first day will open with a keynote by Pierre Matuchet, senior vice president for IT and Digital Transformation at the Adecco Group. Sessions will cover identifying high-value use cases, governance, process redesign and measuring returns, and a panel on sovereign AI will feature Général Dominique Trinquand of DHT Conseil and Marc Valès of Terrespace.

Pierre Moulin, a director at ISG and chair of the summit, said many enterprises are struggling to translate productivity gains from AI into business outcomes. He said European organizations must work out how to capture returns from AI while keeping control of their data, managing risk and preparing their people and systems for increasingly autonomous operations. Day two will open with a keynote by Remi Tromeur of Thales Global Services on AI in vendor management. A panel on human and AI collaboration will feature Valentine Ferreol of Linxens, Ritika Rajpal of WPP and David Rudnianski of Loxam.

The summit is sponsored by DXC Technology, Tata Communications, Tata Consultancy Services, NTT DATA, Inetum, Accenture, Clocate and the TBM Council. ISG describes itself as a global AI-centered technology research and advisory firm with more than 900 clients, including 75 of the world's top 100 enterprises. The firm was founded in 2006 and has 1,500 professionals worldwide. The articles do not say what happens after the summit.

Articles.Title: European Enterprises Face Growing Pressure to Turn AI Investment into Business Value, ISG Says

stories.Headline: Another refrigerator hack in Europe, temperatures raised to as high as 50 degrees causing damage… the inescapable risk of ‘AI-connected appliances’
stories.Summary:
On the 2nd, local time, grocery distribution companies including supermarket chains in several European countries were hit by a cyberattack, and refrigerator and freezer temperatures spiked one after another, according to AP and Reuters. The incidents came after a similar one in France last month and recurred across countries including Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Estonia and Ireland. External hackers reportedly manipulated freezing and refrigeration systems remotely, switching refrigerators and freezers to defrost mode and raising internal temperatures. The article's headline says temperatures were raised to as high as 50 degrees, causing damage. The hacking caused physical damage such as spoilage of stored groceries and supply disruptions, and refrigerators at a supermarket in Brussels, Belgium stood empty.

Hwang Seok-jin, a professor at Dongguk University's Graduate School of International Information Security, said the case is a signal that security threats are expanding beyond personal data leaks to everyday life and industrial facilities, and that attacks are shifting from stealing data or money to manipulating physical environments such as temperature, power and equipment. Um Heung-ryeol, honorary professor in the Department of Information Security at Soonchunhyang University, said cyber attackers newly equipped with AI-based tools can quickly find vulnerabilities and now have the capacity to attack targets from refrigerators and IoT appliances to apartment complexes, and called the refrigerator hacking a representative example that any system with an internet touchpoint can become prey. The article also reports that the red team at Anthropic last month released findings that an AI model can seize home IoT devices without high-performance GPUs and turn them into beachheads for hacking. It notes Samsung Electronics has presented security solutions such as Knox and LG Electronics has offered Shield, while anxiety about hacking grows as AI technology for locating vulnerabilities improves rapidly.

The article says concern is growing that appliances connected via the Internet of Things will be exploited as major intrusion pathways, and that smart home services using AI to centrally control multiple appliances are increasingly likely to become the weak link. It adds that in ordinary households, smart home platforms connecting appliances such as TVs, air conditioners and vacuum cleaners, and devices such as doorbells, door locks and thermostats, could also become intrusion pathways, with attackers possibly seizing AI control privileges or leaking living information collected by appliances. It also reports that the intelligent home network service handling apartment access management and visitor vehicles is a target, and that the reservation management system for community facilities at GS Construction apartment complexes was recently hacked and residents' personal information leaked. Hwang said security must be a priority in an environment where AI connects everything, and that it is necessary to inspect domestic cold-chain logistics and other remote-control systems and establish an independent control architecture that keeps equipment operating safely even if a breach occurs.

Articles.Title: Another refrigerator hack in Europe, temperatures raised to as high as 50 degrees causing damage… the inescapable risk of ‘AI-connected appliances’

stories.Headline: Lee calls deeper Japan cooperation an urgent task as AI reshapes global economy
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that deepening cooperation with Japan is a key task as AI drives global upheaval. He made the remark in a written speech at the Future Economic Forum 2026, hosted by Yonhap News Agency. The speech was read by his press secretary, Seong Ghi-hong. The forum was held under the theme of a fragmenting global economy and bridging the Korean and Japanese markets. Lee pointed to supply chains, AI, aerospace and biotechnology as areas for expanded economic cooperation.

Lee said the world is seeing unprecedented changes in its security situation and trade order. He said AI-driven technological innovation is bringing fundamental changes to people's lives and the future. He said fostering Seoul and Tokyo ties is a timely task against that backdrop. He said his government is strengthening the foundation for trust with Japan based on brisk shuttle diplomacy. He said the scope of Korea-Japan economic cooperation is expanding beyond supply chain stabilization to advanced technologies, including AI, aerospace and biotechnology.

Lee also cited low birthrates and an aging population as social issues the two countries share. He said the two countries are working together to address them through joint responses. He called on participants to explore further ways to deepen bilateral economic cooperation. The article does not say what steps come next.

Articles.Title: Lee calls deeper Japan cooperation an urgent task as AI reshapes global economy

stories.Headline: LG Uplus CTO says S. Korea, Japan could find synergies in voice AI ahead of 6G
stories.Summary:
Lee Sang-yup, the chief technology officer of South Korean mobile carrier LG Uplus, spoke on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at a forum in Seoul hosted by Yonhap News Agency. He said South Korea and Japan could generate synergies in voice artificial intelligence services ahead of the commercialization of sixth-generation, or 6G, networks. He made the remarks when asked about possible areas of technological cooperation between the two countries. The forum was held under the theme of a fragmenting global economy and connecting South Korea and Japan through one market.

Lee said the two countries have considerable room to collaborate in the AI era, particularly in voice AI, because each country has its own linguistic nuances. He said he believes the voice AI field offers opportunities for synergy between the two countries. According to the article, 6G networks are expected to be AI-native, with built-in agentic voice and intelligent calling services. These could shift mobile communications away from traditional app-based interactions toward natural, context-aware voice interfaces and personal AI assistants. Lee said next-generation AI services would be orchestrated through a combination of cloud-based, on-device and platform AI.

Lee said LG Uplus is currently building and testing hybrid AI infrastructure. The forum brought together around 500 participants from the two countries, including political, business and academic leaders. The article does not say what specific steps, agreements or timelines would follow from Lee's remarks. It also does not say what South Korean or Japanese officials plan to do next.

Articles.Title: LG Uplus CTO says S. Korea, Japan could find synergies in voice AI ahead of 6G

stories.Headline: 100 AI, chip, biotech firms to recruit young talent at Seoul Job Fair
stories.Summary:
Around 100 high-tech companies in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, semiconductors and robotics will gather at Dongdaemun Design Plaza in central Seoul on Nov. 9 for the 2026 Seoul Job Fair. The event will run from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and is hosted by the Seoul Metropolitan Government, the Korea Industrial Technology Association and the Korea Student Aid Foundation.

Sixty companies, including pharmaceutical firm Huons and surgical robot maker Meere Company, plan to hire about 400 people. Another 40 or so companies will take part in a youth AI talent festival held alongside the fair. Job seekers can have one-on-one interviews and consultations with recruiters on site. A QR code-based system lets them check their place in line and browse other companies' openings while they wait.

AI-based services will recommend companies that match applicants' preferred jobs and working conditions, and an AI "culture fit" test will help them find workplaces suited to their personalities and values. Visitors can also try AI, robotics, virtual reality and drone technologies at experience booths. Kim Hyun-woo, director general of the city's Economic Policy Office, said the city will strengthen practical hiring links between companies and job seekers so young people can land quality jobs in future industries. The city has held the fair three times since 2022.

In total, 204 companies and about 8,500 job seekers have taken part, and about 1,220 people have been hired. At the same venue, the city will hold an AI talent festival for the Seoul Software Academy, its free job training program for young people. The festival includes lectures on AI-era careers, a startup pitch event, project presentations and a generative AI hackathon. In the hackathon, 12 finalists will propose AI solutions to problems young Seoul residents face, such as finding jobs and housing.

Articles.Title: 100 AI, chip, biotech firms to recruit young talent at Seoul Job Fair

stories.Headline: These rare killer whales are threatened by shipping noise. AI is turning down the din
stories.Summary:
In September, 76 southern resident killer whales arrived in the Salish Sea, the last of an endangered population. Each year the few score left enter Admiralty Inlet and head toward Puget Sound, Washington, moving in and out from late summer until early winter to hunt Chinook salmon. Noise from heavy shipping traffic affects their ability to hunt, communicate and echolocate, and vessels pose a deadly collision risk. Scientists did not realize the southern resident was a genetically distinct group from the more populous Bigg's killer whale until the 1970s.

The first survey in 1974 found 71 whales, the count peaked at 97 in 1996 and declined to 79 in 2001, and the southern resident was listed as endangered in 2005. A 2024 study found that for every one decibel increase in maximum noise level, females were 58% less likely to pursue prey, and males and females were 12.5% less likely to capture prey. In 2022 Quiet Sound introduced a voluntary slow-down program for ships along a 20-mile stretch coming into Seattle, Tacoma and Everett, and Aronson said participation this season has been 73% and underwater noise has fallen by as much as 50% since it began. In July 2025, SMRU Consulting and Microsoft partnered to test whether AI on board a buoy could correctly identify killer whale and humpback whale calls, and in July the Communications Acoustics Buoy was launched in the Haro Strait.

Rachel Aronson, program director of Quiet Sound, an initiative within Maritime Blue, said underwater noise is a pervasive threat and that when it is loud underwater it gets harder for the whales to find food, so they sometimes hunt and miss or forgo hunting, which is a problem especially for a female building up to a pregnancy or nursing a baby. Cormac Booth, managing director of SMRU Consulting, a subsidiary of the University of St Andrews in the UK, said marine acoustic monitoring has been around for decades but the gap between data collection and analysis was once many months, and that the focus has moved away from an after-the-fact archival approach toward reliable insights of what is happening now. Juan Lavista Ferres, chief data scientist and corporate vice president of Microsoft and lab director of the Microsoft AI for Good Lab, said underwater monitoring produces far more audio than people can review manually and that AI helps most with processing this data in near-real time, and he said results so far are encouraging and false positives have decreased. Jason Wood, principal scientist and deputy director of technology at SMRU Consulting, said the Haro Strait offers the biggest bang for your buck for southern residents.

Washington is a trade-dependent state where 40% of jobs are tied to international commerce, so balancing maritime industries with wildlife conservation is a delicate act. SMRU Consulting has developed smart buoys since 2014, used in Scotland, the US East Coast and the Pacific Northwest, and Microsoft's Water SPARROW, an aquatic version of its wildlife monitoring AI launched in 2024, is already used in camera traps. The buoy has three hydrophones anchored underwater, with Microsoft's system floating in the buoy and SMRU's analysis system below the surface, and Wood said the two are engaged in a bake off to see which detects southern resident signals with the greatest accuracy. Wood said that due to the risk of false positives, the buoy, and the article ends there.

Articles.Title: These rare killer whales are threatened by shipping noise. AI is turning down the din

stories.Headline: Kospi dips over 3% following escalating AI concerns
stories.Summary:
Stocks in South Korea fell more than 3 percent on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as heavy selling in technology shares followed growing worries about massive spending on artificial intelligence. The benchmark Kospi opened 2.46 percent lower and extended its losses to close at 5,648.79, down 210.29 points, or 3.59 percent. Trade volume was light at 192.4 million shares worth 14.1 trillion won, or about $10.5 billion. Decliners outnumbered gainers 656 to 220. Foreigners sold a net 1.5 trillion won and institutions sold a net 511.7 billion won, while individuals bought a net 1.7 trillion won.

Overnight on Wall Street, the Nasdaq composite fell 1.07 percent and the S&P 500 fell 0.51 percent, and the PHLX chip index dropped 3.4 percent after a 7.2 percent plunge on Friday. Samsung Electronics slumped 4.15 percent to 219,500 won and SK hynix tumbled 5.03 percent to 1.4 million won. SK Square sank 5.37 percent to 899,000 won and Samsung Electro-Mechanics lost 7.38 percent to 1.1 million won. Naver dipped 3.65 percent to 169,000 won and Kakao slid 3.03 percent to 28,800 won, while oil refiners also fell as crude prices dropped on hopes for a diplomatic solution in the Middle East. SK Innovation plunged 9.36 percent to 119,100 won and S-Oil dived 11.77 percent to 114,700 won.

The won weakened 2.8 won from the previous session's close to 1,341 against the dollar as of 3:30 p.m. The yield on three-year Treasurys fell 0.4 basis points to 3.736 and the return on five-year government bonds dropped 2.2 basis points to 3.87. Kim Seok-hwan, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said concerns about the profitability of AI investments persist and that a sharp drop in U.S. chip shares on the first trading day of November weighed heavily on the Korean market. Investors doubted the productivity and profitability of excessive AI infrastructure spending after some global tech companies reported disappointing earnings. They also stayed cautious ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump's Republican Party faces an uphill challenge to keep its majority in Congress.

Articles.Title: Kospi dips over 3% following escalating AI concerns

stories.Headline: Science ministry, AMD engage in follow-up discussions on AI chip partnership
stories.Summary:
South Korea's science ministry and the U.S. chip company AMD held a steering committee meeting in Seoul on Wednesday, the ministry said. The meeting was a follow-up to a memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in July. Under that agreement, they said they would work together to create an AI research center and heterogeneous computing infrastructure that connects various AI chips. AMD also held its Advancing AI World Tour tech event in Seoul for the first time.

Around 1,300 people preregistered for the AMD event, and local companies that partner with AMD on AI computing infrastructure took part, including LG Electronics. The July agreement covers the AI research center and the computing infrastructure linking different AI chips. The steering committee meeting was held to discuss that partnership agreement, which was signed early this year. The ministry said the meeting was a follow-up measure to the July memorandum.

Ryu Je-myung, the vice science minister, said the ministry will make efforts to ensure the collaborative projects discussed are carried out smoothly. He said the aim is to foster the growth of local AI chip companies and strengthen the competitiveness of the country's AI ecosystem. The ministry did not give further details on what the projects involve. The articles do not say what was decided at the steering committee meeting.

The context is a partnership between the government and AMD on AI chips, set out in the July memorandum and discussed at the steering committee meeting. AMD's first Advancing AI World Tour event in Seoul brought together around 1,300 preregistered attendees and partner companies such as LG Electronics. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the ministry's stated efforts to carry out the projects. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Science ministry, AMD engage in follow-up discussions on AI chip partnership

stories.Headline: [ROUNDTABLE] Korea urged to engage with both US, China on AI, but draw clear lines - The Korea Times
stories.Summary:
The Korea Times hosted a roundtable titled “Beyond U.S.-China AI race: Korea’s strategic edge” in Seoul on Oct. 28, with the article published on Nov. 4, 2026. The participants were Kim Sung-han, former national security adviser and Korea University professor emeritus; Reform Party of Korea Rep. Lee Jun-seok; Lim Jong-in, former presidential cybersecurity adviser and Soongsil University AI committee chair; and Bone AI CEO Lee Do-kyung. Korea Times President-Publisher Oh Young-jin moderated the discussion. The roundtable examined how Korea should navigate the rivalry between the United States and China as artificial intelligence becomes a fiercely contested front.

Kim said Korea should separate consumer AI from technologies used for national security and called for high-level consultations between Cheong Wa Dae and the White House to define the scope of cooperation with China. He said Korea can cooperate with China outside narrowly defined areas involving critical technologies under the “small yard, high fence” strategy, but Seoul realistically needs to consult Washington to ensure such cooperation does not violate U.S. export controls. Lim said that if frontier AI model development capabilities add up to 100 percent, the U.S. would account for 50, China 40 and the rest of the world the remaining 10. He said China has caught up to about 90 percent of the U.S. level with models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, but U.S. equipment restrictions and sluggish domestic demand constrain its ability to develop and deploy AI models.

Rep. Lee warned against excluding China in pursuit of closer cooperation with the U.S., noting that Chinese AI models offer overwhelming cost advantages, particularly in inference. He compared the situation to the U.S. refusing to sell the F-22 fighter jet while still offering the F-16 or F-18, and said areas that do not involve core national interests or critical technology leaks should be opened. Lee Do-kyung stressed that Korea should find areas where it can build its own competitive advantages rather than compete directly with U.S. developers of frontier AI models, pointing to manufacturing capabilities and industry-specific operational knowledge. Participants warned that seeking cooperation with both countries wherever benefits appear would be overly ambitious and stressed the need to draw clear boundaries between areas open to cooperation with China and those involving critical security interests.

Participants cited the Maven Smart System, a U.S. military AI platform developed by Palantir Technologies, which helped U.S. forces hit more than 1,000 targets within the first 24 hours of a campaign against Iran. They said Washington is unlikely to share Maven with Seoul, much like the F-22, while China was unlikely to develop comparable AI-powered command-and-control capabilities soon. Kim said Korea should take such technological gaps into account when discussing the transfer of wartime operational control from the U.S., arguing that Seoul should use its integration with U.S. military systems and standards to learn from American technology and strengthen its own capabilities before the transfer. Rep. Lee warned that Korea’s existing defense posture could become vulnerable if North Korea develops an effective AI-powered command system ahead of Seoul or acquires such technology from China or Russia.
