stories.Headline: India's IT ministry proposes AI model vetting framework
stories.Summary:
India's IT ministry released a draft framework for training AI models on October 29, 2026. The proposal sets out end-to-end safeguards, including verification before deployment. Under the draft, models must be verified as "fit for use" before they are deployed. The framework recommends that a competent government authority carry out the diligence process.

The verification would check compliance with standards for fairness, bias mitigation, and data security, according to the draft Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI Training. Institutions holding valuable AI training data, such as hospitals and banks, are classified as Training Data Providers. Entities seeking to use that data, including startups and researchers, are designated Training Data Consumers. Both would register on a Data Exchange Platform, and actual training would occur within a Secure Data Environment. Models trained under this DEPA network would undergo validation and bias detection, and only those that pass would receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling.

Salman Waris, founder and managing partner at law firm TechLegis, told Moneycontrol that the industry should treat the framework as a proto-licence that could harden into one through future rules or sectoral guidelines. He clarified that participation is voluntary and that the verification obligation would attach only to models trained through the DEPA network, not to all AI models in India. He noted that the trajectory suggests a de facto sector-specific pre-deployment approval if the framework is formalised, especially with planned pilots in regulated sectors like finance and healthcare. Sharad Sharma, co-founder of iSPIRT Foundation and a member of the steering committee that drafted the framework, dismissed the licensing categorisation. He said the proposal aims to establish a self-regulatory, multi-stakeholder governance collective.

That collective would bring together data providers, AI developers, technology providers, domain experts, civil society, and government representatives. Sharma told Moneycontrol that this body would undertake due diligence, oversee, and enforce compliance in alignment with applicable laws, which he distinguished from government licensing. A similar advisory in 2024 was withdrawn after widespread criticism, which cited fears of throttling innovation and creating bureaucratic bottlenecks. Industry stakeholders have expressed concerns that the framework could function as a licensing mechanism.

Articles.Title: India's IT ministry proposes AI model vetting framework

stories.Headline: AI coding agents shift bottleneck to debugging, comprehension
stories.Summary:
AI coding agents now generate code quickly, but engineers struggle to understand and debug what the agents produce. Dr. Greg Law, co-founder and CTO of Undo, described this shift in the development bottleneck. Engineers have trouble grasping what AI-generated code does and how it interacts with existing systems. That makes tracking down bugs and investigating incidents harder.

As AI produces more code, duplicated logic and layers of change create what the article calls a spaghettification of the codebase. Nine in ten engineering leaders say code comprehension and debugging take longer in complex environments such as C/C++ codebases. Despite faster code generation, 79 per cent of engineering leaders report their release cycles are no quicker. AI agents also work from static context like source code and logs, which does not show what the code actually did at runtime. That lack of context can lead to incorrect diagnoses, with 93 per cent of engineering organisations reporting problems from AI hallucinations.

The article says the focus should be on giving agents better evidence rather than more powerful models. Providing a record of what happened when code ran helps an agent understand how an issue occurred. This lets AI trace problems to their root causes and support engineers with debugging. The article adds that AI's effectiveness ultimately depends on the quality of the information it receives.

Articles.Title: AI coding agents shift bottleneck to debugging, comprehension

stories.Headline: Razorpay gets SEBI nod for ₹6,000 Cr IPO
stories.Summary:
Razorpay has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India for its proposed initial public offering worth ₹5,000 to ₹6,000 crore. The fintech firm, founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, secured the regulator's nod for the listing. Sources cited by Inc42 said the listing is expected between January and March 2027. The company is targeting a valuation of around $5 billion for the offering. The IPO is projected to include both a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale, though the split between the two remains undisclosed.

The $5 billion target is below the $7.5 billion valuation Razorpay commanded in its last funding round during 2021. Ahead of the listing, the company shifted its domicile from the US to India. Razorpay reported a net loss in FY25, mainly due to ₹1,209 crore in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs, while operating revenue rose 65 per cent to ₹3,783 crore in the same year. Razorpay has also been expanding its artificial intelligence offerings alongside its IPO preparations. Last month it announced an expanded partnership with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT through its growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage.

The company also introduced Vulcan, a transformer-based AI model for digital payments built with NVIDIA and AWS technology, which it says can score payment routes in real time and identify fraud patterns. It is additionally developing Agent Studio, a platform for deploying task-specific AI agents, which about 200 businesses were using in beta as of August. Razorpay has raised over $800 million to date, with investors including Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the expected listing window and the planned IPO structure.

Articles.Title: Razorpay gets SEBI nod for ₹6,000 Cr IPO

stories.Headline: The United States votes and threatens Trump with charging him for an order singled out by the cost of living and the breakthrough of AI - Demócrata
stories.Summary:
The United States held midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats up for grabs, including 33 regular races and two special elections. Polls before the count showed Democrats ahead nationally, with the RealClearPolling average at 52.1% to 43.3% and Ipsos at 52% to 44% among likely voters. Gasoline averaged 4.15 dollars a gallon, and filling a fifteen-gallon tank cost a little more than 62 dollars. Trump was not on the ballot, and he will remain president after the vote.

Democrats need 218 seats for a House majority and a net gain of four Senate seats to reach 51. A 50-50 Senate tie would leave Republicans with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance. Average inflation between April and September was 3.67%, one point above the average of Biden's last six months, while gasoline cost almost 50% more than in February and diesel about 70% more. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter, and business investment rose 12.7%, driven largely by artificial intelligence. Trump's overall approval stood at 32%, and only 20% approved of his handling of the cost of living, including 48% of Republicans.

Trump returned to the White House promising more affordable living and now faces voters weighing higher bills, a war with Iran that has made energy more expensive through difficulties in the Strait of Hormuz, and tariffs that raise import costs. The articles do not quote him directly. They say a Democratic House would control the agenda and investigative committees, while a Democratic Senate could block presidential and judicial appointments. The first partial results were expected at midnight in peninsular Spain, in areas of Indiana and Kentucky.

Articles.Title: The United States votes and threatens Trump with charging him for an order singled out by the cost of living and the breakthrough of AI - Demócrata

stories.Headline: Sysdig launches AI Defense for runtime security of AI agents
stories.Summary:
Sysdig launched AI Defense on November 5, 2026, according to TechGig. The product is designed to provide automated runtime security and governance for AI agents. Sysdig says the aim is to stop autonomous AI from becoming a business risk without adequate oversight. Loris Degioanni, the founder and CTO of Sysdig, said AI is moving from answering queries to performing actions.

The product monitors every action an agent takes, from its origin to completion, including kernel processes that might invisibly change how the agent works. It provides a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills and plugins, built from runtime telemetry. It can trace every agent to an accountable human. Risky agentic actions can be detected, held for human review or blocked before they complete.

Policy templates with rules mapped to frameworks like the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications can be predefined. Degioanni said blocking responses must happen in real time, in line with the action and before it finishes. Actions taken by an agent and by AI Defense are recorded as they happen, creating audit-quality immutable records. Sysdig warned that an agent deployed in the morning might not be the same one running in the afternoon.

It added that only the operating system kernel accurately shows what actually ran. The IBM Institute for Business Value reported that enterprises expect to deploy an average of 1,661 AI agents by 2027. That is a 38 per cent increase from current deployments, which the article says makes manual governance unsustainable. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch.

Articles.Title: Sysdig launches AI Defense for runtime security of AI agents

stories.Headline: AI Transcription, Note-Taking: Seven Points for Employers
stories.Summary:
A 2025 survey of 1,000 professionals found that one in five respondents said they frequently used AI to draft notes during meetings, according to an article reposted by CBIA from Littler Mendelson. AI note-taking tools can transcribe meetings, outline notes, attribute comments to individual speakers, draft summaries, and assign to-do steps to participants. Agentic versions can also pull information from other sources to help participants complete those steps. A consolidated putative class action, In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation, 5:25-cv-6911 (N.D. Cal. filed Aug. 15, 2025), alleges that Otter AI unlawfully records private conversations and uses the transcripts to train its technology without notice to or consent from participants.

The article lists seven points for employers. On consent, the federal Wiretap Act and state laws prohibit intercepting communications without consent, and the Wiretap Act allows plaintiffs to recover the greater of $10,000 or $100 per day of violation. About a dozen states require all parties to consent, while most states require only one participant to consent. On biometrics, Colorado, Illinois, and Texas require consent before collecting biometric information, and Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act allows up to $5,000 in statutory damages. On accuracy, the article says employees remain responsible for their own work and should review AI-generated records before relying on them.

On discrimination, the article says systemic inaccuracies could disadvantage groups with accents, speech impediments, or other protected characteristics, and it notes accommodation duties under the Americans with Disabilities Act and emerging AI rules in New York City, Illinois, and California. On privilege, it says employers should weigh whether to use the tools in meetings with legal counsel and should ensure vendors commit to confidentiality and data segregation. On retention, it says an hour-long meeting produces about 16 single-spaced pages of transcripts, so employers should consider short retention periods and automatic deletion. On confidentiality, it suggests barring the tools from certain meetings, such as privileged talks, senior executive conversations, and discussions of protected health information.

The article says many employers may have little practical choice about adopting AI note-takers because employees already use them, which makes outright bans ineffective and hard to enforce. It suggests the most reasonable option may be to provide vetted tools that the organization selects, configures, and controls. It also recommends steps such as configuring the technology to obtain consent automatically, training employees to notify participants before recording, and having employees sign consent forms. The article does not say what happens next in the Otter litigation or describe any rulings in the case.

Articles.Title: AI Transcription, Note-Taking: Seven Points for Employers - CBIA

stories.Headline: Designing responsible AI for learning
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026 that it is bringing Guided Learning capabilities to Google Search and Google Classroom, and changing how school controls work. Chris Phillips, Vice President and General Manager of Education, wrote the announcement. Guided Learning coaches students through problems with step-by-step prompts instead of giving them direct final answers. The tool is already available in Gemini, and Google says its research shows measurable learning gains for students.

Guided Learning is globally available in Google Classroom starting today, where it works as a one-to-one study tool anchored in class material and gives teachers real-time insights. A pilot for Search begins later this month in select U.S. schools, with expansion to other school districts in the coming months. Under the new controls, access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on. Google says it will share more specifics with schools in the coming months before the changes roll out.

Phillips said the updates are meant to help students think critically through complex problems and support productive study habits. He said Google believes AI products should support productive struggle, challenging students without overwhelming them. He said Google worked closely with schools and educators to test the Classroom feature and integrate their feedback. He said the goal is to give school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products as they see fit.

Google said it listened to schools, teachers, leading researchers and policymakers before updating its approach to controls. The company said it will continue to listen to feedback and evolve its approach in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts and parents. The Search pilot is meant to gather educator feedback before wider expansion. Google said the controls changes will roll out after schools have time to prepare.

Articles.Title: Designing responsible AI for learning - blog.google

stories.Headline: Agentic AI Foundation aims for rapid AI agent standards
stories.Summary:
The Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation is working to set standards for AI agents, including the Model Context Protocol. Its executive director, Mazin Gilbert, said the foundation must move faster than its member companies to stay relevant. He said protocols like MCP act as plumbing that keeps the ecosystem from becoming a mess that is expensive and prohibitive for companies to deploy at scale. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google contribute to the standards even though they compete on products, and they build products both with and without them.

The MCP specification, which made the protocol stateless, was released in July, and companies updated their entire stacks to it. MCP downloads grew tenfold in its first 10 months at the foundation after Anthropic donated it in December. Fewer than 15 per cent of MCP maintainers now work at Anthropic, while over 1,000 organisations contribute 75 per cent of pull requests, including US retailers and global companies. The AAIF has 305 members, with roughly one new company joining daily, making it the fastest-growing foundation in the Linux Foundation's history.

The foundation launched its Model Context Protocol Associate certification in September to help companies and developers learn about agents. The Gates Foundation, which joined in September, is helping developers in parts of Africa and South Asia access training and certification. The AAIF hosts 10 projects, including Agent Skills from Anthropic, Open Responses from OpenAI, OpenEnv from Hugging Face and OpenSandbox from Alibaba. Gilbert wants to expand the foundation's work to identity, security, trust, observability and agent commerce, including protocols for transactional agents, with physical AI also a future focus.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Foundation aims for rapid AI agent standards

stories.Headline: WorkOS sales app breached by ARTEX AI, customer data accessed
stories.Summary:
WorkOS reported a data breach affecting an internal sales application, identified on October 30, 2026. An attacker used an AI offensive security framework called ARTEX AI to access business contact records and customer communication summaries. The company said its app data and production services were not affected. WorkOS provides APIs and tools for enterprise authentication and identity management.

The accessed data included names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from CRM systems. Customer account histories and summaries of sales calls, support discussions, and Slack conversations were also compromised. Company founder Michael Grinich said the investigating team found user agents such as "artex-enrich/1.0" in web requests from the threat actor. WorkOS disabled external access to the compromised application and engaged an independent forensics firm.

Grinich said the incident is now contained and promised further information once the investigation is complete. WorkOS will directly notify affected customers and advised users to be vigilant for phishing attempts. ARTEX AI was released by Chinese developers as an open-source project and became private after being linked to attacks on South Korean banks. CrowdStrike reported that the cyber-espionage group Vapor Panda used the framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organisations, and the non-profit DIVD said the framework powered its attacks in September.

Articles.Title: WorkOS sales app breached by ARTEX AI, customer data accessed

stories.Headline: Indian IT firms face FDE talent gap for AI projects
stories.Summary:
Indian IT services companies are building workforces of forward-deployed engineers, known as FDEs, for AI projects, TechGig reported on November 5, 2026. These engineers work directly with customers to identify business problems, develop AI-powered solutions, and take them into production. The push has exposed a talent gap, because the role needs hands-on experience that conventional training does not provide. HCLTech, LTM, Wipro, and Coforge are combining external recruitment with internal upskilling to fill it. A report by Scaler and CyberMedia Research found that 88 per cent of surveyed enterprises expect demand for FDE capabilities to rise by 2030, while only 1 per cent of engineers currently hold explicit FDE roles.

During the September quarter of FY27, about 15 per cent of HCLTech's 6,136 freshers were recruited under its elite engineer category for further FDE training. HCLTech is also launching an enterprise-wide FDE Academy, with training tracks aligned to technologies from OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, Google, and Nvidia, plus a programme being developed with Microsoft. Wipro's AI-native business unit has over 2,000 engineers, including FDEs, and Coforge is moving towards hybrid human-agent delivery teams supported by FDEs. HCLTech acknowledged that freshly recruited engineers cannot immediately perform FDE responsibilities. LTM chief executive officer Venu Lambu said the company was accelerating hiring in data and AI areas while upgrading the capabilities of its existing workforce.

Amar Srivastava, CEO of Online Business and Group CPO at Scaler, said companies struggle to find employees with the full range of FDE skills, and suggested that a long-term strategy for 60 to 70 per cent of talent is internal upskilling. Wipro chief executive officer Srinivas Pallia said the company was developing FDE capabilities within its AI-native unit and through technology partnerships, and Coforge chief executive officer Sudhir Singh sees hybrid teams of engineers and AI agents as an important part of its future delivery model. The gap is significant as Indian IT companies reorganise delivery teams around AI agents and smaller groups of engineers responsible for business outcomes. Demand for engineers with a mix of technical expertise, business understanding, and client-facing skills continues to outstrip availability. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the companies' current recruitment, training, and partnership efforts.

Articles.Title: Indian IT firms face FDE talent gap for AI projects

stories.Headline: AI-linked breaches target access tokens, accelerate attacks
stories.Summary:
AI-related cyberattacks are rising, with hackers stealing AI access tokens and using AI tools to speed up intrusions. Over the past month, at least a dozen AI developer platforms were hit, including CommandCode, Northflank, Trigger.dev, Chainstack and WorkOS. The attackers mainly sought stored customer secrets. The Cloud Security Alliance said intruders reach AI provider credentials through intermediary layers such as hosting platforms, evaluation services and developer consoles, and a single intrusion at that layer can expose keys for many inference accounts at once.

Chainstack was hit on October 26, when attackers reached a development environment and parts of its production environment through a third-party component. This exposed customer account information including organization names, account holder names, email addresses and password hashes, and node credentials may also have been exposed, prompting customers to rotate them. On October 30, hackers compromised an internal application used by WorkOS's sales team, accessing business contact details, customer account histories, sales details, customer-relationship information and customer communications. Chainstack and WorkOS disclosed attacks that used the open-source Artex AI penetration testing framework for automation, and multiple companies have linked attacks attributed to the Chinese APT Storm-0940 to Artex.

Wiz's analysis says the surge is driven by the rise of LLM-jacking and LLM broker infrastructure, which makes stolen AI access tokens easily monetizable and attracts more threat actors to credential theft. Wiz also observed hackers abusing enterprise credentials compromised in these attacks, including two cases with identical unauthorized activity within 30 minutes of reported access. Multiple threat actors using the same compromised keys suggest a robust market for this type of credential. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: AI-linked breaches target access tokens, accelerate attacks

stories.Headline: Sam Altman praises Indian AI optimism, calls US pessimistic
stories.Summary:
Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, said on the “Figuring Out” podcast with entrepreneur Raj Shamani that Indians show considerable optimism about artificial intelligence while Americans are generally more pessimistic. He confirmed that India has overtaken the US to become OpenAI’s largest market by user count. The remarks were published in a TechGig report on November 5, 2026. Altman linked the differing attitudes to economic conditions, saying developing economies with rapid growth and high demand for products are more receptive to new technology.

Altman pointed to India’s strong community for AI experimentation and cited Indians using AI tools for practical tasks, including a student who organised a school fundraiser without prior experience. He also said his decision to hold no equity in OpenAI was a mistake. He explained that the choice has caused confusion despite his initial good intentions for the company. The report gave no further figures beyond India passing the US as OpenAI’s largest user market.

Altman is responsible for the comments, which he made in the podcast conversation with Shamani. He described India’s optimism and the US pessimism as a notable contrast in how the two countries see AI. He attributed the gap to economic conditions rather than to anything specific about the technology itself. He also acknowledged the equity decision as an error on his part.

The context is OpenAI’s user base, where India now leads by user count ahead of the US. The report ties the more receptive attitude in developing economies to rapid growth and high demand for products. It does not say what OpenAI plans to do next or whether any policy or product changes follow from the remarks. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Sam Altman praises Indian AI optimism, calls US pessimistic

stories.Headline: Bengaluru leads India in FDE talent with 34 per cent share
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru accounts for 34 per cent of India's Forward Deployed Engineer talent, making it the country's largest hub, according to a report by FDE Academy. Hyderabad follows with 14 per cent of the talent pool, and Delhi NCR contributes 13 per cent. Together these three centres hold 61 per cent of India's FDE talent. Pune and Mumbai add 12 per cent and 11 per cent respectively, while Chennai and other cities each account for 8 per cent.

About 38 per cent of FDE professionals work in Big Tech companies, while product companies and IT services and consulting firms each employ 24 per cent. AI-first startups make up the remaining 14 per cent. Around 70 per cent of FDE professionals have eight years of experience or less, which the report says points to a need for deeper pools of experienced talent as enterprise AI adoption grows. Customer and consulting capabilities appear in 98 per cent of FDE job postings analysed, core engineering skills in 94 per cent, and cloud and AI operations in 84 per cent. Employers are moving beyond conventional coding tests, using deployment case studies, system design interviews, client simulations, and portfolio reviews.

The report gives indicative median annual salaries for field-deployed AI builders of ₹32 lakh for those with zero to three years of experience, rising to ₹1.55 crore for those with more than 15 years. Transformation, governance, and risk roles are the top hiring priority for 28 per cent of employer respondents, though only 18 per cent of professionals said they preferred that career path. Raghav Gupta, Founder and CEO of FDE Academy, said AI deployment requires a mix of engineering depth, business understanding, and the ability to take ownership of outcomes in a customer's environment. He added that access to this combination of skills will become increasingly important as organisations move beyond pilots.

Articles.Title: Bengaluru leads India in FDE talent with 34 per cent share

stories.Headline: AI chatbot answers on data centers vary sharply
stories.Summary:
Research from Five Blocks, a digital reputation management company, found major differences in how eight AI engines described 25 major U.S. data center projects, TechGig reported on November 5, 2026. General descriptions were not negative, but 55 per cent of answers about project challenges were classified as negative. Google AI Mode gave negative responses to challenge questions 88 per cent of the time, while ChatGPT gave negative answers only 6 per cent of the time. A second Five Blocks study found that 83 per cent of answers discussing data centers and their neighbours offered one-sided criticism.

That second study compared the results with other industries, finding the share was similar to oil and gas pipelines but much higher than solar farms, which saw 35 per cent. ChatGPT was an outlier in the second study, consistently giving balanced responses about community concerns, while the other seven AI engines were rated as one-sided in nearly every evaluated answer. The research suggests AI-generated descriptions may not be reliable snapshots of a project's current status. It cited Microsoft's Fairwater Wisconsin project, where Copilot incorrectly claimed it did not exist until September 24.

The findings point to a problem for users trying to understand complicated issues, because two systems can give very different impressions without necessarily inventing any facts. The research underscores the need for critical evaluation, according to the report. The articles do not say who else is responsible or what happens next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI chatbot answers on data centers vary sharply

stories.Headline: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Yuan Feng and Qize Yang, with co-authors Qize Yang, Ruizhe Chen, Sibo Song, Haolin He, Muzhi Zhu, Zihan Liu, Yunfei Chu, Xize Cheng, Yuxuan Wang, Jin Xu and Xike Xie, posted a paper on arXiv on November 5, 2026 describing a method called VisionWeave. The work addresses a cost problem in multimodal large language models, which encode visual inputs into dense, fixed-size patch tokens even though visual information is unevenly distributed across an image. The authors say downsampling loses detail, while existing token pruning and adaptive approaches are limited in content-adaptive granularity, task generalization, and integration with modern models and serving infrastructure. They propose teaching models to learn end to end where, and at what granularity, to allocate visual representations, a capability they call elastic visual representation weaving.

VisionWeave has two parts. A gated spatial pooler builds coarse-grained representations alongside native fine-grained ones within a shared MRoPE coordinate, and a granularity router learns how to allocate them based on content. The authors validated the capability through self-distillation alone on Qwen3.5-4B and scaled to Qwen3.8-27B using over 30K A100 GPU-hours. Based on Qwen3.8-27B, the method saved 43.0% of tokens on average while retaining 98.9% of native performance across eight benchmarks, compared with only 88% performance preserved by token pruning baselines with a fixed 50% savings target. On the SGLang serving engine it achieved a 2.3x throughput gain while reducing mean TTFT by 54.4% and mean TPOT by 60.6%.

The authors state that extensive evaluations confirm robust efficiency-quality trade-offs across diverse tasks, resolutions and video frames. They write that they believe these results position elastic visual weaving as a promising capability for next-generation multimodal models. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, Artificial Intelligence, and Computation and Language. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond presenting the results and the authors' stated belief about the capability's promise.

Articles.Title: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs

stories.Headline: Origins of Universal Machine Learning Force-Field Errors in Multicomponent Materials
stories.Summary:
A study posted on arXiv on November 5, 2026 examines why universal machine learning force fields make errors when applied to multicomponent materials. Hongwei Du and 13 other authors built a benchmark of 7,599 multicomponent configurations, inspired by high-entropy design, elemental substitution and anion mixing. They evaluated eleven pretrained models against density functional theory for energies, forces and stresses, and extended the assessment to elastic, vibrational and adsorption-related properties. The work is listed under materials science, machine learning and computational physics.

The study analyzes force errors through training-reference coverage, local geometric heterogeneity, distance directionality and elemental response. Distances to training-reference environments show a qualitative link between coverage differences and growing errors, though substantial variation remains at similar distances. Higher-error groups show greater local geometric heterogeneity, even though OMat24 covers these environments broadly. Relative to training-reference pair medians, errors stay low near the median, rise steeply on the compression side and increase more weakly on the extension side. After matching element pairs and absolute distance deviations, compression-side force errors are 1.81 to 1.95 times extension-side errors, and model-predicted pairwise interaction curves show greater curvature under compression.

The authors report that fitting difficulty in independent elemental systems correlates with electronic band-energy responses to atomic displacements and Fermi-level shifts, with a similar pattern in multicomponent systems. In parameter-matched comparisons, spherical-harmonic representations with maximum degrees of 2 and 4 lower test force errors for 38 and 40 of 43 elements respectively, while differences in elemental difficulty remain. The authors say the findings can inform force-field selection for experimental compositional design and identify targets for training-data sampling and model representations. The abstract does not state further planned work.

Articles.Title: Origins of Universal Machine Learning Force-Field Errors in Multicomponent Materials

stories.Headline: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
stories.Summary:
Weizheng Zhang, Xunjie Xie, Hao Pan and Lin Lu posted a paper to arXiv on November 5, 2026 describing a new framework called Cova-PINN. The work addresses fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer in complex geometries, a problem that multi-domain physics-informed neural networks, or PINNs, are used to model. Standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports. According to the abstract, this can produce plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures.

Cova-PINN aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. It jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. The authors evaluated it on four triply periodic minimal surface, or TPMS, heat exchangers and on a geometrically distinct DualMS design. They compared it against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol.

Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature errors by 37.7 percent across the four TPMS topologies. It reduces device-level closure errors by 60.2 percent over the same set. The abstract also reports improved full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS. The authors present these results as evidence that the framework improves on the baselines under the shared protocol.

The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2610.11108, and the full PDF and experimental HTML versions are available. The abstract frames the motivation as the gap between plausible temperature fields and accurate end-to-end energy transfer in standard multi-domain PINNs. It does not state any deployment, publication in a journal, or follow-up work. The articles give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries

stories.Headline: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
stories.Summary:
Chuang Yu and 11 other authors posted a paper on arXiv on November 5, 2026, titled From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs. The paper proposes a framework called ReState for multimodal reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models. Most learning-based Multimodal Chain-of-Thought methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. The authors say this results in fragmented reasoning and a gap between training and inference reasoning states.

ReState reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It has two components, Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM treats reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as transitions within a shared state space, so these behaviors are learned jointly. CRSL uses self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, which the authors say mitigates the reasoning-state gap and enables iterative self-refinement without an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. The authors also built VersaCoT-10K, a CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains.

The authors report that experiments show ReState adapts across different MLLM backbones and performs strongly on multiple public reasoning benchmarks. They say the results support a shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. The paper lists Chuang Yu, Xuefei Ma, Yuanhao Feng, Wuxiong Zeng, Bo Wang, Minghong Cai, Dongming Wu, Fei Zhou, Chen Tang, Wenwen Tong, Lewei Lu, and Xiangyu Yue as authors. The abstract does not give further details on the experiments or the benchmarks used.

The paper's data and code are available at a link given in the abstract. The abstract frames the work as addressing the limitations of stage-centric MCoT methods. The posting also includes standard arXivLabs text about the framework for collaborators and its values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the release of the paper and its data and code.

Articles.Title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs

stories.Headline: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
stories.Summary:
Yue Zhao, Shiqi Wu, Yihang Ouyang, Sergey Grebenchuk, Magdalena Grzeszczyk, Xiaoxu Zhao, Kostya S. Novoselov, Maciej Koperski and Qianxiao Li posted a paper titled Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics on arXiv on 5 November 2026. The work introduces a method called DeepMesoD, which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a set coarse-graining scale. The authors say microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but only over small domains and short timescales, while bulk descriptions average those patterns away. Mesoscopic fields keep the spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected systems and scaling limits.

For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied, DeepMesoD learns a free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator tied to the fluctuation-dissipation relation. The method was first checked in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned equation recovered the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts stayed stable well past the training horizon. The authors then treated two systems with no closed-form mesoscopic description. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet under atomistic spin dynamics, predictions matched atomistic references up to 1 ns and a rollout with an unseen initial condition stayed bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr3, the learned kernel captured the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength were not given as inputs.

The authors report that controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing their magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, they say DeepMesoD gives a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics. The paper is listed under Machine Learning, Statistical Mechanics and Computational Physics. The posting also describes arXivLabs, a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site, and says arXiv works only with partners who accept its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy.

Articles.Title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics

stories.Headline: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
stories.Summary:
Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang and Haihua Yang posted a paper titled PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs to arXiv on November 5, 2026. The paper describes a compression framework for native multimodal large language models, which encode visual and linguistic sequences together in one autoregressive Transformer. Unlike conventional models that rely on external vision encoders, these native models tokenize pixel patches directly and can suffer from severe visual token redundancy. The authors say a pilot study confirmed that native models tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance, while ViT-based models degrade under compression.

The paper says existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native models unexplored. The authors introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy. They report that redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and that early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. PACE is described as the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE, and experiments show it maintains near-lossless performance at only 25% to 50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.

The authors are responsible for the work, and the paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence. The abstract says PACE uses dimensional decoupling of positional encoding to decompose attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. The paper is available as a PDF, HTML and TeX source on arXiv.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's availability. They describe arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on the website, and say both individuals and organizations working with it have embraced values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. arXiv says it is committed to working only with partners that adhere to those values. The articles also invite ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community through arXivLabs.

Articles.Title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs

stories.Headline: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Yizhe Zhang and 12 other authors posted a paper titled Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning on arXiv on November 5, 2026. The paper introduces Event-STVG, a task that moves spatio-temporal video grounding from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning. The task unifies long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. The authors say existing STVG benchmarks are largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions and are largely decoupled from long-form reasoning emphasized in multimodal large language models. To support research on the task, the authors built a large-scale benchmark with 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains.

Experiments with state-of-the-art multimodal large language models show substantial difficulty, with the strongest model reaching only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, the authors consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. The paper states that Event-STVG sets a new challenge for visual understanding in multimodal large language models. The authors say the task calls for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time.

They state that code and annotations are available at a URL given in the paper. The paper is listed with a PDF, experimental HTML, and TeX source on arXiv. The abstract page also includes standard text about arXivLabs, a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on the arXiv website. The articles give no further information on what happens next beyond the call for future models and the released code and annotations.

Articles.Title: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning

stories.Headline: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
stories.Summary:
Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang and Jianyuan Guo posted a paper on arXiv on November 5, 2026 describing a framework called GeoReason for remote sensing segmentation. The work addresses instruction-driven perception in Multimodal Large Language Models under the “Embedding-as-Mask” paradigm. The authors say extending this capability to remote sensing reasoning segmentation is exceptionally challenging in cluttered geographical contexts with extreme scale variations. These conditions often lead to what the paper calls Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification.

The paper identifies a bottleneck it describes as the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within autoregressive generation. Because [SEG] is produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, it relies on visual evidence progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. The authors call this information decay particularly catastrophic for remote sensing targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. GeoReason introduces an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor intended to prevent information decay during long-form linguistic inference.

The framework also adds a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes. A Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment Loss explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical remote sensing textures. The authors report that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. They say code is available at a URL given in the paper.

The paper was posted on arXiv under identifier 2610.23416. The abstract page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and lists Cheng Fan and five other authors. The posting appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features on the site. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported benchmark results and the availability of the code.

Articles.Title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation

stories.Headline: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Hao Wang, Zihan Wang, Kai Wu, Jian Yao, Yiwen Ye, Yongcan Luo, Dapeng Wu, Jiale Chen and Haihua Yang posted a paper on arXiv on 5 November 2026 describing CasePlay, a self-play reinforcement learning framework for medical reasoning. The work asks whether self-play grounded in documents can turn clinical case reports into effective training signals for large language models. Case reports trace the full clinical course from first presentation to final treatment decisions, and the authors note that the medical literature holds many such high-quality unlabeled documents. Current pipelines for improving clinical reasoning often depend on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic data generation. The paper identifies two problems with existing self-play methods in this setting.

The first is knowledge-point fixation, where the proposer keeps asking about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report. The second is difficulty-quality mismatch, where questions of suitable difficulty may still be poorly formed or shallow and so are of limited value for training a reasoner. CasePlay addresses these with a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so questions draw on a broader range of evidence, and a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which adds rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth and option quality to answer-accuracy feedback. The authors say this guides the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. The authors report experiments across seven medically related benchmarks.

They say CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average. They highlight a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. The paper is listed under Machine Learning, with Artificial Intelligence and Computation and Language also given as categories. The authors present the approach as an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play reinforcement learning. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond that claim.

Articles.Title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning

stories.Headline: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Xiaoxing Hu and 19 other authors posted a paper titled EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning on arXiv on November 5, 2026. The paper introduces a benchmark for testing whether Omni large language models can find key audio and visual evidence and combine information across modalities. The authors say existing audio-visual benchmarks mostly use multiple-choice questions and score models only on whether the answer is correct. That makes it hard to tell whether a model really builds a reasoning chain from evidence to the right answer.

The benchmark contains 392 videos and 1,027 question-answer pairs, all annotated purely by humans. It covers 15 capabilities across three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. The authors designed annotation procedures in which experts mark audio and visual evidence and build video-based distractors, humans review whether questions meet strict criteria, and models filter out textual and unimodal shortcuts. Models must return both the answer and the supporting evidence intervals, and the authors propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality, with both folded into answer correctness.

The authors tested 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs. Gemini3.7-Flash had the highest overall accuracy at 79.4%, the highest C.G. at 70.8%, and the highest B.G. at 35.1%. At Level 3 it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. The authors say these results show that even the most advanced models still have room to develop in grounded audio-visual reasoning.

The paper appears on arXiv, which also describes arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on the site. The authors state that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy. arXiv says it is committed to these values and works only with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community.

Articles.Title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

stories.Headline: Leveraging Dale's Principle as an Inductive Bias in Recurrent Neural Networks
stories.Summary:
Jiyi Wang, Chenxiao Yang, Yujia Zhao, Jingzhao Zhang and Lu Mi posted a paper to arXiv on 5 November 2026 describing a recurrent neural network called EISep RNN. The paper says biological neurons obey Dale's principle, meaning each neuron sends out only excitatory or only inhibitory signals. It says earlier attempts to impose this rule on artificial networks often caused unstable training or worse performance. The authors present their architecture as a way to implement the principle through a learnable excitatory-inhibitory separation.

The paper reports results across several learning settings, including multi-task learning, continual learning and reinforcement learning. It says EISep gives more stable training dynamics and performance that is competitive with or better than vanilla RNNs and earlier Dale-constrained models. It also reports sparser, more modular connectivity and stable, informative latent dynamics. The authors conclude that Dale's principle works as a biologically grounded and computationally effective inductive bias for recurrent networks.

The work is credited to the five named authors, and the abstract presents the claims as their findings. The paper says the separation of excitatory and inhibitory outputs is learnable in EISep. It frames the results as establishing Dale's principle as a useful inductive bias, in the authors' words. The abstract does not name any other institution or individual as responsible.

The posting is listed with a DOI and a date of 5 November 2026, and the page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The page also describes arXivLabs, a framework where collaborators develop and share features on the site. It says partners in arXivLabs accept values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's availability.

stories.Headline: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers led by Jiafu Tang has released a paper exploring whether computer code can work as a video caption. The work, posted on arXiv on November 5, 2026, has 13 authors in total, including Yifan Xu, Eric Tang and Junjie Zhao. The team compared code captions with ordinary natural language descriptions on two tasks, answering questions about videos and rebuilding videos from their captions. They found that code captions gave better reasoning accuracy and higher reconstruction fidelity.

The paper argues that natural language often struggles to express fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics precisely, which can make descriptions long and ambiguous. Code captions instead use graphical primitives, layout rules and functions of time as an executable program that represents the visual content. To test how well current models can produce such captions, the authors built CodeCap-Bench, which contains 323 videos across five categories of structured 2D content. The benchmark also includes fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework.

The authors report that leading proprietary multimodal large language models show promising code captioning abilities but still struggle to capture complex temporal dynamics faithfully. Open-source models, they say, lag substantially behind. The paper states that realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether these models can generate faithful code captions. The authors present these findings as their own assessment based on extensive experiments.

The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the paper's conclusion that current models fall short on faithful code captioning. The work is published on arXiv, where the full PDF, HTML and TeX source are available. The abstract frames code as a complementary representation of visual content rather than a replacement for natural language. No further steps, follow-up studies or deadlines are mentioned.
